D. CEA is mainly a colorectal cancer marker (and sometimes raised in mucinous ovarian tumors); it has no role in ovarian cancer screening.
key_concept:
Ovarian cancer: no effective screening test.
  • Asymptomatic, family history: risk assessment, genetic counseling, symptom awareness
  • Symptoms or mass: TVUS first, then CA-125
  • Confirmed BRCA carrier: risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy after childbearing
  • Diagnosis: tissue histopathology; staging is surgical
exam_pearl: Symptoms or a mass flip the answer to TVUS then CA-125; without them, screening tests are a trap.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Original recall: 'Post menopause with a family history of ovarian cancer comes for screening for ovarian cancer. What do you do for her?' (options Pelvic US / CA125 / Counseling), Answer: C. Fuller Q version highlights C.

stem: A pregnant lady at 26 weeks, she cannot feel fetal movement anymore. US showed: IUFD at age of 24 weeks. Best management:
why_right: Fetal death at or after 20 weeks is IUFD, and here it occurred at 24 weeks. The preferred route is vaginal delivery by induction, and in the second and early third trimester the cervix is unripe and the uterus is relatively insensitive to oxytocin, so misoprostol (often after mifepristone) is the agent of choice.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV oxytocin works poorly at this gestation because uterine oxytocin receptors are few and the cervix is unripe; it is used near term or once the cervix is favorable.
B. CS adds surgical morbidity and scars the uterus for no fetal benefit; it is reserved for maternal indications such as abruption with instability, uterine rupture or transverse lie that cannot be corrected.
D. D&C is limited to losses up to about 20 weeks (miscarriage); a 24-week fetus is too large and the uterus would be at high risk of perforation.
key_concept:
Pregnancy loss: route depends on gestation.
  • Below 13 weeks: expectant, misoprostol or D&C
  • Up to 20 weeks: misoprostol or D&C (D&C if heavy bleeding or unstable)
  • IUFD (20 weeks or more): induce vaginal delivery, misoprostol ± mifepristone
  • Near term with favorable cervix: oxytocin
  • Check coagulation (risk of DIC with retained dead fetus)
exam_pearl: Gestation is the trap: D&C fits a miscarriage below 20 weeks, oxytocin fits term; 24 weeks means misoprostol.

stem: A 21-year-old woman pregnant at 8 weeks is diagnosed with a missed abortion. Which of the following is the most appropriate management option?
why_right: A missed abortion at "8 weeks" in a stable patient can be managed expectantly (if under 13 weeks), medically with misoprostol (up to 20 weeks), or surgically. Expectant management is not offered here, so misoprostol is the most appropriate option: it is effective, avoids surgery and is the standard medical evacuation agent.
why_wrong_block:
B. Hysterectomy is far too radical for an early miscarriage in a young woman; evacuation is achieved medically or by suction curettage.
C. Methotrexate is used for ectopic pregnancy and post-molar GTN, not for an intrauterine missed abortion.
D. Hypertonic saline infusion is an obsolete intra-amniotic method of second-trimester termination; it has no role at 8 weeks.
key_concept:
Missed abortion (closed os, no fetal heart, no tissue passed): choose by stability and gestation.
  • <13 weeks, stable: expectant management is an option
  • Up to 20 weeks: misoprostol (medical)
  • Heavy bleeding, instability or infection: D&C / suction evacuation
  • Methotrexate: ectopic or GTN only
exam_pearl: If expectant management is listed for a stable early missed abortion, pick it; if it is absent, pick misoprostol.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot (source Q 0391) shown inside the 451 block.

stem: 39 weeks, I think she is not primigravida, her cervix is 4 cm dilated with strong and regular contraction, after 4 hours the cervix dilated to 5 cm, fully effaced cervix (if you calculate the bishop score it would be favorable). What is the management?
why_right: She has strong, regular contractions but progressed only from 4 to 5 cm in 4 hours, which is slower than expected (less than 2 cm in 4 hours) yet is not arrest, because the cervix did change. With intact membranes and adequate contractions, the first step for delay in the first stage is amniotomy, then reassess in about 2 hours.
why_wrong_block:
A. CS for failure to progress needs arrest: no cervical change despite adequate contractions over the defined time (or failed augmentation). Here the cervix is still changing and the fetus is well.
B. Oxytocin is for inadequate contractions or for delay that persists after amniotomy; her contractions are already strong and regular, so adding oxytocin first risks tachysystole.
D. Waiting another 2 hours is right when progress is normal (about 1 cm in 2 hours); 1 cm in 4 hours is delay that needs action.
key_concept:
Slow first stage: ladder of action.
  • Normal progress (about 0.5 cm/hour): reassess
  • Delay with intact membranes: amniotomy, reassess in 2 hours
  • Still slow or weak contractions: oxytocin
  • No change despite adequate contractions or failed oxytocin: CS
exam_pearl: If the same 1 cm gain had taken only 2 hours, progress would be normal and the answer becomes reassess in 2 hours.

stem: 39 weeks, I think she is not primigravida, her cervix is 4 cm dilated with strong and regular contraction, after 2 hours the cervix dilated to 5 cm, fully effaced cervix (if you calculate the bishop score it would be favorable). What is the management?
why_right: Progress from 4 to 5 cm in 2 hours equals about 0.5 cm per hour, which is normal for the first stage. With strong, regular contractions, a fully effaced cervix and no fetal concern, labor is progressing and no intervention is needed: reassess in 2 hours.
why_wrong_block:
A. CS is for arrest of labor or fetal or maternal compromise; she is progressing normally.
B. Oxytocin augments weak or inadequate contractions or persistent delay; her contractions are already strong, so it adds risk of tachysystole without benefit.
C. Amniotomy is the first step when progress is delayed (less than 2 cm in 4 hours); routine amniotomy in normally progressing labor is not recommended.
key_concept:
First-stage progress check.
  • About 0.5 cm/hour (1 cm in 2 hours): normal, reassess
  • Less than 2 cm in 4 hours: delay, amniotomy then reassess in 2 hours
  • Weak contractions or persistent delay: oxytocin
  • No change with adequate contractions: CS
exam_pearl: If the same 1 cm gain had taken 4 hours, that is delay and the answer becomes amniotomy.

stem: A 22-year-old primigravida woman at 38 weeks gestation is in active labor for 4 hours. Cervical dilatation is 5 cm, +1 station. Examination 5 hours later demonstrates no change compared to the previous findings. Contractions occur every 3 minutes and lasts 60 seconds. Fetal heart rate is of category 1 cardiotocograph. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
highlight_terms_source: Contractions occur every 3 minutes and lasts 60 seconds
why_right: At 5 cm she is in the active phase. Contractions every 3 minutes lasting 60 seconds fall within the adequate range (3 to 5 per 10 minutes), yet the cervix has shown no change for 5 hours. Adequate contractions for 4 hours or more without cervical change is active phase arrest, which is an indication for cesarean section.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oxytocin augmentation is for INADEQUATE contractions with no change over 6 hours; her contractions are already adequate, so more uterotonic only risks tachysystole without fixing the arrest.
C. Waiting is right in the latent phase or before the arrest window is reached; here the 4 hour limit with adequate contractions has already passed, so the diagnosis of arrest is made now.
D. Instrumental delivery needs full cervical dilatation with the head at +2 or lower; she is only 5 cm at +1 station.
key_concept:
Active phase arrest: decide by contraction adequacy.
  • Active phase: cervix beyond 4 to 6 cm
  • Adequate = 3 to 5 contractions per 10 min
  • Adequate contractions + no change ≥4 h → C-section
  • Inadequate contractions + no change ≥6 h → oxytocin, then C-section if it fails
  • Instrumental delivery only at full dilatation, head ≥ +2
exam_pearl: Normal (Category 1) CTG does not remove the indication: the C-section here is for arrest of labor, not fetal distress.

stem: 35 weeks gestation, abdomen fundal examination corresponds to 30 cm. Ruptured membrane for 6h, she is stable, no Uterine contractions. Upon vaginal examination, meconium stained liquor found
OptD: Prophylactic Abx and observation for spontaneous delivery
why_right: Membranes ruptured before labor at 35 weeks is PPROM; beyond 34 weeks the fetal lungs and brain are mature enough that delivery is favoured over expectant management. Meconium-stained liquor and a fundal height of only 30 cm at 35 weeks (small for dates) add further reasons to deliver, while a stable mother and no fetal distress mean vaginal delivery can be attempted. With rupture only 6 hours ago, this recall's key is induction alone; its twin card with 16 hours of rupture adds antibiotics.
why_wrong_block:
B. Cesarean section is for fetal distress (non-reassuring CTG), malpresentation or obstructed labor; meconium alone in a stable patient does not mandate it.
C. Induction plus prophylactic antibiotics is this recall's answer once rupture is prolonged (the 16 hour version of this question); at 6 hours the key gives induction alone.
D. Waiting for spontaneous labor fits PPROM below 34 weeks to gain maturity; at 35 weeks with meconium and a small-for-dates uterus there is no benefit to waiting, only infection risk.
key_concept:
PPROM: gestational age sets the plan.
  • <32 wk: MgSO4 for neuroprotection
  • <34 wk: steroids + latency antibiotics, expectant if stable
  • ≥34 wk: deliver (induction if no contraindication to vaginal birth)
  • Deliver at any age if chorioamnionitis, abruption, non-reassuring CTG
  • Fundal height in cm ≈ weeks of gestation; a big lag suggests growth restriction
exam_pearl: Same stem, different hours: short rupture = induce; longer rupture = induce + antibiotics.

stem: 35 weeks gestation, abdomen fundal examination corresponds to 30 cm. Ruptured membrane for 16h, she is stable, no Uterine contractions. Upon vaginal examination, meconium stained liquor found
OptD: Prophylactic Abx and observation for spontaneous delivery
why_right: At 35 weeks with membranes ruptured before labor (PPROM), delivery is favoured beyond 34 weeks, and meconium-stained liquor with a small-for-dates uterus (30 cm) strengthens that. Prolonged rupture (16 hours) in a preterm pregnancy raises the risk of ascending infection, and preterm delivery with unknown GBS status is itself an indication for intrapartum GBS prophylaxis, so antibiotics are added while labor is induced. The mother is stable with no fetal distress, so vaginal delivery is attempted.
why_wrong_block:
A. Induction alone is this recall's answer when rupture is short (the 6 hour twin); with 16 hours of rupture in a preterm pregnancy, antibiotic cover is added.
B. Cesarean is for fetal distress, malpresentation or obstructed labor; meconium in a stable patient without CTG abnormality is not an indication.
D. Expectant management with antibiotics fits PPROM below 34 weeks; at 35 weeks with meconium, waiting adds infection risk without benefit.
key_concept:
PPROM ≥34 weeks: deliver, cover infection.
  • <34 wk stable: steroids + latency antibiotics + expectant care
  • ≥34 wk: induce labor
  • Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis: GBS positive, or status unknown with preterm (<37 wk), rupture ≥18 h or fever
  • Chorioamnionitis: antibiotics + deliver at any gestation
  • C-section only for obstetric indications
exam_pearl: The only difference from the 6 hour twin is rupture duration: longer rupture adds antibiotics.

stem: A 37 weeks GA came to the labor room with PROM for 24 hours, how to prevent postpartum pelvic infection?
why_right: PROM for 24 hours lets vaginal flora ascend, and postpartum pelvic infection (endometritis) is polymicrobial: anaerobes plus gram-negative aerobes. Clindamycin plus gentamicin covers both groups and is the classic regimen for postpartum uterine infection, which is why this recall keys it for preventing pelvic infection after prolonged rupture.
why_wrong_block:
A. Vancomycin covers gram-positive organisms (used for MRSA or GBS in severe penicillin allergy) and misses the anaerobes and gram-negatives of pelvic infection.
B. Clindamycin alone covers anaerobes and some gram-positives but leaves gram-negative aerobes (E. coli) uncovered; gentamicin is added for that.
D. Amoxicillin plus metronidazole covers anaerobes and many gram-positives, but amoxicillin alone gives unreliable cover of the gram-negative aerobes (E. coli is often resistant), which is the gap gentamicin fills.
key_concept:
Obstetric infection regimens.
  • Chorioamnionitis: ampicillin + gentamicin, then deliver
  • After cesarean: add clindamycin for anaerobes
  • Postpartum endometritis: clindamycin + gentamicin
  • PPROM latency: ampicillin + erythromycin
  • Term PROM: deliver within 24 h; GBS prophylaxis if positive or unknown
exam_pearl: Pelvic infection is polymicrobial: you need anaerobe cover (clindamycin) AND gram-negative cover (gentamicin).

stem: A 42-year-old woman presented with pelvic pressure, bloating, and heaviness in the lower abdomen. Her cycle is prolonged with heavy menstrual bleeding (see report). Ultrasound: Presence of uterine fibroid. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: The decisive clue is the combination: pressure, bloating and heaviness PLUS prolonged heavy menstrual bleeding with a fibroid on ultrasound. A submucosal fibroid distorts the endometrial cavity, so it is the type that causes heavy bleeding (and infertility) in addition to bulk symptoms. Pressure alone could be any location; the bleeding makes it submucosal.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cervical fibroid: rare; gives bladder or bowel pressure, dyspareunia or obstructed labor rather than classic heavy menstrual bleeding.
B. Parasitic fibroid: a pedunculated subserosal fibroid that detaches and takes blood supply from omentum or other structures; causes pressure or a mass effect, not menorrhagia.
C. Subserosal fibroid: the commonest type, but it projects outward and causes pressure or heaviness only; it would be the answer if the stem had pressure WITHOUT heavy bleeding.
key_concept:
Fibroid location is predicted by symptoms: bleeding means the cavity is involved.
  • Submucosal: heavy menstrual bleeding + infertility + pressure
  • Intramural: pressure or heaviness (bleeding if large)
  • Subserosal: pressure or heaviness only; most common type
  • Ultrasound (TVUS) is the initial and diagnostic test
  • Submucosal myomectomy is hysteroscopic
exam_pearl: Menorrhagia with a fibroid = submucosal; pressure symptoms alone do not decide the type.

stem: A 39-year-old woman presented with heavy menorrhagia and pelvic pressure with Lower limb heaviness and edema. Pelvic ultrasound confirms the presence of uterine fibroid. What is the most likely location of this fibroid?
why_right: This recall's key is Intramural because the picture combines heavy menorrhagia with bulk effects: pelvic pressure and lower limb heaviness and edema, which suggest a large fibroid compressing pelvic veins. Intramural fibroids sit in the muscle wall, enlarge the uterus and the endometrial surface, so they can produce both heavy bleeding and pressure symptoms.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cervical fibroids are rare; they cause local pressure effects (urinary or bowel symptoms, obstructed labor) rather than heavy menstrual bleeding.
B. Subserosal fibroids grow outward and cause pressure or heaviness but typically NOT menorrhagia, so they do not explain her bleeding.
D. Submucosal fibroids are the classic cause of menorrhagia and infertility; pick them when bleeding dominates without marked bulk symptoms such as leg edema.
key_concept:
Fibroid location by symptom.
  • Submucosal: menorrhagia, infertility, (pressure)
  • Intramural: bulky uterus, pressure, can increase bleeding
  • Subserosal: pressure/heaviness, little bleeding
  • Cervical: rare, urinary/bowel symptoms, obstructed labor
  • Ultrasound is the initial and diagnostic test
exam_pearl: Menorrhagia alone = submucosal; menorrhagia plus large-mass pressure effects (leg edema) is how this recall points to intramural.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1881).

stem: Patient (32 years old i think) had menorrhagia she had subserosal fibroid 3x3 cm what is the management
why_right: A subserosal fibroid grows outward from the uterus and does not distort the cavity, so it is unlikely to be the cause of her menorrhagia. At only 3x3 cm it is far below the surgical threshold, so the bleeding is treated medically first, and NSAIDs reduce menstrual blood loss.
why_wrong_block:
A. Myomectomy is for a fibroid larger than 7 cm or failed medical treatment in a woman wanting fertility; removing a small subserosal fibroid would not treat bleeding it is not causing.
B. Hysterectomy is definitive surgery for a large symptomatic fibroid in a woman who has completed her family; far too radical for a young woman with a small fibroid.
C. Uterine artery embolization is for a symptomatic surgical candidate who refuses surgery; here the fibroid is not the cause and surgery is not indicated.
key_concept:
Fibroid treatment ladder.
  • Asymptomatic/incidental: observe, yearly ultrasound
  • Symptomatic: medical first (NSAIDs, OCP)
  • GnRH analogue: pre-operative shrinkage
  • Surgery: >7 cm or failed medical treatment
  • Myomectomy if fertility wanted; hysterectomy if family complete
  • UAE: surgical candidate refusing surgery
exam_pearl: Subserosal fibroid + menorrhagia: the fibroid is not the culprit, so treat the bleeding medically.

stem: 32-year-old single woman is attending the clinic complaining of menorrhagia for the last few months. The physical examination is unremarkable. Pelvic Ultrasound: Presence of a serosal fibroid, 4 x 4 cm in size. Otherwise, the other parameters of the ultrasound were normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: Her menorrhagia is not explained by the fibroid: a serosal (subserosal) fibroid grows outward and does not distort the cavity, so it rarely causes heavy bleeding, and at 4 x 4 cm it is below the surgical threshold. With a normal examination, the bleeding is treated medically first, and NSAIDs reduce menstrual blood loss.
why_wrong_block:
A. Myomectomy is for fibroids above 7 cm or failed medical therapy; removing a serosal fibroid would not treat bleeding it is not causing.
B. Hysterectomy is far too radical for a young single woman with a small fibroid unrelated to her symptoms, and ends fertility.
C. Embolization is for a symptomatic fibroid needing surgery in a woman who refuses it; here the fibroid is not the cause.
key_concept:
Ask first whether the fibroid explains the symptom.
  • Submucosal: menorrhagia, infertility
  • Intramural: can cause heavy bleeding when large
  • Subserosal: pressure symptoms, rarely bleeding
  • Bleeding not explained by the fibroid: medical treatment (NSAIDs, OCP)
  • Surgery: above 7 cm or failed medical therapy
exam_pearl: Serosal fibroid + menorrhagia = do not blame the fibroid; treat the bleeding medically.

stem: A 39 weeks pregnant female, on examination amniotic fluid was noted to have a dark green color. What's the most appropriate action to be done [[[DURING]]] delivery?
OptC: Oropharyngeal suction before delivering the rest of body
why_right: Dark green amniotic fluid at 39 weeks means meconium-stained liquor, which risks meconium aspiration. This recall's key reflects the traditional teaching for the moment during delivery: suction the mouth and pharynx after the head delivers and before the shoulders and body, aiming to clear meconium before the first breath. Current neonatal resuscitation guidance no longer recommends this routinely; see the concern note.
why_wrong_block:
A. NICU transfer is a post-delivery decision based on the baby's condition; a vigorous baby stays with the mother, and it is not an action during delivery.
B. Immediate intubation for tracheal suction was once advised for a NON-vigorous baby after birth; it is not done during delivery and is no longer routine even then.
D. IV antibiotics treat suspected chorioamnionitis (maternal fever, tachycardia, tender uterus); meconium alone is not an infection.
key_concept:
Meconium-stained liquor at delivery.
  • Have a team skilled in neonatal resuscitation present
  • Vigorous baby: routine care, no suctioning needed
  • Non-vigorous baby: standard resuscitation steps (warm, dry, open airway, ventilate)
  • Old teaching: suction mouth then nose at the perineum; trial evidence showed no benefit
exam_pearl: Exam wording 'DURING delivery' is what pointed old keys to perineal suctioning; after birth the decision depends on whether the baby is vigorous.

stem: A 25-year-old woman was diagnosed to have a complete abortion at 10 weeks of gestation. The patient is a heavy smoker and smokes more than 20 cigarettes a day. She was not taking any folic acid or dietary supplements. Which of the following is the most likely risk that caused the miscarriage?
OptD: Smoking more than 20 cigarettes a day
why_right: The only recognized miscarriage risk factor in this stem is "smokes more than 20 cigarettes a day". Heavy maternal smoking causes placental vasoconstriction and uteroplacental insufficiency, which is linked to miscarriage, fetal growth restriction and other placental complications. The missing folic acid is a deliberate distractor.
why_wrong_block:
A. A diet low in carotene is not an established cause of miscarriage.
B. Folic acid deficiency is mainly linked to neural tube defects; it is not the recognized cause of miscarriage here, whereas heavy smoking is.
C. Most first trimester losses are chromosomal and have no identifiable maternal cause, but this stem explicitly gives a recognized risk factor, so this option does not fit.
key_concept:
Pick the risk factor the stem actually gives you.
  • Heavy smoking: miscarriage, growth restriction, placental problems
  • Folic acid omission: neural tube defects (preconception 0.4 mg daily)
  • Commonest cause of first trimester loss overall: fetal chromosomal abnormality
  • Other recognized factors: advanced maternal age, heavy alcohol, uncontrolled diabetes or thyroid disease
exam_pearl: Folic acid prevents neural tube defects, not miscarriage; do not let the supplement detail pull you away from the smoking.
compiler_note: Compiler note: 'Q:' recall shown under 535 (different question).

stem: A woman was trying to conceive, she is asymptomatic, was found to have serosal fibroid 5x5 cm incidentally on pelvic US. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: She is asymptomatic and the fibroid is serosal and 5x5 cm. Subserosal fibroids grow outward and do not distort the cavity, so they are not a recognised cause of infertility, and 5 cm is below the surgical threshold. An asymptomatic fibroid is managed conservatively with annual follow-up ultrasound, and she can keep trying to conceive.
why_wrong_block:
B. Myomectomy needs a fibroid larger than 7 cm, failed medical therapy, or a cavity-distorting (submucosal) fibroid in infertility; none applies here, and surgery adds uterine scarring before pregnancy.
C. OCPs control bleeding from symptomatic fibroids; she has no symptoms and is trying to conceive, so contraception defeats her goal.
D. Uterine artery embolization is for a symptomatic surgical candidate who refuses surgery, and it is avoided in women who want future pregnancy.
key_concept:
Fibroid + fertility.
  • Asymptomatic: conservative, yearly ultrasound
  • Submucosal distorting cavity: hysteroscopic myomectomy
  • Subserosal: no effect on fertility
  • Surgery: >7 cm or failed medical treatment
  • Avoid UAE if pregnancy desired
exam_pearl: No word 'incidental' is needed: 'asymptomatic' plus a subserosal fibroid under 7 cm is enough for conservative care.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0540).

An asymptomatic fibroid is managed conservatively with annual follow-up ultrasound, and she can keep trying to conceive.

B. Myomectomy needs a fibroid larger than 7 cm, failed medical therapy, or a cavity-distorting (submucosal) fibroid in infertility; none applies here, and surgery adds uterine scarring before pregnancy.
C. OCPs control bleeding from symptomatic fibroids; she has no symptoms and is trying to conceive, so contraception defeats her goal.
D. Uterine artery embolization is for a symptomatic surgical candidate who refuses surgery, and it is avoided in women who want future pregnancy.

Fibroid + fertility.
  • Asymptomatic: conservative, yearly ultrasound
  • Submucosal distorting cavity: hysteroscopic myomectomy
  • Subserosal: no effect on fertility
  • Surgery: >7 cm or failed medical treatment

stem: Baby delivered dead at 38 wks (Stillbirth case). Placenta and baby appear normal Which of the following is best to sent for investigations for chromosomal analysis?
why_right: The baby is already delivered as a stillbirth at 38 weeks, so the sample must come from tissue available after birth. Fetal cells die soon after demise and often fail to grow in culture, whereas placental tissue (taken near the cord insertion) stays viable longer and gives the best chance of a successful karyotype or chromosomal microarray.
why_wrong_block:
A. Umbilical cord sampling (cordocentesis) is a prenatal procedure to draw blood from a LIVING fetus, so it has no role after a stillbirth; a cut segment of cord tissue can be sent as a backup, but placental tissue gives the better yield.
B. Amniotic fluid by amniocentesis is the best sample BEFORE delivery when the dead fetus is still in utero; after birth it is no longer available.
C. Fetal cord blood from a stillborn is clotted and its cells are non-viable, so culture usually fails.
key_concept:
Chromosomal testing in fetal death: timing decides the sample.
  • Fetus still in utero: amniocentesis (amniotic fluid), highest yield
  • After delivery: placental tissue near cord insertion
  • Other post-delivery options: cord segment, internal fetal tissue
  • Fetal blood after death: poor yield
exam_pearl: Delivered = placenta; still inside = amniotic fluid.

stem: A patient with absent fetal heartbeat on ultrasound, which of the following is best to use for chromosomal analysis? (A patient with fetal demise: which of the following is best to use for chromosomal analysis?)
why_right: Absent fetal heartbeat on ultrasound means the dead fetus is still in utero. Amniocentesis before delivery gives amniotic fluid cells that remain viable for culture, making it the highest-yield sample for karyotype or microarray in fetal death; it should be offered before induction.
why_wrong_block:
A. Umbilical cord sampling (cordocentesis) samples blood from a LIVING fetus; after demise there is no circulation and the blood is non-viable.
C. Fetal cord blood after death is clotted and its cells do not grow, so it gives a poor yield.
D. Placental tissue is the best sample AFTER the baby is delivered; while the fetus is still in utero, amniotic fluid is obtained first.
key_concept:
Chromosomal testing in fetal death: timing decides the sample.
  • Fetus still in utero: amniocentesis (amniotic fluid)
  • After delivery: placental tissue near cord insertion
  • Cordocentesis: living fetus only
  • Fetal blood after death: poor yield
exam_pearl: Same options as the stillbirth card: 'absent heartbeat on ultrasound' (still inside) flips the answer to amniotic fluid.

stem: Patient now delivered how to know about the chromosomal analysis from where to take sample
why_right: The lead-in is "now delivered": the fetus is out, so the sample for karyotype comes from fetal tissue directly, and umbilical cord (cord blood or a cord segment) is fetal in origin and easy to obtain at delivery. Prenatal routes are no longer needed once the baby (or stillborn fetus) and placenta are available.
why_wrong_block:
A. "Maternal cord" is not a fetal sample; any maternal tissue or blood gives the mother's karyotype, not the baby's. Maternal blood is used only for cell free fetal DNA screening during pregnancy.
B. Amniotic fluid (amniocentesis) is a prenatal diagnostic route, usually from about 15 weeks; after delivery it is unnecessary and fetal tissue is available directly.
key_concept:
Sample for fetal karyotype depends on timing.
  • First trimester: chorionic villus sampling
  • Second trimester: amniocentesis
  • Later in pregnancy: fetal (cordocentesis) blood
  • After delivery: cord blood or cord segment, placenta, fetal tissue
  • Maternal blood: cell free DNA screening only, not diagnostic
exam_pearl: Read the timing word: "now delivered" removes every invasive prenatal test from the answer list.
compiler_note: Compiler note: 'Q:' recall shown under 543 (after delivery version).

stem: mother presented in OPD concerning for decrease fetal movement, at 18 weeks, there was no fetal heart beat, on her previous visit fetus was normal with normal placenta and fetus heart beat. What the next step for diagnosis?
why_right: She reports decreased fetal movement and no fetal heartbeat was found at 18 weeks; the first diagnostic step is ultrasound to confirm or exclude absent fetal cardiac activity. Ultrasound is the test that diagnoses fetal death, and every other investigation follows only once the diagnosis is confirmed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Amniocentesis is for fetal karyotype (prenatal diagnosis); it is part of the cause workup after demise is confirmed, not the step that diagnoses it.
B. Placental tissue sampling (CVS or placental karyotype after delivery) looks for a cause such as aneuploidy; it does not establish whether the fetus is alive.
C. Umbilical cord sampling gives fetal blood for karyotype or infection studies; it is invasive and only for cause, never the first diagnostic test.
key_concept:
Suspected fetal death: confirm with ultrasound first, then look for the cause.
  • Ultrasound: absent cardiac activity confirms demise
  • Before 20 weeks: classed as pregnancy loss (abortion); at or after 20 weeks: IUFD
  • Decreased movement at viable age: history, kick count, NST, then US or BPP
  • After confirmation: karyotype (amniotic fluid, placenta, cord), infection screen, coagulation profile
exam_pearl: "Next step for diagnosis" = imaging to confirm; genetic sampling answers "why", not "whether".

stem: Primigravida came to antenatal clinic concerned about having a NTD. She Has Prior History Of Anencephaly. What Is Recommended Folic Acid Dose?
why_right: This recall's key is 1000 micrograms because hydrocephalus on its own is not a neural tube defect, so the history is treated as moderate rather than high risk, where some guidelines use about 1 mg daily. The high dose of 4 to 5 mg is reserved for a true NTD history (previous NTD pregnancy, NTD in the woman or her partner) or drug and medical risk factors.
why_wrong_block:
B. 2000 micrograms is not a recognised folic acid dose tier, so it is never the intended answer.
C. 5000 micrograms (5 mg) is the high risk dose; it becomes right if the stem states a previous NTD pregnancy (for example spina bifida or anencephaly) or an NTD in either parent.
key_concept:
Folic acid dose follows NTD risk tier.
  • Average risk: 0.4 mg daily
  • Moderate risk (some guidelines): about 1 mg daily
  • High risk (previous NTD, woman or partner with NTD, antiepileptics, diabetes, SCD/thalassemia): 4 to 5 mg daily
  • Hydrocephalus alone is not an NTD, but it often accompanies spina bifida
exam_pearl: If the stem converts "hydrocephalus" into "spina bifida" or "previous NTD baby", the answer flips to 5000 micrograms.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0560).
Compiler note: Other version (Q): the appropriate dose of folic acid in a woman planning to get pregnant? A) 1 mg B) 5 mg C) 15 mg D) 20 mg. Answer: A.

stem: Primigravida came to antenatal clinic concerned about having a NTD child as her cousin had child with Anencephaly?
highlight_terms_source: her cousin had child with Anencephaly
why_right: The only family history is a cousin's child with anencephaly: she has no personal NTD, no previous affected pregnancy and no affected partner, so she is not in the high risk group that needs 4 to 5 mg. A distant family history at most places her in a moderate risk tier, for which some guidelines use 1 mg (1000 micrograms) daily; this recall keys the lowest listed dose, 1000 micrograms.
why_wrong_block:
B. 2000 micrograms (2 mg) is not a standard folic acid tier; doses are 0.4 mg (average), about 1 mg (moderate), and 4 to 5 mg (high risk).
C. 5000 micrograms (5 mg) is the high risk dose, used for a previous NTD pregnancy, an NTD in the woman or her partner, antiepileptic drugs, diabetes, or hemolytic anemia; a cousin's affected child does not qualify.
key_concept:
Folic acid dose follows NTD risk tier.
  • Average risk: 0.4 mg (400 micrograms) daily
  • Moderate risk (distant family history, some guidelines): about 1 mg daily
  • High risk (previous NTD pregnancy, woman or partner with NTD, antiepileptics, diabetes, SCD/thalassemia): 4 to 5 mg daily
  • Start at least 1 month before conception, continue to 12 weeks (throughout pregnancy in hemolytic anemia)
exam_pearl: Who had the NTD matters: the woman, her partner or her own previous baby = high dose; a cousin's baby = not high dose.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q): Folic acid dose in healthy preg: mg 1, 5, 6 (no answer marked).

stem: Mother On Phenytoin, What Is Folic Acid Dose
why_right: Phenytoin is an enzyme inducing antiepileptic that lowers folate levels and raises NTD risk, which puts her in the high risk group. High risk women need high dose folic acid, 5 mg (5000 micrograms) daily, rather than the standard 0.4 mg.
why_wrong_block:
A. 1000 micrograms (1 mg) is the moderate risk dose in some guidelines (which even place anticonvulsant users there); UK style guidance, and this recall, give 5 mg to women on antiepileptics.
B. 2000 micrograms is not a recognised folic acid dose tier.
key_concept:
High dose folic acid (4 to 5 mg) indications:
  • Antiepileptics (phenytoin, valproate, carbamazepine)
  • Previous NTD pregnancy, or NTD in the woman or her partner
  • Diabetes
  • Sickle cell disease or thalassemia (continue throughout pregnancy)
  • Malabsorption (e.g. coeliac disease)
  • Everyone else: 0.4 mg daily
exam_pearl: Any antiepileptic in the stem = 5 mg folic acid, even with no NTD history.

stem: 37 weeks gestational female having contractions, baby is cephalic, cervix 4cm dilated, baby at 1+ station. Female started bleeding with tender abdomen, ctg normal fetus
why_right: Bleeding with a tender abdomen in labour is placental abruption. At 37 weeks, already labouring (4 cm, station +1, cephalic) with a normal CTG and no maternal instability described, the plan is expedited vaginal delivery, so labour is augmented with oxytocin (with amniotomy) under close fetal and maternal monitoring.
why_wrong_block:
B. Surgical (instrumental) vaginal delivery needs a fully dilated cervix and a low station; at 4 cm it is not possible. It is used in the second stage when delivery must be expedited.
C. Observation is unsafe: an abruption at term should be delivered, as it can extend and cause fetal distress, coagulopathy or hemorrhage. Expectant care is only for a stable preterm abruption (below 34 weeks) with a reassuring fetus.
D. Anesthesia (epidural for analgesia or general for cesarean) does not treat the abruption; cesarean would be chosen if the mother were unstable or the CTG non reassuring, and coagulopathy must be checked before regional block.
key_concept:
Placental abruption: management depends on mother, fetus and gestation.
  • Unstable mother: cesarean section
  • Non reassuring fetus: cesarean section
  • Stable mother, fetal death: vaginal delivery (induction)
  • Stable, reassuring, term or in labour: vaginal delivery, amniotomy plus oxytocin
  • Stable, reassuring, below 34 weeks: admit, steroids, MgSO4 if below 32 weeks
exam_pearl: Abruption plus normal CTG plus stable mother at term = speed up the vaginal birth; a non reassuring CTG flips it to cesarean.

stem: 40 years old pregnant lady, she's in her second pregnancy, her first pregnancy went very well and she has a living child, her past history is unremarkable, she doesn't have any chronic disease, her BMI is 26. She's now in her 12 week of gestation, And she presented now in her first antenatal care visit, which of the following is the best thing to council her about?
OptA: Do a 50 oral glucose tolerance test
OptB: Council her about the current best options for genetic abnormalities or something like the prenatal care screening.
OptC: Give her low dose aspirin to prevent pre-eclampsia.
why_right: At 40 years the main extra risk of this otherwise low risk pregnancy is fetal aneuploidy, and at her 12 week first visit she is in the window for first trimester screening. So the priority counselling is her options for aneuploidy screening and diagnostic testing (combined screening or cell free DNA, then CVS or amniocentesis if needed).
why_wrong_block:
A. A 50 g glucose challenge is routine at 24 to 28 weeks; early testing is for risk factors such as previous GDM or BMI ≥30, and she has a BMI of 26 with an uneventful first pregnancy.
C. Low dose aspirin is for women at high risk of pre-eclampsia (e.g. previous pre-eclampsia, chronic hypertension, diabetes, renal disease) or with two or more moderate factors; age 40 alone is a single moderate factor.
D. Tdap is given later in each pregnancy (third trimester, about 27 to 36 weeks), not at the 12 week booking visit.
key_concept:
First antenatal visit at advanced maternal age:
  • Confirm dating with ultrasound
  • Offer aneuploidy screening: first trimester combined test or cell free DNA
  • Positive screen: diagnostic CVS (10 to 13 weeks) or amniocentesis (from 15 weeks)
  • GDM test: 24 to 28 weeks unless previous GDM or obesity
  • Aspirin: one high risk factor or two moderate factors
exam_pearl: Age alone in a healthy parous woman = counsel on genetic screening; add a second risk factor before thinking aspirin.

stem: A 16-week primigravida who is medically free presented to the clinic with fears of delivering a macrosomic baby. Her BMI is 35. What is the appropriate test?
why_right: A BMI of 35 is obesity, a recognised risk factor for gestational diabetes and macrosomia, so she qualifies for glucose testing with an OGTT rather than routine reassurance. The 75 g OGTT is the one step diagnostic test for GDM and is the appropriate test for her concern.
why_wrong_block: A. Fasting glucose alone misses many cases of GDM, because much of pregnancy hyperglycemia is post load; it is not the standard diagnostic test, though a high fasting value can flag overt diabetes.
key_concept:
GDM testing:
  • Routine: 24 to 28 weeks
  • One step: 2 hour 75 g OGTT (diagnostic)
  • Two step: 50 g challenge, then 3 hour 100 g OGTT if positive
  • Risk factors: BMI ≥30, previous GDM, previous macrosomic baby, first degree relative with diabetes, PCOS
  • HbA1c and random glucose are not GDM diagnostic tests
exam_pearl: Obesity plus fear of a big baby = OGTT, not a single fasting glucose.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Only two options recorded.

stem: G2P1 came at 23 weeks of gestation. Completely normal, O+ blood type, all test unremarkable. She Has 2 Prior Uncomplicated Deliveries. She said her mother was diagnosed with diabetes mellitus type 2. She is concerned about her having it as well. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient's concern? (They emphasized type 2 diabetes, not gestational)
highlight_terms_source: mother was diagnosed with diabetes mellitus type 2
why_right: She is at 23 weeks, completely normal, with 2 prior uncomplicated deliveries (no previous GDM or macrosomia); a mother with type 2 diabetes alone does not justify early or immediate testing. The right step is the standard screen, a 75 g OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks, which is only a week away and also detects diabetes declaring itself in pregnancy.
why_wrong_block:
A. HbA1c is not a reliable diagnostic test in pregnancy (red cell turnover lowers it) and misses GDM; it is used to look for pre existing diabetes at booking in high risk women, not for this concern at 23 weeks.
B. A random glucose is neither sensitive nor diagnostic for GDM; it is only useful when classic symptoms of hyperglycemia are present.
D. The 3 hour 100 g OGTT is step 2 of the two step approach, done only after an abnormal 50 g challenge; it is not the first test.
key_concept:
When to screen for GDM:
  • Everyone: 24 to 28 weeks
  • Early (first visit): previous GDM, previous macrosomia, obesity, or several risk factors combined
  • One step: 75 g 2 hour OGTT
  • Two step: 50 g challenge, then 100 g 3 hour OGTT
  • Family history alone: routine timing
exam_pearl: Family history alone keeps her on the routine 24 to 28 week OGTT; a previous GDM or big baby would pull testing earlier.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot on next page within 576 block. Answer: C (Confirmed). Family history alone OR overweight alone are not indications for early DM screen. Beside, she has 2 prior uncomplicated deliveries (no macrosomia, no GDM); if these were present, then we might consider early screen.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with a leiomyoma associated with heavy menstruation (see image and lab result). [Labs Showed Low Hb And CT Showing Fibroid] Which of the following is the most appropriate next management step?
why_right: The fibroid is causing heavy menstruation and the labs show low Hb; the lead-in asks for the next step. A symptomatic fibroid with significant anemia is stabilised first by correcting the anemia (transfusion if severe, then iron), and only then is definitive treatment planned.
why_wrong_block:
A. Myomectomy is definitive treatment for a symptomatic fibroid in a woman wanting fertility, but operating on a severely anemic patient is unsafe; it follows correction of the anemia.
C. Oral contraceptive pills can reduce bleeding in mild cases, but they do not treat an already low Hb and are a later option.
D. Uterine artery embolization is an alternative definitive option for women who decline surgery; it also comes after the anemia is corrected.
key_concept:
Fibroid management ladder:
  • Asymptomatic, incidental: observe and follow up
  • Symptomatic with significant anemia: correct anemia first
  • Medical: NSAIDs or tranexamic acid, hormonal options, GnRH agonist before surgery
  • Wants fertility: myomectomy
  • Completed family: hysterectomy
  • Declines surgery: uterine artery embolization
exam_pearl: "Next step" plus a low Hb = fix the anemia before any procedure.

stem: A young woman in the childbearing age presents with chronic pelvic pain and heavy menstrual bleeding. {There was a picture of a sagittal view CT scan showed a gray, well-defined circle in the uterus} What is the best next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: gray, well-defined circle in the uterus
key_concept:
Fibroid management depends on symptoms, size, anemia and fertility wishes.
  • Asymptomatic, incidental: observe with yearly ultrasound
  • Symptomatic bleeding: medical first (OCP, LNG-IUD, tranexamic acid)
  • Severe anemia: correct the anemia before definitive treatment
  • Surgery if large (>7 cm) or medical failure: myomectomy if fertility wanted, hysterectomy if family complete
  • Wants to avoid surgery: uterine artery embolization
  • GnRH agonist: pre-operative shrinkage, short term
exam_pearl: If the stem adds a very low Hb, the next step flips to correcting the anemia, not any of these three.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: No option highlighted; compiler comment 'C??'.
Other marked answers: Compiler comment: C??
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 45-years old female in 5th day post-hysterectomy the patient have fever, she does not complain of anything and the wound is clean. What is your next step of measurement?
why_right: This recall's key is medication review because the patient is on day 5 with fever but "does not complain of anything" and the "wound is clean": there are no urinary, chest or wound clues to direct tests. Drug fever is a non-invasive, often overlooked cause to check first in an asymptomatic postoperative patient.
why_wrong_block:
A. CBC and blood cultures are right when the patient looks septic (rigors, tachycardia, hypotension) or has a line or clear source; in a well, asymptomatic patient they are not the first step in this recall.
B. Urinalysis and culture is right for fever with urinary symptoms or a catheter, typically on days 2 to 3; here the patient has no complaints.
C. A chest X-ray is right for cough, dyspnoea, crackles or reduced breath sounds, mostly in the first days after surgery (atelectasis, pneumonia); there are no chest findings here.
key_concept:
Asymptomatic postoperative fever: start with the history, examination and drug chart before blind tests.
  • Day 1: atelectasis
  • Days 2 to 3: pneumonia, UTI, thrombophlebitis
  • Days 4 to 5: wound infection, DVT
  • After hysterectomy: also vaginal cuff cellulitis or pelvic collection
  • Drug fever: diagnosis of exclusion; patient often looks well
exam_pearl: Symptoms or signs pointing to a source (dysuria, cough, red wound) move the answer to the matching test.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1985B).

stem: A pregnant woman at 11 weeks gestation is found to have a positive anti-E antibody titer of 1:16. What is the next best step in management ?
key_concept:
Alloimmunized pregnancy: titer first, then Doppler, then treat by gestation.
  • Below critical titer: repeat titers serially
  • At or above critical titer: stop relying on titers; check paternal antigen status / fetal genotype and start serial MCA Doppler from mid second trimester
  • MCA PSV >1.5 MoM = severe fetal anemia: fetal blood sampling and intrauterine transfusion, or delivery near term
  • Hydrops (ascites + skin edema) = severe disease
  • Anti-D prophylaxis only prevents D sensitization in unsensitized women
  • Anti-Kell is the exception: severe anemia even with low titers
exam_pearl: Anti-D immunoglobulin is a trap for any already sensitized woman and for any non-D antibody.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: No answer marked; compiler put question marks next to A and C.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 43-year-old woman presented with intermenstrual bleeding in the last 3 months (see report). Ultrasound: A 13 mm long echogenic structure in the endometrium. Which of the following is the most appropriate management option?
OptD: Hysteroscopy and removal of the structure
highlight_terms_source: 13 mm long echogenic structure in the endometrium
why_right: An echogenic intracavitary structure in a woman with intermenstrual bleeding is an endometrial polyp. It is both symptomatic and 13 mm (over 1 cm), so the management is hysteroscopic polypectomy. Hysteroscopic removal treats the bleeding and gives the whole lesion for histology in one step.
why_wrong_block:
A. Blind endometrial sampling can miss a focal polyp and does not remove it; sampling is the step for AUB over 45 or thickened endometrium without a focal lesion.
B. Repeat scanning (observation) is only for polyps that are asymptomatic AND under 1 cm; this one is symptomatic and 13 mm.
C. Progestogens do not remove a structural lesion; they are used for anovulatory bleeding or hyperplasia without atypia, not for a polyp.
key_concept:
Endometrial polyp: TVUS first, hysteroscopy confirms and treats.
  • Presents with menorrhagia or intermenstrual bleeding
  • Asymptomatic AND under 1 cm: observe
  • Symptomatic OR over 1 cm: hysteroscopic polypectomy
  • Removal gives histology (excludes hyperplasia or cancer)
exam_pearl: Symptoms OR size over 1 cm alone is enough to remove; only small AND silent polyps are watched.

stem: A woman in her 30s with heavy menstrual bleeding, she had 13mm?? polyp, and hemoglobin of 7 g/dL. What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: Heavy menstrual bleeding with a 13 mm polyp means a symptomatic polyp larger than 1 cm, and the treatment of a symptomatic or large endometrial polyp is hysteroscopic polypectomy. It removes the cause of the bleeding, gives tissue for histology, and preserves the uterus in a woman in her 30s. The Hb of 7 is managed alongside (iron, or transfusion if she is symptomatic or unstable), while removal of the polyp is the definitive management the recall keys.
why_wrong_block:
B. Hysterectomy is far too radical for a benign polyp in a young woman; it is kept for failed conservative treatment, completed family with other pathology, or malignancy.
C. Blood transfusion treats the consequence, not the cause. It becomes the first step when the anemia is symptomatic (fatigue, dizziness, tachycardia, hypotension) or bleeding is ongoing and heavy, which the stem does not describe; the source also highlighted this option.
key_concept:
Endometrial polyp: TVUS to detect, hysteroscopy to confirm and treat.
  • Presents with heavy or intermenstrual bleeding
  • Initial imaging: transvaginal ultrasound
  • Small (<1 cm) and asymptomatic: observe
  • Symptomatic or >1 cm: hysteroscopic polypectomy
  • Symptomatic or unstable anemia: transfuse first, then treat the cause
exam_pearl: If the stem says she is dizzy, tachycardic or hypotensive with this Hb, transfusion comes first.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Screenshot (numbered 41 in its source file) embedded under 633. Option A is bold with 'removal' red-highlighted; 'transfusion' in option C is also red-highlighted.
Other marked answers: Screenshot red highlight also on: C. Blood transfusion

stem: 62-year-old patient presented with vaginal bleeding. Investigations revealed a malignant tumor of uterine fundus. Which of the following groups of lymph nodes is likely affected in this condition and to be dissected during surgery?
why_right: A 62-year-old with vaginal bleeding and a malignant tumor of the uterine fundus has endometrial cancer. Lymph from the fundus follows the ovarian vessels in the infundibulopelvic ligament up to the para-aortic nodes, so these are at risk and are sampled or dissected during surgical staging.
why_wrong_block:
A. Superficial inguinal nodes drain the vulva, lower vagina and the uterine cornu along the round ligament; they are not the main drainage of the fundus.
B. Deep inguinal nodes receive lymph from the superficial inguinal nodes and the lower limb; they are not a staging group for uterine cancer.
C. Internal iliac nodes drain the cervix and lower uterine body; they would be the answer for a cervical or lower uterine tumor, not a fundal one.
key_concept:
Pelvic organ lymph follows the arterial supply.
  • Uterine fundus and ovary: para-aortic (via ovarian vessels)
  • Uterine cornu: superficial inguinal (via round ligament)
  • Cervix and lower uterus: internal and external iliac, obturator
  • Vulva and lower vagina: superficial inguinal
  • Endometrial cancer: biopsy to diagnose, surgical staging with pelvic and para-aortic nodes
exam_pearl: Fundus or ovary = para-aortic; cervix = iliac; vulva = inguinal.

stem: A 30-year-old woman P1+0 presented to Obstetrics and Gynecology Clinic complains of inability to conceive for the last 3 years. During that time, she was not on contraceptive and her menstrual periods every 45 days but no period for the last 6 months (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? TSH 9.2 U/L (0.4 - 5.0); FSH 5.3 U/L; LH 7.2 U/L; Prolactin 140 ng/ml (< 25 ng/ml)
why_right: The labs show a high TSH 9.2 with a raised prolactin 140 and normal FSH and LH. Primary hypothyroidism raises TRH, which stimulates prolactin release, and the hyperprolactinemia suppresses ovulation, giving oligomenorrhea, then amenorrhea and infertility. The single diagnosis that explains both abnormal results is hypothyroidism.
why_wrong_block:
B. Hypopituitarism lowers pituitary output (TSH, FSH, LH, prolactin); here TSH and prolactin are high.
C. Hyperprolactinemia is present but is secondary; a primary prolactinoma would not raise TSH, so always check TSH before blaming the pituitary.
D. PCOS needs hyperandrogenism or polycystic ovaries and often a raised LH:FSH ratio; none is given and it does not raise TSH.
key_concept:
High prolactin: check pregnancy and TSH before imaging the pituitary.
  • High TSH + high prolactin = primary hypothyroidism (TRH drives prolactin)
  • Normal TSH + very high prolactin = consider prolactinoma, drugs
  • Low FSH/LH/TSH together = hypopituitarism
  • High FSH = ovarian failure
  • PCOS: 2 of 3 (oligo/anovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries); a raised LH:FSH ratio is supportive only
  • Treat with levothyroxine: prolactin and cycles normalise
exam_pearl: Raised prolactin with raised TSH is hypothyroidism, not a prolactinoma.

stem: A 35-year-old woman is complaining of vaginal discharge and burning with urination. Her husband was recently diagnosed with gonorrhea. Which of the following tests has the highest diagnostic value?
why_right: Her husband has gonorrhea and she has discharge with dysuria, so the question is where Neisseria gonorrhoeae lives in a woman. Gonococci infect columnar epithelium of the endocervix, so an endocervical swab (NAAT or culture) gives the highest diagnostic yield.
why_wrong_block:
A. A routine urine culture does not grow gonococci; first void urine NAAT is acceptable but less sensitive than a genital swab in women.
B. Rectal or anogenital swabs are added when there is anal exposure or anorectal symptoms; they are not the primary site in this presentation.
D. The vagina is lined by squamous epithelium that gonococci do not infect; a high vaginal swab is for candida, bacterial vaginosis and trichomonas.
key_concept:
Sample the site the organism infects.
  • Gonorrhea / Chlamydia in women: endocervical swab (culture or NAAT); vulvovaginal NAAT swab is equivalent
  • Men: first void urine or urethral swab
  • Candida, BV, trichomonas: high vaginal swab
  • Anal or oral exposure: add rectal or pharyngeal swabs
exam_pearl: Cervicitis organisms (gonorrhea, chlamydia) = endocervical swab; vaginitis organisms = high vaginal swab.

stem: A 35-week pregnant woman presents with vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound shows placenta previa covering the os completely. She was stabilized, and the bleeding stopped. What is the most appropriate management?
OptC: Wait until 37 weeks, then do cesarean section
highlight_terms_source: placenta previa covering the os completely
why_right: A complete previa at 35 weeks whose bleeding has stopped in a stabilized mother is managed expectantly (admission and observation), aiming for planned cesarean at 36 to 37 weeks. This avoids prematurity while timing delivery before labor starts. Delivery is by cesarean only because the placenta covers the os.
why_wrong_block:
A. Induction of labor means vaginal delivery, which is contraindicated when the placenta covers the internal os.
B. Immediate cesarean is right for severe active bleeding, maternal instability or fetal distress before 37 weeks; here bleeding has stopped and she is stable.
D. Awaiting labor is unsafe and vaginal birth is impossible with a complete previa; delivery must be a planned cesarean before labor.
key_concept:
Placenta previa: cesarean only; timing depends on bleeding and gestation.
  • No vaginal exam until ultrasound localizes the placenta
  • Severe bleeding, unstable mother or fetal distress: stabilize and cesarean now
  • Mild or stopped bleeding before term: admit, steroids if <34 wk, MgSO4 if <32 wk
  • Then planned cesarean at 36 to 37 weeks
  • At term with bleeding: cesarean
exam_pearl: Bleeding stopped and stable = wait; active heavy bleeding or fetal distress = cut now.

stem: A woman planning for conception presented to the clinic concerned about vitamin D deficiency. She is dark skinned and vegetarian, and does not get adequate exposure to sunlight. What is the recommended daily dose of vitamin D?
highlight_terms_source: does not get adequate exposure to sunlight
why_right: She has several risk factors for deficiency: dark skin, a vegetarian diet and little sunlight. Women at high risk of vitamin D deficiency who are planning or in pregnancy are advised a higher prophylactic dose of about 1000 IU daily, rather than the routine dose given to low-risk women.
why_wrong_block:
A. 600 IU is the general recommended daily allowance for adults and pregnant women without risk factors; it is not enough for this high-risk woman.
C. 2000 IU is a higher dose used in some regimens for those with documented low levels; it is not the standard prophylactic dose for risk factors alone.
D. 4000 IU is the usual tolerable upper intake for adults, a ceiling, not a routine daily recommendation.
key_concept:
Vitamin D dose depends on risk.
  • Low-risk adult or pregnant woman: about 400 to 600 IU daily
  • High risk (dark skin, covered or indoors, vegetarian, obese): about 1000 IU daily
  • Confirmed deficiency: treatment doses, then maintenance
  • 4000 IU: upper limit, not a target
  • Pair with folic acid 0.4 mg preconception
exam_pearl: Risk factors listed (dark skin, low sun, vegetarian) push the answer above the routine dose to 1000 IU.

stem: A 19 years old primigravida complaining of abdominal cramps and vaginal spotting. LMP 6 weeks ago with a positive home pregnancy test. Speculum examination closed os and abdominal pain with cervical manipulation. What's the appropriate next step?
OptD: Further deeper vaginal examination to rule out masses
why_right: A woman 6 weeks after her LMP with a positive pregnancy test, cramps and spotting, a closed os and pain on cervical manipulation could have a threatened miscarriage or an ectopic pregnancy. After history and speculum examination, the next step is transvaginal ultrasound to show whether the pregnancy is intrauterine and viable, and to look for an adnexal mass or free fluid.
why_wrong_block:
A. CBC is supportive (anemia, blood loss) but cannot locate the pregnancy or decide the diagnosis.
C. CT exposes the fetus to radiation and is inferior to ultrasound for early pregnancy; it has no role here.
D. Further deep vaginal examination adds pain and, with a possible ectopic, risks rupture; imaging, not repeated palpation, is needed to rule out masses.
key_concept:
First-trimester bleeding: history and exam, then TVUS, then treat by type.
  • Closed os + viable intrauterine pregnancy: threatened miscarriage
  • Open os, products retained: inevitable or incomplete
  • Closed os, nonviable pregnancy on scan, often few symptoms: missed
  • Empty uterus + positive hCG: suspect ectopic, add serial beta-hCG
  • Cervical motion tenderness: think ectopic
exam_pearl: Cervical motion tenderness in early pregnancy means ectopic until TVUS proves otherwise.

stem: A 20-year-old primigravida in her first trimester is a heavy smoker. You advise her about the risks of smoking during pregnancy, but she refuses to quit. What is the most appropriate next step?
OptC: Join her to a smoking cessation support group
why_right: She is a 20-year-old adult who has been counselled and refuses to quit. In pregnancy, behavioural support is the first-line cessation intervention, and offering referral to a cessation support group keeps her engaged and builds motivation without coercion or breaching confidentiality.
why_wrong_block:
A. Informing her father breaches the confidentiality of a competent adult; family can be involved only with her consent.
B. Informing her mother is the same breach of confidentiality; her age makes her the decision maker.
D. NRT in pregnancy is considered only when she wants to quit and behavioural support alone has failed; drugs are pointless for someone not ready to stop.
key_concept:
Smoking in pregnancy: advise, support, then medicate if needed.
  • Risks: low birth weight and IUGR, miscarriage, preterm birth, abruption, stillbirth, SIDS
  • First line in pregnancy: counselling and behavioural support
  • Not ready to quit: motivational support, keep the door open
  • NRT: if behavioural support fails and she wants to quit
  • Varenicline and bupropion: generally avoided in pregnancy
  • Outside pregnancy: varenicline or combination NRT first line, bupropion an alternative
exam_pearl: An adult patient's refusal never justifies calling her parents; offer support and keep counselling.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant recall (Q:): 'She has not thought about quitting.' Same options; C. Join her to a smoking cessation support group highlighted.

stem: A 32-year-old patient became pregnant through in-vitro fertilization. She is now 7 weeks pregnant and is scheduled for laparoscopic surgical excision of an ectopic pregnancy (see report). Ultrasound: Presence of a right-sided 4-cm ectopic pregnancy. Which of the following is the most appropriate procedure?
OptC: Excision of both right and left tubes
why_right: This recall's key is right-sided salpingotomy alone: the aim is to remove the right ectopic while conserving tubal tissue in an IVF patient who wants a future pregnancy. Surgery itself is correct because a 4 cm mass fails the methotrexate size criterion (<4 cm). Note that the same scenario with a left hydrosalpinx on the report is keyed elsewhere to excision of both tubes; see the concern below.
why_wrong_block:
B. Hysterectomy is never the procedure for a tubal ectopic in a woman seeking fertility; it is reserved for uncontrollable uterine haemorrhage (e.g. cornual or scar rupture) when nothing else works.
C. Removing both tubes is justified only when the report shows a left hydrosalpinx, because hydrosalpinx fluid refluxes into the uterus and lowers IVF implantation; the recall's key chose tubal conservation instead.
D. Methotrexate needs a stable patient, hCG ≤5000, no cardiac activity and a mass <4 cm; a 4 cm ectopic fails the size rule, and an intraoperative injection is not a substitute for removing it.
key_concept:
Ectopic ≥4 cm or unstable: surgery; small, stable, criteria met: methotrexate.
  • MTX criteria: stable, hCG ≤5000, no fetal heart, mass <4 cm, reliable follow-up
  • Salpingectomy: usual surgical choice when the other tube is healthy
  • Salpingotomy: considered to preserve fertility, needs hCG follow-up for persistent trophoblast
  • IVF patient + hydrosalpinx: remove the hydrosalpinx to improve implantation
exam_pearl: Read the report: a left hydrosalpinx in an IVF patient flips the answer to excising both tubes.

stem: A 30-year-old primigravida presents to the Emergency Room complaining of vaginal spotting for the last few days, her history reveals irregularity of the menstrual cycles and that she has been trying to conceive for the last 3 years. Abdominal examination reveals tenderness in the lower abdomen and the pelvic examination reveals a closed cervical Os with cervical motion tenderness (see lab results). Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, Heart rate 105/min, Temperature 36.6 °C, Weight 60 kg, Height 160 cm. Hb 130 g/L; HCT 0.38; MCH 19; MCHC 330; MCV 85; Platelets 155; WBC 4.6. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
OptA: Perform an abdominal ultrasound of the pelvis
OptC: Know about the reason of infertility
why_right: A woman of reproductive age with spotting, irregular cycles, lower abdominal tenderness, cervical motion tenderness and a heart rate of 105 could have an ectopic pregnancy. Before any imaging or treatment, the first step is to confirm whether she is pregnant with a β-hCG; the result then directs the ultrasound and management.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ultrasound comes after β-hCG, which tells you what to look for (and transvaginal, not abdominal, is preferred in early pregnancy); it would be first only once pregnancy is already confirmed.
C. The cause of her 3 year infertility is an elective outpatient work-up; it is irrelevant until an acute ectopic or other emergency is excluded.
D. Analgesia treats the symptom, not the cause; it is supportive and would never replace establishing pregnancy status first.
key_concept:
Any woman of reproductive age with pelvic pain or bleeding: β-hCG first.
  • β-hCG positive → transvaginal ultrasound for location
  • No intrauterine sac with hCG above the discriminatory level → suspect ectopic
  • Unstable + positive hCG → surgery after resuscitation
  • CMT also fits PID, which is considered once pregnancy is excluded
exam_pearl: Infertility history and IVF are ectopic risk factors; they raise, not lower, the need to check hCG first.

stem: A primigravida at 38 weeks gestation presented with irregular contractions. Upon assessment she had 4 cm cervical dilation, -2 station, intact membranes, and normal CTG. Three hours later there was no change and she was still having mild irregular contractions. What is the appropriate management?
OptC: Ask her to come later when she is in active labor
why_right: She has mild irregular contractions, 4 cm with -2 station, intact membranes and a normal CTG, and no change after 3 hours. That is the latent phase (or prodromal labor), not active labor, and the latent phase can normally last many hours. With mother and fetus well, there is nothing to correct, so she can be sent home and asked to return when contractions become regular and painful.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oxytocin augmentation is for the active phase when contractions are inadequate and the cervix has not changed for about 6 hours; it is not used to speed up a normal latent phase.
B. Amniotomy is an augmentation step in established labor; with the head high at -2 and no active labor, it risks cord prolapse and commits her to delivery without an indication.
key_concept:
Latent phase with reassuring mother and fetus: reassure and send home; augment only in the active phase.
  • Latent phase: up to 4 to <6 cm; may last up to about 20 h in a nullipara
  • Active phase: >4 to 6 cm with regular contractions
  • Active phase, adequate contractions, no change 4 h → C-section
  • Active phase, inadequate contractions, no change 6 h → oxytocin, then C-section if it fails
  • Ruptured membranes at term not in labor → induction
exam_pearl: Prolonged latent phase is not a labor arrest; arrest rules apply only once she is in the active phase.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q:): Women in labor 1 cm dilated with irregular contraction evaluated for 3 hours with no progression. A. Amniotomy, B. Send her home and come back if ready (not by word but something like that) [highlighted], C. Induction of labor.

stem: A female pregnant at 23 weeks gestation came to antenatal clinic all previous pregnancy uncomplicated, her mother have T2DM and she is asking about GDM screening?
OptB: Random blood sugar at this visit
OptC: 75g oral glucose tolerance test at 28-32 weeks
why_right: She is 23 weeks, has a first-degree relative with T2DM and no previous GDM, so she needs routine GDM testing in the usual third-trimester window rather than anything today. The one-step diagnostic test is the 75 g, 2-hour OGTT, which is what this option offers.
why_wrong_block:
A. HbA1c is not used to diagnose GDM; it is used to detect pre-existing diabetes early in pregnancy or to judge control in known diabetics.
B. A random glucose is neither a screening nor a diagnostic test for GDM in an asymptomatic woman; it would only matter if she had symptoms of overt hyperglycaemia.
D. The 3-hour 100 g test is the second (diagnostic) step of the two-step approach, done only after an abnormal 1-hour 50 g challenge; it is not the first test offered.
key_concept:
GDM testing: 24 to 28 weeks; early testing if previous GDM.
  • One-step: 2-hour 75 g OGTT
  • Two-step: 1-hour 50 g challenge → if positive, 3-hour 100 g OGTT
  • HbA1c: not diagnostic for GDM
  • Diagnosed GDM: diet and exercise first, insulin if targets not met
exam_pearl: The standard window is 24 to 28 weeks; the 28 to 32 in the option is likely how it was recalled, so pick by the test type (75 g OGTT).

stem: 60 female has post menopausal bleeding for 8 months what confirm diagnosis
why_right: A 60-year-old with post-menopausal bleeding for 8 months has endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. Only tissue confirms the diagnosis, and that tissue comes from the endometrium, so endometrial biopsy is the confirmatory test (AUB over 45 → endometrial sampling).
why_wrong_block:
A. Cervical biopsy is for a visible cervical lesion or an abnormal Pap/colposcopy (postcoital bleeding points to the cervix); it does not sample the endometrium.
C. A vaginal (speculum) exam is part of the initial assessment to find the bleeding source, but it gives no tissue and cannot confirm a diagnosis.
key_concept:
Endometrial sampling rules:
  • AUB at age >45 → endometrial biopsy
  • Post-menopausal bleeding + endometrial thickness >5 mm → biopsy
  • Asymptomatic post-menopausal + thickness ≥11 mm → biopsy
  • <45 with unopposed estrogen (PCOS, obesity) or failed medical therapy → biopsy
  • MRI and CA-125 are not diagnostic; MRI is for staging
exam_pearl: "Confirm diagnosis" = tissue; ultrasound triages but never confirms endometrial cancer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Same question shown twice. Numbered 727: '70 or 80 female has post menopausal bleeding for 8 months. I dont remember if next step or most appropriate or highest diagnostic?' A. cervical biopsy / B. endometrial biopsy (highlighted). The 'Q:' version adds C. Vaginal exam and also highlights endometrial biopsy.

stem: 22 years old female coming for annual care. She is has no complaint, married for 2 years, on OCP, have depression on fluoxetine, no family history of cancer or cardiac disease. What screening should be done at this time?
why_right: She is 22, asymptomatic, and here for annual care. Cervical cancer screening starts at 21, with Pap cytology every 3 years from 21 to 29, so a Pap smear is the screening due now. Her OCP use, fluoxetine and negative family history do not change this.
why_wrong_block:
B. Mammography is not a screening test at 22 in an average-risk woman; routine screening starts at 40, earlier only with high genetic or family risk.
C. The option text was not recalled; whatever it was, Pap cytology is the screening test indicated at this age.
D. Pelvic ultrasound is not a screening test in asymptomatic women; it is used to investigate symptoms or an abnormal exam.
key_concept:
Cervical screening schedule:
  • Starts at 21, regardless of sexual history
  • 21 to 29: Pap cytology every 3 years
  • 30 to 65: co-test every 5 years or Pap alone every 3 years
  • >65 with adequate negative screening: stop
exam_pearl: Age, not marriage or sexual activity, starts cervical screening.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q:): female recently married, she is 23-24 (anyway more than 21), otherwise normal, what is screening or health promotion now: A. Pap smear [highlighted], B. Mammo.

stem: A 20-year-old divorced woman came for a Pap test. When is it recommended?
why_right: She is 20. Cervical screening begins at 21 regardless of sexual history, marriage or divorce, so a screening Pap is not recommended now but is due in about one year when she turns 21.
why_wrong_block:
A. Screening under 21 is not recommended even if sexually active, because cervical changes at this age usually regress and treatment causes harm; she would be screened now only if she were already 21 or older.
C. Three years is the repeat interval after a normal Pap between 21 and 29, not the time to the first screen.
D. Symptoms (postcoital bleeding, discharge) call for a diagnostic exam at any age; screening does not wait for symptoms.
key_concept:
First Pap at 21, then every 3 years until 29.
  • <21: no screening, whatever the sexual history
  • 21 to 29: cytology every 3 years
  • 30 to 65: co-test every 5 years or cytology every 3 years
exam_pearl: At 20 the answer is "wait until 21", which this recall phrases as "after 1 year".

stem: A 30-year-old married, nulligravid woman with symptomatic multiple uterine fibroids, all subserosal, underwent myomectomy. According to her operative note, the endometrial cavity was entered during surgery. What is the risk of placenta accreta during future pregnancies?
why_right: This recall's key is "Not affected", presumably reasoning that the fibroids were "all subserosal" and the patient is "nulligravid" with no cesarean scar. However, the stem stresses that the "endometrial cavity was entered", and standard teaching holds that any uterine surgery breaching the endometrium damages the endometrial and myometrial interface and raises placenta accreta risk. Learn the key, but be ready for exams keyed to "Increase".
why_wrong_block:
A. Increase is the answer most standard sources favour, because cavity entry at myomectomy leaves an endometrial scar like a cesarean; it is not the key on this recall.
B. Decrease is never correct: uterine scarring can only raise accreta risk or leave it unchanged.
C. Unknown is wrong because the association between prior uterine surgery and accreta is well established.
key_concept:
Placenta accreta spectrum: placenta invades because the decidua is deficient at a scar.
  • Strongest risk: previous cesarean section(s), especially with placenta previa
  • Other scars: myomectomy entering the cavity, curettage, Asherman syndrome
  • Subserosal myomectomy without cavity entry: little effect on the endometrium
  • Accreta (attached to myometrium), increta (into myometrium), percreta (through serosa)
exam_pearl: The clue "endometrial cavity was entered" is what makes the standard answer Increase; the key here says Not affected.

stem: A 39-year-old G8 P5126 at 38 weeks' gestation presents for induction of labor due to decreased fetal movement. She is started on oxytocin and begins having contractions. After several hours of labor, her cervix dilates to 6 cm, but she then develops a fever and fetal tachycardia. A diagnosis of chorioamnionitis is entertained. She delivers a baby boy vaginally 4 hours later, but afterward, there is a large continuous vaginal bleeding. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her bleeding?
why_right: Large continuous bleeding after delivery is PPH, and atony is the commonest cause. This woman also stacks atony risk factors: grand multiparity (G8), prolonged oxytocin exposure, and chorioamnionitis, all of which impair myometrial contraction.
why_wrong_block:
B. Placenta accreta presents with failure of placental separation and bleeding during attempted removal; usually linked to prior cesarean with previa, which is not described.
C. Cervical laceration follows instrumental or precipitous delivery and bleeds despite a firm uterus; nothing here suggests it.
D. Vaginal laceration likewise needs trauma clues (instrumental delivery, macrosomia, visible tear); none are given.
key_concept:
Uterine atony risk factors:
  • Overdistension: twins, polyhydramnios, macrosomia
  • Grand multiparity
  • Prolonged or augmented labor, prolonged oxytocin
  • Chorioamnionitis
  • Tocolytics (MgSO4) or general anesthesia
exam_pearl: Oxytocin exposure + chorioamnionitis + grand multipara = atony.

stem: A 30-year-old woman had a spontaneous vaginal delivery for a term twin pregnancy 2 hours ago. Now she has active vaginal bleeding. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her bleeding?
why_right: Active bleeding 2 hours after delivery is primary PPH, and atony is the commonest cause. A twin pregnancy overdistends the uterus, which then contracts poorly after delivery, making atony even more likely.
why_wrong_block:
B. Coagulopathy is an uncommon cause and nothing (abruption, preeclampsia, DIC, bleeding history) suggests it.
C. Genital tract trauma is the second commonest cause; it needs clues such as instrumental delivery, a visible tear, or bleeding with a firm uterus.
D. Retained tissue is less common and no incomplete placenta is described.
key_concept:
PPH is atony until proven otherwise.
  • Primary PPH: within 24 hours of delivery
  • Secondary PPH: 24 hours to 12 weeks
  • Overdistension (twins, polyhydramnios, macrosomia) predisposes to atony
  • First step: check tone, massage, oxytocin
exam_pearl: Twins = overdistended uterus = atony.

stem: A 38-year-old woman, known for low-lying placenta, delivered a normal vaginal delivery. One hour post-delivery, she had postpartum hemorrhage. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: PPH one hour after a normal vaginal delivery is most likely due to uterine atony, the commonest cause of PPH. The low-lying placenta does not change this; if anything, the placenta implanted on the poorly contractile lower segment makes placental-bed bleeding more likely.
why_wrong_block:
A. Coagulopathy is uncommon and nothing in the stem suggests a clotting problem.
C. Uterine inversion is rare, occurs at placental delivery (often with cord traction on a fundal placenta), and presents with shock, a vaginal mass and an absent fundus.
D. Genital tract trauma is the second commonest cause; no instrumental delivery, laceration or firm uterus is described.
key_concept:
PPH cause by clue:
  • No specific clue: atony
  • Firm uterus or visible tear: trauma
  • Mass in vagina, absent fundus, shock: inversion
  • Oozing from all sites, DIC trigger: coagulopathy
  • Low-lying placenta: lower segment contracts poorly, still atony/placental bed
exam_pearl: Do not let 'low-lying placenta' distract you: atony remains the answer.

stem: A 24-year-old woman just delivered her first baby with a birth weight of 2.7 kg while she was at 38 weeks of gestation. She is not known to have any medical or surgical history. She has a heavy gush of bleeding postpartum. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: not known to have any medical or surgical history
why_right: A "heavy gush of bleeding postpartum" is postpartum hemorrhage, and uterine atony is by far its most common cause. With no history pointing to a bleeding disorder, no traumatic or instrumental delivery, and no incomplete placenta described, the default answer is atony: PPH is atony until proven otherwise.
why_wrong_block:
B. Cervical injury is the next most common cause, suspected when bleeding continues despite a FIRM, well contracted uterus or after instrumental or precipitous delivery; none of that is described here.
C. Coagulation defects would be suspected with a known bleeding disorder, abruption, severe preeclampsia/HELLP, sepsis or massive transfusion; she has no medical history.
D. Retained placental fragments are suspected when the placenta is incomplete on inspection or bleeding is delayed/secondary; no incomplete placenta is mentioned.
key_concept:
PPH causes, the 4 Ts (most to least common):
  • Tone: atony, soft boggy uterus, most common
  • Trauma: cervical/vaginal laceration, uterus firm
  • Tissue: retained placenta or fragments, incomplete placenta
  • Thrombin: coagulopathy
  • First step: check uterine tone, then massage and uterotonics
exam_pearl: If the stem says the uterus is FIRM and contracted, atony is out; think genital tract laceration next.

stem: A 24-year-old woman primigravida undergoes an uneventful vaginal delivery at term. After placental delivery, she has 1000 cc of vaginal bleeding. She is alert, and her vital signs are stable, with the uterus noted to be firm. Which of the following is the most common cause?
why_right: Bleeding of 1000 mL after placental delivery is postpartum hemorrhage.
