  • CXR: diagnosis (consolidation) and complications
  • ABG: severity and type 2 respiratory failure in COPD
  • Cultures: organism, for admitted or severe cases
  • CBC/CRP: supportive, non-specific
exam_pearl: "Initial investigation" to diagnose = CXR; "assess severity / need for ventilation" in COPD = ABG.

stem: A female on warfarin presents with bloody stool, is pale, hypotensive, and has cool extremities. Her lab results show: Hb = 6 g/dL; PT and PTT prolonged; BP = 90/65. What is the initial step in fluid management?
why_right: This recall's key is PCC because the patient is on warfarin with a major bleed (bloody stool, hypotension, cool extremities) and prolonged PT/PTT. Warfarin with active bleeding requires urgent reversal with IV vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate (or FFP if PCC is unavailable); PCC works fastest and in a small volume, so the source treats correcting the coagulopathy as the first step to stop ongoing loss.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ringer's lactate is a crystalloid for initial volume resuscitation; it restores volume but does not reverse the warfarin coagulopathy driving the bleed.
C. Normal saline is the first resuscitation fluid in an unstable GI bleed without coagulopathy (e.g. NSAID ulcer); here bleeding continues until warfarin is reversed.
D. Packed RBCs will also be needed (Hb 6 with shock) and replace oxygen-carrying capacity, but they do not reverse the warfarin effect that keeps her bleeding; this recall puts reversal first.
key_concept:
Warfarin + bleeding: admit, IV vitamin K + PCC (or FFP).
  • Bleeding on warfarin: IV vitamin K plus PCC (preferred) or FFP
  • No bleeding, INR above 10: hold warfarin, oral vitamin K
  • No bleeding, INR 4 to 10: hold warfarin, consider low-dose oral vitamin K
  • Unstable GI bleed: crystalloid resuscitation
  • Transfuse RBCs if Hb below 7 (below 8 with cardiac disease)
exam_pearl: Same shocked GI bleeder NOT on anticoagulants with Hb above 7 = normal saline; on warfarin = reverse with PCC + vitamin K.

stem: 76-year-old man, known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and dyslipidemia, presented to the clinic with exertional shortness of breath for 1 year. He has to slow down his walk and stop after 10 meters. He denied any history of syncope, chest pain, or palpitation. Precordium examination revealed a forceful apex beat and a crescendo- decrescendo ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotid. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: crescendo- decrescendo ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotid
why_right: A crescendo-decrescendo ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotid is the signature of aortic stenosis. The forceful (heaving) apex reflects concentric LVH from pressure overload, and the age (76) with diabetes, hypertension and dyslipidemia fits calcific degenerative AS. Exertional dyspnea is one of the classic AS symptoms (with angina and syncope), signalling severe disease.
why_wrong_block:
A. Mitral stenosis gives a mid-diastolic rumble with an opening snap at the apex, not a systolic murmur radiating to the carotids.
C. Pulmonary stenosis is an ejection systolic murmur at the left 2nd intercostal space that increases with inspiration and does not radiate to the carotids; it is usually congenital in younger patients.
D. Aortic regurgitation is an early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal edge with a collapsing pulse, not a systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur.
key_concept:
Ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids = aortic stenosis.
  • Elderly with atherosclerotic risk factors → calcific AS; young → bicuspid valve
  • Signs: slow-rising pulse, heaving apex, soft S2
  • Symptoms: exertional dyspnea, angina, syncope (severe disease)
  • Diagnosis: transthoracic echocardiography
  • Symptomatic severe AS → valve replacement
exam_pearl: Systolic + carotid radiation = AS; if the systolic murmur rises on standing/Valsalva and falls with handgrip, think HOCM instead.

stem: A 25 years old male presented with progressive SOB and wheezing. On auscultation: wheezy chest, no crackles. History of previous hospitalization and intubation last year. Was given systemic steroids but no benefit which of the following is the most appropriate rescue (something like that) drug
highlight_terms_source: History of previous hospitalization and intubation
key_concept:
Acute severe asthma ladder: O2 → SABA → SAMA → systemic steroid → reassess/ICU → IV MgSO4 → intubation.
  • SABA: best bronchodilator
  • Systemic steroid: needed, but slow, not the rescue
  • IV MgSO4: refractory attack
  • Deteriorating after MgSO4: intubate
  • Previous intubation = high-risk, ICU
exam_pearl: "Given steroids but no benefit" + "rescue" points to the step after steroids (IV MgSO4); "already given MgSO4, still worse" = intubation.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Middle age pt with migraine headaches Ask about medication What medication is used for acute attacks ??
key_concept:
Headache: acute vs prophylaxis.
  • Migraine acute: mild/moderate NSAIDs, moderate/severe triptan
  • Migraine prophylaxis: beta blocker (propranolol)
  • Cluster acute: 100% oxygen; prophylaxis verapamil
  • Tension acute: NSAIDs; prophylaxis amitriptyline
exam_pearl: Triptans are contraindicated in ischemic heart disease or uncontrolled hypertension; then use NSAIDs.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 22 year old woman presented to the clinic with 2 months history of polyarthralgia, skin rash, mucosal ulcers and Fatigue. Her clinical examinations revealed malar rash over her face and active arthritis at several joints. Hb 100 (120-160 g/L female); Platelets count 100 (150-400) ×109/L; WBC 3 (4.5-10.5 ×109/L); ESR 35 (2-10 mm/h female); Lupus anticoagulant positive; Urea 5 (2.75-7.4 mmol/L); Creatinine 78 (44-115 umol/L); C-reactive peptide 5 (<8.2 mg/L); Complement C3 0.3 (0.7-1.5 g/L); Complement C4 0.13 (0.15-0.45 g/L). Which of the following test obtained at this visit is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
why_right: This recall's key is ANA. The young woman has a classic SLE picture: malar rash, mucosal ulcers, arthritis, pancytopenia, low C3/C4 and a positive lupus anticoagulant. ANA is positive in nearly all SLE patients, so it is the test used to establish the autoimmune basis; a negative ANA practically excludes SLE.
why_wrong_block:
A. Anti-Ro (SSA) is linked to Sjögren syndrome, subacute cutaneous lupus and neonatal lupus/congenital heart block; it is not the test that confirms systemic lupus.
C. Anti-dsDNA is highly specific for SLE and tracks disease activity and nephritis, but it is negative in a sizeable share of patients, so it cannot exclude lupus; this recall keys the sensitive test, ANA.
D. Anti-RNP confirms mixed connective tissue disease (SLE features overlapping with myositis, Raynaud, scleroderma); there is no myositis or overlap here.
key_concept:
SLE antibodies: ANA most sensitive, anti-Sm and anti-dsDNA most specific.
  • ANA: most sensitive, screening; negative ANA practically excludes SLE
  • Anti-Sm: most specific
  • Anti-dsDNA: specific, activity and nephritis
  • Low C3/C4: activity, nephritis
  • Anti-histone: drug-induced lupus
  • Anti-Ro/La: neonatal lupus, Sjögren
exam_pearl: "Most sensitive / screening" = ANA; "most specific" = anti-Sm (then anti-dsDNA); SLE plus myositis overlap = anti-RNP.

stem: abdominal pain after meals no medical surgical or family history Next step in investigation:
key_concept:
Dyspepsia: age and red flags decide.
  • Young, no red flags: H. pylori test and treat
  • Red flags or older age at onset: urgent endoscopy
  • Barium study: dysphagia or EGD not possible
  • CT: complications, pancreatic or mesenteric causes
exam_pearl: Anemia or isolated high urea with normal creatinine (GI bleed) turns the same dyspepsia stem into endoscopy.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: male elderly with diabetes, on follow up not adhere to medx bc he is not believing in medx what to do?
OptA: explain diabetes and lifestyle by simple visual diagrams
key_concept:
Non-adherence from disbelief: explore beliefs, explain simply, build trust.
  • Use lay language, no jargon
  • Visual aids help low literacy and older patients
  • Written material only reinforces verbal teaching
  • Shared decision making improves compliance
exam_pearl: The answer that spends time with the patient (explain, check understanding, gain trust) usually beats a passive handout.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Pt Newly dignosed with diabetes mellitus, Hb1C 7.9. His BMI 34. What is the first line for him?
why_right: A newly diagnosed type 2 diabetic with HbA1c 7.9 and BMI 34 starts lifestyle modification plus metformin. Metformin is first-line: effective, weight-neutral, no hypoglycemia, cheap. An HbA1c between 7.5 and 10% at diagnosis justifies starting it with lifestyle advice rather than lifestyle alone.
why_wrong_block:
A. DPP-4 inhibitors are weight-neutral add-on agents (or used when metformin is not tolerated or eGFR is low); they are not first line.
B. Liraglutide (GLP-1 agonist) is an injectable add-on, favoured with established cardiovascular disease or when weight loss is a priority after metformin; it is not first-line monotherapy.
D. Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycemia and weight gain, a poor choice in an obese patient; they are second-line add-ons.
key_concept:
New T2DM: lifestyle + metformin.
  • HbA1c below 7.5%: lifestyle first
  • 7.5 to 10%: lifestyle plus metformin
  • Above 10% or symptomatic catabolic: insulin
  • Stop metformin if eGFR below 30
  • ASCVD/HF/CKD: add GLP-1 agonist or SGLT2 inhibitor
exam_pearl: Gestational diabetes = diet first; hospitalized patient = insulin, not oral agents.

stem: 28-year-old woman, not known to have any medical illness, complains of increased sleepiness, fatigue and does not drink alcohol. Examination reveals an overweight patient, not in distress, with no lymphadenopathy or masses (see lab results). high tsh, low t4 (dont remember numbers) +ve anti tpo. HBsag -ve. Anti hbs +ve. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Sleepiness, fatigue, overweight in a young woman with high TSH, low T4 is primary hypothyroidism, and positive anti-TPO confirms autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis, the commonest cause in iodine-sufficient areas. HBsAg negative with anti-HBs positive just means hepatitis B immunity, a distractor.
why_wrong_block:
A. Graves' disease causes hyperthyroidism (low TSH, high T4, TSH-receptor antibodies), not hypothyroid symptoms.
B. Subacute thyroiditis presents with a painful tender thyroid and transient thyrotoxicosis after a viral illness, with high ESR; not a painless hypothyroid picture.
C. Sick euthyroid syndrome needs an acute non-thyroidal illness (ICU, sepsis) and shows low T3 with normal or low TSH; this woman has no illness and a high TSH.
key_concept:
High TSH + low T4 + anti-TPO = Hashimoto.
  • Hashimoto: hypothyroid, anti-TPO, painless
  • Graves: low TSH, TRAb, diffuse uptake
  • Subacute: painful, high ESR, low uptake
  • Sick euthyroid: low T3, acute illness
exam_pearl: Anti-TPO can also be positive early in Hashimoto with a transient hyperthyroid phase; the high TSH here settles it.

stem: An elderly patient presents with chest pain, shortness of breath, and hypotension. On examination, there is a systolic murmur radiating to the axilla. ECG shows ST elevation in leads V2–V4, and troponin is markedly elevated. What is the most likely cause of hypotension?
highlight_terms_source: systolic murmur radiating to the axilla
why_right: After an acute STEMI (ST elevation V2 to V4, high troponin), a new systolic murmur radiating to the axilla with hypotension means acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle dysfunction or rupture. The question asks for the cause of hypotension, and the murmur identifies the mechanism: sudden regurgitant volume drops forward cardiac output and floods the lungs.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cardiogenic shock describes the hemodynamic state, not its cause; the axillary-radiating murmur names the specific mechanism (acute MR).
B. Pulmonary embolism gives sudden dyspnea and hypotension with right heart strain (S1Q3T3, RBBB), not anterior ST elevation and an MR murmur.
C. Drug-induced hypotension (nitrates, morphine, beta blockers) is possible after MI but would not produce a new murmur radiating to the axilla.
key_concept:
Post-MI new murmur + shock: find the mechanism.
  • Apical pansystolic to axilla + pulmonary edema: papillary muscle rupture/acute MR
  • Harsh parasternal systolic + thrill, step-up in O2: VSD
  • Hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds: free wall rupture/tamponade
  • Papillary rupture typically 2 to 7 days, more with inferior MI
exam_pearl: Murmur to axilla = MR; loud harsh murmur at left sternal border with thrill = ventricular septal rupture.

stem: 42 Y. O women taking chemotherapy for breast cancer, come in flu season and ask for vaccines due her weak immunity. What vaccine to give and which type
OptD: Avoid all vaccine untill complete chemotherapy
key_concept:
Immunosuppressed patient: inactivated vaccines YES, live vaccines NO.
  • Inactivated (killed) influenza injection: safe, cannot cause flu
  • Live attenuated: intranasal flu, MMR, varicella, zoster live, yellow fever: avoid
  • Live vaccines deferred until immune recovery (e.g., at least 1 month off high dose steroids)
  • Response to vaccine may be reduced during chemo, but benefit still outweighs risk
exam_pearl: Immunocompromised does not mean no vaccines; it means no LIVE vaccines.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 22-year-old man presents with altered sensorium for the last 2 days and headaches for 5 days, with a history of fever for the preceding month. On examination, there is nuchal rigidity (see lab results). Hb 100 (130-170 g/L); WBC 11 (4.5-10.5 x 10^9/L); Glucose, fasting 7.22 (3.5-6.5 mmol/L). Cerebrospinal Fluid: Appearance turbid (clear); Cells 240 (0-3 /uL); Total protein 3.6 (0.22-0.33 g/L); Glucose 2.7 (2.50-3.89 mmol/L); Neutrophils 23%; Lymphocytes 73%. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: history of fever for the preceding month
why_right: A month of fever before meningitis signs points to a subacute cause, classically TB. The CSF shows lymphocyte predominance (73%) with very high protein (3.6 g/L) and glucose 2.7 that is low relative to serum glucose 7.22 (ratio below 0.5). Lymphocytes plus low glucose plus high protein in a subacute course = tubercular meningitis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Septicemia: does not explain nuchal rigidity with a lymphocytic, high protein CSF; it would be right for systemic sepsis without CSF meningitis findings.
C. Pyogenic (bacterial) meningitis: acute (hours to days) with neutrophil predominant CSF and very low glucose; here the course is a month and lymphocytes dominate.
D. Viral meningoencephalitis: acute course with lymphocytes but normal glucose and only mildly raised protein; not a month of fever with protein this high.
key_concept:
Read CSF by cell type + glucose (compare with serum).
  • Neutrophils + low glucose: bacterial
  • Lymphocytes + low glucose + high protein: TB (or fungal)
  • Lymphocytes + normal glucose: viral
  • CSF/serum glucose ratio below 0.5 = low
exam_pearl: A 'normal' CSF glucose number can still be low if the serum glucose is high; always calculate the ratio.

stem: pt symptomatic came to er, pic provided with heart block, what to do to diagnose (not sure tho)?
why_right: In a symptomatic patient in the ER with a new heart block, an ischemic cause (especially inferior MI involving the right coronary artery, which supplies the AV node) must be excluded. Invasive coronary angiography is the definitive test to diagnose coronary occlusion and allows treatment in the same sitting, so the recall keys it as the diagnostic step.
why_wrong_block:
A. Myocardial perfusion scan: a non-invasive test for stable patients with suspected chronic ischemia; not appropriate for an acutely symptomatic ER patient.
B. Coronary CT angiogram: suits low to intermediate risk stable chest pain to rule out CAD; it cannot treat a lesion and is less suitable in an unstable patient with conduction disease.
D. Chest X-ray: gives no information on coronary anatomy or the cause of the block; useful only for complications such as pulmonary edema.
key_concept:
Heart block on ECG: recognise degree, stabilise, then find the cause.
  • 1st degree: long PR, no dropped beats
  • 2nd degree: some P waves not followed by QRS
  • 3rd degree: P and QRS independent (AV dissociation)
  • Unstable bradycardia: atropine, then pacing
  • Suspected ischemic cause (inferior MI/RCA): coronary angiography
exam_pearl: The recall itself is uncertain: if the question asks for treatment of unstable complete heart block, the answer shifts to atropine/pacing, not a diagnostic test.

stem: male in his 50s, smoker complaining of cough with clear mucus and breathlessness. This attack lasted for 3-4 days and similar attacks 1 year ago. Chest x ray hyperinflation (not sure what else). Diagnosis?
key_concept:
How to decide in a smoker with recurrent cough and breathlessness:
  • Chronic bronchitis: productive cough at least 3 months in 2 consecutive years
  • Emphysema: barrel chest, hyperresonance, air trapping/hyperinflation
  • Bronchiectasis: large volumes of purulent sputum, clubbing, HRCT tram tracks
  • Cancer: hemoptysis, weight loss, mass or collapse on X-ray
  • PE: sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, hypoxia, often clear X-ray
  • Spirometry is the diagnostic test for COPD
exam_pearl: Large volumes of purulent sputum with clubbing point to bronchiectasis rather than chronic bronchitis.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A patient presents with signs & symptoms of meningitis. Lumbar puncture findings are as follows: CSF glucose: 3.5mmol/L, CSF protein: 500 mg/L (reference range: 100–400 mg/L), Predominant lymphocytes. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for the specific causative organism?
why_right: The CSF shows predominant lymphocytes, normal glucose (3.5 mmol/L) and only mildly raised protein (500 mg/L), which is a viral pattern. When the LP result is given, treat according to it: the treatable viral cause to cover is herpes simplex, so IV acyclovir is the specific therapy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ceftriaxone and vancomycin: the bacterial meningitis regimen, right with neutrophil predominant CSF, low glucose and high protein; not a lymphocytic CSF with normal glucose.
B. IV methylprednisolone: steroids (dexamethasone) are an adjunct in bacterial meningitis, and high dose methylprednisolone is for relapses of demyelinating disease; neither treats a viral organism.
C. Antifungal therapy: right for cryptococcal meningitis, typically in immunocompromised (HIV) patients with lymphocytes and LOW glucose; no such clue here.
key_concept:
If the CSF result is given, treat the organism it points to, not the empirical cocktail.
  • Neutrophils + low glucose: ceftriaxone + vancomycin + dexamethasone
  • Lymphocytes + normal glucose: viral, IV acyclovir (HSV)
  • Lymphocytes + low glucose: TB (or fungal if immunocompromised)
  • Unknown CSF, sick patient: empirical ceftriaxone + vancomycin + dexamethasone + acyclovir
exam_pearl: Confusion, seizures or temporal lobe changes with a lymphocytic CSF = HSV encephalitis; acyclovir should never be delayed.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q: version: 22-year-old man, 4 days fever, headache, confusion, Kernig's sign, T 39, CSF cells 380, protein 0.8, glucose 3.7, 90% lymphocytes, culture pending; options Ceftriaxone+vancomycin+steroid / Ceftriaxone+vancomycin / Ceftriaxone / Acyclovir, Acyclovir highlighted. Screenshot on next page (4 year old, convulsion, decreased LOC, viral illness few days ago, clear CSF, normal protein, lymphocytosis, low glucose): A- Acyclovir (HSV encephalitis); normal protein and clear CSF favor HSV over TB; 25% of HSV cases have low CSF glucose.

stem: Patient is planning a long flight. He is concerned about developing deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Which of the following is the most appropriate preventive measure?
OptA: Keep legs elevated throughout the flight
OptC: Perform periodic leg exercises and ambulate during the flight
why_right: For a traveller on a long flight, the recommended general prevention is to keep the calf muscle pump active: periodic leg/calf exercises, walking in the aisle when possible, and staying hydrated. This reduces venous stasis, the main mechanism of travel related DVT.
why_wrong_block:
A. Keeping legs elevated throughout the flight is impractical and does not replace muscle activity; prolonged immobility in any position promotes stasis.
B. Aspirin is not recommended for travel DVT prophylaxis; in selected high risk travellers (prior VTE, recent surgery, active cancer) compression stockings or LMWH are considered instead.
key_concept:
Long haul travel DVT prevention by risk level:
  • All travellers: calf exercises, walk periodically, aisle seat, hydration, avoid tight clothing and sedatives
  • Higher risk: properly fitted below knee compression stockings
  • Very high risk: LMWH may be considered individually
  • Aspirin: not recommended for this purpose
exam_pearl: Aspirin is the tempting 'drug' option, but for travel DVT the answer is mobilisation, not antiplatelets.

stem: X-ray (image) with lower lobe involvement. What is the most likely organism?
why_right: A focal lobar (lower lobe) consolidation on X-ray is the typical pneumonia pattern, and Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of community acquired lobar pneumonia. Without other clues pointing elsewhere, the 'most likely organism' is pneumococcus.
why_wrong_block:
A. Staphylococcus aureus: suspect after influenza, in IV drug users or with cavitating/multiple lesions and abscesses; not the default for a single lobar consolidation.
B. Mycoplasma: atypical pneumonia in young people with dry cough and bilateral patchy interstitial infiltrates, not a dense lobar consolidation.
C. Legionella: suspect with severe pneumonia plus diarrhea, confusion, hyponatremia or exposure to water systems/air conditioning; the X-ray alone does not point to it.
key_concept:
Typical (lobar) vs atypical (interstitial) pneumonia:
  • Typical: productive cough, fever, lobar consolidation; most common S. pneumoniae
  • Atypical: dry cough, bilateral interstitial infiltrates; Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, viruses
  • Post influenza or cavitation: S. aureus
  • GI symptoms, hyponatremia: Legionella
  • Foul sputum, aspiration risk: anaerobes
exam_pearl: Bilateral interstitial pattern with dry cough switches the answer from pneumococcus to Mycoplasma.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recall mentions an X-ray image (not shown on page).

stem: A patient presented with green sputum and fever. The chest X-ray shows consolidation. What is the most likely cause?
key_concept:
Pick the organism from the extra clue, otherwise pneumococcus.
  • No special clue: Streptococcus pneumoniae
  • Water exposure, GI symptoms, hyponatremia: Legionella
  • Young, dry cough, bilateral infiltrates: Mycoplasma
  • Post influenza, cavitation: Staph aureus
exam_pearl: Sputum colour does not identify the organism; look for an exposure or extrapulmonary clue (water systems, diarrhea, hyponatremia) before moving away from pneumococcus.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Patient has mycoplasma infection with low Hb.
why_right: Mycoplasma can cause immune mediated hemolysis (cold agglutinins), explaining the low Hb. This recall's key is corticosteroids on the reasoning that the anemia is autoimmune, so immunosuppression is chosen over doing nothing.
why_wrong_block: A. Reassurance is the source's distractor on the basis that the hemolysis needs active treatment; it would be right for mild, transient post Mycoplasma hemolysis managed by treating the infection and keeping the patient warm.
key_concept:
Warm vs cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia:
  • Warm: IgG, Coombs IgG ± C3, spherocytes; causes autoimmune disease, lymphoma; treatment corticosteroids first line
  • Cold: IgM, Coombs C3 only, agglutination; causes Mycoplasma, EBV, lymphoproliferative; treatment keep warm, treat cause, plasmapheresis if severe
  • Mycoplasma hemolysis is usually transient
exam_pearl: Steroids treat WARM (IgG) AIHA; Mycoplasma gives COLD (IgM) agglutinin hemolysis, which responds poorly to steroids.

stem: (21 years age) present with knee pain and mild fever and systolic murmur after 3 weeks of URTI. What gives?
key_concept:
Acute rheumatic fever: Jones criteria after group A strep pharyngitis (typically 2 to 4 weeks later).
  • All patients: penicillin to eradicate strep, then secondary prophylaxis
  • Arthritis and mild carditis: aspirin (high dose NSAID)
  • Severe carditis / heart failure: corticosteroids, plus diuretics
  • Echocardiography to assess carditis
  • Prophylaxis without carditis: 5 years or to age 21, whichever is longer
  • Carditis without residual disease: 10 years or to age 21, whichever is longer
exam_pearl: Fever + migratory large joint arthritis + new murmur weeks after a sore throat = rheumatic fever: aspirin for joints, steroids only if carditis is severe, penicillin for everyone.
compiler_note:
⚠ Image audit: p317: no highlight or Answer line; option '_ ACETYLSALICYLIC ACID' is written in all caps while others are normal case, which may be an emphasis mark. Card_answer null; reviewer to decide whether caps = endorsement (would be D. Acetylsalicylic acid).
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 45-year-old man under investigation for hypertension was prescribed a drug for his lipid disorder. One week later, he returned with intense facial flushing after taking the medication. He was advised to take a full dose of aspirin three times daily instead of a low dose once daily, which completely relieved the flushing. [HDL 0.72 mmol/L (<1.03), LDL 5.30 mmol/L (<3.36), total cholesterol 6.12 mmol/L (<5.1), triglycerides 2.20 mmol/L (<2.16); ALT 35 IU/L (5-40), CK 205 IU/L (24-195)] Which drug was he prescribed?
why_right: Intense facial flushing within a week of starting a lipid drug that is relieved by aspirin is the signature of niacin (nicotinic acid). The flush is prostaglandin mediated (mainly PGD2), so a cyclooxygenase inhibitor like aspirin taken beforehand prevents it. Niacin also suits this profile: it is the most potent HDL raiser and lowers LDL and triglycerides, matching his low HDL with high LDL.
why_wrong_block:
B. Clofibrate: a fibrate whose typical effects are gallstones, myopathy (especially with statins) and GI upset, not prostaglandin flushing. Right when the question features a drug for severe hypertriglyceridemia.
C. Atorvastatin: causes myalgia/myopathy and raised transaminases, not flushing that aspirin abolishes. Right when the stem describes muscle pain or a rising CK on a lipid drug.
D. Cholestyramine: a bile acid sequestrant causing bloating, constipation, raised triglycerides and reduced absorption of other drugs and fat-soluble vitamins. Right when the side effect is GI or malabsorptive.
key_concept:
Match the lipid drug to its signature side effect.
  • Niacin: flushing (prevented by aspirin), hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia/gout, hepatotoxicity
  • Statins: myopathy, raised transaminases
  • Fibrates: gallstones, myopathy with statins
  • Bile acid sequestrants: GI upset, raised TG, reduced drug and fat-soluble vitamin absorption
  • Ezetimibe: generally well tolerated, mild diarrhea
exam_pearl: Flushing relieved by aspirin = niacin; the aspirin clue is the giveaway, not the lipid numbers.

stem: A 28-year-old patient presents with a history of 10-day of palpitations, sweating and neck discomfort. BP 110/70, HR 116, RR 18, temperature 37.7 C, SpO2 95%. Free T4 76.5 (8.5-15.2 pmol/L), TSH 0.15 (0.4-5.0), WBC 5.2, ESR 73 (2-10 mm/h). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Neck discomfort is the keyword for subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis. Combined with 10 days of thyrotoxic symptoms, low-grade fever (37.7 C), high free T4 (76.5), suppressed TSH (0.15) and a markedly raised ESR (73) with a normal WBC, the picture is an inflammatory, destructive thyroiditis rather than overproduction of hormone.
why_wrong_block:
A. Graves' disease: painless hyperthyroidism with diffuse goiter, eye signs and positive TSH receptor antibodies; ESR is normal. Right when there is a painless diffuse goiter or ophthalmopathy and high uptake on scan.
C. Hashimoto's thyroiditis: painless and usually presents with hypothyroidism (high TSH, fatigue, weight gain); it does not give a high ESR with neck pain.
D. Multinodular toxic goiter: painless hyperthyroidism in an older patient with a nodular goiter and patchy uptake; no neck pain, no raised ESR.
key_concept:
Thyrotoxicosis + painful/tender thyroid + high ESR = subacute thyroiditis.
  • Often follows an URTI; fever, malaise
  • Low TSH, high T4/T3, raised ESR
  • Radioactive iodine uptake: low (vs high in Graves)
  • Treatment: NSAIDs (steroids if severe) for pain, beta-blocker for symptoms
  • No antithyroid drugs: the problem is hormone leak, not synthesis
  • Course: hyper, then possible transient hypo, then usually normal
exam_pearl: Neck pain + thyrotoxicosis + high ESR: subacute thyroiditis, and do not reach for carbimazole.

stem: A 33-year-old man with a history of severe asthma is admitted to the Emergency Department with an asthma attack. He received high-flow oxygen and nebulized salbutamol. He is unable to complete sentences, has bilateral expiratory wheeze, and is unable to perform a peak flow reading. He was immediately given intravenous hydrocortisone and nebulized salbutamol continuously. After 10 minutes, there is no improvement, and intravenous magnesium sulfate was given. His condition continues to deteriorate (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: He has at least acute severe asthma (cannot complete sentences, too breathless to perform a peak flow) and has already received oxygen, continuous salbutamol, IV hydrocortisone and then IV magnesium sulfate, yet he "continues to deteriorate". Magnesium is the last medical step in the acute asthma ladder, so deterioration after it means securing the airway with intubation and mechanical ventilation (ICU).
why_wrong_block:
A. NIV is the rescue for hypercapnic COPD exacerbations in an alert patient; in deteriorating acute asthma it is not standard and only delays definitive airway control.
B. IV aminophylline is a senior or ICU option with a narrow therapeutic window and little added benefit; a patient deteriorating after magnesium needs ventilation, not another bronchodilator.
C. Nebulized ipratropium belongs early in the ladder alongside salbutamol; it would not rescue a patient who is still worsening after magnesium.
key_concept:
Acute severe asthma ladder (escalate when not improving):
  • Oxygen
  • Nebulized SABA (back to back if needed)
  • Add nebulized ipratropium
  • Systemic steroid (IV hydrocortisone or oral prednisolone)
  • IV magnesium sulfate, involve ICU
  • Still deteriorating: intubate and ventilate
exam_pearl: Asthma worsening after IV magnesium = intubate; COPD with hypercapnic acidosis in an alert patient = NIV.

stem: Elderly patient who recently underwent major surgery is now presenting with shortness of breath, chest pain, and has a confirmed DVT. The patient also had an ischemic stroke two months ago. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: Breathlessness and chest pain with a confirmed DVT after recent major surgery means venous thromboembolism, most likely PE. The key is the bleeding profile: recent major surgery plus an ischemic stroke two months ago is read by this question as a contraindication to anticoagulation and an absolute bar to fibrinolysis (stroke within 3 months). When DVT/PE coexists with a contraindication to anticoagulation, an IVC filter is placed to stop further emboli reaching the lungs.
why_wrong_block:
A. Start warfarin: warfarin is never started alone in acute VTE (slow onset and an early prothrombotic phase) and needs heparin/LMWH overlap; here anticoagulation is considered contraindicated anyway. Right as long-term therapy after LMWH in a patient who can be anticoagulated.
C. Administer fibrinolytics: reserved for massive PE with shock, and ischemic stroke within 3 months and recent major surgery are contraindications. Right when PE causes hypotension and there is no bleeding contraindication.
key_concept:
PE / DVT management by circulation and bleeding risk.
  • Stable, no contraindication: heparin or LMWH, then oral anticoagulant
  • Stable, anticoagulation contraindicated: IVC filter
  • Recurrent emboli despite adequate anticoagulation: IVC filter
  • Massive PE (shock): thrombolysis
  • Massive PE with thrombolysis contraindicated or failed: embolectomy
exam_pearl: If LMWH/heparin is offered and there is no real bleeding contraindication, it beats a filter; the filter is the answer only when the stem makes anticoagulation unsafe, as here.

stem: 26 yo man, complaining of intermittent wheezing after exercise, he mentioned he always gets wheezing after exercising, on exam diffuse bilateral wheeze. What is the appropriate management?
why_right: A young man with intermittent wheezing after exercise that he always gets, and diffuse bilateral wheeze, has exercise-induced bronchoconstriction. The inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist salbutamol is the reliever: it relaxes bronchial smooth muscle within minutes and is also taken shortly before exercise to prevent attacks. Nothing in the stem suggests a severe attack needing IV therapy.
why_wrong_block:
B. Inhaler fluticasone: an inhaled steroid controller with no immediate bronchodilator effect. Right when asthma is persistent (frequent reliever use, night waking) and needs regular controller therapy.
C. IV Mg: reserved for acute severe or life-threatening asthma not responding to nebulized bronchodilators and steroids.
D. IV steroid: systemic steroids are for moderate to severe exacerbations (oral usually suffices); not for a mild, intermittent exercise-triggered wheeze.
key_concept:
Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction: SABA (salbutamol) as reliever and before exercise.
  • Step 1 mild intermittent: SABA as needed
  • Persistent symptoms: add regular low-dose ICS (controller)
  • Uncontrolled on ICS: add LABA; never LABA alone
  • Acute severe attack: oxygen, nebulized SABA, ipratropium, systemic steroid, then IV Mg if poor response
  • Current GINA discourages SABA-only treatment for ongoing asthma; frequent symptoms warrant an ICS-containing regimen
exam_pearl: Wheeze triggered by exercise = salbutamol before exercise; IV magnesium and IV steroids belong to the severe attack, not this one.

stem: A 30-40 man getting blood transfusion in the ER and minutes after he got skin rash and facial flushes. How to prevent this?
OptD: Matching the recipient with the donor ethnicity
why_right: Skin rash and facial flushing starting minutes after a transfusion is a mild allergic (urticarial) reaction to donor plasma proteins, mediated by histamine release. For a patient who has had such reactions, pre-medication with an antihistamine before future transfusions is the preventive step this recall keys.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pushing the bag quickly does nothing to prevent allergy and risks circulatory overload; a slow rate is used to prevent TACO.
C. Warming blood prevents hypothermia and arrhythmias in rapid or massive transfusion, not allergic skin reactions.
D. Donor ethnicity is irrelevant; compatibility depends on ABO/Rh and antibody screening, and these do not prevent plasma-protein allergic reactions.
key_concept:
Transfusion reactions and prevention:
  • Urticaria, flushing, itch: allergic; antihistamine (premedicate next time)
  • Anaphylaxis (IgA deficiency): washed or IgA-deficient products
  • Fever, chills (febrile non-hemolytic): leukoreduced blood, antipyretic
  • Fever, hypotension, hemoglobinuria: acute hemolytic (ABO mismatch); stop transfusion
  • Rapid or massive transfusion: blood warmer
exam_pearl: Rash only, stable vitals: pause, give antihistamine, may resume; add hypotension or wheeze and it is anaphylaxis, stop and give adrenaline.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-2477B).

stem: 35-year-old male with chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea, and weight loss. Endoscopy: blunting of villi. Diagnosis:
why_right: Chronic diarrhea, steatorrhea and weight loss describe small bowel malabsorption, and blunting of villi (villous atrophy) on duodenal biopsy is the hallmark of celiac disease. The full histology is villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytes; treatment is a lifelong gluten-free diet.
why_wrong_block:
B. Whipple's disease: also causes malabsorption, but biopsy shows PAS-positive foamy macrophages in the lamina propria, usually in a middle-aged man with arthralgia, fever and neurological signs. Right when the stem mentions PAS-positive macrophages or Tropheryma whipplei.
C. Crohn's disease: transmural inflammation with skip lesions, aphthous/deep ulcers, strictures and non-caseating granulomas, often terminal ileum with RLQ pain, fistulas or perianal disease. Villous blunting is not its defining finding.
key_concept:
Malabsorption + villous atrophy = celiac disease.
  • Screen: IgA tTG (check total IgA)
  • Confirm: duodenal biopsy on gluten (villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intraepithelial lymphocytes)
  • Associations: type 1 DM, dermatitis herpetiformis, iron deficiency
  • Treatment: gluten-free diet
  • Whipple: PAS-positive macrophages
  • Crohn: granulomas, skip lesions, transmural
exam_pearl: Blunted villi = celiac; foamy PAS-positive macrophages = Whipple; granulomas = Crohn.

stem: Question about old male with hyperlipidemia and hypertension on medication. He came with progressive abdominal distention. He had AST elevated months ago, and now he came with progressive abdominal distention. No other symptoms were mentioned. Labs, AST and ALT were high, almost 100 both. Asking what is the best next step or image.
highlight_terms_source: AST and ALT were high, almost 100 both
why_right: An older man with hyperlipidemia and hypertension (metabolic risk), persistently raised AST/ALT (around 100, a mild chronic rise) and now progressive abdominal distention is most likely developing chronic liver disease (e.g. fatty liver progressing to cirrhosis) with ascites. The lead-in asks for the next step / imaging: abdominal ultrasound is the initial test, showing liver texture and size, ascites, splenomegaly and focal lesions, cheaply and without radiation. Biopsy is the confirmatory test later, not the first step.
why_wrong_block:
A. Echo: right when ascites is suspected to be cardiac (raised JVP, edema, heart failure signs, high SAAG with high ascitic protein). The stem points to the liver via the long history of raised transaminases.
C. CT abdomen: not the first-line test; it follows ultrasound when a focal lesion needs characterizing (e.g. multiphasic CT for a nodule in a cirrhotic liver) or when ultrasound is inconclusive.
key_concept:
Suspected chronic liver disease or new ascites: ultrasound first.
  • Initial: abdominal ultrasound (liver, spleen, ascites, portal vein, focal lesions)
  • New ascites: also diagnostic paracentesis (SAAG, protein, cell count)
  • Focal lesion over 1 cm in cirrhosis: multiphasic CT or MRI
  • Confirmatory / staging: liver biopsy (or elastography for fibrosis)
  • Cardiac cause suspected (raised JVP): echocardiography
exam_pearl: "Next step" or "initial imaging" for a liver problem = ultrasound; "best/gold/confirmatory" = biopsy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler note: Initial = US; BEST/GOLD/CONFIRMATORY = BIOPSY. (No option highlighted; the note endorses ultrasound as the initial step.) A separate 'Q:' version (60-year-old female, options incl. 'Ultrasound liver and spleen' highlighted) follows as its own card.

stem: A 60-year-old female with history of HTN, DLP, DM, came with increased abdominal distention, no history of alcohol use, he reported 10 years history of high aminotransferase, upon examination she has ascites no organomegaly. What is the next step? There were labs of elevated LFTS I think 3-fold NOT in the thousands but don't remember them unfortunately. And question asked for next step.
highlight_terms_source: elevated LFTS I think 3-fold NOT in the thousands
why_right: A 60-year-old with HTN, DLP and DM, no alcohol and a 10-year history of raised aminotransferases (mild, not in the thousands) now has ascites: this is the story of metabolic fatty liver disease progressing to cirrhosis. The next step is ultrasound of the liver and spleen to look for a cirrhotic liver, splenomegaly/portal hypertension, ascites and any focal lesion. Biopsy confirms and stages later; it is not the first move.
why_wrong_block:
A. Echocardiography: right when ascites may be from right heart failure or constrictive pericarditis (raised JVP, edema, cardiac history); here the decade of abnormal liver enzymes in a metabolic patient points to the liver.
C. Ct abdomen: second line after ultrasound, mainly to characterize a focal liver lesion (multiphasic CT) or when ultrasound is inconclusive.
D. Maybe liver biopsy: the gold standard to confirm and stage chronic liver disease, but it is invasive and comes after non-invasive imaging; ascites also increases its risk.
key_concept:
Metabolic risk factors + chronic mild transaminase rise + ascites = suspect MASLD/NAFLD cirrhosis.
  • Initial: ultrasound liver and spleen
  • New ascites: diagnostic paracentesis with SAAG
  • Fibrosis: elastography or non-invasive scores
  • Focal lesion over 1 cm in cirrhosis: multiphasic CT or MRI
  • Confirmatory / gold: liver biopsy
exam_pearl: Initial = ultrasound, gold = biopsy: read the lead-in verb before choosing.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Unnumbered 'Q:' variant printed under 1277. Compiler note for the block: Initial = US; BEST/GOLD/CONFIRMATORY = BIOPSY.

stem: 50 years old man in the clinic with stressful job and high sodium diet and no physical activity bp: high (i guess it was 150/90? Im not sure) Sodium:high
OptB: ask him to monitor his bp and follow up
OptC: lifestyle changes (was more specific like less sodium and more activity)
OptD: tell him his bp is okay and nothing to worry about
highlight_terms_source: stressful job and high sodium diet and no physical activity
why_right: A 50-year-old with a high sodium diet, no physical activity and a stressful job has a mildly raised clinic BP (about 150/90, grade 1 range in ESC/WHO terms) with no organ damage, diabetes or cardiovascular disease mentioned. The first step is lifestyle modification targeted at his risk factors: salt restriction, regular aerobic exercise, weight control and stress reduction, with repeat measurements to confirm sustained hypertension before drugs are considered.
why_wrong_block:
A. Prescribed anti hypertensive immediately: right when BP is markedly high (grade 2 or more, e.g. ≥160/100), or with target organ damage, diabetes, CKD or established cardiovascular disease, or when lifestyle measures have failed.
B. Ask him to monitor his bp and follow up: confirming the reading is reasonable, but it misses the modifiable causes clearly planted in the stem; monitoring without advice is incomplete management.
D. Tell him his bp is okay and nothing to worry about: false reassurance; a BP around 150/90 is raised and needs action and follow up.
key_concept:
Mild hypertension, low risk: lifestyle first, then reassess.
  • Lifestyle: less salt, aerobic exercise, weight loss, DASH-style diet, limit alcohol, stop smoking
  • Confirm with repeated clinic, home or ambulatory readings
  • Drugs now: grade 2+ BP, organ damage, diabetes, CKD or high CV risk
  • Drugs later: lifestyle fails over a few months
  • Note: ACC/AHA calls ≥140/90 stage 2 and pairs lifestyle with a drug; ESC/NICE allow lifestyle first in low risk grade 1
exam_pearl: When the stem lists salt, inactivity and stress with mildly raised BP, the exam wants lifestyle change; drugs first only if BP is very high or there is organ damage or high risk.

stem: Pt came with cough and frothy pink sputum BP 80/40 HR 125 O2 (I think low) I think the question is asking what is true regarding the condition
why_right: Cough with frothy pink sputum means acute pulmonary edema, and with BP 80/40, HR 125 and hypoxia this is cardiogenic shock from a failing left ventricle. The body compensates for the low cardiac output with sympathetic vasoconstriction, so systemic vascular resistance rises (cold, clammy peripheries). An increased SVR is therefore the true statement.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cardiac output is decreased in cardiogenic shock (the pump has failed). A high cardiac output is the pattern of distributive shock such as sepsis (warm peripheries, low SVR).
C. Central venous pressure is normal or raised in cardiogenic shock because blood backs up behind the failing heart. A low CVP fits hypovolemic or distributive shock.
D. PCWP is raised in cardiogenic shock; that high left sided filling pressure is exactly what pushes fluid into the alveoli and causes pink frothy sputum. Low PCWP is seen in hypovolemic, septic and neurogenic shock.
key_concept:
Shock hemodynamics: identify the type, then predict CO, PCWP and SVR.
  • Cardiogenic: CO low, PCWP HIGH, SVR high
  • Hypovolemic: CO low, PCWP low, SVR high
  • Septic: CO HIGH, PCWP low, SVR low
  • Neurogenic: CO low, HR LOW (bradycardia), SVR low
  • High PCWP points to cardiogenic; high CO points to distributive (septic) shock
exam_pearl: Pink frothy sputum + hypotension = cardiogenic shock: low CO, high PCWP, high SVR.

stem: 59 have fever chills copd , dm , we give fluid bolus and bp still low
highlight_terms_source: we give fluid bolus and bp still low
why_right: Fever and chills in a 59 year old with COPD and DM who stays hypotensive after a fluid bolus is fluid refractory septic shock. Once adequate fluid has failed to restore pressure, the next step is a vasopressor to keep MAP at 65 mmHg or above, and norepinephrine is the first line vasopressor in septic shock.
why_wrong_block:
A. Dobutamine is an inotrope for low cardiac output states (cardiogenic shock, or septic shock with myocardial dysfunction despite pressors). It can vasodilate and drop BP further, so it is not the first agent for distributive hypotension.
B. Hydrocortisone is added only for refractory septic shock that persists despite adequate fluids AND ongoing vasopressor therapy. It is not given before a vasopressor.
D. More fluid is right if the initial resuscitation volume has not yet been given and the patient is still fluid responsive. Here the stem says BP is still low after fluids, which is the trigger to start a vasopressor rather than keep loading (risk of pulmonary edema).
key_concept:
Septic shock ladder:
  • Step 1: crystalloid resuscitation + cultures + early antibiotics
  • Step 2: still hypotensive after fluids → norepinephrine (target MAP ≥ 65)
  • Step 3: rising pressor needs → add vasopressin
  • Step 4: refractory shock on pressors → hydrocortisone
  • Low cardiac output despite pressors → add dobutamine
exam_pearl: No fluids yet → fluids; fluids given and BP still low → norepinephrine.

stem: janduice and 2 Liver lesion in the right lobe what is the disease that is risk factor for this condition
highlight_terms_source: 2 Liver lesion in the right lobe
why_right: Jaundice with two right lobe liver lesions (classically in a nodular cirrhotic liver) is hepatocellular carcinoma until proven otherwise. The question asks for the risk factor, and chronic hepatitis B is the most common and strongest cause of HCC worldwide and in Saudi Arabia; it can cause HCC even without cirrhosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Aflatoxin (Aspergillus contaminated grain) is a real HCC carcinogen and acts synergistically with HBV, but it is far less common than hepatitis B as the driving cause. It would be the answer only if the stem stressed moldy stored grain exposure.
B. Lead is not a recognised risk factor for HCC. Lead poisoning causes anemia with basophilic stippling, neuropathy and abdominal colic.
C. Wilson disease causes cirrhosis, but its HCC risk is low compared with viral hepatitis. Think Wilson in a young patient with liver disease, neuropsychiatric signs and Kayser Fleischer rings.
key_concept:
Liver mass in a cirrhotic liver = HCC; know the causes in order of importance.
  • Hepatitis B: most common cause, can cause HCC without cirrhosis
  • Hepatitis C, alcohol, NASH: via cirrhosis
  • Hemochromatosis: high HCC risk among metabolic causes
  • Aflatoxin: environmental carcinogen, synergistic with HBV
  • Diagnosis: multiphase (triphasic) CT/MRI ± AFP
exam_pearl: 'Strongest/most common risk factor for HCC' = hepatitis B, not aflatoxin or Wilson.

stem: Pt treat his rheumatoid arthritis with methotrexate and have mouth ulcer and rigor what is the cause
why_right: The stem links the symptoms to the drug: a patient on methotrexate who develops mouth ulcers (mucositis) and rigors (infection). Methotrexate is a folate antagonist that causes bone marrow suppression and mucosal toxicity, so neutropenia with a febrile infection is the explanation. Management is to stop methotrexate, check a CBC, treat as febrile neutropenia and give folinic acid (leucovorin) rescue.
why_wrong_block: A. Felty syndrome also causes neutropenia with infections, but it needs long standing seropositive RA with splenomegaly (SANTA: splenomegaly, anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, arthritis). Nothing here points to it, while mouth ulcers in a patient taking methotrexate point to drug toxicity.
key_concept:
Neutropenia in an RA patient: drug toxicity vs Felty.
  • Methotrexate: mucositis/mouth ulcers, cytopenias, hepatotoxicity, pneumonitis
  • Toxicity worsens with renal impairment, folate deficiency, trimethoprim co prescription
  • Prevention: weekly dosing + folic acid; overdose/toxicity: folinic acid
  • Felty: long standing seropositive RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia
  • Other options a student may weigh: septic arthritis, opportunistic infection on immunosuppression
exam_pearl: Mouth ulcers + fever on methotrexate = marrow toxicity; Felty needs splenomegaly.

stem: women with MVP and sever MR without endocarditis , want dentist procedure what to give?
key_concept:
IE prophylaxis = high risk heart + high risk (dental) procedure.
  • High risk: prosthetic valve/material, prior IE, cyanotic or incompletely repaired CHD, transplant valvulopathy
  • NOT indicated: MVP with MR, acquired valve disease, bicuspid valve, ASD, HCM, rheumatic fever without prosthesis
  • Drug of choice: oral amoxicillin before the procedure (penicillin allergy: alternative such as azithromycin/clarithromycin or doxycycline)
  • Metronidazole is not an IE prophylaxis drug
exam_pearl: Severity of MR does not change the rule: native MVP/MR alone never earns prophylaxis.
compiler_note:
⚠ Image audit: Page 328 printed Q1302 is 'Miatral valve prolapse and regurge and he want to do dentist procedure and no hx of endocarditis what to give for prophylaxis for endocarditis' with options 'Amoxicillin 2m before and 12 after surgery' / 'Metronidazole 500 before and after 6 hours of surgery' and NO mark. Card was built from the appended 'Q:' variant (MVP + severe MR, options no need to prophylaxis / amoxicillin, A highlighted), which is internally consistent. Decide whether card should represent primary or variant.
Compiler note: Typed version (unmarked): Miatral valve prolapse and regurge, wants dentist procedure, no hx of endocarditis, what to give for endocarditis prophylaxis? Options: Amoxicillin 2m before and 12 after surgery; Metronidazole 500 before and after 6 hours of surgery. The 'Q:' restatement highlights 'no need to prophylaxis'.

stem: A 69-year-old man complains of shortness of breath and weight loss for the last 6 months. He has a 40-pack-year smoking history and no TB or HIV risk factors (see reports). Chest X-ray: A large left-sided pleural effusion. Thoracentesis: 1,500 mL of bloody fluid that is strongly exudative by Light's criteria. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: A 69-year-old, 40 pack-year smoker with 6 months of weight loss and a large bloody exudative effusion most likely has lung cancer (or pleural malignancy). The next step is contrast CT of the chest to show the underlying mass, nodes and pleural thickening and to plan an image-guided biopsy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Empirical antibiotics suit a parapneumonic effusion with fever, cough and raised inflammatory markers, not a bloody effusion with months of weight loss.
C. Blind pleural biopsy has low yield; when malignancy is suspected, biopsy should be CT-guided or thoracoscopic after CT has mapped the pleura.
key_concept:
Pleural effusion work-up:
  • Step 1: diagnostic thoracentesis, apply Light's criteria
  • Transudate: treat the cause (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic)
  • Exudate unexplained: contrast CT chest
  • Suspected malignancy: CT-guided pleural biopsy or thoracoscopy
  • Bloody effusion: malignancy, trauma, PE, TB
exam_pearl: Smoker + weight loss + bloody exudate = malignancy until proven otherwise; image before you biopsy.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0674).

stem: A 69-year-old man complains of shortness of breath and weight loss for the last 6 months. He has a 40-pack-year smoking history and no TB or HIV risk factors (see reports). Chest X-ray: A large left-sided pleural effusion. Thoracentesis: 1,500 mL of bloody fluid that is strongly exudative by Light's criteria. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: A 69 year old, 40 pack year smoker with 6 months of weight loss and a large bloody, strongly exudative effusion has malignancy (lung cancer or mesothelioma) until proven otherwise. After the tap has been done, contrast CT chest is the next step: it shows the underlying mass, pleural thickening or nodules and lymph nodes, and maps the best target for a guided biopsy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Empirical antibiotics fit a parapneumonic effusion or empyema (fever, acute illness, purulent or low pH fluid). Six months of weight loss with a bloody effusion is not an infection picture.
C. Tissue is eventually needed, but a pleural biopsy should be image guided (CT guided or thoracoscopic) and planned after the CT; a blind biopsy before imaging has a lower yield.
key_concept:
Exudative effusion work up order:
  • Diagnostic thoracentesis: Light's criteria, cytology, culture, cell count
  • Suspected malignancy → contrast CT chest (ideally before draining the fluid fully)
  • Then tissue: CT guided or thoracoscopic pleural biopsy, or biopsy of the primary
  • Bloody effusion: malignancy, PE, trauma, TB
exam_pearl: Smoker + weight loss + bloody exudate → CT chest with contrast before any biopsy.

stem: 2 years old male presented in annual checkup with start to have abnormal fasting glucose result and high blood preesure readings (No numbers just like this) . His BMI is 31 classifying him as obese with history of significant smoking and frequent fast food eating with sedentary lifestyle. LDL:4.03 Total cholesterol: 7.04 What is initial step in managing the patient ?
OptA: Focus in weight loss to reduce BMI.
OptB: Start antihypertensive medication and lipid lowering agent
OptC: smoking cessation , exercise , reduce weight and follow up him
why_right: This young man has a cluster of modifiable risk factors: impaired fasting glucose, high BP readings (not yet confirmed or staged), BMI 31, significant smoking, fast food and a sedentary lifestyle, with raised cholesterol. The lead in asks for the initial step, which is comprehensive lifestyle change addressing every factor (stop smoking, exercise, diet and weight loss) with follow up to recheck BP, glucose and lipids before deciding on drugs.
why_wrong_block:
A. Weight loss is part of the plan but only one item; it ignores smoking, a major modifiable cardiovascular risk factor in this patient. The best answer is the one covering all his risks.
B. Drugs come later: the BP has not been confirmed by repeated readings, and in a young patient without diabetes or established cardiovascular disease an LDL of 4.03 mmol/L is below the very high threshold (4.9 mmol/L, 190 mg/dL) that mandates a statin regardless of risk. Drugs would be right if lifestyle change fails or risk is high on reassessment.
D. Reassurance is wrong because he has several cardiovascular risk factors and prediabetes that need active intervention now; reassurance fits only a fully normal check up.
key_concept:
Metabolic risk cluster on screening: lifestyle first, then reassess.
  • Stop smoking, exercise, diet, weight loss
  • Confirm hypertension on repeated readings before labelling or treating
  • Stage 1 HTN without target organ damage → lifestyle first, drugs if no response
  • Statin regardless of risk: LDL ≥ 4.9 mmol/L (190 mg/dL), diabetes age 40 to 75, clinical ASCVD
exam_pearl: 'Initial step' + several risk factors = the answer that bundles ALL lifestyle measures, not weight loss alone.

stem: A 61-year-old man comes to the clinic with a 2-day history of dyspnoea on exertion. He has a long standing hypertension and a 30-pack-year smoking history. Physical examination is unremarkable except for rare crackles at the bases of the lungs. Which of the following ( something like most specific most helpful in diagnosing )
highlight_terms_source: rare crackles at the bases of the lungs
why_right: A long standing hypertensive smoker with exertional dyspnea and basal crackles is suspected of left ventricular dysfunction (heart failure). BNP (or NT pro BNP) is released by stretched ventricular myocardium, so it is the most helpful blood test to detect ventricular dysfunction; a normal level makes heart failure unlikely. The same applies to the recalled variant (COPD patient with SOB, crackles and leg edema → pro BNP).
why_wrong_block:
B. CRP is a non specific inflammatory marker; it would support pneumonia or another inflammatory process, not ventricular dysfunction.
C. CK (CK MB) is a marker of myocardial injury and ischemia, used for infarction rather than for heart failure.
D. Troponin T marks myocardial necrosis and is the test for acute coronary syndrome (chest pain, ischemic ECG), not the test for ventricular dysfunction.
key_concept:
Cardiac biomarkers by question asked:
  • Ventricular dysfunction / heart failure → BNP or NT pro BNP
  • Myocardial injury / MI → troponin (CK MB older)
  • Inflammation → CRP
  • BNP also raised by: older age, renal failure, ACS, PE, cor pulmonale
  • BNP lower than expected: obesity, flash pulmonary edema, mitral stenosis/acute MR
exam_pearl: Dyspnea + crackles, 'detect LV dysfunction' → BNP; chest pain/ischemia → troponin.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q: Patient known case of COPD with SOB, crackles and lower limb oedema, most appropriate lab investigation: pro bnp.

stem: 59 years old patient came to ED with fever chils And worsening coough with yellow to greenish phlegm which started 4-5 days before the presentation Patient knows case of COPD DM OA(knee) On examination respiratory distress and crackles in all lungs felid GCS12/15 Chest x ray PA( hyperinflated lung with lower lobe infiltration and air bronchogram ) What the most appropriate next step in management ??? Bp90/50 Hr 128 Rr24 Temp 39 His MAP is 63, Wbs 18k Neutrophil 80% Hg 10.1 Cr 190 (normal up to 115) Lactic acid venous 4 (notmal up to 2) FBG very high ( sorry don't remember) CRP 190
why_right: This is severe community acquired pneumonia with sepsis induced hypoperfusion: fever, purulent sputum, lobar infiltrate with air bronchogram, BP 90/50 (MAP 63), HR 128, lactate 4, raised creatinine and GCS 12. The stem mentions no fluid given yet, so the first step to restore perfusion is IV crystalloid resuscitation; antibiotics and cultures are started in the same first hour, but the immediate threat is circulatory.
why_wrong_block:
B. A vasopressor (norepinephrine) is right when hypotension persists after adequate fluid resuscitation (septic shock). Starting it before any fluid in a volume depleted septic patient is premature.
C. Hb 10.1 is above the usual transfusion threshold of 7 g/dL in sepsis without active bleeding or acute coronary ischemia, so transfusion is not indicated.
D. Antibiotics are essential and must be given within the first hour, alongside fluids, after cultures. When the question asks for the single next step in a hypotensive, hypoperfused patient, circulation (fluids) is prioritised; antibiotics would be the answer if the patient were hemodynamically stable.
key_concept:
Sepsis first hour bundle: hypotension or lactate ≥ 4 → fluids now.
  • Measure lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics
  • Broad spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour
  • Crystalloid resuscitation for hypotension or high lactate
  • Vasopressor (norepinephrine) if MAP stays < 65 after fluids
  • Transfuse only if Hb < 7 g/dL (no bleeding or ischemia)
exam_pearl: No fluid given yet → fluids; BP still low after fluids → vasopressor (compare the norepinephrine card).
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other recalled versions (unmarked): elderly DM/OA patient with fever, chills, yellowish green phlegm, respiratory distress, GCS 12/15, Hb 10.6, hypotension (90s/60s), left lower infiltration with air bronchogram; options Vasopressor / Give antibiotic(s) / Blood transfusion / Fluid resuscitation. Also: 55y with 5 day SOB, pneumonia, BP 90/70, HR 123, SpO2 95 on 3L, Temp 38; options Vasopressor / IV Fluid / ABx / Antipyretics.

stem: COPD AND HAVE ACIDOSIS WHAT IS THE INITIAL INVESTIGATION
why_right: A COPD patient with acidosis (respiratory acidosis already shown on the blood gas) is having an acute exacerbation with ventilatory failure. The initial investigation is a chest X-ray to find the trigger or complication that changes management: pneumonia, pneumothorax, pulmonary edema or effusion. It is quick, bedside and done in every admitted exacerbation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Contrast CT is not an initial test in COPD exacerbation; CT pulmonary angiography is reserved for suspected PE after initial assessment, and it delays care in an acidotic patient.
C. CBC is part of routine admission bloods (white count, polycythemia, anemia) but it is supportive and does not identify the precipitant the way a chest X-ray does.
D. Sputum culture is sent when sputum is purulent or the patient is admitted, to guide antibiotics, but results are delayed and it is not the initial investigation.
key_concept:
Acute COPD exacerbation work up:
  • ABG: defines respiratory acidosis and need for NIV
  • Chest X-ray: pneumonia, pneumothorax, edema, effusion
  • ECG, CBC, electrolytes; sputum culture if purulent
  • pH < 7.35 with high PaCO2 despite treatment → NIV (BiPAP)
  • CT only for specific questions (e.g. suspected PE)
exam_pearl: Acidosis already known → next/initial investigation is the CXR to find the trigger.

stem: 40 years old famle came to follow up clinic , she was in good health 2 years old when examined Past medical hx of Rheumatic fever 15 years ago she smokes 10 cigarettes for 15 years On current examination she have good heart rhythm and blowing Diastolic decrescendo murmur at aortic area BP 154/56 HR 68 What the most appropriate advice for future preventive health maintenance ?
OptD: prophylaxis Abx before the dental procedure
highlight_terms_source: blowing Diastolic decrescendo murmur at aortic area
why_right: The "blowing diastolic decrescendo murmur at the aortic area" with a wide pulse pressure (BP 154/56) after "rheumatic fever 15 years ago" points to rheumatic aortic regurgitation. A newly heard valvular murmur must first be characterised by transthoracic echo, which shows severity, LV size and EF, and decides surveillance or surgery timing. Every later preventive decision for this valve depends on that echo, so it is the key step here.
why_wrong_block:
A. An annual chest X ray is not a screening or surveillance tool for valve disease or for smokers; it cannot grade the regurgitation or LV function. Lung cancer screening, when indicated, uses low dose CT in older heavy smokers.
B. Colorectal screening is not the issue raised by this vignette, and an annual flexible sigmoidoscopy is not a recommended interval. It would be right only for a colorectal screening question at screening age.
D. Native valve disease from rheumatic heart disease without prior endocarditis is not an indication for dental antibiotic prophylaxis under current guidance. It is reserved for prosthetic valves, previous infective endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease and cardiac transplant valvulopathy.
key_concept:
New murmur = transthoracic echo first.
  • Diastolic decrescendo murmur at aortic area + wide pulse pressure = aortic regurgitation.
  • TTE: first test for a murmur; TEE gives better detail when needed.
  • Asymptomatic valve disease: follow up and medical treatment; symptomatic or low EF: surgery.
  • Dental prophylaxis: prosthetic valve, prior IE, selected congenital disease only.
  • Rheumatic carditis with residual valve disease: secondary prophylaxis for 10 years after last attack or until age 40, whichever is longer.
exam_pearl: Rheumatic valve disease alone does not earn dental prophylaxis; prosthetic valve or prior endocarditis does.

stem: 28-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 2-week history of bloody diarrhea, lower abdominal cramps, and tenesmus. Physical examination reveals abdominal distension with mild tenderness (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to establish the diagnosis?
why_right: A 28 year old with 2 weeks of bloody diarrhea, cramps and tenesmus has a subacute colitis picture typical of ulcerative colitis (tenesmus reflects rectal involvement). The lead in asks for the investigation that establishes the diagnosis: colonoscopy with biopsy shows continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum and gives histology to confirm UC.
why_wrong_block:
B. CT shows bowel wall thickening and complications (perforation, toxic megacolon, abscess) but cannot confirm mucosal disease or give histology.
C. C. difficile toxin testing is for diarrhea after antibiotics or hospitalization (or a flare in known IBD); no such exposure is given here, and it does not diagnose UC.
D. Stool culture is done to exclude infective colitis, but a negative culture only rules out infection; it does not establish the diagnosis.
key_concept:
Suspected IBD: stool studies exclude infection, colonoscopy with biopsy confirms.
  • UC: continuous from rectum, bloody diarrhea, tenesmus, mucosal disease
  • Crohn: skip lesions, transmural, terminal ileum, fistulas
  • CT: complications or severe disease
  • Severe colitis or suspected toxic megacolon: avoid full colonoscopy, use flexible sigmoidoscopy and X-ray or CT
exam_pearl: If the stem adds fever, tachycardia and marked colonic dilatation (toxic megacolon), full colonoscopy becomes dangerous; none of these is described here.

stem: A 22-year-old man presented to the Emergency Room with left leg swelling and pain that started 2 days ago and is getting worse. It involves the whole left leg. He also complains of chest tightness and shortness of breath. Examination reveals left lower limb pitting edema extending to the thigh (see report). ECG: Sinus tachycardia. Which of the following is the most appropriate management at this time?
highlight_terms_source: chest tightness and shortness of breath
why_right: Whole left leg swelling to the thigh is a proximal DVT, and new chest tightness, dyspnea and sinus tachycardia indicate it has embolized (PE). In a stable patient the immediate step is parenteral anticoagulation; LMWH is first line, and when it is not offered, unfractionated heparin is the correct choice "at this time".
why_wrong_block:
A. Aspirin: an antiplatelet; it has no role in treating venous thromboembolism, which is fibrin rich clot needing anticoagulation.
B. Clopidogrel: also an antiplatelet, used for arterial disease (ACS, stents, stroke), not DVT or PE.
C. Warfarin: used for longer term anticoagulation and must overlap with heparin; started alone it is slow and briefly prothrombotic.
key_concept:
VTE management ladder:
  • Stable DVT or PE: LMWH first line (or DOAC); UFH if LMWH not offered or renal failure or possible thrombolysis
  • Warfarin: start with heparin overlap until INR therapeutic
  • Unstable (hypotension) PE: thrombolysis
  • Anticoagulation contraindicated: IVC filter
exam_pearl: "At this time" asks for the acute agent: heparin, never warfarin alone and never an antiplatelet.

stem: 71-year-old man is evaluated after a recent hospitalization 10 days ago for pneumonia and was discharged with a 10-day course of appropriate antibiotics. For the past 5 days, he has had a low-grade fever and increased shortness of breath. Pulmonary examination reveals decreased fremitus, dullness to percussion, and decreased breath sounds over the lower third of the right hemithorax (see lab results and report). Chest radiograph: Moderate right-sided pleural effusion. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: recent hospitalization 10 days ago for pneumonia
why_right: He was "hospitalized 10 days ago for pneumonia" and now has "low-grade fever and increased shortness of breath" with a moderate effusion, so this is hospital acquired infection complicated by a parapneumonic effusion or empyema. Piperacillin-tazobactam covers Pseudomonas and other hospital organisms, and the infected fluid must be drained for source control.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ceftriaxone + azithromycin is a community acquired pneumonia regimen, and it leaves the infected effusion undrained. Right for a fresh CAP admission without recent hospitalisation.
B. Drainage is correct, but levofloxacin alone is a weaker choice: it gives unreliable anaerobic cover for an infected effusion or empyema, and he has just finished an antibiotic course, so resistance is likely. Piperacillin-tazobactam covers Pseudomonas, gram negatives and anaerobes in one agent.
C. Watchful waiting is unsafe with fever, worsening breathlessness and a moderate effusion suggesting a complicated parapneumonic effusion. A repeat film is for a resolving, asymptomatic simple effusion.
key_concept:
Post-hospital pneumonia + effusion = drain + antipseudomonal antibiotic.
  • Hospital acquired pneumonia: onset 48 to 72 hours or more after admission.
  • Cover Pseudomonas: piperacillin-tazobactam.
  • CAP regimens (ceftriaxone + azithromycin, levofloxacin) are inadequate here.
  • Infected/complicated effusion or empyema: drain (small-bore drain or chest tube).
exam_pearl: "Hospitalized recently" is the clue that turns a CAP regimen into a wrong answer.

stem: A 71-year-old man is evaluated after a recent hospitalization 10 days ago for pneumonia and was discharged with a 10-day course of appropriate antibiotics. For the past 5 days, he has had a low-grade fever and increased shortness of breath. Pulmonary examination reveals decreased fremitus, dullness to percussion, and decreased breath sounds over the lower third of the right hemithorax (see lab results and report). Chest radiograph: Moderate right-sided pleural effusion. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: recent hospitalization 10 days ago for pneumonia
why_right: Fever and dyspnea starting days after discharge from a pneumonia admission, with dullness, reduced fremitus and a "moderate right-sided pleural effusion", point to a complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema in a recently hospitalized patient. Infected pleural fluid must be drained, and a small-bore drain is adequate for most such collections. Because he was recently in hospital and already had a full antibiotic course, empiric cover must be broad (Pseudomonas, resistant gram-negatives and anaerobes), which piperacillin-tazobactam provides.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is a community-acquired pneumonia regimen; it lacks antipseudomonal cover after recent hospitalization and does not drain the infected effusion.
B. Drainage is right, but levofloxacin is a community-acquired pneumonia agent here: it lacks reliable anaerobic cover for a pleural infection after recent hospitalization and antibiotics; a large-bore chest tube is also not needed when a small-bore drain usually suffices.
C. Watchful waiting suits a small, resolving effusion in a well patient; persistent fever with a moderate effusion after pneumonia needs drainage and antibiotics now.
key_concept:
Pneumonia plus effusion that fails to settle: drain the pleural space and give antibiotics suited to where the infection was acquired.
  • New effusion with pneumonia: diagnostic thoracentesis first
  • Pus, positive Gram stain/culture, or complicated fluid: drain (small-bore tube usually enough)
  • Community-acquired: ceftriaxone plus azithromycin
  • Hospital-acquired or recent admission/antibiotics: antipseudomonal agent (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam)
exam_pearl: Recent hospital stay + fever + effusion = drain it and cover Pseudomonas; antibiotics alone or a CAP regimen are traps.

stem: Female pt k/c of COPD presented with hepatomegaly, increasing SOB, +ve shifting dullness, LL edema and raised JVP with giant 'a' wave (I am not sure but I think also there is finding in heart auscultation). What is causing these symptoms?
why_right: In a "k/c of COPD" patient, raised JVP, hepatomegaly, ascites and leg edema are systemic venous congestion, the picture of right heart failure. Chronic hypoxic lung disease causes pulmonary hypertension and then right ventricular failure (cor pulmonale). A giant a wave reflects the stiff, hypertrophied right ventricle that the right atrium must push against.
why_wrong_block:
B. Left heart failure presents with pulmonary congestion: orthopnea, PND, basal crackles, S3. It is right only when those findings dominate; here the findings are systemic congestion in a COPD patient.
C. Chronic liver disease gives ascites and edema but a normal or low JVP and stigmata of liver disease. A raised JVP with giant a wave points to the heart, not the liver.
key_concept:
COPD + raised JVP + hepatomegaly + edema = cor pulmonale (right heart failure).
  • Pulmonary hypertension sign: loud P2, parasternal heave.
  • Giant a wave: RV hypertrophy/pulmonary hypertension or tricuspid stenosis.
  • Giant v wave: tricuspid regurgitation; cannon a waves: complete heart block; absent a: AF.
  • Next step for suspected cor pulmonale: echocardiogram.
  • Raised JVP separates cardiac ascites from cirrhosis.
exam_pearl: Ascites with a RAISED JVP is cardiac; ascites with a normal JVP is liver.

stem: Case of a woman in her 30's presenting with shortness of breath and chest pain for one day. There is no cough or fever, vitally stable, labs all normal except D dimer 800 high. ECG showed peaked P wave in lead II and right deviation with right bundle branch block. What is the most helpful investigation to be done?
highlight_terms_source: shortness of breath and chest pain for one day
right deviation with right bundle branch block
why_right: Sudden "shortness of breath and chest pain" with no cough or fever, a raised D dimer, and ECG right heart strain (peaked P in II, right axis deviation, RBBB) make pulmonary embolism the working diagnosis. She is "vitally stable", so she can go to CT, and CT pulmonary angiography is the test that confirms the diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Echo shows only indirect signs (RV strain) and cannot confirm PE. It is the choice in a hemodynamically unstable patient who cannot be moved to CT.
B. A V/Q scan is used when CT contrast is contraindicated (renal impairment, contrast allergy), in pregnancy, when CTPA is inconclusive, or for chronic PE. None applies here.
D. MR angiography is not a standard first line test for PE; it is less sensitive and less available than CTPA.
key_concept:
Stable suspected PE with raised D dimer = CT pulmonary angiography.
  • D dimer: rules out PE only when negative in low probability; cannot confirm.
  • ECG: sinus tachycardia (commonest), S1Q3T3, RBBB, right axis, P pulmonale.
  • Unstable PE: bedside echo.
  • V/Q: contrast contraindicated, pregnancy, inconclusive CT, chronic PE.
exam_pearl: "Vitally stable" sends her to CTPA; hypotension would switch the answer to bedside echo.

stem: 51 yo pt, k/c of DM, HTN, renal impairment 3, compliant on his medications. Diagnosed as AF and the physician decides to give him anticoagulant, what is the best to add?
why_right: With HTN and DM he already scores at least 2 on CHA2DS2-VA, so anticoagulation is indicated, and DOACs are first line. The decisive clue is "renal impairment 3": among the DOACs apixaban depends least on renal clearance and has the most favourable bleeding and safety data in CKD, so it is the best choice.
why_wrong_block:
B. Rivaroxaban is a reasonable DOAC but is more renally cleared than apixaban and needs dose reduction in moderate CKD. Right for a patient with normal renal function who prefers once daily dosing.
C. Dabigatran is mostly renally excreted, so it accumulates and raises bleeding risk in CKD. It suits patients with good renal function.
D. Edoxaban also needs renal dose adjustment and has reduced efficacy at very high creatinine clearance. It is not the preferred agent when renal function is the issue.
key_concept:
AF anticoagulation in CKD: apixaban is the DOAC least dependent on the kidney.
  • Anticoagulate when CHA2DS2-VA is 2 or more.
  • First line: DOAC; warfarin (INR 2 to 3) for mechanical valve or moderate/severe mitral stenosis.
  • Renal dependence: dabigatran highest, apixaban lowest.
  • Severe renal failure/dialysis: warfarin is the traditional choice.
exam_pearl: Kidney in the stem = avoid dabigatran, pick apixaban.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler added a 'Q:' variant: 'Female known case of A-fib, it was decided she start anticoagulation. What is the most appropriate? a-Apixaban b-Rivaroxaban c-Edoxaban d-Dabigatran' (unmarked).

stem: 45 k/c of HTN and 20 pack smoker, BMI 28, asymptomatic, came for check up. Best prevention for patient care? BP 150/95. Labs: HDL 1.1, LDL 4.5, Cholesterol 6.5, Triglycerides 2.1.
OptD: Lifestyle modification and follow up in 3 months
why_right: He is a "k/c of HTN" whose BP is still 150/95, and he also smokes and has LDL 4.5 mmol/L, so his cardiovascular risk is high and both factors need drug treatment. Antihypertensive therapy plus a statin is the preventive step that lowers his risk, alongside smoking cessation and lifestyle advice.
why_wrong_block:
A. Stress testing is not a screening test in an asymptomatic person; it is used to investigate exertional chest pain or other ischemic symptoms.
B. Option not recalled, so it cannot be judged.
D. Lifestyle alone with review is for newly found mild hypertension in a low risk patient without other risk factors. Here he is already hypertensive, uncontrolled, a smoker and has high LDL, so delaying drugs is inadequate.
key_concept:
Multiple risk factors + uncontrolled BP + high LDL = drug therapy for both, plus lifestyle.
