Random glucose 25 (3.9-5.5 mmol/L). ABG: HCO3 10 (22-28 mmol/L), pH 7.10 (7.36-7.45). RBC 5 (4.7-6.1 x10^12/L male; 4.2-5.4 female). Hb 130 (130-170 g/L male; 120-160 female). WBC 14 (4.5-10.5 x10^9/L). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management?
why_right: Glucose 25, pH 7.10 and bicarbonate 10 with polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss in a 17-year-old is diabetic ketoacidosis from new-onset type 1 diabetes. Saline has "already been initiated" and potassium is 4.4 (not below 3.3), so the next step is IV insulin to stop ketogenesis and lower glucose, with potassium added to fluids as it falls.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV ceftriaxone: afebrile with a clear chest and normal radiograph; mild leukocytosis is common in DKA. Antibiotics are right only when an infective trigger is found.
C. IV potassium chloride: K 4.4 is normal; potassium is added to the fluids once insulin starts and K falls. Replacing potassium before insulin is needed only when K is below 3.3.
D. IV sodium bicarbonate: reserved for very severe acidosis (pH below 6.9); pH 7.10 corrects with fluids and insulin.
key_concept:
DKA order: fluids, check K, insulin, then treat the trigger.
  • Diagnosis: hyperglycemia + metabolic acidosis + ketosis
  • Step 1: 0.9% saline resuscitation
  • K below 3.3: replace potassium before insulin
  • K 3.3 or above: start IV insulin infusion (low dose, 0.1 IU/kg/hr)
  • Bicarbonate only if pH below 6.9
  • Then find the precipitant (missed insulin, infection)
exam_pearl: If the stem had K below 3.3, potassium replacement would come before insulin.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer: B (MG).

stem: A patient presents with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Laboratory results show: Blood glucose 380 mg/dl, pH 7.15, Bicarbonate 15 mEq/L. What is the most appropriate initial management?
why_right: The labs confirm DKA (glucose 380 mg/dl, pH 7.15, bicarbonate 15). The initial management is IV fluid resuscitation plus IV regular insulin infusion, after checking potassium is not low, because fluids correct the profound dehydration and fixed-rate IV insulin stops ketogenesis and closes the anion gap.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV bicarbonate is reserved for very severe acidosis (pH below 6.9); at pH 7.15 it adds no benefit and risks hypokalemia and paradoxical CNS acidosis.
B. Subcutaneous insulin is used once DKA has resolved (overlapping with the infusion before stopping it); absorption is unreliable in a dehydrated acidotic patient, so it is not the initial treatment here.
key_concept:
DKA ladder: fluids, potassium, insulin, find the trigger.
  • Fluids first: 0.9% saline bolus, then 0.45% saline
  • Check K: if below 3.3, replace before insulin
  • Regular insulin IV infusion 0.1 U/kg/hr
  • Add dextrose when glucose falls, continue insulin until acidosis resolves
  • Bicarbonate only if pH below 6.9
  • Switch to SC basal insulin with overlap once resolved
exam_pearl: If the options separate fluids from insulin, fluids alone come first; if potassium is low, potassium comes before insulin.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0693).
Compiler note: Related variant listed under 2536 (Q: block).

stem: A 50-year-old man is complaining of pain affecting the wrist joints bilaterally, second and third proximal interphalangeal joints, and right knee joint for the last 4 months. His examination revealed active arthritis at both wrists and second and third proximal interphalangeal joints (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
highlight_terms_source: wrist joints bilaterally, second and third proximal interphalangeal joints
why_right: Symmetric arthritis of both wrists and 2nd/3rd PIPs for 4 months with active arthritis on exam is new rheumatoid arthritis. This recall's key combines DMARD maintenance (methotrexate as the anchor, with hydroxychloroquine) and short-term prednisone as a bridge, because steroids control synovitis within days while DMARDs take weeks to months to work. The steroid is then tapered once the DMARDs take effect.
why_wrong_block:
A. Methotrexate: the correct anchor DMARD, but alone it gives no rapid control of active synovitis while it takes effect; in this recall the bridge is the missing piece.
B. Methotrexate and sulfasalazine: an acceptable DMARD combination, but it still lacks the steroid bridge for active arthritis.
C. Methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine: good maintenance DMARDs, but no bridging glucocorticoid for the currently active joints.
key_concept:
New active RA = DMARD (methotrexate based) for maintenance + short-term prednisone as a bridge.
  • Methotrexate is the cornerstone; hydroxychloroquine alone is not enough
  • Steroids act in days, DMARDs in weeks to months
  • Taper steroids once controlled; do not continue long term
  • Refractory or erosive disease: add a TNF inhibitor
  • Anti-CCP confirms RA; RA spares DIP joints
exam_pearl: When the stem says 'active arthritis' at diagnosis, choose the option that includes the steroid bridge.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer: D (GB). Lab results referenced but not shown.

stem: Child fell from tree, vomiting, head swelling, he became drowsy. What is the MOST APPROPRIATE management?
why_right: A child who fell from a tree, is vomiting and has "become drowsy" has a deteriorating level of consciousness after head injury. Trauma care follows ABC, so securing the airway (intubation) to protect against aspiration and hypoxia comes before any definitive neurosurgical step. The hematoma has not even been confirmed on CT yet.
why_wrong_block: A. Hematoma evacuation: needs a CT showing a surgical lesion (e.g. epidural hematoma with midline shift) and a secured airway; it becomes the answer when the stem already gives that CT and the airway is not the problem.
key_concept:
Head injury with falling consciousness: Airway first, then CT, then surgery.
  • Intubate: GCS 8 or less, unconscious, SpO2 below 88%, or aspiration risk (vomiting with drowsiness)
  • Then non-contrast CT head
  • Epidural hematoma: lens-shaped, middle meningeal artery, lucid interval
  • Surgical hematoma with mass effect: craniotomy and evacuation
exam_pearl: When the stem gives no CT and only symptoms of deterioration, the answer is the airway; when it gives CT with midline shift and a stable child, the answer is evacuation.

stem: 12/16 years old girl fall 2 meters while playing, The loss of consciousness then vomited many times and then become sleepy, in examination there is head hematoma and left limb weakness and sign of lateralization, CT brain show extra dural hematoma with midline shift. ( no GCS in the Qs) What is the best next management?
OptD: repeat the CT scan after 12 hours.
highlight_terms_source: left limb weakness and sign of lateralization
extra dural hematoma with midline shift
why_right: Fall from 2 meters, loss of consciousness, repeated vomiting, sleepiness, "left limb weakness" and lateralizing signs with CT showing an "extradural hematoma with midline shift" means a surgical lesion with mass effect. The definitive and time-critical treatment is urgent craniotomy and hematoma evacuation; midline shift over 5 mm is an accepted indication.
why_wrong_block:
B. Intubate and secure the airway: the first step when GCS is 8 or less or the airway is at risk, and it may be done on the way to theatre, but no GCS is given and the question has already reached the CT stage; the decision being tested is surgery.
C. Admit and observe: right for a small epidural hematoma without midline shift or neurological deficit in an alert patient; focal weakness and shift rule it out.
D. Repeat CT after 12 hours: right for a minor stable lesion being monitored; waiting with lateralizing signs and shift risks herniation and death.
key_concept:
Epidural hematoma: arterial bleed that needs evacuation once it causes mass effect.
  • Source: middle meningeal artery (temporal fracture)
  • CT: biconvex, lens-shaped
  • Clinical: lucid interval, ipsilateral blown pupil, contralateral weakness
  • Midline shift over 5 mm or focal deficit: craniotomy and evacuation
  • Small, no shift, alert: observe with repeat CT
exam_pearl: CT already showing shift plus lateralizing signs moves the answer from airway or observation to evacuation.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Short version: child fell from 2 meters, vomiting multiple times and sleepy, left side weakness, CT shows extradural hemorrhage; options hematoma evacuation (highlighted) vs intubate and secure the airway. Related: Hematoma with 6mm midline shift -> Craniotomy. Midline shift > 5mm -> Craniotomy.

stem: 28-year-old patient presented to the clinic complaining of perianal discharge. He reported history of on-off abdominal pain. He reported family history of Crohn's disease. On examination, three fistula openings at 3, 7 and 9 o'clock. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: A 28-year-old with "three fistula openings", recurrent abdominal pain and a family history of Crohn's has multiple, complex perianal fistulae that point to undiagnosed Crohn's disease. This recall's key is colonoscopy (with ileoscopy and biopsies) to confirm the underlying disease, because fistula management is very different in Crohn's (medical therapy, setons, avoiding fistulotomy).
why_wrong_block:
B. MRI: the gold-standard imaging to map fistula tracts and find abscesses; it is the answer when Crohn's is already known and the question asks for fistula anatomy or a suspected abscess.
C. Fistulogram: an older, less accurate way to outline a tract, largely replaced by MRI and endoanal ultrasound.
D. US: endoanal ultrasound can assess simple tracts and sphincters, but transabdominal US does not diagnose Crohn's or map complex perianal disease.
key_concept:
Multiple or recurrent perianal fistulae: think Crohn's.
  • Suspected Crohn's not yet diagnosed: colonoscopy with ileoscopy and biopsy
  • Fistula anatomy or abscess: MRI pelvis
  • Abscess: drain before escalating immunosuppression
  • Fistulizing Crohn's: anti-TNF (infliximab), setons
  • Simple low non-Crohn's fistula: fistulotomy
exam_pearl: Known Crohn's with perianal sepsis: MRI pelvis; suspected but undiagnosed Crohn's: colonoscopy.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-2100B).

stem: concerning and warrants further evaluation for possible malignancy. Which of the following types of nipple discharge is most concerning?
OptD: Spontaneous unilateral, from a single duct, and clear
why_right: Pathological nipple discharge is "spontaneous", "unilateral" and from a "single duct", and is usually serous (clear) or bloody. These three features suggest a localized ductal lesion (intraductal papilloma or carcinoma) and need imaging and evaluation whatever the colour. The other options each have a feature that makes them physiological or benign.
why_wrong_block:
A. Spontaneous and bilateral red: blood is worrying, but bilateral, multi-duct discharge suggests a systemic or diffuse benign process; unilateral single-duct bloody discharge would be the concerning version (classically intraductal papilloma).
B. Spontaneous bilateral milky: galactorrhea from prolactin excess, drugs, pregnancy or lactation; it needs a prolactin and drug review, not a malignancy work-up.
C. Induced unilateral green: discharge produced by squeezing, especially green or dark, is typical of duct ectasia or fibrocystic change and is benign.
key_concept:
Nipple discharge red flags: spontaneous, unilateral, single duct, bloody or serous.
  • Physiological: bilateral, multi-duct, expressed only, milky or green
  • Bloody single duct: intraductal papilloma most common cause
  • Green/dark with inverted nipple: duct ectasia
  • Milky bilateral: galactorrhea (check prolactin, drugs, pregnancy)
  • Pathological pattern: imaging (US with or without mammogram), then biopsy or duct excision
exam_pearl: Colour alone does not make discharge malignant; spontaneity, laterality and single-duct origin do.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Stem is truncated in the source (begins mid-sentence).

stem: child was riding a bicycle, and then he sustained a handlebar injury, he presented to the ER with abdominal pain and tenderness And Nausea & Vomiting FAST Was Done And It Was Inconclusive. What’s Most Likely Injured Abdominal Organ?
highlight_terms_source: FAST Was Done And It Was Inconclusive
why_right: A "handlebar injury" is a focused blow to the epigastrium that crushes the pancreas (and duodenum) against the vertebral column, classically in children. The pancreas is retroperitoneal, so FAST is often "inconclusive" because early free intraperitoneal fluid may be absent; CT abdomen with contrast is the test when this is suspected.
why_wrong_block:
A. Spleen: the most commonly injured solid organ in blunt abdominal trauma overall, with left upper quadrant pain and usually free fluid on FAST; the handlebar mechanism points elsewhere.
B. Liver: commonly injured in right upper quadrant blows and usually produces hemoperitoneum visible on FAST.
D. Urinary bladder: injured with pelvic fractures or a blow to a full bladder, presenting with hematuria or inability to void, not an epigastric handlebar impact.
key_concept:
Mechanism predicts organ in blunt trauma.
  • Handlebar (epigastric) blow: pancreas and duodenum
  • Retroperitoneal injury: FAST may be negative or inconclusive
  • Suspected pancreatic or duodenal injury, stable: CT abdomen with contrast
  • Lap belt: small bowel, mesentery, lumbar (Chance) fracture
  • Overall most common solid organ: spleen
exam_pearl: "Most commonly injured organ" in blunt trauma is spleen, but a handlebar mechanism with negative FAST is pancreas.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer: C. Pancreas ✅ (also highlighted; 'Soft tissue' written beside C). Handlebar injury (direct epigastric blow) causes pancreatic injury, especially in children. FAST is often inconclusive because pancreatic injuries are retroperitoneal and may not produce significant free intraperitoneal fluid early. UpToDate, ATLS (may not be detected on FAST; CT abdomen with contrast if suspected), Nelson.

stem: A diabetic patient presents with a NON-HEALING foot ulcer. The patient complains of numbness. On exam, The ulcer shows central erythema. (no mention of "with signs of healing", no mention of pulse). He's unable to perceive touch and sensation. What is the most critical test to perform to reach the diagnosis?
why_right: The stem already shows neuropathy ("numbness", "unable to perceive touch"), so the open question for a "NON-HEALING" diabetic ulcer with no pulse findings given is whether the limb has enough blood supply. Peripheral arterial disease is the main reason a diabetic ulcer fails to heal, and the ABI is the critical bedside test for it; it decides referral for revascularization and whether the wound can heal.
why_wrong_block:
B. Monofilament test: screens for loss of protective sensation; it is the answer for routine diabetic foot screening, but here the sensory loss is already evident and does not explain failure to heal.
C. Assessment of pressure points: important for offloading and preventing ulcers, but it does not diagnose the cause of a non-healing ulcer.
key_concept:
Non-healing diabetic foot ulcer: check perfusion first.
  • First step: palpate pulses, then ABI
  • ABI 0.9 to 1.4: normal; below 0.9: PAD; below 0.5: severe
  • ABI above 1.4: calcified vessels (common in diabetes), use toe pressures or Doppler
  • Absent pulse: arterial Doppler; intact pulse with dark skin: venous duplex
  • Monofilament: annual neuropathy screening
exam_pearl: In diabetics a falsely high ABI from calcified arteries can hide PAD; that is when toe pressures or Doppler are used.

stem: A 12-year-old presents with left sided lower abdominal pain. Examination confirms a slightly elevated, tender left testis with redness and edema of the scrotum. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A 12-year-old with lower abdominal pain and a slightly elevated, tender testis has testicular torsion: the twisted cord pulls the testis upward, and adolescent torsion commonly refers pain to the lower abdomen. Redness and edema of the scrotum come from venous congestion. The alternate recall adds an absent cremasteric reflex and no transillumination, which point the same way.
why_wrong_block:
B. Epididymo-orchitis has a gradual onset with fever or urinary symptoms, a preserved cremasteric reflex and pain relieved by elevation; the testis is not high riding. Think of it in a sexually active young man, or in a child with a UTI or urinary tract anomaly.
C. An incarcerated inguinal hernia is a tender, irreducible lump that extends from the scrotum up into the groin, typically in an infant; here the finding is an elevated tender testis, not a groin mass.
D. Torsion of a testicular appendage gives tenderness localized to the upper pole (blue dot sign) with a normally positioned, vertical testis; the whole testis being elevated and tender points to true torsion.
key_concept:
Acute scrotum: decide by testis position, reflex and site of tenderness.
  • Torsion: sudden, high riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex
  • Appendage torsion: upper pole tenderness, blue dot, vertical testis
  • Epididymo-orchitis: gradual, fever, dysuria, reflex present
  • Incarcerated hernia: irreducible tender lump into the groin
  • Torsion: urgent exploration, imaging must not delay surgery
exam_pearl: Vertical testis with focal upper pole tenderness flips the answer to appendage torsion; an elevated whole testis keeps it at torsion.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Alternate recall (Q:): sudden hemiscrotal pain with swelling and tenderness, cremasteric reflex absent, no transillumination (didn't mention 'high riding'): A testicular torsion (highlighted), B epididymo-orchitis, C hydrocele.

stem: Elderly women with previous laparotomy for sigmoidectomy after complicated diverticulitis, with incisional hernia symptomatic painful What is the best next step?
why_right: An incisional hernia after a previous laparotomy that is symptomatic and painful needs repair, and incisional hernias are repaired with mesh because suture repair alone has a high recurrence rate. A laparoscopic approach with mesh reinforcement gives a lower wound infection rate and faster recovery, which suits an elderly patient with a scarred abdomen.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance is only for a small asymptomatic hernia in a patient unfit or unwilling for surgery; this hernia is painful, so it should be repaired.
B. Open repair without mesh (primary suture) has an unacceptably high recurrence for incisional hernias; tissue repair is reserved for very small defects or a contaminated field where mesh is avoided.
C. Laparoscopic repair is the right approach, but without mesh it is incomplete: the laparoscopic incisional repair is by definition a mesh repair, so the option that names the mesh is the best answer.
key_concept:
Symptomatic hernia = repair; incisional hernia = mesh.
  • Laparoscopic mesh indications: bilateral, recurrent, need for fast recovery, incisional/ventral
  • Primary unilateral inguinal hernia in a fit patient: open mesh repair
  • Suture repair alone: high recurrence for incisional hernias
  • Strangulated or obstructed hernia: emergency surgery
exam_pearl: When one option says repair and another says the same repair with mesh, the mesh option wins for an incisional hernia.

stem: Old female + Weight loss & Stool +ve for occult blood + Constipation
why_right: An older woman with weight loss, change in bowel habit (constipation) and a positive fecal occult blood test has colorectal cancer until proven otherwise. A positive occult blood test always needs a full colonoscopy, which views the entire colon, allows biopsy and detects synchronous lesions.
why_wrong_block: A. Sigmoidoscopy only examines the rectum and sigmoid, so a right sided (proximal) tumor, which often presents with occult bleeding and anemia, would be missed. Even when sigmoidoscopy finds a distal cancer, a full colonoscopy is still required to look for synchronous tumors.
key_concept:
Positive FOBT or red flags (age, weight loss, bowel habit change, iron deficiency anemia) = colonoscopy.
  • Colonoscopy: whole colon, biopsy, synchronous lesions
  • Cancer found on sigmoidoscopy: next step colonoscopy, then CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for staging
  • Iron deficiency anemia in an older adult: upper and lower GI endoscopy
  • Multiple liver lesions with constitutional symptoms: colonoscopy to find the primary
exam_pearl: Occult blood plus weight loss is never followed up with a limited scope; the answer is the full colonoscopy.

stem: A patient underwent a dental procedure and subsequently develops jaundice and chills. Ultrasound reveals a 6 cm hypoechoic lesion in the liver. What is the most appropriate initial management?
highlight_terms_source: 6 cm hypoechoic lesion in the liver
why_right: A "dental procedure" followed by "jaundice and chills" and a "6-cm hypoechoic lesion in the liver" points to a pyogenic liver abscess from bacteremic seeding. An abscess of this size will not resolve on antibiotics alone, so the appropriate initial management is image guided percutaneous drainage combined with IV broad spectrum antibiotics, which also gives pus for culture.
why_wrong_block: A. Oral antibiotics are inadequate for a septic patient with a large pyogenic abscess; therapy starts IV and is combined with drainage. Antibiotics alone suit small abscesses (roughly under 3 cm) or an amoebic abscess treated with metronidazole.
key_concept:
Liver abscess: decide pyogenic vs amoebic, then size.
  • Pyogenic: biliary disease, bacteremia (dental, GI source); chills, high fever
  • Pyogenic, larger abscess: percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics
  • Pyogenic, small abscess: IV antibiotics (aspiration if needed)
  • Amoebic (travel, Entamoeba serology): metronidazole first, even if large
  • Open surgery: rupture, failed percutaneous drainage, multiloculated thick pus
  • Hydatid: albendazole, avoid blind aspiration
exam_pearl: Amoebic abscess = metronidazole first regardless of size; pyogenic large abscess = drain.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0163).

stem: A patient sustained a high-velocity trauma and is hypotensive despite receiving IV fluids. Xray shows an openbook pelvic fracture. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: A high-velocity injury with an open-book pelvic fracture and hypotension despite IV fluids means ongoing pelvic bleeding from the widened pelvic ring. The immediate step in the primary survey (circulation) is a pelvic binder over the greater trochanters: it closes the ring, reduces pelvic volume and tamponades venous and bony bleeding, while blood transfusion is started.
why_wrong_block:
B. External fixation stabilizes the pelvis more definitively but takes time and theatre resources; it follows the binder in an unstable patient, not before it.
C. Surgery (laparotomy or pre-peritoneal packing) is for persistent instability after the binder and transfusion, or for a positive abdominal source; it is not the first step for a pelvic bleed.
D. Internal fixation is definitive, delayed fixation done once the patient is resuscitated and stable; it has no place in the acute management of a hypotensive patient.
key_concept:
Unstable pelvic fracture: binder first, then control the bleeding.
  • Step 1: pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters + blood products
  • Still unstable: angioembolization (arterial bleed) or pre-peritoneal packing
  • External fixation: temporary skeletal stabilization
  • Internal fixation: definitive, once stable
exam_pearl: In a hypotensive pelvic fracture, the simplest bedside device (the binder) beats every operative option as the next step.

stem: A 60 (70) years old Male was found to have inguinal hernia incidentally on physical examination. The hernia is reducible and causes no pain but slight discomfort. What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: A reducible inguinal hernia in a 60 to 70-year-old man that causes slight discomfort is symptomatic, and the exam rule is that symptomatic inguinal hernias in fit adults are referred for elective surgical repair (open mesh repair for a primary unilateral hernia). Repair relieves symptoms and removes the risk of incarceration and strangulation; the similar recall marked referral for elective repair.
why_wrong_block:
B. Observation (watchful waiting) is mainly for a painless hernia, or for a patient who is unfit for or declines surgery; most watched hernias in older men end up needing repair, and this one already causes discomfort.
C. Increasing physical activity does not treat a hernia and may increase intra-abdominal pressure; there is no conservative exercise treatment for an inguinal hernia.
key_concept:
Inguinal hernia management by state and patient.
  • Symptomatic, reducible, fit adult: elective repair (open mesh if primary unilateral)
  • Bilateral or recurrent: laparoscopic mesh repair
  • Femoral hernia: repair even if asymptomatic (high strangulation risk)
  • Irreducible tender or obstructed: urgent or emergency surgery
  • Infant umbilical hernia: observe, most close spontaneously
exam_pearl: Even mild discomfort makes an inguinal hernia symptomatic; observation is for a painless hernia in a patient who declines or cannot have surgery.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Embedded screenshot of a similar recall (62-year-old man, reducible right inguinal hernia with mild discomfort, Australian guidelines) marks 'B. Referral to a general surgeon for elective repair' (consistent with surgical repair).

stem: 27 YO female presented to OPD with painful swelling in tip of her right thumb 2 days ago, she work as hairdresser and trimming hangnail. Examination show tense tender swelling in pulp of “Nail FOLD Is Intact” which of the following is most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A tense, tender swelling of the pulp of the thumb tip after minor trauma, with the nail fold intact, is a felon: an abscess in the closed septated compartments of the distal pulp. The key discriminator is location: pulp involvement means felon, whereas infection of the nail fold means paronychia.
why_wrong_block:
B. Paronychia is infection of the nail fold around the nail, classically after trimming a hangnail or manicure; here the stem stresses that the nail fold is intact and the swelling is in the pulp.
C. Onychomycosis is a chronic fungal infection of the nail plate causing thickening and discoloration, not an acute tense painful pulp swelling over 2 days.
D. Cellulitis is diffuse, poorly demarcated spreading redness of skin and subcutaneous tissue; a tense, localized pulp swelling is a closed space abscess, which is a felon.
key_concept:
Fingertip infections by site.
  • Felon: pulp space abscess, tense throbbing tip, needs incision and drainage
  • Paronychia: nail fold, often after hangnail or manicure
  • Herpetic whitlow: vesicles, do not incise
  • Flexor tenosynovitis: Kanavel signs, along the whole finger
  • Onychomycosis: chronic nail plate change
exam_pearl: Hangnail history tempts you to paronychia; the words 'pulp' and 'nail fold intact' make it a felon.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version: Hairdresser came to the emergency department with a swollen bulb of the thumb finger after stick injury with a tool. Same options, Felon highlighted.

stem: A Patient with Fatigue, Recurrent ureteric stones and bone pain Ca: 3.50 mmol Parathyroid adenoma: 2cm parathyroid adenoma What's Most Appropriate NEXT Step In Management?
why_right: This recall's key is bisphosphonate, read as the immediate step: a calcium of 3.50 mmol/L is markedly raised, at the threshold of severe hypercalcemia, and the acute management is to lower calcium (aggressive IV normal saline, then an IV bisphosphonate) before anything else. The compiler marked this answer with question marks and also flagged parathyroidectomy, so the key is uncertain in the source.
why_wrong_block:
B. A calcimimetic (cinacalcet) lowers PTH and calcium in patients who cannot or will not have surgery, or in parathyroid carcinoma; it is not the first choice in a surgical candidate and acts too slowly for a severe acute rise.
C. Increasing dietary calcium would worsen hypercalcemia and stone formation; it has no role here.
D. Parathyroidectomy is the definitive treatment and is clearly indicated (symptomatic disease with renal stones and bone pain, calcium markedly raised, localized adenoma); in this card it is treated as the step after calcium is controlled.
key_concept:
Primary hyperparathyroidism from an adenoma: control severe calcium, then operate.
  • Severe hypercalcemia: IV normal saline first, then IV bisphosphonate (calcitonin for rapid short-term effect)
  • Definitive: parathyroidectomy, after sestamibi localization
  • Surgery indications: any symptomatic PHPT, stones, osteoporosis or fragility fracture, age under 50, calcium well above normal
  • Unfit for surgery: cinacalcet
exam_pearl: If the question says 'definitive management' or omits a high calcium crisis, the answer flips to parathyroidectomy.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Compiler highlighted Bisphosphonate but put question marks on both A and D (uncertain).
Other marked answers: Compiler question-marked: D. Parathyroidectomy ??

stem: (Long scenario) after IV fluid how to confirm that the pt is well resuscitated?
why_right: Adequate resuscitation is shown by restored tissue perfusion, and serum lactate is the most direct marker of it: a lactate of about 2 mmol/L (normal or cleared) means oxygen delivery now meets demand. Among these options it is the only value that confirms successful resuscitation; the source also notes that CVP measures volume, while lactate measures perfusion.
why_wrong_block:
A. A CVP of 8 mmHg only estimates intravascular filling; it was an older sepsis target (early goal-directed therapy) but correlates poorly with fluid responsiveness and does not prove the tissues are perfused. The compiler suggested it for a sepsis version, but when lactate is offered, lactate is preferred.
B. A MAP of 45 mmHg is hypotension and indicates ongoing shock; the target is a MAP of at least 65 mmHg.
C. Urine output is an excellent resuscitation marker (classically the best one in burns, target at least 0.5 ml/kg/h in adults), but 0.1 ml/kg/h is severe oliguria and shows inadequate resuscitation.
key_concept:
Endpoints of resuscitation: perfusion beats pressure and volume.
  • Lactate normal or clearing (about 2 mmol/L or less)
  • MAP ≥ 65 mmHg
  • Urine output ≥ 0.5 ml/kg/h adults, ≥ 1 ml/kg/h children (best in burns)
  • Improving mental status and capillary refill
  • CVP: volume estimate only, not an endpoint
exam_pearl: In a burn question that offers an adequate urine output (such as 0.5 to 1 ml/kg/h), choose urine output; here it is 0.1, so lactate wins.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Compiler: If burn case = lactate 2; if Sepsis = CVP 8 (Central Venous Pressure = 8 mmHg). 'If burn case D. Lactate = 2 ✅': lactate reflects tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery; normal or clearing lactate (<2 mmol/L) indicates successful resuscitation, best marker among choices. CVP = volume estimate, lactate = perfusion (more important); CVP 8 is normal but does not confirm adequate resuscitation. Targets: MAP ≥ 65, UO ≥ 0.5 ml/kg/hr (0.1 = severe oliguria), improving mental status, lactate clearance. If choices include CVP vs lactate, pick lactate. Embedded burn recall (40% deep flame burn in ICU, indicator of good response) marks C. Urine output.
Other marked answers: Embedded burn recall screenshot: C. Urine output (red; D. CVP also red); Compiler, if sepsis scenario: A. CVP 8

stem: Currently presenting with jaundice, and RUQ tenderness. Her LFT and bilirubin are elevated. What is the most appropriate diagnostic imaging?
why_right: This recall's key is MRCP because the lead-in asks for the most appropriate (not the initial) diagnostic imaging: in a patient with jaundice, RUQ tenderness and raised bilirubin and LFTs, MRCP is a non-invasive, accurate way to show the whole biliary tree and detect common bile duct stones or strictures. The compiler stresses the split: initial = ultrasound, most appropriate = MRCP.
why_wrong_block:
B. Abdominal ultrasound is the INITIAL imaging for jaundice with RUQ pain (cheap, quick, shows gallstones and duct dilatation); choose it when the question says 'initial' or 'first'. Its weakness is poor views of the distal CBD.
C. CT abdomen is better for suspected malignant obstruction (pancreatic head mass), complications or staging; it misses many non-calcified CBD stones.
key_concept:
Biliary imaging ladder: read the lead-in verb.
  • Initial: abdominal ultrasound (stones, CBD dilatation)
  • Diagnostic for CBD stones/biliary anatomy: MRCP
  • Therapeutic (stone extraction, stenting): ERCP
  • Suspected malignancy or complications: CT
exam_pearl: 'Initial' or 'first' flips the answer to ultrasound; 'confirm CBD stone' or 'most appropriate' in this recall points to MRCP.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot answer: A. This question comes in multiple formulas: most appropriate INITIAL = US; most appropriate = MRCP. Compiler note: 'It is most appropriate'.

stem: 1 week ago and complaining of mild abdominal pain after the accident. O/E: Vitally stable. Mild abdominal pain mainly in the right upper quadrant. No other complaints or findings. What is the most appropriate initial step?
OptB: Refer him to emergency department for further evaluation
OptC: Do blood work to rule out hemorrhage
why_right: This recall's key is referral to the emergency department: the patient is being seen outside the ED a week after an accident with new RUQ pain ("after the accident", "mild abdominal pain mainly in the right upper quadrant"). Even though he is "vitally stable", delayed pain over the liver after trauma can reflect a contained liver injury, subcapsular hematoma or delayed bleeding, so he needs a setting that can image (CT with contrast for the stable patient), monitor serially and intervene if he deteriorates.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ultrasound (FAST) is a quick bedside screen for free fluid, mainly in unstable patients; it is operator dependent and poor at grading solid organ injury. In a stable trauma patient the definitive study is CT, and it is done as part of the ED work-up, not as an isolated outpatient test.
C. Blood work (Hb, LFTs) supports the work-up but cannot exclude or localise an injury on its own; a normal early Hb does not rule out bleeding. It would be ordered inside the ED evaluation, not instead of it.
key_concept:
Abdominal trauma work-up depends on hemodynamic status.
  • Unstable + positive FAST: laparotomy
  • Stable blunt trauma: CT abdomen with IV contrast
  • Stable penetrating RUQ wound: CT abdomen
  • Delayed RUQ pain after trauma: think liver injury or subcapsular hematoma
  • Patient seen outside the ED with a possible intra-abdominal injury: send to ED for full evaluation
exam_pearl: If "CT abdomen with contrast" is among the options for a stable trauma patient, it beats both ultrasound and referral.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Compiler: If CT with contrast in choices I will chose it. (Both A and B highlighted; B has ✅.)
Other marked answers: Compiler highlight: A. Do Abdominal ultrasound

stem: 67 year old man 6hours post femoral artery surgery developed swelling and worsening neurological signs (Stem exactly like this)
why_right: This recall's key is the decompression procedure for acute compartment syndrome: "6 hours post femoral artery surgery" with limb "swelling and worsening neurological signs" is classic reperfusion injury after revascularisation. Capillary leak raises compartment pressure, muscle and nerve become ischemic, and irreversible damage follows within hours, so the treatment is emergency release of the fascial compartments (fasciotomy).
why_wrong_block:
A. A backslab (plaster splint) immobilises a fracture; applying any cast or tight dressing to a limb with rising compartment pressure makes it worse. In suspected compartment syndrome all casts and dressings are removed, not added.
B. Traction is used to align or hold fractures (e.g. femoral shaft); it does nothing for compartment pressure and can even raise it.
D. Nerve repair is for a transected nerve. Here the nerve deficit is ischemic from pressure, and it recovers only if the compartment is decompressed promptly.
key_concept:
Post revascularisation swelling + pain + neuro deficit = compartment syndrome until proven otherwise.
  • Early sign: pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch
  • Late signs: paresthesia, paralysis, pallor; pulse may still be present
  • Diagnosis is clinical; compartment pressure measurement if unclear
  • First: remove casts and dressings, keep limb at heart level
  • Definitive: emergency fasciotomy of all involved compartments
exam_pearl: A palpable distal pulse does not exclude compartment syndrome; do not wait for pulselessness.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler: 'fasciotomy ??'. Suspect acute compartment syndrome due to reperfusion injury after vascular surgery: capillary leak increases compartment pressure; muscle and nerve ischemia cause neurologic deficits; permanent damage within 6-8 hours. Emergency fasciotomy to decompress compartments and restore perfusion. Post vascular surgery + pain/swelling + neuro deficit = compartment syndrome: Fasciotomy (cutting open the fascia to relieve pressure inside a muscle compartment; saves the limb).

stem: A patient presents with an open femur fracture with a 5-cm wound. What is the first step in management?
OptB: IV antibiotics within the first hour
why_right: An "open femur fracture with a 5-cm wound" is contaminated from the moment of injury, and the single most effective step against deep infection and osteomyelitis is early IV antibiotics. The lead in is "first step", so antibiotics within the first hour (with tetanus cover, wound photo, saline dressing and splinting) come before the trip to theatre.
why_wrong_block: A. Surgical debridement and irrigation is essential but is the next step, done urgently (within about 12 hours for high energy injuries such as an open femur, within 24 hours for others, immediately for gross contamination) after antibiotics have been started. It would be the answer if the stem says antibiotics are already given and asks for the next step.
key_concept:
Open fracture sequence: antibiotics first, then theatre.
  • 1: ATLS assessment, IV antibiotics within 1 hour, tetanus prophylaxis
  • 2: Photograph wound, cover with saline soaked dressing, splint/reduce
  • 3: Formal debridement and irrigation in theatre
  • 4: Fixation (IM nail if stable patient; external fixator for damage control or heavy contamination)
  • Any wound over a fracture, even 1 cm, = open fracture
exam_pearl: Read the lead in: "first step" = antibiotics; "antibiotics given, next step" = surgical debridement.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Another version (Q:): patient fell from a high place and developed a 5 cm thigh wound with dirt. What will you do? A. Wound clean B. Blood transfusion (no answer marked for this version).

stem: A patient undergoes a dental procedure and subsequently develops jaundice and chills. Abdominal ultrasound reveals a 6-cm hypoechoic lesion in the liver. What is the most appropriate initial management?
why_right: A "dental procedure" followed by "jaundice and chills" and a "6-cm hypoechoic lesion in the liver" points to a pyogenic liver abscess from bacteremic seeding. An abscess of this size will not resolve on antibiotics alone, so the appropriate initial management is image guided percutaneous drainage combined with IV broad spectrum antibiotics, which also gives pus for culture.
why_wrong_block: A. Oral antibiotics are inadequate for a septic patient with a large pyogenic abscess; therapy starts IV and is combined with drainage. Antibiotics alone suit small abscesses (roughly under 3 cm) or an amoebic abscess treated with metronidazole.
key_concept:
Liver abscess: decide pyogenic vs amoebic, then size.
  • Pyogenic: biliary disease, bacteremia (dental, GI source); chills, high fever
  • Pyogenic, larger abscess: percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics
  • Pyogenic, small abscess: IV antibiotics (aspiration if needed)
  • Amoebic (travel, Entamoeba serology): metronidazole first, even if large
  • Open surgery: rupture, failed percutaneous drainage, multiloculated thick pus
  • Hydatid: albendazole, avoid blind aspiration
exam_pearl: Amoebic abscess = metronidazole first regardless of size; pyogenic large abscess = drain.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0083).

stem: 70 years old male with history of dyslipidemia, on atorvastatin. He also has a history of recurrent TIA, but now he is asymptomatic. He came complaining of his last TIA symptoms. His labs are all normal except for LDL (slightly above the normal range). He did carotid US and showed narrowing 70-90%. What is your management?
why_right: This is symptomatic carotid disease: "recurrent TIA" with a fresh episode ("his last TIA symptoms") and carotid ultrasound showing "narrowing 70-90%". Symptomatic 70 to 99% stenosis in a surgical candidate is the strongest indication for carotid endarterectomy, ideally within 2 weeks of the event, because it reduces recurrent stroke far more than medical therapy alone.
why_wrong_block:
A. Surveillance ultrasound is for asymptomatic or low grade stenosis. Repeating the scan in 3 to 6 months leaves a high risk of stroke in the early weeks after a TIA untreated.
C. Intensifying statin therapy (e.g. rosuvastatin) is part of best medical therapy, which every patient gets, but it does not replace revascularisation in symptomatic high grade stenosis; he is already on a statin.
D. Unrecalled option (another version: lifestyle modification). Lifestyle change and risk factor control are always added but are not the definitive management for symptomatic 70 to 99% stenosis.
key_concept:
Carotid stenosis: symptoms + degree decide.
  • Symptomatic 70 to 99%: CEA, ideally within 2 weeks
  • Symptomatic 50 to 69%: consider CEA (patient factors)
  • Symptomatic below 50%: best medical therapy
  • Total occlusion (100%): no CEA
  • Asymptomatic: medical therapy; selected high grade cases may be considered for CEA
  • All: antiplatelet, high intensity statin, BP and diabetes control, smoking cessation
exam_pearl: "Now asymptomatic" after a TIA still means symptomatic carotid disease; do not route to surveillance.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Second version lists D as Lifestyle modification, with a check on B. This is a symptomatic high-grade carotid stenosis. AHA/ASA and UpToDate: symptomatic 70-99% stenosis = CEA strongly recommended, best within 2 weeks of TIA/stroke if surgical candidate; symptomatic 50-69% = consider CEA; <50% = medical therapy. CEA reduces future stroke risk vs medical therapy alone. A: surveillance is for asymptomatic/mild stenosis. C: already on statin, lipid therapy alone insufficient. D: lifestyle always recommended but not definitive.

stem: Diabetic patients present with an inflamed, tender right leg. On examination: skin discoloration, Fluctuance. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
why_right: In a "diabetic" patient an "inflamed, tender" leg with "skin discoloration" and "fluctuance" indicates a pus collection or a necrotizing soft tissue infection. The lead in is "immediate management", and this is a surgical emergency: surgical exploration with drainage and debridement (plus IV broad spectrum antibiotics) both confirms the diagnosis and controls the source; delaying for tests worsens outcome.
why_wrong_block:
A. CBC (and LRINEC style labs) are adjuncts sent in parallel; they never delay surgery once fluctuance and skin changes make the diagnosis clinically obvious.
C. MRI helps define deep infection or osteomyelitis when the diagnosis is uncertain and the patient is stable; it wastes hours in an obvious abscess or suspected necrotizing infection.
D. CT abdomen examines the wrong region; it is unrelated to a leg infection (CT of the limb can show gas, but still should not delay exploration).
key_concept:
Diabetic limb infection with fluctuance or skin necrosis = operate now.
  • Cellulitis without collection: IV antibiotics
  • Fluctuance: incision and drainage / exploration
  • Necrotizing fasciitis clues: pain out of proportion, rapid spread, dusky skin, bullae, crepitus, systemic toxicity
  • Necrotizing fasciitis: urgent debridement + broad spectrum IV antibiotics + ICU support
  • Imaging only if diagnosis unclear and patient stable
exam_pearl: When fluctuance or discoloration is stated, choose the knife over any scan.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Diabetic + inflamed tender leg + skin discoloration + fluctuance = abscess or necrotizing infection (especially necrotizing fasciitis); rapid progression possible. IDSA/UpToDate: fluctuance + skin changes in diabetic limb = surgical emergency; immediate I&D or surgical exploration. Imaging/labs are adjuncts, not first line in obvious cases. Nec fasc: pain out of proportion, bullae, systemic signs; Type I polymicrobial, Type II Group A Strep; diagnosis mostly clinical. Management: immediate surgical debridement, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, supportive care/ICU.

stem: Female comes for screening of breast cancer asking what type of nipple discharge should worry her?
OptD: Spontaneous unilateral single duct and clear
why_right: Pathological nipple discharge has a recognisable pattern: "spontaneous" (not expressed), "unilateral" and from a "single duct". That pattern suggests a ductal lesion such as intraductal papilloma or, less often, carcinoma and needs imaging. Serous (clear) or bloody fluid with these features is concerning; colour matters less than being spontaneous, unilateral and single duct.
why_wrong_block:
A. Bilateral discharge usually has a systemic or physiological cause; even blood stained bilateral discharge (e.g. in pregnancy) is commonly benign. It would worry you if it were unilateral from a single duct.
B. Spontaneous bilateral milky discharge is galactorrhea: think pregnancy, hyperprolactinemia, hypothyroidism or drugs, not breast cancer. Work-up is prolactin and TSH.
C. Discharge that appears only when squeezed, especially green, typically reflects duct ectasia or fibrocystic change; induced discharge is generally benign.
key_concept:
Worrying discharge = spontaneous + unilateral + single duct (+ serous or bloody, older age, mass).
  • Bloody single duct, young/middle age: intraductal papilloma most common
  • Green/black, multiple ducts, inverted nipple: duct ectasia
  • Milky bilateral: galactorrhea, check prolactin and TSH
  • Pathological pattern: mammogram + ultrasound, then core biopsy of any lesion
exam_pearl: Bilateral and induced = reassuring; a spontaneous single duct discharge is worrying even if it is clear.

stem: Hairdresser came to the emergency department with a swollen bulb of the thumb finger after getting a stick from the tools she's using, Nail bed is intact?
why_right: A swollen, tense "bulb" (pulp) of the thumb after a puncture ("a stick from the tools") with the "nail bed" intact is a felon: an infection of the closed septated pulp space of the distal phalanx, usually Staphylococcus aureus introduced by penetrating injury. The septa make it a tense, very painful collection that needs incision and drainage if pus has formed.
why_wrong_block:
B. Paronychia: infection of the nail fold at the side or base of the nail, typically after nail biting or manicure; here the nail region is spared and the pulp is affected.
C. Onychomycosis: a chronic fungal infection causing thick, discoloured, crumbling nails, not an acute painful pulp swelling after a puncture.
D. Cellulitis: diffuse spreading erythema of skin and subcutaneous tissue without a tense loculated collection; the localized tense pulp swelling points to a felon.
key_concept:
Fingertip infections by location.
  • Pulp of distal phalanx, tense, after puncture: felon (incision and drainage)
  • Nail fold: paronychia
  • Vesicles on fingertip, herpes exposure: herpetic whitlow (do NOT incise)
  • Fusiform swollen finger, flexed posture, pain on passive extension: flexor tenosynovitis
  • Chronic thick discoloured nail: onychomycosis
exam_pearl: Pulp = felon, nail fold = paronychia, vesicles = herpetic whitlow which must not be incised.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0344).
Compiler note: Felon: deep infection of the distal pulp (fingertip pad); tense, swollen, very painful bulb; usually follows penetrating injury (common in hairdressers, barbers); nail bed intact. Paronychia = infection around nail fold; onychomycosis = fungal nail infection; cellulitis = diffuse skin infection. Pulp divided into septal compartments so pressure builds up = risk of ischemia and osteomyelitis; most common organism S. aureus. Management: early = oral antibiotics; abscess = incision and drainage.

stem: A 55-year-old man with a history of heart disease presents with a small lesion on the ear pinna for 2 months. What is the safest and most appropriate type of anesthesia for excision?
OptD: Local anesthesia with ropivacaine and adrenaline
why_right: A "small lesion on the ear pinna" is a minor excision that needs only local anesthesia, and the patient has "heart disease". Plain 1% lidocaine infiltration is fast in onset, effective and has a wide safety margin, and it avoids adrenaline, which can cause tachycardia and arrhythmia in cardiac patients and is traditionally avoided in the ear and other end artery sites. That makes it the "safest and most appropriate" choice.
why_wrong_block:
B. A regional block is unnecessary for a small superficial lesion, and long acting agents like levobupivacaine carry more systemic toxicity risk if absorbed. A regional technique suits larger areas where infiltration would need large volumes.
C. Bupivacaine is the most cardiotoxic local anesthetic, a poor choice in a patient with heart disease, and a regional block is overkill for a tiny pinna lesion.
D. Adrenaline is avoided here: classic teaching avoids it in end artery areas (ears, fingers, toes, nose, penis), and it adds cardiac stress in a patient with heart disease. Adrenaline containing local is useful for vascular areas without these concerns.
key_concept:
Choose the simplest, safest anesthesia that covers the field.
  • Small skin lesion: local infiltration with lidocaine
  • Lidocaine with adrenaline: longer action and less bleeding; traditionally avoided in end artery sites and used cautiously in cardiac disease
  • Bupivacaine: long acting, most cardiotoxic
  • Regional blocks: larger fields or when infiltration volume would be high
exam_pearl: Cardiac patient + ear lesion: plain lidocaine, no adrenaline, no bupivacaine.

stem: A 75-year-old man presents to the Outpatient Department complaining of back pain and increasing difficulty with passing urine (see lab results). Prostate-specific antigen 84 (0–4), Alkaline phosphatase 410 (39–117 IU/L), Albumin 41, Gamma glutamyltransferase 19 (6–37 IU/L). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A 75-year-old man with outflow symptoms ("increasing difficulty with passing urine") plus "back pain" suggests prostate cancer with spinal bone metastases. The PSA of 84 is far beyond what BPH produces, and a high alkaline phosphatase (410) with normal GGT and albumin means the ALP is coming from bone, not liver, which fits osteoblastic metastases.
why_wrong_block:
A. Prostatitis can raise PSA, but it presents with fever, dysuria and perineal or pelvic pain with a tender prostate; it does not explain bony back pain and a bone ALP rise.
C. Bladder cancer classically presents with painless hematuria in a smoker and does not raise PSA.
D. BPH causes outflow symptoms with only a mild PSA rise; it does not cause back pain or a raised bone ALP. It fits LUTS with a normal or slightly raised PSA.
key_concept:
Elderly man + LUTS + back pain + very high PSA + high ALP with normal GGT = metastatic prostate cancer.
  • Bone (spine) is the commonest metastatic site; lesions are osteoblastic
  • High ALP + normal GGT: bone source; high ALP + high GGT: liver source
  • Diagnosis: DRE, MRI prostate, transrectal or transperineal biopsy; bone scan for staging
  • BPH: LUTS, smooth enlarged prostate, PSA low; alpha blocker first
exam_pearl: Back pain in an old man with urinary symptoms is spinal metastasis until proven otherwise.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (screenshot): Old male with back pain and high PSA and urine retention (since 2 months) - prostatitis / prostatic cancer / BPH / idk. Comment: His PSA was something in 60s (very high for BPH). Anyhow, answer is prostate cancer due to back pain.

stem: A diabetic patient presents with a well-demarcated plantar foot ulcer. The patient has nearly diminished sensation and intact peripheral pulses. The ulcer shows central erythema with signs of healing. What is the most critical test to perform to reach the diagnosis?
why_right: A "plantar" ulcer in a diabetic with "diminished sensation" and "intact peripheral pulses" is a neuropathic ulcer: weight bearing site, adequate perfusion, loss of protective sensation. The test that establishes that diagnosis is the 10-g monofilament test, which confirms loss of protective sensation and therefore the neuropathic cause.
why_wrong_block:
A. ABI assesses arterial insufficiency; it is the key test for an ulcer with absent or weak pulses, a non-healing course, or a dorsal, toe tip or heel location. Here pulses are intact and the ulcer is healing (note ABI can be falsely high in diabetics due to calcified vessels).
C. CT does not diagnose the ulcer type; deep infection or osteomyelitis is assessed with X-ray first and MRI, not CT, and only if suspected.
D. Finding pressure points guides offloading and prevention once neuropathy is established; it is management, not the test that makes the diagnosis.
key_concept:
Diabetic foot ulcer: location + pulses + sensation decide the type.
  • Neuropathic: plantar, under metatarsal heads, painless, intact pulses: monofilament test, offloading
  • Arterial: toes, heel, dorsum, painful, absent pulses: ABI then duplex/CT angiography
  • Venous: gaiter area/medial malleolus, intact pulses: venous duplex
  • Suspect osteomyelitis: probe to bone, X-ray, MRI
exam_pearl: Same stem with a malleolar or dorsal non-healing ulcer flips the answer to ABI.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Plantar ulcer + intact pulses + sensory loss = diabetic neuropathic ulcer = monofilament test (10-g monofilament assesses loss of protective sensation). Screenshot versions: examiner says pulse was not mentioned, only diminished sensation; ulcer regular, peri-wound erythema; Answer: B. Other examiners: ulcer on malleoli (Dec) / dorsal not plantar (Apr); if non-healing, malleoli and dorsal locations favor arterial ulcer and answer is ABI. Recalls 'plantar, non-healing, sharply demarcated/regular margin, surrounding erythema, diminished sensation': Alhomrani says monofilament (though cannot say ABI is wrong).
Other marked answers: Screenshot variant (ulcer on malleoli/dorsal, non-healing): A. ABI

stem: Old patient came with leg swelling and absent or diminished pulses. What you will do next?
highlight_terms_source: leg swelling and absent or diminished pulses
why_right: An old patient with absent or diminished pulses has suspected arterial disease, and the leg problem must first be characterised non-invasively. Doppler ultrasound (with ABI) is the first-line bedside test: it confirms reduced arterial flow, localises the level of disease and can also assess the veins as a cause of the swelling. It is cheap, quick and radiation-free, so it comes before any cross-sectional imaging.
why_wrong_block:
B. MRI (MRA) is a second-line anatomical study used for planning intervention once Doppler has shown significant disease; not the first step.
C. CT (CT angiography) is the confirmatory/gold-standard roadmap test, used after Doppler or directly in acute limb ischemia when intervention is planned; it is not the initial test for diminished pulses.
D. HbA1c screens for diabetes as a risk factor, but it does not evaluate the limb or explain the absent pulses; risk-factor work-up comes after the vascular assessment.
key_concept:
Diminished pulses = vascular assessment starts non-invasive.
  • PAD ladder: ABI, then Doppler/duplex US (non-invasive vascular lab), then CT angiography
  • Acute limb ischemia: heparin, then US, then CTA (gold standard)
  • Leg ulcer/swelling: check pulses first; absent = arterial Doppler, intact = venous duplex
  • MRA/conventional angiography = planning or when CTA not possible
exam_pearl: If the lead-in says 'most appropriate/confirmatory' in sudden-onset acute ischemia, CTA wins; for 'what next' with diminished pulses, Doppler first.

stem: 14 years old boy came with sudden severe left abdominal and groin pain. On examination you find out transillumination test negative, severe tender on touch, slight elevated testicle. What is diagnosis?
why_right: A 14-year-old boy (peak age for torsion) with sudden severe groin/lower abdominal pain, an exquisitely tender testis that is elevated (high-riding) and a negative transillumination test has testicular torsion. The twisted spermatic cord shortens and pulls the testis up, and adolescents often report the pain in the lower abdomen. Diagnosis is clinical and needs urgent surgical exploration without waiting for imaging.
why_wrong_block:
B. Direct inguinal hernia is an adult (older male) acquired defect through Hesselbach triangle, usually a painless reducible bulge; it does not cause a tender, elevated testis in a teenager.
C. Indirect inguinal hernia gives a groin/scrotal swelling with a cough impulse; if incarcerated it is tender, but the lump extends from the groin into the scrotum and the testis is separate, not high-riding and acutely tender.
D. Hydrocele is a painless, fluctuant swelling that transilluminates; here pain is severe and transillumination is negative.
key_concept:
Acute scrotum in a boy: torsion until proven otherwise.
  • Torsion: sudden severe pain, high-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex; explore surgically
  • Torsion of appendage: upper pole pain, blue dot sign; conservative
  • Epididymo-orchitis: gradual, swollen testis, increased flow on Doppler; antibiotics
  • Hydrocele: painless, transilluminates
  • Hernia: groin-to-scrotum swelling, cough impulse
exam_pearl: Lower abdominal pain in an adolescent boy: always examine the testes; delaying for Doppler costs the testis.

stem: A 90-year-old female with long-standing incisional hernia presents to ER with abdominal pain and fecalith discharge. Her hernia is strangulated with ulcers and necrosis. All vitals are normal. Management?
why_right: A strangulated incisional hernia with necrosis, ulceration and fecal discharge means compromised, likely perforated bowel with a fecal fistula. Strangulation is an absolute indication for emergency surgery, and a large, complex, contaminated hernia with dead bowel needs an open laparotomy to resect the non-viable bowel and deal with the defect. Normal vitals and age 90 do not change this: dead bowel will not recover without surgery.
why_wrong_block:
A. Dressing is only for superficial wound problems (seroma, minor wound discharge); it ignores necrotic, strangulated bowel.
B. Laparoscopy suits elective, uncomplicated, bilateral or recurrent hernias; a strangulated, necrotic, fecally contaminated incisional hernia requires open access for bowel resection.
C. MRI adds delay and nothing to management; the diagnosis of strangulation with necrosis is already clinical and surgery is mandatory.
key_concept:
Hernia state decides urgency.
  • Reducible: elective repair (open mesh first-line)
  • Irreducible: non-tender, not obstructed; early repair
  • Obstructed: tender, vomiting, distension; urgent surgery
  • Strangulated: tense, very tender, discoloured, systemic signs; emergency open surgery
  • Laparotomy indications in obstruction: peritonitis, strangulation, failed conservative care
exam_pearl: Normal vitals do not buy time once necrosis or feces are visible: strangulation always means emergency open surgery.

stem: Old male came for routine exam; doctor accidentally found a mild swelling in inguinal region when he coughs or lies straight, which is not tender and causes no symptoms. What to do?
highlight_terms_source: mild swelling in inguinal region when he coughs
not tender and causes no symptoms
why_right: An old man with an incidental, non-tender, reducible inguinal swelling that appears on coughing and causes no symptoms has an asymptomatic reducible inguinal hernia. In such men watchful waiting with routine follow-up is an accepted, safe option because the risk of acute complications is low and surgery carries its own risks in the elderly. The patient is taught warning signs (pain, irreducibility) and reviewed, with repair offered if symptoms develop.
why_wrong_block:
B. Open (mesh) repair is the standard operation for symptomatic primary unilateral hernia or when surgery is chosen; not mandatory for an asymptomatic hernia in an old man.
C. Laparoscopic mesh repair is preferred for bilateral or recurrent hernias or when fast recovery is needed; none applies, and surgery is not yet indicated.
D. Simple reassurance with no follow-up is unsafe: a hernia can enlarge, become symptomatic or incarcerate, so the patient needs planned surveillance and red-flag advice.
key_concept:
Asymptomatic reducible inguinal hernia in an older man: watchful waiting is acceptable.
  • Symptomatic hernia: repair (open mesh first-line)
  • Bilateral, recurrent or fast recovery needed: laparoscopic mesh
  • Femoral hernia: repair even if asymptomatic (high strangulation risk)
  • Children: herniotomy, never watchful waiting
  • Tender/irreducible: urgent surgery
exam_pearl: 'Watchful waiting' beats 'reassure' because it includes follow-up; femoral or pediatric hernias are never watched.

stem: What is appropriate after trauma history with decreased pulses and ulceration on arm?
key_concept:
Trauma + limb at risk: decide arterial vs compartment.
  • Hard signs of arterial injury (absent pulse, pallor, cold, expanding hematoma): surgical exploration/repair
  • Compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, tense limb; fasciotomy
  • After revascularisation of prolonged ischemia: consider prophylactic fasciotomy
  • Never elevate an ischemic or compartment-syndrome limb above the heart; keep at heart level
exam_pearl: Pulseless + pale, cold limb after trauma points to the artery (explore); pulseless + severe pain, paresthesia and a tense compartment after a fracture is late compartment syndrome (fasciotomy).
compiler_note:
⚠ Image audit: The compiler marked this answer tentatively ('??' / 'not sure' / needs re-correction) — see the compiler note.
Compiler note: Not sure. A. Fasciotomy: done for compartment syndrome (pain out of proportion, tense compartment, pain with passive stretch); decreased pulses alone after trauma suggests arterial injury first. B. Surgery (check): urgent vascular surgical exploration/repair is required in trauma with reduced pulses; limb-threatening ischemia. C. Elevation above heart worsens arterial perfusion in ischemia.
Other marked answers: Typed highlight: A. Fasciotomy ?

stem: Old man fell down and then came to the ER confused, CT brain showed: crescent shaped lesion, most likely dx?
why_right: An old man who fell and is now confused, with a crescent-shaped (concave) collection on CT, has a subdural hematoma. Tearing of the bridging veins in the elderly (brain atrophy stretches them) produces blood between dura and arachnoid that spreads along the hemisphere and crosses suture lines, giving the crescent. Elderly and alcoholic patients are the classic group, often after minor trauma.
why_wrong_block:
B. Epidural hematoma is biconvex (lens-shaped), limited by sutures, from the middle meningeal artery after a temporal fracture, classically with a lucid interval; not crescent-shaped.
C. Subarachnoid hemorrhage shows blood in the sulci, fissures and basal cisterns, not a crescent collection over the hemisphere; it classically presents as a thunderclap headache.
key_concept:
CT shape gives the bleed.
  • Subdural: crescent/concave, crosses sutures, bridging veins, elderly/alcoholics (suB = Banana)
  • Epidural: biconvex/lens, does not cross sutures, middle meningeal artery, lucid interval (Epi = lEmon)
  • SAH: blood in cisterns/sulci, berry aneurysm or trauma, worst headache of life
exam_pearl: Elderly + fall + gradual confusion = subdural even if the trauma was trivial; lucid interval + temporal fracture = epidural.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other recall: CT scan picture showing crescent shape asking for diagnosis: A. Subdural Hematoma. Differentiate from epidural hematoma: biconvex (lens-shaped), does NOT cross suture lines, often due to rupture of the middle meningeal artery. Figure: epidural = lens-shaped, convex inner border, between skull and dura; subdural = crescent, concave inner border, crosses sutures, not midline, between dura and arachnoid.

stem: 10 year old boy with cushing syndrome due to left adrenal adenoma, scheduled for adrenalectomy. What is the most important post operative management?
OptC: Give stress dose steroid, then gradually taper down
OptD: Initiate fludrocortisone to maintain sodium balance
highlight_terms_source: cushing syndrome due to left adrenal adenoma
why_right: A cortisol-secreting adrenal adenoma suppresses ACTH, so the contralateral adrenal is atrophied. After the tumour is removed the patient suddenly has too little cortisol and the stress of surgery raises demand, risking an Addisonian crisis. Hence a stress dose of hydrocortisone peri/postoperatively, then a gradual taper over weeks to months while the suppressed axis recovers.
why_wrong_block:
A. Lifelong corticosteroids are for bilateral adrenalectomy or permanent adrenal insufficiency; after unilateral adenoma removal the remaining gland usually recovers, so steroids are tapered off.
B. Stopping steroids immediately is dangerous: the suppressed contralateral gland cannot respond, causing adrenal crisis.
D. Fludrocortisone replaces aldosterone, which is regulated by the renin-angiotensin system and stays intact after unilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing; it is needed in primary adrenal failure, not here.
key_concept:
Unilateral adrenalectomy for cortisol-secreting adenoma: cover then taper.
  • Low ACTH Cushing = primary adrenal source; contralateral gland suppressed
  • Perioperative stress-dose hydrocortisone, then slow taper
  • Bilateral adrenalectomy: lifelong glucocorticoid plus fludrocortisone
  • Pheochromocytoma (not Cushing): alpha blockade before surgery
exam_pearl: Cortisol adenoma removal = iatrogenic adrenal insufficiency; aldosterone is spared, so no fludrocortisone.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other recall: adrenalectomy for left cortisol-secreting adenoma causing Cushing's; highlighted: Stress dose IV hydrocortisone and taper gradually (other options: lifelong steroid, stop steroids, fluconazole to maintain sodium).

stem: A 38 year old female with intermittent RUQ pain for several months, associated with nausea, vomiting and jaundice. On examination, there is mild right upper quadrant tenderness. Labs: high bilirubin and LFTs. What is the most appropriate diagnostic imaging?
key_concept:
Suspected biliary obstruction ladder.
  • Step 1: transabdominal US (stones, CBD dilation)
  • Step 2: MRCP or EUS if CBD stone suspected but not proven
  • Step 3: ERCP for confirmed stone or cholangitis (diagnostic and therapeutic)
  • Fever + RUQ pain + jaundice = Charcot triad, cholangitis; US first, then ERCP
  • CT: for malignancy or complications
exam_pearl: 'Initial imaging' = US; 'most appropriate to confirm CBD stone after US' = MRCP; watch the lead-in.
compiler_note:
⚠ Image audit: The compiler marked this answer tentatively ('??' / 'not sure' / needs re-correction) — see the compiler note.
Compiler note: Suggests biliary obstruction, most likely choledocholithiasis. For RUQ pain or suspected gallstones: 1) Ultrasound first; 2) If CBD stone suspected = MRCP or EUS; 3) If confirmed = ERCP (treatment).
Other marked answers: Explanation: B. Abdominal US (ultrasound first)

stem: Elderly (I think smoker k/c of hypertension and DM) presents with diminished right leg pulse (not sure, maybe with calf pain, it was something pointed to acute limb ischemia or acute on top of chronic), there is popliteal bypass scar (smth like that) on his left leg (yes left, and I'm sure the present complain on his right leg not left) Which of the following indicates acute limb ischemia? (It was acute not chronic I'm sure)
why_right: The question asks which finding points to an acute (or acute-on-chronic) threatened limb rather than stable chronic disease. Among the options, only pain at rest reflects perfusion too low to meet the limb's needs without exercise, i.e. ischemia severe enough to threaten the limb; new rest pain with diminished pulses is the 'pain' of the 6 Ps. The other options are history or risk factors, not markers of acute ischemia.
why_wrong_block:
A. Intermittent claudication (pain on walking, relieved by rest) is the hallmark of stable chronic PAD, managed with exercise and risk-factor control; it does not indicate acute ischemia.
C. A previous left popliteal bypass shows established atherosclerotic disease (and can be a site of graft thrombosis on that side), but the current complaint is the right leg, so it is history, not a sign of acute right-leg ischemia.
D. Smoking is a risk factor for PAD and thrombosis; risk factors raise likelihood but do not indicate that ischemia is acute.
key_concept:
Ischemia severity spectrum.
  • Claudication: chronic, stable PAD; exercise + risk factors
  • Rest pain (relieved by hanging foot down), ulcer, gangrene: limb-threatening
  • Acute ischemia: sudden 6 Ps (pain, pallor, paresthesia, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paralysis)
  • Acute ALI ladder: heparin, then US, then CTA; paralysis = skip imaging
  • Embolic (AF) = embolectomy; in situ thrombosis on atheroma = catheter-directed thrombolysis
exam_pearl: Rest pain alone classically defines chronic limb-threatening ischemia; what makes it acute is a sudden onset with the 6 Ps, so read the timing in the stem.

stem: A patient with diabetes presents with swelling of the big toe and warmth and tenderness of the (calf) for 4 days. There is 2 cm ulcer over the first metatarsal area. No discharge is noted. Distal pulses are intact. What is the most appropriate investigation?
highlight_terms_source: 2 cm ulcer over the first metatarsal area
key_concept:
Diabetic foot/leg: pick the test for the threat the stem emphasises.
  • Leg ulcer: check pulses first; absent = arterial Doppler, intact = venous duplex
  • Calf warmth/tenderness/swelling: venous duplex for DVT
  • Suspected osteomyelitis: X-ray first, MRI most accurate, bone biopsy definitive
  • Angiography: arterial disease needing revascularisation
exam_pearl: If the lead-in centres on the calf, think DVT and duplex; if it centres on the ulcer and bone, think MRI.
compiler_note:
⚠ Image audit: Page says 'Answer: C or A not sure'; explanation discusses both Duplex (DVT) and MRI (osteomyelitis) without concluding. Card has C.
Compiler note: Answer line: 'C or A not sure'. A. Duplex US: best for DVT evaluation; calf tenderness means DVT must be ruled out; non-invasive, first-line. C. MRI: gold standard for osteomyelitis; indicated if bone involvement suspected (ulcer >2 cm, chronic, deep, non-healing). Other recall: big toe swelling and discharge for 4 days, 2 cm ulcer on first metatarsal, distal pulses intact; options Duplex US, conventional angio, MRA, CT with contrast (no answer marked).
Other marked answers: Answer line: A. Duplex ultrasound

stem: Elderly women with previous laparotomy for sigmoidectomy after complicated diverticulitis, she had a mild incisional hernia (There was mention of cough impulse and that it doesn't bother her but not exactly). It became painful with exercise and expanded. But no signs of strangulation (this was stated in the scenario). What is the best action?
highlight_terms_source: became painful with exercise and expanded
why_right: An incisional hernia after laparotomy that has become "painful with exercise" and has "expanded" is symptomatic and enlarging, so it needs elective repair even though there is "no signs of strangulation". Incisional hernias should be repaired with mesh because suture repair alone has a high recurrence rate, and the laparoscopic approach avoids re-opening the scarred midline and gives faster recovery with fewer wound complications in an elderly patient.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassure: acceptable only for a small, asymptomatic hernia that does not bother the patient; this one is now painful and growing, which increases the risk of incarceration.
B. Open repair without mesh: primary suture repair of an incisional hernia has an unacceptably high recurrence; it is reserved for very small defects or a contaminated field where mesh is unsafe.
C. Laparoscopic repair: incomplete answer, because the laparoscopic incisional repair is a mesh repair; closing the defect without mesh reinforcement recurs frequently.
key_concept:
Symptomatic or enlarging incisional hernia = elective repair with mesh.
  • Asymptomatic, small: observation is possible
  • Painful, enlarging: elective mesh repair
  • Tender, irreducible, signs of obstruction or strangulation: emergency open repair
  • Laparoscopic mesh repair: smaller wounds, fewer wound infections, faster recovery
  • Suture repair without mesh: high recurrence
exam_pearl: "Painful" or "expanding" turns observation into repair; any repair of an incisional hernia should include mesh.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Asymptomatic hernia: observation possible. Symptomatic or enlarging hernia: surgical repair. Incisional hernia: mesh repair (often laparoscopic).

stem: 65 years man with reducible inguinal hernia, mild discomfort without significant pain.
why_right: The hernia is "reducible" with only "mild discomfort without significant pain", so it is minimally symptomatic. In an older man with a minimally symptomatic inguinal hernia, watchful waiting with review is an accepted option because the risk of acute incarceration is low; surgery is offered if symptoms increase or the hernia becomes irreducible.
why_wrong_block:
A. Surgical repair: right once the hernia is clearly symptomatic (pain limiting activity), enlarging, irreducible, or the patient wants repair; mild discomfort alone does not mandate it.
B. Lifestyle modification: general advice (weight loss, avoid straining) may accompany follow-up but is not itself a management plan for the hernia.
C. Activity modification: does not treat or monitor the hernia; restricting activity is not required and would fit only as supportive advice, not the chosen strategy.
key_concept:
Inguinal hernia management depends on symptoms and state.
  • Asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic, reducible (adult man): watchful waiting is acceptable
  • Symptomatic: elective repair (open mesh for primary unilateral)
  • Bilateral or recurrent: laparoscopic mesh repair
  • Femoral hernia: repair even if asymptomatic
  • Tender, irreducible, obstructed or strangulated: emergency surgery
exam_pearl: "Mild discomfort" = watch; "pain limiting activity", irreducible, or femoral = repair.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Printed label '312-313' covers this single screenshot.

stem: Man who experienced a road traffic accident (RTA), had a lucid interval, and then lost consciousness, with a convex lesion found on CT scan. What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: Head trauma with a "lucid interval" followed by loss of consciousness and a "convex" (lens shaped, biconvex) lesion on CT is an epidural hematoma, usually from a torn middle meningeal artery. This is an expanding arterial bleed causing mass effect, so the definitive and most appropriate management is urgent craniotomy and evacuation of the hematoma.
why_wrong_block:
A. Shunt: a ventriculoperitoneal shunt treats hydrocephalus; it does not remove an extradural clot compressing the brain.
C. Mannitol: a temporizing measure to lower intracranial pressure while arranging surgery; it does not stop the arterial bleed or remove the hematoma.
D. Intubation: protects the airway when GCS is 8 or less and is done as part of ABC resuscitation, but it is supportive; the question asks for the management of the lesion itself, which is surgical evacuation.
key_concept:
Epidural vs subdural hematoma.
  • Epidural: convex, lens shaped; middle meningeal artery; lucid interval; often temporal fracture
  • Subdural: concave, crescent shaped; bridging veins; elderly, alcoholics, gradual
  • Symptomatic epidural hematoma: urgent craniotomy and evacuation
  • Mannitol and intubation are bridges, not definitive treatment
exam_pearl: Lens (convex) + lucid interval = epidural; the answer is craniotomy, with airway and mannitol only as bridges.

stem: Patient was involved in a motor vehicle accident and presents with Paradoxical chest wall movement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: "Paradoxical chest wall movement" after blunt trauma means a segment of the chest wall has lost bony continuity: flail chest, from several adjacent ribs each fractured in two or more places. The free segment is sucked in on inspiration and pushed out on expiration.
why_wrong_block: B. Cardiac contusion: presents with arrhythmias, new ECG changes or hypotension after a sternal blow; it does not cause paradoxical movement of the chest wall.
key_concept:
Chest trauma pattern recognition.
  • Paradoxical movement: flail chest
  • Flail chest treatment: analgesia, oxygen, assisted ventilation if hypoxic
  • Hyperresonance, tracheal shift, raised JVP, hypotension: tension pneumothorax
  • Raised JVP, hypotension, muffled heart sounds, equal air entry: cardiac tamponade
  • Arrhythmia or ECG changes after sternal impact: cardiac contusion
exam_pearl: The hypoxia in flail chest comes mainly from the underlying pulmonary contusion, not the loose segment itself.

stem: A hairdresser came to the emergency department with a swollen bulb of the thumb finger after getting a stick from the tools she's using. Nail bed is intact.
highlight_terms_source: swollen bulb of the thumb finger
why_right: A swollen, tense "bulb" (pulp) of the thumb after a puncture ("a stick from the tools") with the "nail bed" intact is a felon: an infection of the closed septated pulp space of the distal phalanx, usually Staphylococcus aureus introduced by penetrating injury. The septa make it a tense, very painful collection that needs incision and drainage if pus has formed.
why_wrong_block:
B. Paronychia: infection of the nail fold at the side or base of the nail, typically after nail biting or manicure; here the nail region is spared and the pulp is affected.
C. Onychomycosis: a chronic fungal infection causing thick, discoloured, crumbling nails, not an acute painful pulp swelling after a puncture.
D. Cellulitis: diffuse spreading erythema of skin and subcutaneous tissue without a tense loculated collection; the localized tense pulp swelling points to a felon.
key_concept:
Fingertip infections by location.
  • Pulp of distal phalanx, tense, after puncture: felon (incision and drainage)
  • Nail fold: paronychia
  • Vesicles on fingertip, herpes exposure: herpetic whitlow (do NOT incise)
