The lead-in asks how to "avoid missed diagnosis": the safest strategy is admission for active observation with repeated abdominal examination by the same team, which reveals evolving appendicitis while avoiding an unnecessary operation. In a girl, a pregnancy test and pelvic ultrasound are usually added during this period.
why_wrong_block:
B. Discharging an equivocal RLQ pain risks missing early appendicitis that progresses to perforation; discharge with return advice fits only clearly non-surgical, resolving pain.
C. Analgesia should be given and does not mask appendicitis, but on its own it does not establish or exclude the diagnosis; it is part of care, not the strategy that prevents a miss.
key_concept:
Equivocal RLQ pain: observe, re-examine, then decide.
  • Clear clinical appendicitis: surgery
  • Equivocal (mild signs, normal WBC, afebrile): admit, serial exams and labs
  • Female: pregnancy test and pelvic ultrasound (torsion, ovarian cyst, ectopic)
  • Children and pregnancy: ultrasound first; CT if still unclear in adults
  • Analgesia is safe and does not hide peritonitis
exam_pearl: Serial examination is the best tool for an unclear appendix; analgesia is safe and should never be withheld while observing.

stem: A 60-year-old woman with recent history of feeling tiredness, fatigue and weight loss. She noticed as well worsening of her chronic constipation. Stool for occult blood was positive (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values RBC 3 4.7-6.1 x 1012/L (Male) 4.2-5.4 x 1012/L (Female) Hb 89 130-170 g/L (Male) 120-160 g/L (Female) HCT 0.25 0.42-0.52 (Male) 0.37-0.48 (Female) Platelets count 234 150-400 × 109/L Which of the following is the best next step in diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: Stool for occult blood was positive
why_right: A "60-year-old" with fatigue, weight loss, worsening constipation (change in bowel habit), anemia (Hb 89) and a positive stool occult blood test has colorectal cancer until proven otherwise. Colonoscopy is the best next step because it visualizes the entire colon and allows biopsy and removal of polyps in the same session.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT enterography images the small bowel (Crohn disease, obscure small bowel bleeding) and cannot take tissue; it is not the test for a suspected colon cancer.
B. Barium enema is outdated, misses small lesions and cannot biopsy; it is used only when colonoscopy is impossible.
C. Sigmoidoscopy sees only the distal colon and would miss a right-sided cancer, which typically causes anemia; a positive occult blood test needs full colonoscopy.
key_concept:
Positive FOBT/FIT or iron deficiency anemia with red flags = colonoscopy.
  • Colonoscopy: whole colon + biopsy + polypectomy
  • Sigmoid cancer found on sigmoidoscopy: still need full colonoscopy for synchronous lesions
  • After diagnosis: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging
  • Barium enema or CT colonography: only if colonoscopy not possible
exam_pearl: Never repeat a positive occult blood test or settle for a partial exam; go to colonoscopy.

stem: Patient presented with weight loss (and other dyspepsia Symptoms) Gastric antrum Histopathology confirmed Adenocarcinoma. How to stage the “T”?
why_right: The lead-in asks specifically how to stage the "T", which is the depth of tumour invasion through the gastric wall layers. Endoscopic ultrasound resolves the individual wall layers and nearby nodes, so it is the most accurate test for T (and local N) staging of gastric cancer. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis is still done first overall to look for distant metastases (M).
why_wrong_block:
B. Transabdominal ultrasound cannot resolve the layers of the stomach wall; at most it may show liver metastases or ascites.
C. A nuclear (bone) scan looks for skeletal metastases when symptoms suggest them; it says nothing about depth of invasion.
D. A contrast (Gastrografin) study outlines the lumen and mucosa or shows a leak, but cannot measure how deep the tumour penetrates the wall.
key_concept:
TNM staging tools for upper GI cancer.
  • Diagnosis: upper endoscopy with biopsy
  • M (distant spread): CT chest, abdomen and pelvis first
  • T and local N: endoscopic ultrasound
  • Occult peritoneal disease: staging laparoscopy
  • PET-CT: occult distant metastases (more in esophageal cancer)
exam_pearl: "Next investigation after biopsy" = CT CAP; "how to assess T / depth of invasion" = EUS.

stem: A 62-year-old man has been noticing progressive difficulty swallowing, first solid food and now liquids as well. A barium study shows a ragged narrowing just below the carinal level. Endoscopic biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma. Which of the following provides the most accurate information regarding the T stage of an esophageal carcinoma?
highlight_terms_source: T stage of an esophageal carcinoma
why_right: The lead-in asks for "the most accurate information regarding the T stage", which is depth of invasion through the esophageal wall. Endoscopic ultrasound visualizes each wall layer and periesophageal nodes, making it the most accurate test for T (and local N) staging of esophageal cancer once biopsy has confirmed the diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT is the first staging scan for distant metastases and gross invasion of neighbouring organs, but it cannot separate the wall layers to define early T stage.
B. PET is best for detecting occult distant metastases (M stage); its spatial resolution is too low to judge depth of wall invasion.
C. MRI is not a routine staging tool for esophageal cancer and is less accurate than EUS for wall depth.
E. Bronchoscopy checks for tracheobronchial invasion in tumours at or above the carina; it shows airway involvement, not the tumour's depth in the esophageal wall.
key_concept:
Esophageal cancer workup: biopsy, then stage in layers.
  • Diagnosis: endoscopy with biopsy (barium shows a ragged stricture)
  • Distant spread: CT chest and abdomen, then PET-CT
  • T and local N: endoscopic ultrasound
  • Upper or mid tumour near the airway: bronchoscopy for tracheal invasion
  • SCC: upper/mid esophagus, smoking, alcohol, achalasia; adenocarcinoma: lower, Barrett, GERD
exam_pearl: T = EUS, M = CT/PET; bronchoscopy only answers "is the airway invaded".

stem: Case Of Post-Operative Fever - 4 days post abdominal surgery, pale, hypotensive with cold extremities. how to confirm iV fluid level in patient who is being treated for dehydration?
why_right: This recall's key is CVP 8 because the question asks how to confirm the "IV fluid level" (intravascular filling) in a hypovolemic patient, and CVP is the classic direct estimate of right-sided filling pressure. A CVP of 8 sits in the traditional resuscitation target range of 8 to 12 mmHg, whereas each of the other values is either clearly abnormal or a perfusion marker rather than a volume measure.
why_wrong_block:
B. A MAP of 45 is profound hypotension; the usual resuscitation target is a MAP of at least 65, so this value shows ongoing shock, not adequate fluid.
C. Urine output of 0.1 mL/kg/h is severe oliguria; adequate resuscitation is shown by at least 0.5 mL/kg/h in adults.
D. Lactate reflects tissue perfusion and anaerobic metabolism rather than intravascular volume, and a value of 2 sits at the upper limit of normal, so on this key's logic it does not confirm fluid status.
key_concept:
Resuscitation endpoints: know the target for each number.
  • CVP: traditional target 8 to 12 mmHg (static, limited predictor)
  • MAP: at least 65 mmHg
  • Urine output: at least 0.5 mL/kg/h adults, at least 1 mL/kg/h children
  • Lactate: normal up to 2 mmol/L; falling lactate = improving perfusion
  • Burns: urine output is the main endpoint
exam_pearl: The same four options appear in a burn recall keyed to lactate 2; read whether the question asks for "fluid level" (CVP here) or "good resuscitation".

stem: Patient came to ER with burns all over the body after intubation and resuscitation what will indicate good fluid…
why_right: After intubation and resuscitation of extensive burns, the question asks which value indicates "good fluid" resuscitation. Urine output is the usual burn endpoint, but here it is only 0.1 mL/kg/h, so the remaining sign of adequate tissue perfusion is a lactate of 2, which is at the upper limit of normal and shows no significant anaerobic metabolism. CVP is unreliable in burns and MAP 45 is shock.
why_wrong_block:
A. Urine output is the best burn endpoint, but the target is at least 0.5 mL/kg/h in adults (1 mL/kg/h in children); 0.1 mL/kg/h means under-resuscitation.
B. A MAP of 45 is severe hypotension and indicates inadequate resuscitation; the target is a MAP of at least 65.
C. CVP is invasive and a poor predictor of volume status in burns, where massive capillary leak and fluid shifts distort it; it is not used as the resuscitation endpoint.
key_concept:
Burn resuscitation: titrate fluids to perfusion endpoints.
  • Main endpoint: urine output at least 0.5 mL/kg/h adults, 1 mL/kg/h children
  • Supporting: normal or falling lactate
  • Heart rate and BP: unreliable (pain, catecholamines)
  • CVP: poor predictor, not a target
  • Fluid: Ringer lactate by Parkland formula, then adjust to urine output
exam_pearl: If the urine output option is below target, pick the next perfusion marker that is normal (lactate), not CVP.

stem: 10 years old girl came to the ER complaining from RLQ abdominal pain that associated with nausea and 3 times vomiting, there is pain and rebound tenderness in examination. What is the diagnosis?
why_right: A school-age child with RLQ pain, nausea and vomiting, and rebound tenderness on examination has the classic picture of acute appendicitis. Rebound tenderness signals localized peritoneal irritation in the right iliac fossa, which fits an inflamed appendix. In a child, ultrasound is the first imaging if confirmation is needed, followed by appendectomy.
why_wrong_block:
B. Intussusception: typically an infant or toddler (about 6 months to 3 years) with episodic colicky crying, drawing up the legs, a sausage-shaped mass and red currant jelly stool; a 10-year-old with localized RLQ peritonism does not fit.
C. Meckel's diverticulum: classically presents in young children with painless rectal bleeding; Meckel's diverticulitis can mimic appendicitis but is far rarer, so it is not the diagnosis for this classic picture.
key_concept:
RLQ pain + nausea/vomiting + rebound tenderness = acute appendicitis until proven otherwise.
  • Pain often starts periumbilical, then migrates to the RLQ
  • Anorexia, low-grade fever, McBurney point tenderness, Rovsing sign
  • Imaging: US in children and pregnancy; CT best in non-pregnant adults
  • Uncomplicated: laparoscopic appendectomy
  • Abscess: percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics + interval appendectomy
exam_pearl: Age flips the answer: infant with colicky pain and a mass = intussusception; toddler with painless bleeding = Meckel's; school-age child with RLQ peritonism = appendicitis.
compiler_note: Compiler note: A 'Q:' variant: 14 years old female with periumbilical pain shifting to the right, anorexia, mild diarrhea + dysuria, no vomiting/fever, right tenderness increasing with cough; options Appendicitis / Gastroenteritis / Right ureteric stone / UTI; highlighted A) Appendicitis.

stem: 90 year old male living in residential community comes complaining of severe abdominal pain in the last 24 hours. The abdomen was soft and lax, tender all over, hyperactive abdominal sounds. (no rigidity) What is the next step:
highlight_terms_source: soft and lax, tender all over
why_right: A 90-year-old from a residential (care) home with diffuse tenderness, a soft, lax abdomen with no rigidity and hyperactive bowel sounds needs a complete bedside examination before any test, and that includes a digital rectal examination. In frail, immobile elderly patients DRE quickly detects fecal impaction (a common cause of pain and obstructive symptoms), rectal masses and blood (hinting at ischemia or malignancy). It is cheap, immediate and guides the choice of further investigation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Colonoscopy: an elective, preparation-requiring investigation, not the next step in acute severe abdominal pain; it is used for bleeding or suspected colorectal cancer once the acute picture is clarified.
B. Sigmoidoscopy: useful for suspected sigmoid volvulus (huge tympanic distension, coffee bean sign) or distal lesions, but should follow examination, not replace it.
C. US abdomen: reasonable imaging for biliary or pelvic causes, but the bedside examination (including DRE) is completed first; in a frail elderly patient with diffuse pain, CT is usually the more informative imaging.
key_concept:
Acute abdomen in the elderly: complete the examination (including DRE) before imaging.
  • Nursing home + immobility: think fecal impaction
  • DRE: impaction, rectal mass, blood on the glove
  • Pain out of proportion with a soft abdomen: think mesenteric ischemia (CT angiography)
  • Massive tympanic distension + coffee bean sign: sigmoid volvulus (sigmoidoscopic decompression)
exam_pearl: Soft, non-rigid abdomen in an elderly patient does not exclude serious pathology; the elderly often lack peritoneal signs.

stem: 32 years old male admitted for motor vehicle accident, after initially stabilization and multiple surgical interventions for fractures. He is in pos-op care Which of the following is the most appropriate preventive measures?
why_right: After major trauma and multiple fracture surgeries, the main preventable complications are those of immobility: DVT/PE, pneumonia and atelectasis, pressure ulcers, muscle wasting and joint stiffness. Early mobilization and physiotherapy address all of these, which is why it is the most appropriate preventive measure in the post-operative phase (alongside pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis when bleeding risk allows).
why_wrong_block:
A. Extended bed rest: increases the risk of DVT/PE, pneumonia, pressure sores and deconditioning; it is the opposite of prevention.
B. High-dose corticosteroids: no preventive role after trauma surgery; they impair wound and fracture healing and raise infection risk.
D. Empirical antibiotics for 5 days: surgical prophylaxis is short (a single pre-incision dose, at most about 24 h for closed fractures); prolonged empirical courses promote resistance and C. difficile without benefit.
key_concept:
Post-operative prevention after polytrauma = fight immobility.
  • Early mobilization and physiotherapy
  • VTE prophylaxis: LMWH when bleeding risk allows, mechanical devices otherwise
  • Incentive spirometry / chest physiotherapy against atelectasis and pneumonia
  • Pressure area care
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis: short, peri-incisional only
exam_pearl: Bed rest is never the preventive answer post-op; mobilization is.

stem: A 25-year-old patient sustained a blunt trauma to the right chest wall; there was paradoxical movement of the right side of the chest (see report). Heart rate 96 /min Respiratory rate 35 /min Oxygen saturation 84 % Chest X-ray: Fracture 2nd through 4th ribs at more than 1 site. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
highlight_terms_source: Fracture 2nd through 4th ribs at more than 1 site
why_right: Ribs 2 to 4 fractured at more than one site with paradoxical chest movement is flail chest. The danger is hypoxia from the unstable segment and the underlying pulmonary contusion, here shown by SpO2 84% and RR 35. Initial management is supportive: adequate analgesia plus oxygenation and assisted ventilation, with intubation when hypoxia persists (SpO2 below about 88% is a trauma intubation trigger).
why_wrong_block:
A. Fluid resuscitation: the patient is not hypotensive (HR 96, no shock); the problem is respiratory, and excess fluid worsens pulmonary contusion. Fluids would lead if he were in hemorrhagic shock.
C. Needle decompression: treats tension pneumothorax (hyperresonance, absent breath sounds, tracheal shift, raised JVP, hypotension), none of which is described.
D. Thoracostomy chest tube: for pneumothorax or hemothorax seen on examination or X-ray; the film here shows only rib fractures.
key_concept:
Flail chest = 2 or more adjacent ribs fractured in 2 or more places + paradoxical movement.
  • Problem: hypoxia from the flail segment and pulmonary contusion
  • Treatment: analgesia (including regional blocks), oxygen, assisted ventilation
  • Intubate if hypoxia persists or respiratory failure develops
  • Avoid fluid overload (contusion worsens)
  • Tension pneumothorax: needle decompression then chest tube
exam_pearl: Paradoxical movement means flail chest (ventilate and give analgesia); hyperresonance with tracheal shift means tension pneumothorax (decompress).
compiler_note: Compiler note: A second version (option B 'Assistant ventilation') also gives 'Answer: B'.

stem: Pelvic fracture with BP 88/55. Next step?
why_right: A pelvic fracture with BP 88/55 means hemorrhagic shock from pelvic bleeding, which can be massive. Current trauma resuscitation favors early blood products (balanced transfusion) over large-volume crystalloid in a hypotensive bleeding trauma patient, together with a pelvic binder and definitive hemorrhage control (angioembolization or preperitoneal packing). The key here is therefore blood transfusion.
why_wrong_block:
A. Bed rest: appropriate only for a stable, minor (e.g. pubic ramus) fracture; useless in a hypotensive patient.
B. Laparotomy: pelvic bleeding is retroperitoneal and is not controlled by laparotomy; laparotomy is for intra-abdominal bleeding with a positive FAST in an unstable patient.
C. IV fluids: a limited initial crystalloid bolus may be given while blood is prepared, but large-volume crystalloid dilutes clotting factors and worsens bleeding; ongoing shock from pelvic hemorrhage needs blood.
key_concept:
Unstable pelvic fracture = hemorrhagic shock until proven otherwise.
  • Pelvic binder to close the pelvic volume
  • Early blood products (massive transfusion protocol if needed)
  • Limit crystalloid
  • Hemorrhage control: angioembolization or preperitoneal packing / external fixation
  • Positive FAST + unstable: laparotomy for the abdomen, not the pelvis
exam_pearl: If 'pelvic binder' appears among the options, it usually comes first; otherwise blood beats crystalloid in hemorrhagic shock.

stem: A nurse is reviewing a patient’s file before surgery and notices that the allergy history is not documented. According to the surgical safety checklist, at which stage should allergies be confirmed?
why_right: In the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, Sign In is done before induction of anesthesia and includes confirming identity, site, procedure and consent, the site marking, the anesthesia safety check, pulse oximetry, and explicitly "Does the patient have a known allergy?", along with airway and blood-loss risk. Allergies must be known before any anesthetic agent or antibiotic is given, so they are confirmed at Sign In.
why_wrong_block:
B. Sign Out: done before the patient leaves the operating room; it covers the procedure name, instrument, sponge and needle counts, specimen labeling, equipment problems and recovery concerns.
C. Time Out: done before skin incision; the team introduces itself, reconfirms patient, site and procedure, antibiotic prophylaxis within the last 60 minutes, anticipated critical events and imaging. Allergy is checked earlier, before induction.
D. Postoperative: not a phase of the checklist, and too late; anesthetic drugs and antibiotics would already have been given.
key_concept:
WHO Surgical Safety Checklist: 3 phases.
  • Sign In (before induction): identity, site, consent, site marking, anesthesia check, oximeter, allergy, airway/aspiration risk, blood-loss risk
  • Time Out (before incision): team introductions, confirm patient/site/procedure, antibiotics within 60 min, critical events, imaging
  • Sign Out (before leaving OR): procedure recorded, counts, specimen labeling, equipment issues, recovery plan
exam_pearl: Allergy, airway and blood-loss risk = Sign In; antibiotics within 60 minutes = Time Out; counts and specimens = Sign Out.

stem: A 28 year old female presented following radiation of neck with neck swelling. Ultrasound showed swelling in the left lobe of the thyroid of 3x4cm of papillary thyroid cancer. Which of the following is the best management?
why_right: This is confirmed papillary thyroid cancer (3x4 cm) in a patient with a history of neck radiation. Prior head and neck irradiation raises the risk of multifocal and bilateral disease, and is a standard indication for total thyroidectomy rather than lobectomy, even for a tumor that would otherwise allow a lobectomy. Total thyroidectomy also allows radioactive iodine therapy and thyroglobulin surveillance afterwards.
why_wrong_block:
A. Left lobectomy: an option for low-risk, unifocal differentiated cancer (roughly 1 to 4 cm) without risk factors, or for an indeterminate Bethesda IV nodule; the radiation history removes this option.
B. Left lobectomy with isthmusectomy: still a unilateral procedure, with the same limitation as lobectomy; it leaves the contralateral lobe at risk in a radiation-exposed gland.
C. Subtotal thyroidectomy: leaves residual thyroid tissue, which is inadequate oncologically and interferes with radioactive iodine; it is an old operation for benign goiter or Graves disease.
key_concept:
Differentiated thyroid cancer: extent of surgery.
  • <1 cm, low risk: active surveillance or lobectomy
  • 1 to 4 cm, low risk: lobectomy or total thyroidectomy
  • >4 cm, extrathyroidal extension, nodal or distant metastases, prior radiation, bilateral nodules: total thyroidectomy
  • Bethesda VI (malignant): near-total / total thyroidectomy
  • Medullary cancer: total thyroidectomy
exam_pearl: History of neck irradiation pushes any thyroid cancer toward total thyroidectomy.

stem: An elderly man with a known history of BPH presents to OPD with difficult urination, frequency, urgency, and a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying. He has been treated with an alpha-blocker for the past 2 years, with persistent symptoms. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptA: Adjust the dose of the alpha-blocker
highlight_terms_source: alpha-blocker for the past 2 years, with persistent symptoms
why_right: BPH is treated initially with an alpha-blocker, and TURP is the definitive treatment when medical therapy fails. Here the man has been on an alpha-blocker for 2 years with persistent symptoms (hesitancy, frequency, urgency, incomplete emptying), which is failure of medical therapy, so the most appropriate next step among these options is TURP.
why_wrong_block:
A. Adjust the alpha-blocker dose: alpha-blockers have a quick, largely dose-limited effect; after 2 years of persistent symptoms, a higher dose adds side effects (orthostatic hypotension) without meaningful benefit.
B. Suprapubic catheterization: used for acute retention when urethral catheterization fails or is contraindicated (e.g. urethral trauma or stricture); this patient is voiding, not in retention.
C. Clean intermittent catheterization: for neurogenic bladder or chronic retention in patients unfit for surgery; it is not the next step for symptomatic BPH failing medication.
key_concept:
BPH management ladder.
  • Initial: lifestyle measures + alpha-blocker (tamsulosin, doxazosin)
  • Large gland: add a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor (finasteride)
  • Failed medical therapy or complications (retention, recurrent UTI, stones, hematuria, renal impairment): TURP
  • Very large gland: open or enucleation prostatectomy
  • Acute retention: Foley catheter + urine culture
exam_pearl: New LUTS with an enlarged prostate = alpha-blocker; persistent symptoms despite long medical treatment = TURP.

stem: A patient with spinal metastasis presents with rapidly progressive paraparesis and fecal incontinence (level T something). His symptoms continue to worsen despite medical management. What is the most appropriate initial management?
highlight_terms_source: rapidly progressive paraparesis and fecal incontinence
continue to worsen despite medical management
why_right: This is metastatic spinal cord compression with "rapidly progressive paraparesis" and sphincter loss ("fecal incontinence") that keeps worsening despite medical management (steroids). Progressive deficit despite steroids is the indication for urgent surgical decompression (usually with stabilization, followed by radiotherapy), which gives the best chance of preserving or regaining walking and continence.
why_wrong_block:
A. Chemotherapy acts too slowly to relieve an acute compression; it is used only for very chemosensitive tumors alongside definitive local treatment.
B. Steroids are the first step to reduce cord edema, but they have already failed here; escalating them does not decompress the cord.
C. Conservative care would be right only for a patient unfit for surgery or with very poor prognosis; with a progressing deficit it risks permanent paraplegia.
key_concept:
Metastatic cord compression: steroids immediately, MRI whole spine, then decompress.
  • Red flags: back pain, leg weakness, sensory level, bladder/bowel dysfunction.
  • Immediate: high-dose dexamethasone.
  • Imaging: urgent MRI whole spine.
  • Progressive deficit, instability or failed medical therapy: urgent surgery then radiotherapy.
  • Unfit for surgery or radiosensitive tumor: radiotherapy.
exam_pearl: Worsening despite steroids is the trigger that turns the answer from radiotherapy/steroids to surgery.

stem: Pts in the 4th post op day complaining of fever only what is the best next ?
why_right: By the postoperative fever timeline, fever on days 4 to 5 points to surgical site (wound) infection or DVT. On the 4th post-op day with fever as the only complaint, the best next step is to examine the wound for redness, warmth, discharge or collection; if infection is found, the wound is opened and drained.
why_wrong_block:
A. CBC: may support infection but does not localize the source; the decisive next step is the targeted bedside examination of the surgical site.
B. Urine culture: UTI is the classic cause on days 2 to 3 (especially after catheterization); on day 4 the wound comes first.
D. Review medication: drug fever is a diagnosis of exclusion, considered later when no infectious source is found.
key_concept:
Post-operative fever by day.
  • Day 1: atelectasis (or early necrotizing wound infection)
  • Days 2 to 3: UTI, superficial thrombophlebitis, pneumonia
  • Days 4 to 5: surgical site infection, DVT
  • Day 6 and beyond: wound dehiscence, deep collection or abscess (CT)
  • SSI management: open the wound and drain; CT if deep infection suspected
exam_pearl: Day 3 fever pushes you to the urine; day 4 to 5 fever pushes you to the wound.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler note: It Was "Wound Exploration", Not "Wound Assessment".

stem: A 70-year-old female presents with a complaint of rectal pain and passing mucus. This exact picture was shown: What is the diagnosis?
why_right: The image shows circumferential, concentric mucosal folds protruding through the anus in a 70-year-old woman with mucus discharge and rectal discomfort. Full-thickness rectal prolapse is typical of elderly women (weak pelvic floor, chronic straining), and the exposed mucosa secretes mucus. Concentric rings indicate the whole rectal wall has prolapsed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Skin tag: a small, soft, skin-covered flap at the anal verge, often painless or linked to a fissure; it is not a mucosal, circumferential protrusion.
C. Haemorrhoid: prolapsed hemorrhoids appear as separate cushions with radial grooves between them, and classically present with painless bright red bleeding, not concentric circular folds.
key_concept:
Anal protrusion: read the folds.
  • Concentric (circular) folds: full-thickness rectal prolapse
  • Radial folds, separate cushions: prolapsed hemorrhoids or mucosal prolapse
  • Small skin-covered tag: skin tag (sentinel tag with a posterior fissure)
  • Rectal prolapse: elderly women, straining, mucus, incontinence
  • Treatment: surgical (perineal approach in frail elderly, abdominal rectopexy if fit)
exam_pearl: Concentric rings = rectal prolapse; radial grooves = hemorrhoids.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Photo shows circumferential concentric mucosal folds protruding from the anus.

stem: Patient in 60s diagnosed with prostate cancer presenting with back pain (and maybe lower limb weakness). What is the appropriate next step for him?
why_wrong_block:
A. IV hydrocortisone captures the steroid idea, but the steroid of choice for cord edema is dexamethasone, and steroid alone without urgent MRI leaves the level and cause of compression undefined.
B. MRI is the right test, but outpatient timing is wrong: suspected cord compression needs same-day imaging, because delay risks permanent paralysis and sphincter loss. Outpatient MRI suits chronic mechanical back pain without red flags.
key_concept:
Back pain in a patient with cancer = spinal cord compression until proven otherwise.
  • Commonest culprits: prostate, breast, lung (bone metastases to spine)
  • Immediate: high-dose IV dexamethasone
  • Imaging: urgent whole spine MRI (not outpatient)
  • Definitive: radiotherapy or surgical decompression after MRI
  • A normal neuro exam does not exclude impending compression
exam_pearl: Right idea, wrong detail: hydrocortisone instead of dexamethasone, or MRI booked outpatient, are both traps in a cancer patient with back pain.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Both options crossed out with pen X marks. Embedded AI note: suspected spinal cord compression (oncologic emergency); neither A nor B correct; correct: urgent (not outpatient) whole spine MRI and high-dose IV corticosteroids, typically dexamethasone not hydrocortisone. Outpatient MRI inappropriate given urgency.
Other marked answers: Screenshot Answer line: A (IV hydrocortisone)

stem: A young man was brought to the Emergency Department after he was hit in the chest while playing football. On examination, he was dyspneic and drowsy with GCS 11/15. Tracheal shifting to the left and raised JVP were noted. He has barely audible breath sounds on the right side. Blood pressure 80/50 mmHg Heart rate 130 /min Respiratory rate 32 /min Temperature 36.6 °C Oxygen saturation 90% Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: barely audible breath sounds on the right side
why_right: After a chest blow, this man has barely audible breath sounds on the right, trachea shifted to the left (away from the silent side), raised JVP and shock (BP 80/50, HR 130). That combination of unilateral silent chest, contralateral tracheal deviation, distended neck veins and hypotension is a right tension pneumothorax, an obstructive shock needing immediate decompression.
why_wrong_block:
A. Flail segment needs multiple rib fractures with paradoxical chest wall movement; it causes hypoxia and pain but does not shift the trachea or raise the JVP.
B. Cardiac tamponade also gives raised JVP and hypotension (Beck triad with muffled heart sounds), but breath sounds stay equal and the trachea stays central; it is typical of penetrating injury.
C. Pulmonary contusion causes hypoxia and crackles developing over hours, but no tracheal deviation, raised JVP or obstructive shock.
key_concept:
Raised JVP + hypotension after chest trauma: decide tension vs tamponade by the lungs and trachea.
  • Tension pneumothorax: silent hyperresonant side, trachea shifted away, raised JVP, shock
  • Tamponade: equal breath sounds, central trachea, muffled heart sounds, pulsus paradoxus
  • Massive hemothorax: silent DULL side, flat neck veins
  • Flail chest: paradoxical segment, supportive care
  • Tension treatment: needle decompression then chest tube (clinical diagnosis, no X-ray first)
exam_pearl: Silent side + distended neck veins = tension; silent side + flat neck veins and dullness = massive hemothorax.
compiler_note: Compiler note: 'Q:' variant: MVA with distended neck vein, trachea shifted to the other side, absent sound, hyperresonance on percussion, BP 80/60; options Cardiac tamponade / Massive hemithorax / Tension pneumothorax (highlighted, consistent).

stem: Lesser sac 9 cm cyst posterior to the stomach
highlight_terms_source: 9 cm cyst posterior to the stomach
key_concept:
Lesser sac cyst behind the stomach: the history and cyst features decide pseudocyst versus neoplasm.
  • Pseudocyst: homogenous, thin wall, more than 4 weeks after pancreatitis; CT is the best imaging
  • Small, young or asymptomatic: observe; large, persistent or growing: endoscopic (internal) drainage
  • Fever, leukocytosis, gas or thick irregular wall: abscess or infected collection, percutaneous drainage
  • Septations, solid parts, no pancreatitis history: think cystic neoplasm
exam_pearl: Without a pancreatitis history and with septations or solid components, the same location points to a cystic neoplasm, not a pseudocyst.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 6 or 7 years old child fell and subsequently became drowsy, nauseated, and started vomiting. GCS is decreased but not ≤8 (I don't remember exactly) CT scan shows a crescent shaped intracranial bleeding. What is the best management?
why_right: After a fall, the child became drowsy, nauseated and vomiting with a reduced GCS, and CT shows a crescent-shaped bleed, which is a subdural hematoma (torn bridging veins). A symptomatic acute traumatic hematoma with neurological deterioration and raised intracranial pressure signs needs urgent neurosurgical evacuation to relieve mass effect. Because the GCS is not ≤8 and the airway is maintained, definitive decompression takes priority over intubation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Intubation is indicated for GCS ≤8, inability to protect the airway, hypoxia or aspiration risk; here the GCS is reduced but above 8, so the airway is not the immediate problem.
C. Reassurance fits a minor head injury with normal GCS and no imaging findings; a child with vomiting, drowsiness and an intracranial bleed on CT cannot be reassured.
D. CT already made the diagnosis and is the test of choice for acute head trauma; MRI only delays treatment and is reserved for subacute or subtle injuries (for example diffuse axonal injury).
key_concept:
Acute intracranial bleed on CT + deterioration = surgical evacuation.
  • Subdural: crescent (concave), bridging veins
  • Epidural: lens (biconvex), middle meningeal artery, lucid interval
  • CT without contrast is the first imaging in head trauma
  • Intubate if GCS ≤8 or airway not protected
  • Small, asymptomatic hematoma without shift: may be observed with serial CT
exam_pearl: If the stem gave GCS ≤8, airway first; with GCS above 8 and a symptomatic bleed, go to evacuation.

stem: A 23-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department after he fell down from 3 m height on his right leg. Examination revealed a deformity of the leg with an open wound in the mid-leg and devitalized tissue and dirt in the wound. The leg was put in a splint Blood pressure 112/70 mmhg Heart rate 99 /min Respiratory rate 22 /min Oxygen saturation 95 % Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
highlight_terms_source: devitalized tissue and dirt in the wound
key_concept:
A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to Surgical debridement (antibiotics-first is argued as the alternative).
  • Open fracture sequence: IV antibiotics + tetanus, splint or reduce
  • Then urgent debridement and irrigation in theatre
  • Then definitive fixation: IM nail, or external fixator if soft tissues are badly damaged
  • Lead-in decides: first step in ED = antibiotics; surgical next step = debridement
exam_pearl: If the stem says antibiotics were already given, debridement is unequivocally next.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: BP printed as '11270 mmhg' (likely 112/70).
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A patient with diabetes presents with swelling of the big toe and warmth and tenderness of the calf for 4 days. There is a 2-cm ulcer over the first metatarsal area. No discharge is noted. Distal pulses are intact. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
highlight_terms_source: warmth and tenderness of the calf
why_right: The decisive clues are warmth and tenderness of the calf for 4 days with limb swelling and intact distal pulses: arterial insufficiency is unlikely and deep vein thrombosis (or venous disease) must be excluded. Duplex ultrasound is the non-invasive, first-line test that assesses venous flow and thrombus (and can also assess arterial flow), so it is the most appropriate initial investigation.
why_wrong_block:
B. Conventional angiography is invasive arterial imaging used for intervention planning in established arterial disease; with intact pulses it is not an initial test.
C. ABI is the first test for suspected peripheral arterial disease (claudication, absent pulses, arterial ulcer); it does not detect DVT and is often falsely high in diabetics with calcified vessels.
D. CT with contrast (or CT angiography) suits acute limb ischemia or deep abscess or osteomyelitis planning; it is not the initial test for a warm tender calf and carries contrast risk in a diabetic.
key_concept:
Leg problem: check the pulses first, then pick the test.
  • Pulses intact + calf swelling, warmth, tenderness: duplex ultrasound for DVT
  • Pulses intact + gaiter ulcer: venous duplex
  • Absent pulses, claudication: ABI first, then arterial duplex, then CT angiography
  • Acute ischemia (sudden pain, absent pulses): CT angiography
exam_pearl: A diabetic foot ulcer is a distractor here; the warm tender calf with intact pulses makes it a venous question.

stem: Patient post op 6 days of colectomy. Have muscle weakness fatigue and palpitation Potassium 2.5 (low) What is most critical to check?
OptC: Check diet in the past week
why_right: A patient 6 days after colectomy (GI losses, ileus, NG drainage) has K 2.5 with muscle weakness, fatigue and palpitations, meaning severe symptomatic hypokalemia. Severe hypokalemia can paralyze the respiratory muscles and cause arrhythmia, so in an ABC order the most critical thing to check first is respiratory distress (airway and breathing), alongside cardiac monitoring and IV potassium replacement.
why_wrong_block:
B. ABG is useful later (metabolic alkalosis often accompanies GI potassium loss), but it is a laboratory test, not the immediate life-threat assessment.
C. Dietary history helps explain chronic low potassium, but it does not change emergency management of a symptomatic K of 2.5 after surgery.
D. Monitoring urine output matters before giving potassium (to avoid hyperkalemia in renal failure), but it is not the most critical danger to check in a weak patient whose breathing may be failing.
key_concept:
Severe hypokalemia: secure ABC, monitor the heart, replace IV.
  • Features: weakness, cramps, ileus, palpitations, flattened T waves and U waves
  • Danger: respiratory muscle weakness and arrhythmia
  • Postop causes: GI losses, NG suction, diarrhea, diuretics
  • Treatment: IV potassium if severe (below 2.5), symptomatic or ECG changes; oral if mild
  • Check magnesium if potassium does not correct
exam_pearl: If ECG or cardiac monitoring were offered, it would compete strongly; among these options, breathing comes first.

stem: Patient presented to the ER with pelvic fracture, he is actively bleeding with a large hematoma in the pelvis, his BP = 80/50 (or something near to this), most appropriate management?
key_concept:
Unstable pelvic fracture: resuscitate, bind, then control the bleeding vessel.
  • Hemorrhagic shock: blood products early (balanced transfusion)
  • Pelvic binder to reduce pelvic volume
  • FAST to look for an abdominal source
  • FAST positive: laparotomy; FAST negative: angioembolization or preperitoneal packing
  • Most pelvic bleeding is venous or from fracture surfaces; arterial bleeding suits angioembolization
exam_pearl: A pelvic hematoma alone is not an indication for laparotomy; a positive FAST is.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 72 year old female underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Post operatively she complains of fever, tachycardia and leukocytosis. In examination of the wound there was slight erythema and no pus formation. Temperature: 38.6, HR: 116, BP: 90/60. Which of the following is most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: slight erythema and no pus formation
why_right: She meets several SIRS criteria at once: temperature "38.6" (above 38), "HR 116" (above 90) and "leukocytosis". The wound shows only "slight erythema and no pus", so no infective source is confirmed, which makes SIRS the best label rather than an infection diagnosis. SIRS is the body's systemic response to the surgical insult itself and is common early after an operation. The "BP 90/60" is not a SIRS criterion; it signals possible evolving sepsis, but sepsis still needs an identified or suspected infective source.
why_wrong_block:
A. Thrombophilia is a predisposition to clotting, not a cause of fever with leukocytosis; it would matter only if she presented with DVT or PE.
B. UTI is a classic cause of fever around postoperative days 2 to 3, but nothing here points to it (no urinary symptoms, no catheter or urinalysis findings).
C. Surgical site infection needs real wound signs such as purulent discharge, spreading cellulitis or a collection, typically around days 4 to 5; slight erythema without pus does not establish it.
key_concept:
SIRS = 2 or more criteria; sepsis = SIRS plus a confirmed or suspected infection.
  • Temperature above 38 or below 36
  • HR above 90
  • RR above 20 or PaCO2 below 32 mmHg
  • WBC above 12,000, below 4,000 or more than 10% bands
  • Severe sepsis = sepsis plus organ dysfunction; septic shock = refractory hypotension
  • Postop fever: D1 atelectasis; D2 to 3 UTI, pneumonia, thrombophlebitis; D4 to 5 wound infection, DVT
exam_pearl: Criteria met but no proven source = SIRS; add a pus-draining wound or positive urine and it becomes sepsis.

stem: A patient presents after total thyroidectomy with numbness around the mouth and in the peripheral limbs. What is the most likely cause?
OptD: Hypocalcemia due to vitamin D deficiency
why_right: "Numbness around the mouth and in the peripheral limbs" after "total thyroidectomy" is the classic picture of hypocalcaemia. The cause is hypoparathyroidism from injury, devascularisation or inadvertent removal of the parathyroid glands, usually appearing within 24 to 72 hours. Look for Chvostek and Trousseau signs and check serum calcium.
why_wrong_block:
B. Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes hoarseness, aspiration or stridor (if bilateral), not perioral and limb paresthesia.
C. Postoperative hypothyroidism develops over weeks as stored hormone runs out and gives fatigue, cold intolerance and weight gain, not acute tingling.
D. It does produce hypocalcaemia, but vitamin D deficiency is a chronic background cause; symptoms starting right after total thyroidectomy point to parathyroid damage.
key_concept:
Post-thyroidectomy complications by presentation:
  • Neck swelling with stridor within hours: hematoma, open the wound at the bedside
  • Hoarseness or aspiration: recurrent laryngeal nerve
  • Loss of high-pitched voice: superior laryngeal nerve
  • Perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm: hypoparathyroidism, so hypocalcaemia
  • Refractory hypocalcaemia: check magnesium
exam_pearl: Tingling after thyroidectomy = parathyroids, not nerves; voice change = nerves.

stem: 14 year old pt with ulcerative colitis failed to respond to many medical therapies. Patient has fulminant disease complicated by toxic megacolon, which of the following is the most appropriate URGENT treatment?
highlight_terms_source: fulminant disease complicated by toxic megacolon
why_right: UC that has "failed to respond to many medical therapies" and is now "fulminant" with "toxic megacolon" carries a high risk of perforation, so the URGENT definitive treatment is surgery. The emergency operation is a subtotal/total colectomy with end ileostomy, done after rapid resuscitation (IV fluids, nil by mouth, IV antibiotics and steroids). These supportive measures stabilise the patient for surgery but do not replace it once medical therapy has failed.
why_wrong_block:
B. Methotrexate is a slow-acting maintenance immunomodulator with no role in acute severe colitis or toxic megacolon.
C. IV broad-spectrum antibiotics are part of supportive care for toxic megacolon, but they treat translocation and sepsis risk, not the failing colon; alone they are not the urgent treatment after failed medical therapy.
D. TPN or bowel rest is supportive nutrition only and does nothing for the toxic dilated colon; it would only be the answer for nutritional support questions.
key_concept:
Toxic megacolon in UC: resuscitate, then decide surgery early.
  • Toxic megacolon: colon dilated above 6 cm plus systemic toxicity (fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis)
  • Initial: IV fluids, NPO, bowel decompression, IV steroids, IV antibiotics
  • Failed medical therapy, perforation or worsening: urgent colectomy
  • Emergency operation: subtotal/total colectomy with end ileostomy
  • Ileal pouch reconstruction is a later elective stage, never in the emergency
exam_pearl: If the stem says medical therapy has already failed, the answer is colectomy, not more drugs.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Original recall: '14 y old boy with ulcerative colitis have toxic megacolon. Urgent management? A - IV fluid and avoid oral intake, B - colectomy, C - Antibiotics, D - Methotrexate' (unmarked).

stem: A 68-year-old man has been advised to undergo surgical treatment for a left reducible inguinal hernia. He is otherwise healthy. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
why_right: An "otherwise healthy" man with a primary, unilateral, "reducible inguinal hernia" who has been advised surgery gets a tension-free open mesh repair (Lichtenstein). Mesh lowers recurrence compared with suture repair, and the open approach is the standard default for a first unilateral hernia.
why_wrong_block:
A. Simple (suture or tissue) repair without mesh has a higher recurrence rate; it is reserved for situations where mesh is avoided, such as a contaminated field.
C. Laparoscopic repair is preferred for bilateral or recurrent hernias, when faster recovery is a priority, or for femoral hernia; none applies here.
D. Non-surgical management (watchful waiting) suits minimally symptomatic patients or those unfit for surgery; this patient is healthy and already advised to have surgery.
key_concept:
Choosing the inguinal hernia repair:
  • Primary unilateral, healthy adult: open mesh (Lichtenstein)
  • Bilateral: laparoscopic
  • Recurrent after open repair: laparoscopic (operate through fresh planes)
  • Need for faster return to work: laparoscopic
  • Strangulated or contaminated: emergency open repair, mesh often avoided
exam_pearl: Bilateral or recurrent flips the answer to laparoscopic; a single primary hernia stays open mesh.

stem: Patient did thyroidectomy he developed a peri oral tingling so diagnosis?
key_concept:
Match the post-thyroidectomy symptom to its cause:
  • Perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm: hypoparathyroidism, check calcium
  • Fever, tachycardia, agitation: thyroid storm
  • Hoarseness: recurrent laryngeal nerve
  • Loss of high pitch: superior laryngeal nerve
  • Neck swelling with stridor: hematoma
exam_pearl: Paresthesia = calcium problem; hyperthermia and tachycardia = thyroid storm.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Patient hypertensive, tachycardic, no obvious external injury. What is the type of shock?
key_concept:
Read HR and skin to type the shock.
  • Hypovolemic: HR up, cold peripheries, SVR up
  • Neurogenic: HR normal or low, warm peripheries, SVR down, neuro deficit
  • Septic: HR up, warm early, infection source
  • Cardiogenic: HR up, cold, raised PCWP
  • Obstructive: tamponade, tension pneumothorax, massive PE
exam_pearl: Tachycardia rules toward hemorrhage; bradycardia with warm skin after trauma is the neurogenic clue.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Recall says 'hypertensive' (likely meant hypotensive).
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Hypotensive tachycardic GCS low
key_concept:
ATLS order: treat what kills first.
  • A: airway with cervical spine protection; intubate if GCS 8 or less
  • B: breathing, decompress tension pneumothorax
  • C: circulation, stop bleeding, IV fluids or blood
  • D: disability, GCS and pupils
  • E: exposure with temperature control
  • Secondary (head-to-toe) survey and imaging only after stabilisation
exam_pearl: Fluids are part of C; when asked for the first step, the whole ABCDE primary survey beats any single intervention.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Numbered 1234 is a fragmentary recall with no marked answer.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 25 year-old MVA patient. Suffering head trauma in the process. He is conscious but disoriented
why_right: Any "MVA" trauma patient starts with the primary survey (ABCDE) to find and treat immediate life threats, even when "conscious". Being "disoriented" after "head trauma" is assessed under D (GCS, pupils), but airway, breathing and circulation must be secured first. Imaging and detailed examination come only after the primary survey and resuscitation.
why_wrong_block:
B. Head CT is indicated (GCS below 15 after head injury), but only once the primary survey is complete and the patient is stable enough for the scanner.
C. Head-to-toe examination is the secondary survey, done after the primary survey and resuscitation, not first.
D. Observation is unsafe in a disoriented patient after a road traffic accident; it suits a fully alert patient with minor head injury and no CT criteria.
key_concept:
Trauma sequence: primary survey, resuscitation, secondary survey, definitive care.
  • Primary: Airway with C-spine, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure
  • Disability: GCS and pupils identify head injury severity
  • GCS 8 or less: secure a definitive airway
  • Secondary survey: head-to-toe exam and history
  • Imaging such as head CT follows stabilisation
exam_pearl: Head CT is tempting with confusion after head injury, but nothing comes before ABCDE.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Unnumbered 'Q:' follow-up printed under 1234; lead-in question not recalled.

stem: 55-year-old woman presents with a scaly, oozing lesion on the right nipple for the past few weeks. On physical examination, no palpable breast masses are found. Breast ultrasound and mammogram are normal. What is the next best step in management?
highlight_terms_source: scaly, oozing lesion on the right nipple
why_right: A "scaly, oozing lesion" of the nipple persisting for weeks in a "55-year-old" is Paget disease of the nipple until proven otherwise. Normal mammogram and ultrasound do not exclude it, since it may be confined to the nipple or associated with occult DCIS. The diagnosis is confirmed by a nipple (punch, wedge or full-thickness) biopsy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Referring to dermatology delays tissue diagnosis of a possible malignancy; eczema that is bilateral, itchy and spares the nipple or responds to treatment may suit dermatology, a unilateral nipple lesion does not.
B. A topical steroid trial can falsely improve Paget disease and delay diagnosis; it is reasonable only for typical bilateral areolar eczema, with biopsy if it fails.
key_concept:
Paget disease of the nipple vs eczema:
  • Paget: unilateral, starts on the nipple then spreads to areola, older woman
  • Eczema: often bilateral, itchy, starts on the areola, spares the nipple
  • Normal imaging does not exclude Paget
  • Diagnosis: nipple biopsy
  • Most cases have underlying DCIS or invasive cancer
exam_pearl: Persistent unilateral nipple eczema in an older woman = biopsy, not steroids.

stem: A 45-year-old obese woman presented with 1-week history of jaundice, anorexia and abdominal pain. She has no chronic illnesses and not on any medications. On examination, she is jaundiced with stable vital signs and no fever. Abdomen exam showed mild tender liver with span of 13 cm, no splenomegaly. Labs: RBC 4 (4.2-5.4 female), Hb 110 g/L (120-160 female), platelets 212, WBC 18 (4.5-10.5), direct bilirubin 79 (1.5-6.5), total bilirubin 98 (3.5-16.5), AST 70 (12-40), ALT 150 (5-40), alkaline phosphatase 1000 (39-117). Which of the following is the next step in the management?
OptD: Abdominal CT scan of the liver
why_right: A raised "direct bilirubin 79" with a markedly raised "alkaline phosphatase 1000" and only modest transaminase rise is a cholestatic pattern. The first step is abdominal ultrasound to check whether the bile ducts are dilated, separating extrahepatic obstruction (such as stones in an "obese" 45-year-old woman) from intrahepatic cholestasis. It is cheap, noninvasive and widely available.
why_wrong_block:
A. MRCP is second-line imaging, used when ultrasound is equivocal or to define the level and cause of an obstruction before intervention.
B. Liver biopsy is invasive and only considered for intrahepatic cholestasis after imaging excludes duct obstruction.
D. CT is less sensitive than ultrasound for gallstones and adds radiation and contrast; it suits suspected malignancy or staging after ultrasound.
key_concept:
Approach to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia:
  • High AST and ALT: hepatocellular injury
  • High ALP and GGT: cholestasis, then ultrasound
  • Dilated ducts: obstruction (stones, tumor, PSC), then MRCP or ERCP
  • Normal ducts: intrahepatic causes (PBC, drugs, sepsis, pregnancy)
exam_pearl: Cholestatic labs always mean ultrasound first; MRCP and ERCP come after.

stem: A 20-30s male patient presented to the ER complaining of a perianal painful lump for 12 hours, which he felt after the passage of a hard stool. On exam, there is a 1 x 1 cm dome-shaped, bluish, tender swelling just beneath the perianal skin. What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: This recall is keyed to lateral sphincterotomy, reasoning that the lump followed straining with a "hard stool", which links it to anal sphincter spasm as in fissure disease. Note that the actual findings (a "painful lump" for "12 hours", "1 x 1 cm dome-shaped, bluish, tender" swelling "just beneath the perianal skin") describe a perianal hematoma (thrombosed external hemorrhoid). Sphincterotomy is the standard operation for a chronic anal fissure; see the concern note before relying on this key.
why_wrong_block:
A. Conservative care (analgesia, stool softeners, sitz baths) is the standard approach for a perianal hematoma that presents late (beyond about 72 hours) or with mild pain; this recall's key instead targets the sphincter.
B. Rubber band ligation is for internal hemorrhoids above the dentate line (grade I to III); it must never be applied to an external, sensate lump below the dentate line, which is what this is.
D. Aspiration does not empty a thrombosed external hemorrhoid because the content is clotted blood; early evacuation is done by incision or excision, not needle aspiration.
key_concept:
Painful bluish perianal lump after straining = perianal hematoma (thrombosed external hemorrhoid).
  • Early (within about 72 h), severe pain: incision/excision and evacuation of the clot under local anesthesia
  • Late or mild: conservative (analgesia, sitz baths, stool softeners)
  • Same lump + fever + raised WBC = perianal abscess: incision and drainage
  • Chronic fissure (>6 weeks): lateral internal sphincterotomy
  • Acute fissure (<6 weeks): topical diltiazem plus constipation treatment
  • Rubber band ligation: internal hemorrhoids only
exam_pearl: A LUMP points to hematoma or abscess; sharp pain on defecation with NO lump points to fissure, the only one where sphincterotomy applies.

stem: Old age male with lesion on right thigh. Lesion was well demarcated, red, painful to touch. What's the next investigation?
highlight_terms_source: well demarcated, red, painful to touch
why_right: A "well demarcated, red, painful to touch" lesion on the thigh of an older man is an inflammatory or infective skin picture (erysipelas or cellulitis), not a pigmented tumour. The question asks for the "next investigation", and ultrasound is the quick bedside test that shows whether there is an underlying abscess (which would need drainage) and helps exclude a deeper collection. It is cheap, fast and radiation free.
why_wrong_block:
A. Punch biopsy is for a suspicious skin lesion needing histology (an atypical rash or a possible tumour); an acute tender red area is an infection picture, not a reason for biopsy.
B. MRI is reserved for suspected deep infection such as necrotizing fasciitis (only if it does not delay surgery), osteomyelitis or a soft tissue mass; it is not the first test for a superficial red lesion.
C. X-ray helps only if gas in soft tissues, a foreign body or bone involvement is suspected; it cannot show a soft tissue fluid collection.
key_concept:
Red, tender, demarcated skin lesion = soft tissue infection; image to look for pus.
  • Erysipelas: sharply demarcated, raised, tender, fever; group A strep; penicillin
  • Cellulitis: ill-defined redness after minor trauma
  • Suspected abscess: ultrasound, then drain any collection
  • Necrotizing infection: surgery first, imaging must not delay it
  • Pigmented irregular lesion: excisional biopsy, not ultrasound
exam_pearl: Red and painful = infection, so ultrasound for pus; dark and irregular = melanoma, so excisional biopsy.

stem: Female came to the ER after MVA with severe abdominal pain, BP 83/50 (no Hb level was mentioned). What is the initial step?
why_right: After an "MVA" with "severe abdominal pain" and "BP 83/50", this patient is in hemorrhagic shock from presumed intra-abdominal bleeding. Current trauma resuscitation (ATLS) favours early blood products over large volumes of crystalloid in a hypotensive trauma patient, so packed RBC transfusion is the initial step while the bleeding source is identified. A normal Hb at this point would not be reassuring, because Hb lags behind acute blood loss.
why_wrong_block:
A. Crystalloid may be started as a limited bolus, but "observe" is unsafe in a hypotensive trauma patient; large crystalloid volumes dilute clotting factors and worsen bleeding.
B. Laparotomy is the definitive step for an unstable patient with a positive FAST or peritonitis, but resuscitation with blood starts first and runs alongside the decision to operate.
key_concept:
Hypotensive blunt abdominal trauma: resuscitate with blood, then FAST decides.
  • Stable: CT abdomen
  • Unstable blunt: FAST
  • Unstable + FAST positive: laparotomy
  • Unstable + FAST negative: DPL / look for another source
  • Unstable stab wound: laparotomy
  • Hemorrhagic shock: early blood products, limit crystalloid
exam_pearl: Do not wait for an Hb result in a hypotensive trauma patient; Hb lags behind acute bleeding.

stem: Young female presented to ER with severe shoulder pain, with visible deformity of the shoulder, inability to abduct the arm. What is the next step in evaluation?
why_right: "Severe shoulder pain", a "visible deformity" and "inability to abduct the arm" suggest a shoulder dislocation (most often anterior) or a proximal humerus fracture. Plain X-ray (AP plus a lateral or axillary view) is the first investigation: it confirms the dislocation and its direction and shows any associated fracture before reduction is attempted.
why_wrong_block:
A. MRI is for soft tissue injury such as a rotator cuff or labral tear, usually after reduction or for persistent symptoms; it is not the first test for an acute deformity.
B. CT is used for complex fractures (for example of the glenoid or humeral head) when X-ray is inconclusive or for surgical planning, not as the first step.
D. Surgical exploration is for hard signs of vascular injury (pulseless limb, expanding hematoma); nothing here suggests a vascular injury, and a dislocation is reduced closed after X-ray.
key_concept:
Suspected dislocation or fracture: X-ray first, then reduce.
  • Anterior dislocation (most common): arm held abducted and externally rotated, squared-off shoulder
  • Posterior dislocation: seizure or electric shock, arm adducted and internally rotated
  • Check axillary nerve (sensation over the deltoid) before and after reduction
  • Post-reduction X-ray to confirm position
  • MRI later for rotator cuff or labral tears
exam_pearl: Always X-ray before reducing a shoulder: a hidden fracture changes the plan.

stem: Patient underwent sigmoidectomy using previously used surgical instruments. Which measure now helps reduce the risk of surgical site infection? (it was written what will reduce in this scenario)
why_right: The scenario's problem is that "previously used surgical instruments" were used, so the measure that removes this source of contamination is proper sterilization of instruments before the next operation. The question is general rather than about this patient: nothing done now reverses the exposure, but correct instrument sterilization is what prevents surgical site infection going forward.
why_wrong_block:
A. Antibiotic prophylaxis works when given before incision (within about an hour); continuing antibiotics after surgery does not lower SSI rates and promotes resistance, so it is not recommended.
B. Keeping the patient warm during surgery is a genuine SSI-reducing measure in general, but it does not address this scenario's specific failure, which is contaminated instruments.
D. Unsterile instruments clearly raise infection risk, so saying there is no effect on the wound is false.
key_concept:
SSI prevention bundle (match the measure to the failure in the stem).
  • Sterile instruments and aseptic technique
  • Prophylactic antibiotic before incision, not prolonged afterwards
  • Hair removal by clipping, not shaving
  • Normothermia and glucose control
  • Skin antisepsis (chlorhexidine-alcohol)
exam_pearl: Prophylactic antibiotics count only BEFORE the incision; postoperative antibiotics are a classic wrong answer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: The Q is general, not about this patient.

stem: 56 year old male, past history of peptic ulcer, present to ER with severe abdominal pain, tenderness all abdomen, guarding, Rebound, Skin cool and clammy, Hypotensive 87/60, Heart rate 120, Initial management?
why_right: A "past history of peptic ulcer" with generalized tenderness, "guarding, Rebound" points to a perforated peptic ulcer with peritonitis. The patient is in shock ("Skin cool and clammy", BP "87/60", HR "120") from fluid loss into the peritoneum, so the initial step is IV fluid resuscitation. Laparotomy is the definitive treatment, but it follows resuscitation.
why_wrong_block:
B. Laparotomy (omental patch for a duodenal ulcer) is the definitive treatment of a perforated ulcer, but it comes after fluid resuscitation; operating on a hypovolemic patient is dangerous.
C. Vasopressors are only for shock that persists after adequate fluid; giving them to a volume-depleted patient worsens organ perfusion.
key_concept:
Perforated peptic ulcer: resuscitate, confirm, operate.
  • Clinical picture: sudden severe pain, rigidity, rebound, absent bowel sounds
  • Initial: IV fluids, NPO, NG tube, IV PPI, IV antibiotics
  • Imaging: erect chest X-ray for free air under the diaphragm
  • Duodenal perforation: omental (Graham) patch
  • Gastric perforation: biopsy the edge (exclude cancer) and patch or excise; gastrectomy only for large or malignant ulcers
exam_pearl: "Initial" management in any shocked surgical abdomen is fluid; "definitive" is surgery.
compiler_note: Compiler note: A follow-up 'Q:' version (BP 85/55, options IV fluid / vasopressor / blood transfusion / antibiotic) is carded separately; it also highlights IV fluid.

stem: Known case of peptic ulcer presented with abdominal pain tenderness and rebound tenderness with guarding blood pressure was 85/55 and tachycardia 120 what the initial management?
why_right: A "known case of peptic ulcer" with tenderness, "rebound tenderness with guarding" means a perforated ulcer with peritonitis, and "85/55" with "tachycardia 120" means shock. The "initial management" is IV fluid (crystalloid) to restore circulating volume; antibiotics, imaging and surgery follow once resuscitation is under way.
why_wrong_block:
B. Vasopressors are added only when hypotension persists despite adequate fluid; in a volume-depleted patient they worsen tissue perfusion.
C. Blood transfusion is for hemorrhagic shock (for example a bleeding ulcer with melena or hematemesis and a low Hb); here the picture is perforation with peritonitis, not bleeding.
D. IV antibiotics are part of managing perforation and peritonitis, but restoring circulation comes first in a hypotensive patient.
key_concept:
Peptic ulcer complications: the picture decides the first move.
  • Perforation + shock: IV fluid first, then antibiotics, PPI, laparotomy
  • Bleeding ulcer + shock: fluid resuscitation, transfuse if Hb low, then endoscopy
  • Vasopressors: only after adequate volume
  • Erect chest X-ray: free air confirms perforation
exam_pearl: Peritonitis signs point to perforation (fluid, then surgery); melena or hematemesis points to bleeding (fluid or blood, then endoscopy).
compiler_note: Compiler note: Unnumbered 'Q:' variant printed under 1281 (numbered version had options IV fluid / laparotomy / vasopressor).

stem: After minor Injury painful swelling in forearm with warmth Next step?
key_concept:
Warm painful swelling after minor injury: decide by fluctuance and toxicity.
  • Diffuse, no fluctuance: cellulitis, antibiotics (IV if systemic or severe)
  • Fluctuant or collection on ultrasound: abscess, incision and drainage
  • Pain out of proportion, toxicity, purple skin: necrotizing fasciitis, urgent surgery + IV antibiotics
  • Firm enlarging mass, not inflamed: imaging + biopsy, then wide excision if sarcoma
exam_pearl: Fluctuance is the switch: no pus means antibiotics, pus means drainage.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: No answer marked for the numbered recall. The following unnumbered 'Q:' (5-year-old, pain out of proportion, purple discoloration) is a different question carded separately.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 5-year-old child presents to the emergency department with a rapidly progressive painful skin lesion. The pain is severe and disproportionate to the physical findings. Over a short period, the lesion has increased in size with progressive swelling and discoloration. On examination, the child is febrile and appears toxic, and the affected area shows erythema with patches of purple discoloration and marked tenderness. What to do?
OptB: surgical consultation and iv antibiotic (exactly like this)
highlight_terms_source: pain is severe and disproportionate to the physical findings
why_right: "Rapidly progressive" painful lesion, pain "disproportionate to the physical findings", a "toxic" febrile child and "patches of purple discoloration" describe necrotizing fasciitis. It is a surgical emergency: urgent surgical consultation for debridement plus broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, because the infection spreads along fascia faster than the skin shows.
why_wrong_block:
A. MRI can show fascial involvement, but waiting for imaging delays debridement and raises mortality; the diagnosis is clinical and confirmed in theatre. Imaging is only for unclear cases in a stable patient.
C. Topical antibiotics and analgesia suit only minor superficial infections such as impetigo; they have no role in a deep, life-threatening, toxic soft tissue infection.
key_concept:
Pain out of proportion + rapid spread + toxicity + skin discoloration = necrotizing fasciitis.
  • Treatment: urgent surgical debridement + broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
  • Usually polymicrobial; group A strep can cause it alone
  • Crepitus and foul smell suggest gas-forming organisms
  • Perineal and genital form: Fournier gangrene
  • Cellulitis: localized redness and pain, no toxicity, antibiotics alone
exam_pearl: Pain out of proportion to what you see is the flag that turns "cellulitis" into a surgical emergency.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Unnumbered 'Q:' variant printed under 1317 (numbered 1317 is a different forearm swelling recall).

stem: Patient presented with symptoms of appendicitis. Imaging: appendicitis, fecolith, appendicular abscess 1 x 15 cm reaching the flank. What is the management?
why_right: Imaging shows appendicitis with a fecolith and an established "appendicular abscess" (large, "reaching the flank"). An organized appendiceal abscess is treated by image-guided percutaneous drainage with IV antibiotics, followed by interval appendectomy. Operating early in this inflamed, friable field risks bowel injury, fistula and unplanned bowel resection.
why_wrong_block:
A. Open drainage is more invasive and is reserved for collections that cannot be reached percutaneously or when percutaneous drainage fails.
C. Removing the appendix now means dissecting through an inflamed, friable abscess cavity, with more complications (bowel injury, fistula, bowel resection); the appendix is taken out later as an interval procedure.
D. Laparoscopic appendectomy is right for uncomplicated appendicitis, but with an established abscess the appendix is removed later, after drainage.
key_concept:
Complicated appendicitis: match treatment to the CT finding.
  • Uncomplicated: laparoscopic appendectomy
  • Phlegmon (mass, no collection): IV antibiotics, conservative
  • Abscess: percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics + interval appendectomy
  • Small collection: antibiotics alone
  • Unstable or generalized peritonitis: surgery
exam_pearl: Abscess is drained first and the appendix removed later; phlegmon is treated with antibiotics only.

stem: 70 years old, 4 days post knee replacement No symptoms only labs HR 115 Temp 38.9 WBC 15 Xray: right lower lobe infilteration What is the most appropriate “INITIAL” step in management? (BP NOT MENTIONED) (It Literally Said INITIAL , NOT NEXT)
key_concept:
Post-op fever: think by day, then treat the cause; shock always takes priority.
  • Days 1 to 2: wind (atelectasis, early pneumonia, aspiration)
  • Days 3 to 5: water (UTI, catheter or line infection)
  • Days 5 to 7: wound (surgical site infection); DVT/PE from about day 5
  • Fever + tachycardia + WBC + new infiltrate = pneumonia with SIRS
  • Hypotensive: fluids and antibiotics together, within the first hour
  • Normotensive: cultures then broad-spectrum antibiotics
exam_pearl: "Initial" with no BP stated: fluids only if you are told about hypotension or poor perfusion; otherwise the infection itself is treated.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Typed version: Post op day 4 fever and + xray. What is the initial? A. IV fluids, B. Broad spectrum antibiotics. Fuller 'Q:' restatement continues on next page. No answer marked.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 22 year old female, has non tender, mobile, firm thyroid noqdule moves with tongue protrusion (She is not complaining of anything) US: Hypo echoic and inside it microcalcifications Size: 3 cm Most appropriate next step?
OptB: give thyroxine then reassess in 2 months
highlight_terms_source: Hypo echoic and inside it microcalcifications
why_right: A 3 cm nodule that is "hypoechoic" with "microcalcifications" has suspicious ultrasound features and is well above the size threshold for sampling, so the next step is FNA for cytology. Being young, asymptomatic and non-tender does not lower the concern; the ultrasound pattern decides. Cytology (Bethesda category) then dictates surgery or follow-up.
why_wrong_block:
B. TSH-suppressive thyroxine is not used to treat or shrink a suspicious nodule; it delays diagnosis of a possible carcinoma.
C. Discharge (or US follow-up) fits a sub-centimetre or purely benign-looking (e.g. spongiform, purely cystic) nodule; this one is 3 cm with malignant features.
D. Thyroidectomy follows cytology (e.g. suspicious or malignant Bethesda result) or compressive symptoms; operating before FNA skips the diagnosis.
key_concept:
Thyroid nodule workup: TSH + neck US, then decide on FNA.
  • Low TSH: scintigraphy (hot nodule rarely malignant)
  • Normal or high TSH: check FNA criteria
  • Suspicious US (hypoechoic, microcalcifications) ≥1 cm: FNA
  • Below criteria: US follow-up
  • FNA result (Bethesda) decides surgery
exam_pearl: If the stem gives a low TSH, the next step flips to a thyroid scan, not FNA.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Hypo-Echoic → FNA if 1 cm; if below 1 cm → Follow Up.

stem: diabetic patient presents with a foul-smelling ulcer. What is the most beneficial initial management step?
why_right: A "foul-smelling" diabetic ulcer implies infected, necrotic or sloughy tissue, and no wound heals or clears infection while dead tissue remains. Debridement is therefore the most beneficial initial step: it removes the bacterial load, lets you assess depth (bone, abscess) and obtain deep cultures. Every adjunct listed works only on a clean, debrided bed.
why_wrong_block:
B. Advanced dressings support a clean granulating wound after debridement; on necrotic, infected tissue they do not address the cause.
C. Hyperbaric oxygen is an adjunct for selected refractory or ischemic diabetic foot wounds that fail standard care, not a first step.
D. Negative pressure (VAC) therapy is for a non-healing wound or one at risk of non-healing, applied after debridement; it is contraindicated over untreated necrotic or grossly infected tissue.
key_concept:
Wound ladder: clean it first, then help it close.
  • Necrotic or foul tissue: debridement
  • Then secondary closure or grafting
  • Diabetic ulcer or bed sore at risk of non-healing: VAC after debridement
  • Infected diabetic foot: add antibiotics, check for osteomyelitis
  • HBOT: refractory cases only
exam_pearl: VAC is the answer only when the stem says the wound is already debrided or clean but not healing.

stem: post MI developed signs of DVT femoral pulse intact but all pulses below cannot be felt What is the most appropriate next step?
highlight_terms_source: femoral pulse intact but all pulses below cannot be felt
why_right: "Femoral pulse intact but all pulses below cannot be felt" is acute arterial occlusion, not DVT (the "DVT" wording is almost certainly a recall slip). After an MI, a left ventricular mural thrombus is a classic embolic source, so this is an embolus lodged at the femoral bifurcation, and the definitive treatment of embolic acute limb ischemia is (Fogarty balloon) embolectomy. Heparin would be given immediately, but it is not among the options.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oral warfarin is for long-term prevention after the event (e.g. mural thrombus or AF); it does nothing for an acutely threatened limb. The acute anticoagulant would be IV heparin.
C. Angiography helps when the cause is unclear (e.g. thrombosis on chronic PAD with claudication history) and the limb is not immediately threatened; a clear embolic source with sudden loss of pulses goes straight to embolectomy, and imaging should not delay surgery if there is a motor or sensory deficit.
D. Catheter-directed thrombolysis suits in situ thrombosis on atherosclerotic disease or distal small-vessel occlusion in a viable limb; a fresh cardiac embolus at a proximal bifurcation is removed surgically, which is faster and more reliable.
key_concept:
Acute limb ischemia: heparin first, then revascularize according to cause.
  • Embolic (AF, post-MI mural thrombus, no claudication history): embolectomy
  • Thrombotic (prior claudication, PAD risk factors): imaging, then thrombolysis or bypass
  • Irreversible limb (fixed paralysis, mottling): amputation
  • Pulse level localizes: femoral present, popliteal absent = femoral bifurcation or below
exam_pearl: "Next step" with heparin among the options: pick heparin; "definitive management" of an embolus: embolectomy.

stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because his parents noticed that his asymptomatic small olive shape mass and . On examination, the right testis is not palpable in the scrotum. What is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: right testis is not palpable in the scrotum
why_right: A 2-year-old with the "right testis not palpable in the scrotum" has an undescended testis well past the age at which spontaneous descent can be expected (about 6 months). Surgery is ideally done by 18 months, so at 2 years it is already due and should be done now to protect fertility, reduce torsion risk and allow future examination for malignancy. A palpable undescended testis is brought down by orchidopexy; a truly non-palpable one is located by diagnostic laparoscopy, then fixed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Waiting until age 5 increases the risk of germ cell damage and infertility; delay is never preferred once the window for spontaneous descent has passed.
C. Observation fits a newborn or infant under about 6 months, when spontaneous descent still occurs, or a retractile testis that can be brought into the scrotum and stays there.
key_concept:
Undescended testis: operate early, not late.
  • Under about 6 months: observe for spontaneous descent
  • Orchidopexy ideally by 6 to 18 months
  • Palpable (e.g. inguinal canal): orchidopexy
  • Non-palpable: diagnostic laparoscopy
  • Hormonal therapy: not recommended
  • Post-pubertal unilateral: consider orchidectomy
exam_pearl: Retractile testis (can be manipulated into the scrotum and stays) needs only reassurance, not surgery.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recall stem is garbled (mentions an 'olive shape mass'); compiler added a separate pyloric stenosis question after it (see 1340b).

stem: A 5-month-old baby was admitted with an inability to tolerate food and non-bilious vomiting over the past 2 days. On examination, he appears to be dehydrated. There is an olive-shaped mass palpable in the epigastric region measuring 2 × 2 cm. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: olive-shaped mass palpable in the epigastric region
why_right: "Non-bilious vomiting", dehydration and a palpable "olive-shaped mass" in the epigastrium are hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. The definitive treatment is Ramstedt pyloromyotomy, splitting the hypertrophied muscle. It is not an emergency: dehydration and the hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis are corrected with normal saline (plus potassium) first, then surgery. The age of 5 months is older than typical (2 to 8 weeks), but the findings are classic.
why_wrong_block:
B. Balloon dilatation is used for acquired adult pyloric stenosis (e.g. peptic scarring); infantile muscular hypertrophy is cured by pyloromyotomy.
C. Gastrojejunostomy is a bypass for adult gastric outlet obstruction such as malignancy; it is unnecessary and more morbid in an infant.
key_concept:
Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
  • First-born male, 2 to 8 weeks, projectile non-bilious vomiting, hungry after
  • Olive mass, visible peristalsis left to right
  • Labs: hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis
  • Diagnosis: ultrasound
  • Step 1: fluids and electrolytes (normal saline)
  • Step 2: Ramstedt pyloromyotomy
exam_pearl: If the lead-in asks "immediate" or "initial" step, the answer is correcting dehydration and electrolytes, not pyloromyotomy.
