compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's 'Q:' block under 1340 (unnumbered); a different question (pyloric stenosis).

stem: Qs about pediatric patient, I think the case was testicular torsion. Asking about golden hour for treatment.
why_right: Testicular torsion twists the spermatic cord and cuts off arterial inflow, so viability depends on time to detorsion. Salvage is highest when the testis is untwisted within about 6 hours of pain onset, which is why 6 hours is taught as the golden window. This is why a clinical diagnosis goes straight to scrotal exploration without waiting for imaging.
why_wrong_block:
B. 8 hours is already beyond the golden window; salvage falls progressively after 6 hours, although exploration is still performed.
C. By 12 hours salvage rates are much lower; this is not the window to aim for.
D. At 24 hours the testis is usually non-viable and often needs orchidectomy; still explore, but salvage is unlikely.
key_concept:
Torsion is a time-critical clinical diagnosis.
  • Sudden severe pain, high-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex
  • High suspicion: scrotal exploration, no imaging delay
  • Doppler US only if diagnosis uncertain
  • Surgery: detorsion + bilateral orchidopexy; orchidectomy if non-viable
  • Golden window: about 6 hours
exam_pearl: Torsion can present as lower abdominal pain only; always examine the scrotum in a boy with abdominal pain.

stem: Scenario about testicular torsion, imaging of choice:
why_right: When imaging is used for suspected torsion, the study of choice is scrotal Doppler ultrasound: it is fast, bedside, radiation-free and shows absent or reduced flow to the affected testis. Remember the order of priorities: torsion is a clinical diagnosis, and with high suspicion the patient goes to exploration without imaging; Doppler is reserved for uncertain cases.
why_wrong_block:
A. Plain X-ray cannot show the testis or its blood flow; it has no role in scrotal pain.
B. MRI can show testicular perfusion but is slow and not readily available, so it wastes the ischemic window.
D. CT exposes the gonads to radiation and does not assess testicular flow; CT suits renal colic or abdominal pathology, not the scrotum.
key_concept:
Acute scrotum: Doppler pattern separates the causes.
  • Torsion: absent or reduced flow; treat by exploration
  • Epididymo-orchitis: increased flow; antibiotics + NSAID
  • Torsion of appendix testis: upper pole pain, blue dot sign; NSAID
  • Clear clinical torsion: skip imaging, go to surgery
exam_pearl: If "Scrotal exploration" appears as an option in a classic torsion case, it beats ultrasound.

stem: Patient presents with swelling, the overlying skin was erythematous and fluctuance after a minor injury. What is the next step in management?
why_right: "Fluctuance" under erythematous skin after a minor injury means a collected abscess, not just cellulitis. Pus in a closed cavity is not penetrated well by antibiotics, so source control by incision and drainage is the treatment and the next step.
why_wrong_block:
A. Antibiotics alone treat cellulitis (redness, warmth, no fluctuance); for an abscess they are only an adjunct after drainage when there is systemic illness, extensive surrounding cellulitis or immunosuppression.
C. A CBC does not change management of a localized abscess; it may help in a systemically unwell patient, but drainage is still needed.
key_concept:
Skin and soft tissue infection: is there pus?
  • Redness, warmth, no fluctuance: cellulitis, antibiotics
  • Fluctuant collection: incision and drainage
  • Breast abscess, small with healthy skin: needle aspiration
  • Crepitus, rapid spread, severe pain: necrotizing infection, surgical debridement
exam_pearl: No fluctuance = cellulitis = antibiotics; fluctuance = abscess = drain it.

stem: A 46-year-old man, whose father was recently diagnosed with prostate cancer, comes for advice on screening. On digital rectal examination, the prostate is smooth, regular, and the sulcus is palpable. What is the next best step in management?
highlight_terms_source: father was recently diagnosed with prostate cancer
smooth, regular, and the sulcus is palpable
key_concept:
Prostate screening start depends on risk.
  • Average risk: shared decision from about 50
  • First-degree relative diagnosed before 65, or Black: from about 45
  • Several relatives diagnosed young: earlier still
  • Screening test: PSA (DRE only as adjunct)
  • Abnormal DRE or raised PSA: further evaluation (MRI, biopsy)
exam_pearl: Same stem, different key: father diagnosed young or Black patient means PSA; father diagnosed old means reassurance.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Compiler rule: If his father diagnosed before age of 65: B) PSA in 2 week. If father diagnosed after age of 65: A) reassurance. If he is Black: B) PSA in 2 week (regardless of family hx). Father's age not given in this recall, so no option marked. See 1356b/1356c variants (father 73 / 76: Reassurance).
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 42-year-old male screened for prostate cancer. Father had prostate cancer at age 73. DRE mid? and soft. Most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: Father had prostate cancer at age 73
why_right: A 42-year-old with no symptoms and a soft prostate on DRE has no finding that needs work-up. His father was diagnosed at 73, i.e. after 65, so he does not count as a high-risk family history and he is below the usual age for average-risk screening discussion. Reassurance is therefore the most appropriate management.
why_wrong_block:
A. Immediate biopsy is reserved for an abnormal DRE (hard, nodular, asymmetric gland) or a raised PSA; this gland is soft and he has no PSA result.
C. Routine yearly DRE is not recommended as a screening tool in an average-risk man this young; screening, when chosen, is a shared decision based on PSA at an older age.
key_concept:
Prostate cancer screening depends on age and true risk, not on any family history.
  • Average risk: shared decision on PSA screening from about age 50 to 55
  • High risk (first-degree relative diagnosed before 65, or Black ethnicity): start earlier, around 40 to 45
  • Relative diagnosed after 65: treat as average risk
  • Hard or nodular DRE, or raised PSA: proceed to imaging and biopsy
exam_pearl: The age of the relative at diagnosis is the trap: a father diagnosed before 65 would change the answer toward early PSA screening.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's 'Q:' variant under 1356; options printed as A, B, D (third option lettered D in source). Father diagnosed after 65: reassurance.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the primary care clinic concerned about prostate cancer because his father was diagnosed with prostate cancer at the age of 76. The patient is completely asymptomatic with no urinary complaints. On digital rectal examination (DRE), the prostate is soft, smooth, of normal size, and the medial sulcus is easily palpable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: father was diagnosed with prostate cancer at the age of 76
soft, smooth, of normal size, and the medial sulcus is easily palpable
why_right: This 45-year-old is completely asymptomatic and has a soft, smooth, normal-sized prostate with a preserved median sulcus, so the exam is normal. His father was diagnosed at 76, after age 65, which does not make him high risk. With no indication for testing, reassurance is the most appropriate next step.
why_wrong_block:
A. Annual DRE is not a recommended screening strategy and adds nothing for an average-risk man with a normal examination.
B. Transrectal ultrasound is used to guide biopsy or assess gland size, not to screen an asymptomatic man with a normal DRE.
D. PSA testing would be offered to a high-risk man at this age (relative diagnosed before 65) or to an average-risk man at an older age after shared decision making; neither applies here.
key_concept:
Normal DRE + no symptoms + relative diagnosed after 65 = average risk, reassure.
  • Abnormal DRE: hard, nodular, obliterated median sulcus
  • Early PSA screening only if first-degree relative diagnosed before 65 or other high-risk group
  • TRUS is a biopsy guide, not a screening test
exam_pearl: If the stem changes the father's age at diagnosis to under 65, PSA testing becomes the answer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's second 'Q:' variant under 1356.

stem: 10yo boy with large swelling on the left side of his neck. On examination: 10 cm in size, soft and spongy. US FNA: clear lymphatic fluid. What is the appropriate management?
why_right: A soft, spongy lateral neck swelling in a child with clear lymphatic fluid on aspiration is a cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformation). A 10 cm lesion will not regress and risks airway compression, infection and bleeding, so it needs active treatment. Of the listed options, surgical excision is the only definitive treatment.
why_wrong_block:
B. Observation is acceptable only for small, asymptomatic lymphatic malformations; a 10 cm mass needs treatment.
C. Chemotherapy treats malignant neck masses such as lymphoma, which would give lymphoid cells on FNA rather than clear lymphatic fluid.
D. Radiotherapy has no role in a benign lymphatic malformation in a child and carries growth and malignancy risks.
key_concept:
Cystic hygroma = lateral, soft, transilluminant neck mass with clear lymphatic fluid.
  • Thyroglossal cyst: midline, moves with tongue protrusion, surgery (Sistrunk)
  • Branchial cyst: anterior border of sternocleidomastoid, cholesterol crystals
  • Cystic hygroma treatment: sclerotherapy, then surgery
exam_pearl: If sclerotherapy appears as an option it is usually preferred first for a macrocystic lesion; without it, surgery is the answer.

stem: Diabetic patient come with lateral leg ulcer, warm leg and there is discharge and black base and pulseless in distal dorsalis. The most likely cause is:
why_right: This recall's key is venous, most likely reflecting the lateral leg location, the warm leg and the discharge (exudate), all of which fit venous ulceration. However, the stem also says pulseless dorsalis pedis and a black base, which are the textbook features of an arterial ulcer. The card is kept as keyed, but compare it with the near-identical recall where the pulse is intact.
why_wrong_block:
A. Neuropathic ulcers sit on pressure points of the sole (metatarsal heads, heel) in a warm foot with palpable pulses and loss of sensation, not on the lateral leg.
C. Malignancy (Marjolin ulcer) is suspected in a long-standing non-healing ulcer with rolled or everted edges; nothing here suggests it.
D. Arterial ulcers have absent pulses, a cold limb and a deep, punched-out, necrotic (black) base; the cold limb is missing here, but the absent pulse and black base point this way.
key_concept:
Leg ulcer: check the pulse first.
  • Absent pulse: arterial ulcer, arterial Doppler
  • Intact pulse: venous ulcer, venous duplex
  • Venous: gaiter area, shallow, irregular edge, pink granulating base, exudate, pigmentation
  • Arterial: pressure or trauma sites, punched out, deep, necrotic or sloughy base, cold limb
  • Neuropathic: plantar pressure points, painless, warm foot, pulses present
exam_pearl: In exam stems the distal pulse decides: absent = arterial, intact = venous.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Page marks Venous despite 'pulseless' in the stem (compare 1379, same options with intact pulse).

stem: 36 y/o male DM came complaining of ulcer in the medial site of the foot. WOTF is the highest risk of this ulcer?
highlight_terms_source: ulcer in the medial site of the foot
why_right: The key reads this as an ulcer over the medial aspect of the ankle/foot, the gaiter region, which is the classic site of venous ulceration. Venous ulcers result from sustained venous hypertension caused by valve incompetence, so venous hypertension is the strongest risk factor for an ulcer at this site. The patient is also young (36), making atherosclerotic disease less likely.
why_wrong_block:
A. Diabetes mainly causes neuropathic ulcers over plantar pressure points (metatarsal heads, heel) and contributes to arterial disease; it is not the main driver of a medial gaiter ulcer.
B. Atherosclerosis causes arterial ulcers on distal pressure or trauma sites (toes, heel, lateral malleolus) with absent pulses and pain, usually in older smokers.
key_concept:
Ulcer site points to the cause.
  • Medial malleolus / gaiter area: venous (venous hypertension)
  • Toes, heel, lateral malleolus, shin: arterial
  • Plantar metatarsal heads: neuropathic (diabetes)
exam_pearl: If the stem places the ulcer on the sole over a pressure point in a diabetic, the answer flips to diabetes (neuropathy).

stem: Diabetic patient come with lateral leg ulcer, warm leg and there is discharge and black base (in my exam there was sign of epithelization or something like that) and pulse is intact distal dorsalis (and another pulse also intact). The most likely cause is:
why_right: The deciding clue is the intact dorsalis pedis (and other distal pulses): a leg ulcer with intact pulses is treated as venous. A warm leg, discharge (exudate) and signs of epithelialisation also fit a venous ulcer. Even in a diabetic, intact pulses point to venous disease, and the next step would be venous duplex.
why_wrong_block:
A. Neuropathic ulcers occur over plantar pressure points with loss of sensation, not on the lateral leg.
C. Malignant change (Marjolin ulcer) is considered in a long-standing non-healing ulcer with rolled edges or rapid growth; epithelialisation argues against it.
D. Arterial ulcers require absent or reduced pulses and a cold limb; here the pulses are intact and the leg is warm.
key_concept:
Leg ulcer first step = check distal pulses.
  • Intact pulse: venous, venous duplex
  • Absent pulse: arterial, arterial Doppler / ABI
  • Diabetes does not override the pulse finding
exam_pearl: Same options with a pulseless foot would point to arterial; the pulse is the switch.

stem: 45 y old came with severe pain during and after defecation, along with bright red blood on toilet paper, on examination posterior midline tear in the anal canal with increased sphincter tone. Most appropriate initial treatment?
highlight_terms_source: severe pain during and after defecation
bright red blood on toilet paper
posterior midline tear in the anal canal
why_right: Severe pain during and after defecation, bright red blood on the paper and a posterior midline tear with increased sphincter tone are classic for an anal fissure. The lead-in is initial treatment, which is medical: stool softeners and fibre plus a topical agent that relaxes the internal sphincter (chemical sphincterotomy), such as topical nitroglycerin or diltiazem.
why_wrong_block:
A. Colonoscopy is not needed for a typical midline fissure; it is indicated for atypical (lateral or multiple) fissures suggesting Crohn disease, or for red flags like age-related cancer risk.
C. Lateral internal sphincterotomy is for chronic fissures (over 6 weeks, sentinel tag) that fail medical therapy, not the initial step.
D. Antibiotics treat perianal abscess or infection (fever, fluctuant swelling, discharge), which is not present here.
key_concept:
Anal fissure: sharp pain on defecation + fresh blood + posterior midline tear.
  • All: fibre, fluids, stool softeners, sitz baths
  • Acute (under 6 weeks) or initial: topical nitrates or calcium channel blocker (diltiazem)
  • Refractory: botulinum toxin injection
  • Chronic failing medical therapy: lateral internal sphincterotomy
exam_pearl: Painless bleeding suggests hemorrhoids; painful bleeding with a midline tear is a fissure, and surgery only comes after medical failure.

stem: Pt post thyroid surg prez w numbness around lips and other hypocalcemia symptoms. Stated "Chovsteks sign". What's the cause?
key_concept:
Post-thyroidectomy complication by presentation.
  • Neck swelling + stridor within hours: hematoma, bedside wound exploration
  • Perioral numbness, spasm, Chvostek/Trousseau: hypocalcaemia, check calcium and replace
  • Hypocalcaemia refractory to replacement: check magnesium
  • Hoarseness, aspiration: recurrent laryngeal nerve
  • Loss of high pitch: superior laryngeal nerve
exam_pearl: Chvostek and Trousseau signs mean calcium, not nerve injury, even though both follow thyroid surgery.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Patient in hypovolemic shock, what do you monitor?
why_right: In hypovolemic shock the best bedside marker of end-organ perfusion and adequacy of resuscitation is urine output, monitored hourly via a urinary catheter. It reflects renal perfusion and falls progressively with each class of hemorrhage, so a target urine output is used to guide fluid resuscitation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Blood pressure is maintained by compensation and only falls once about 30 to 40% of volume is lost, so a normal BP can hide ongoing hypoperfusion.
C. Heart rate is an early sign but is unreliable as a resuscitation endpoint: it is blunted by beta blockers, age or pacemakers and raised by pain or anxiety.
key_concept:
Resuscitation adequacy = organ perfusion, best tracked by hourly urine output.
  • Class I: urine output normal
  • Class II: tachycardia, narrowed pulse pressure, BP normal, urine output mildly reduced
  • Class III: BP first drops, urine output markedly reduced
  • Class IV: urine output negligible
exam_pearl: BP is the last vital sign to fall in hemorrhage, so it is a poor monitor; urine output is the classic answer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: In hypovolemic shock, the most reliable indicator of adequate tissue perfusion and resuscitation is urine output. (Recall marked B with '??'.)

stem: Post total thyroidectomy (4 days) c/o of stridor and cough and SOB; upon inspection the nerve was damaged or stuck, I don't recall much. What's the management
why_right: This recall's key is cricothyroidotomy, read as the need for an immediate surgical airway in a patient with stridor and SOB after total thyroidectomy, where bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury leaves both cords near the midline and obstructs the airway. The source itself is debated: laryngoscopy is the step that confirms cord palsy, and tracheostomy is the definitive airway for persistent bilateral palsy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tracheostomy is the definitive airway when bilateral cord palsy persists; it is a planned procedure rather than the crash airway, which is why the source split on it.
B. Laryngoscopy confirms vocal cord paralysis and is the answer when the lead-in asks for the initial or next diagnostic step in a stable patient.
D. Repair of the recurrent laryngeal nerve is done only when a transection is recognised during surgery; it is not the management of airway compromise days later.
key_concept:
Post-thyroidectomy stridor: match the timing and the lead-in.
  • Hours post-op + neck swelling: hematoma, open the wound at the bedside
  • Stridor from bilateral RLN palsy: secure airway (intubation), surgical airway if intubation fails
  • Confirm palsy: laryngoscopy
  • Persistent bilateral palsy: tracheostomy
  • Unilateral RLN injury: hoarseness, aspiration, usually no stridor
exam_pearl: Read the verb: diagnosis or next step = laryngoscopy; definitive airway = tracheostomy; emergency when intubation fails = cricothyroidotomy.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: If asking about initial/next: Laryngoscopy to confirm the diagnosis of recurrent LN injury. If asking about definitive: Tracheostomy.
Other marked answers: Compiler explanation: B. Laryngoscopy (initial/next); Compiler explanation: A. Tracheostomy (definitive)

stem: Pt complains of bulge in his anus with fever, don't remember
why_right: The decisive clue is fever with a perianal bulge. A painful perianal swelling plus systemic signs of infection (fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis) is a perianal abscess, which needs incision and drainage.
why_wrong_block: B. Thrombosed pile: a very painful, tender bluish swelling at the anal verge, usually after straining or constipation, and the patient is typically afebrile. Here the fever points to infection, not thrombosis.
key_concept:
Perianal swelling: fever or not decides.
  • Painful swelling + fever ± high WBC: perianal abscess, incision and drainage
  • Painful tender bluish swelling, afebrile: thrombosed external pile
  • Sharp pain with defecation, fresh blood, no swelling: anal fissure
  • Chronic discharging opening after an abscess burst: fistula in ano
exam_pearl: Remove the fever and the same painful perianal lump becomes a thrombosed pile.

stem: A 36-year-old patient presented with a neck mass that has been present for 3 years. Physical examination confirmed a palpable left thyroid gland; with no palpable cervical lymph nodes. Neck Ultrasound: Left thyroid nodule occupying most of the left lobe, measures 3.4 x 3.8 cm and has mixed cystic and solid components, the right lobe is normal. Fine Needle Aspiration: Finding is coded as Bethesda IV (suspicious for follicular neoplasm). Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: FNA coded Bethesda IV (suspicious for follicular neoplasm) cannot separate follicular adenoma from carcinoma on cytology, because that needs capsular or vascular invasion seen on histology. The answer is a diagnostic lobectomy of the affected side: a left hemithyroidectomy, since the nodule is confined to the left lobe, the right lobe is normal and there are no nodes.
why_wrong_block:
A. Thyroid scan: used when TSH is low to look for a hot (autonomous) nodule before FNA. No suppressed TSH is given here and cytology is already available.
B. Total thyroidectomy: for Bethesda VI (malignant), medullary cancer, or bilateral disease. Here the disease is unilateral and not yet proven malignant, so removing the normal right lobe is overtreatment.
D. Repeat FNA: the step for Bethesda I (nondiagnostic) and Bethesda III. Repeating cytology for Bethesda IV will not resolve the question of invasion.
key_concept:
Bethesda category drives thyroid nodule management.
  • I nondiagnostic: repeat FNA
  • II benign: ultrasound follow up
  • III: repeat FNA
  • IV follicular neoplasm: hemithyroidectomy (lobectomy)
  • V: manage as IV or VI
  • VI malignant: (near) total thyroidectomy
exam_pearl: Follicular lesion on FNA means you need the capsule, so take the lobe; only Bethesda VI earns a total thyroidectomy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recaller: not sure the recall was exactly this GB/MG one, but 100% sure it said Bethesda IV and asked for management.

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with a groin swelling that appears when she stands and disappears when lying down. On examination, the swelling is located below and lateral to the Pubic Tubercle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: below and lateral to the Pubic Tubercle
key_concept:
Pubic tubercle rule for groin hernias.
  • Above and medial: inguinal (direct or indirect)
  • Below and lateral: femoral
  • Indirect vs direct: lateral vs medial to inferior epigastric vessels; deep ring occlusion controls indirect
  • Femoral: women, high strangulation risk, repair even if asymptomatic
exam_pearl: Women get inguinal hernias more often than femoral, so decide by the pubic tubercle, not by sex.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Acute limb ischemia what is the risk for it?
key_concept:
Acute limb ischemia: embolus vs thrombosis.
  • Embolic: AF, recent MI, valve disease; sudden onset, normal other limb; treat with embolectomy
  • Thrombotic: prior claudication or PAD (smoking, diabetes); acute on chronic; catheter directed thrombolysis
  • Features: 6 Ps (pain, pallor, paresthesia, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paralysis)
exam_pearl: If the option list includes AF, that is the classic answer for embolic acute limb ischemia; claudication history points to thrombosis.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Patient 2 months claudication pain, ABI was 0.3 CTA showed 3cm occlusion in popliteal artery, what's the most app step
key_concept:
Limb ischemia treatment fork.
  • Chronic claudication: exercise program, risk factor control, antiplatelet; revascularize if disabling or critical
  • Short focal lesion, viable limb: endovascular angioplasty or stenting
  • Long or diffuse lesion: surgical bypass
  • Acute embolic (AF): embolectomy
  • Acute thrombotic (on PAD): catheter directed thrombolysis
  • Nonviable limb: amputation
exam_pearl: Viability decides: a viable limb is revascularized, only a dead or unsalvageable limb is amputated.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Old patient long history of leg claudication *for 2 months*, present with leg pain and ABI <0.3 and, *CTA show artery occlusion more than 3 cm* what to do?
why_right: This recall's key is amputation because the scenario is framed as acute on chronic ischemia: a long history of claudication, new leg pain, an ABI below 0.3 and an occlusion longer than 3 cm. The teaching rule used for this question is that acute on chronic ischemia with ABI below 0.3 (or an irreversibly paralysed limb) is managed by amputation.
why_wrong_block:
B. Thrombolysis: chosen for acute on chronic in situ thrombosis when the limb is still salvageable; here the severity markers in the stem (ABI below 0.3, long occlusion) are used to signal an unsalvageable limb.
C. Embolectomy: for embolic acute ischemia (AF, recent MI) in a previously normal artery; this patient has long standing atherosclerotic disease, not an embolic source.
key_concept:
Acute limb ischemia treatment by cause.
  • Cardiac embolus (AF): embolectomy
  • In situ thrombosis on PAD: catheter directed thrombolysis
  • Acute on chronic with ABI below 0.3 or irreversible paralysis: amputation
  • Initial step in all: heparin
exam_pearl: Embolus means embolectomy, thrombosis means thrombolysis, nonviable limb means amputation.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot of another recall of the same scenario (see 1433) with printed Answer: A.

stem: 65 yo male came complaining with sudden lower fossa pain that is increasing. Labs: Wbc 23, Hb normal. CT shows diverticulitis + collection. What is the initial and most appropriate?
why_right: CT shows diverticulitis with a collection (a diverticular abscess, Hinchey I or II) and the stem does not describe generalized peritonitis or instability. A drainable abscess (about 4 cm or more) is treated with IV antibiotics plus image guided percutaneous drainage, which is both the initial and the most appropriate step.
why_wrong_block:
A. Laparoscopy: reserved for failed percutaneous drainage, an undrainable abscess, or purulent peritonitis (Hinchey III) where laparoscopic lavage or resection is considered.
B. Open laparotomy: for perforated diverticulitis with generalized (purulent or feculent) peritonitis, Hinchey III or IV, or an unstable patient; not for a contained, drainable collection.
key_concept:
Diverticulitis management by Hinchey stage.
  • Uncomplicated: antibiotics (or observation if mild and immunocompetent)
  • Small abscess (about 3 cm or less): IV antibiotics alone
  • Larger abscess (about 4 cm or more): percutaneous drainage + antibiotics
  • Purulent or feculent peritonitis: surgery (laparotomy, Hartmann)
  • After recovery: colonoscopy at 6 to 8 weeks to exclude cancer
exam_pearl: A contained collection is drained through the skin; free perforation with peritonitis goes to theatre.
compiler_note:
Terse recall of the same question: Diverticulitis with fluid collection about 20/13 cm what to do next??
Compiler note: Compiler typed 'A. Percutaneous drain.' under the recall. Rule: 4 cm -> drain; 3 cm -> conservative (if there is fever or SIRS, choose IV Abx over conservative). Options taken from the 'Diverticulosis with collection management' restatement.

stem: Q: Patient with acute diverticulitis fluid collection What is your next step
key_concept:
Diverticular collection: size and sepsis decide.
  • Small collection: IV antibiotics (conservative)
  • Larger collection (about 4 cm or more): percutaneous drainage + antibiotics
  • Generalized peritonitis: laparotomy
  • Colonoscopy: 6 to 8 weeks later, never in the acute phase
exam_pearl: Colonoscopy is the right answer only when the stem says the attack has resolved.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Additional version inside 1447 block; size of collection not stated. Rule given: 4 cm -> drain; 3 cm -> conservative, IV Abx if fever/SIRS.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 19-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of frequent attacks of per-rectal fresh bleeding. Physical examination confirmed clotted blood in the rectum. Nasogastric tube was draining greenish coloured fluids. Hb 85. Colonoscopy: no colorectal pathology. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic tool to localize source of bleeding?
why_right: A 19-year-old with painless recurrent fresh rectal bleeding, a nasogastric tube draining bile (greenish fluid) that argues against an upper GI source, and a normal colonoscopy points to a small bowel source, most likely a Meckel diverticulum. A technetium 99m pertechnetate (Meckel) scan localizes it by detecting ectopic gastric mucosa.
why_wrong_block:
A. Diagnostic laparoscopy: may be used to confirm and resect a Meckel diverticulum once suspected, but it is invasive and not the first test to localize bleeding.
B. Gastrografin follow through: a contrast study for obstruction or fistula; it does not show the bleeding point or the ectopic gastric mucosa.
C. Upper GI endoscopy: first line when an upper source is suspected (melena, blood in the NG aspirate); here bilious NG drainage makes an upper source unlikely.
key_concept:
Bleeding with negative colonoscopy: think small bowel.
  • Young, painless bright red bleeding: Meckel scan (Tc 99m pertechnetate)
  • Bilious NG aspirate without blood: upper source unlikely
  • Older, stable, negative EGD and colonoscopy: capsule endoscopy
  • Active brisk bleeding: CT angiography or tagged RBC scan
exam_pearl: Meckel rule of 2: about 2 feet from the ileocecal valve, presents before age 2, may contain gastric or pancreatic tissue.
compiler_note:
Terse recall of the same question: Young with 12 years age bloody diarrhea colonoscopy negative what next?
Compiler note: Screenshot marks **D.

stem: 16 years old female presented to the ER after sustaining a trauma due to fall from 10 metres height; she identifies site of pain by moaning; what is the best way to secure Airway?
highlight_terms_source: identifies site of pain by moaning
why_right: A fall from 10 metres with a patient who only moans and merely localises pain has a depressed conscious level and cannot protect her airway, which is an indication for a definitive airway. In trauma the definitive airway is a cuffed tube in the trachea, i.e. endotracheal intubation (done orally with manual in-line cervical spine stabilisation). This recall's key is the general term "endotracheal" as the definitive, aspiration-protecting airway.
why_wrong_block:
B. Nasotracheal: a blind technique that is unsafe after major head and facial trauma (possible base of skull fracture, bleeding) and needs a breathing patient; it is not the trauma airway of choice.
C. Orotracheal: this is in fact the usual route of endotracheal intubation in trauma; the recall keys the broader term "endotracheal", so learn the key as the definitive cuffed tube in the trachea.
key_concept:
Trauma airway: who needs a definitive airway and which one.
  • Indications: GCS 8 or less / unconscious, SpO2 <88%, risk of aspiration (oral bleeding, secretions)
  • Default: endotracheal (oral) intubation with in-line C-spine stabilisation
  • Intubation needed + severe facial injury (e.g. mandibular fracture) = cricothyroidotomy
  • Avoid nasotracheal route with suspected base of skull or midface fracture
exam_pearl: Add severe facial or mandibular injury to the stem and the answer flips from endotracheal intubation to cricothyroidotomy.
compiler_note:
Terse recall of the same question: Patient fall from height how to intubate it / secure airway.
Compiler note: Answer A (green) - probably confirmed by Abdulmajeed, he got 100 WO 120 in surgery (2 years ago) and he has 1 probably confirmed mistake elsewhere.

stem: Pt with massive hematemesis all are normal except WBC and Blood urea nitrogen is high diagnosis ?
why_right: Peptic ulcer disease is the most common cause of hematemesis, and a massive bleed fits an ulcer eroding into a vessel (e.g. a posterior duodenal ulcer and the gastroduodenal artery). The raised BUN with otherwise normal labs reflects digested blood protein absorbed from the gut, a marker of upper GI bleeding, not liver or kidney disease. With no alcohol, liver or vomiting clue, PUD is the default answer.
why_wrong_block:
A. Erosive gastritis: usually causes low-volume oozing; it is the classic answer in an alcoholic or NSAID/stress setting, which the stem does not give.
C. Mallory-Weiss syndrome: needs a history of forceful or repeated vomiting before the hematemesis; that trigger is absent here.
D. Esophageal varices: right when there are signs of chronic liver disease or portal hypertension (alcohol, abnormal LFTs, ascites, splenomegaly); here everything except WBC and BUN is normal.
key_concept:
Upper GI bleed: pick the cause from the history clue.
  • No clue / default = peptic ulcer disease (most common)
  • Vomiting first, then blood = Mallory-Weiss tear
  • Liver disease, portal hypertension = varices
  • Alcohol binge, NSAIDs, ICU stress = erosive gastritis
  • High BUN with normal creatinine = blood digested in the upper GI tract
exam_pearl: An isolated high BUN in a bleeding patient points to an upper GI source, not renal failure.

stem: Patient with 3 day hx of colectomy present with fever and tenderness mainly LLQ and have abdominal distension + absent bowel sound Asking about most initial study
why_right: On day 3 after colectomy the patient has distension and absent bowel sounds with fever and LLQ tenderness: the first question is ileus or obstruction versus a complication such as an anastomotic leak. The lead-in asks for the most initial study, and a plain abdominal X-ray is the quick bedside first image to show dilated loops, air-fluid levels or gross free air. This recall's key is the plain film as the first imaging step, with CT as the follow-on test.
why_wrong_block:
B. CBC + lactate: useful bloods for sepsis and ischemia and usually drawn alongside, but the recall treats the question as asking for the first imaging study.
C. Re-exploration: reserved for a clear surgical emergency (generalised peritonitis, hemodynamic instability, a confirmed large leak); no instability is described here, so you investigate first.
key_concept:
Post-operative distension with absent bowel sounds: is it ileus, obstruction or a leak?
  • Ileus: check and correct electrolytes (especially potassium), bowel rest, NG tube
  • Plain abdominal X-ray: first quick image for distension
  • Suspected anastomotic leak (fever, focal peritonism after day 3 to 5): CT with contrast
  • Unstable or generalised peritonitis: return to theatre
exam_pearl: Free air on X-ray is expected for some days after open abdominal surgery, so it does not by itself prove a leak.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presented to the ED with 18-hour history of severe epigastric pain associated with vomiting. She is known to have multiple small gallstones. Upper abdominal tenderness. Labs: WBC 13.4; ALP 289; Amylase 488; Direct bilirubin 19; Total bilirubin 34. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
why_right: Severe epigastric pain with vomiting and amylase 488 (more than 3 times normal) in a woman with multiple small gallstones is acute gallstone pancreatitis. The lead-in asks for the most appropriate initial management, and the first priority is early IV crystalloid resuscitation (Ringer lactate preferred), together with analgesia. Everything else follows once fluids are running.
why_wrong_block:
A. Abdominal ultrasound: done to confirm the gallstone cause and assess the CBD, but it is an investigation, not the initial management; the diagnosis is already made on pain plus enzymes.
C. Broad-spectrum antibiotics: not given routinely in acute pancreatitis; right when there is cholangitis or infected necrosis.
D. ERCP: right for gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction (e.g. dilated CBD, rising jaundice); the mildly raised bilirubin here does not demand it as the first step.
key_concept:
Acute pancreatitis = 2 of 3: typical pain, amylase/lipase ≥3x normal, imaging findings.
  • Initial: IV crystalloid (Ringer lactate), analgesia
  • Ultrasound: look for gallstones / CBD dilation
  • Urgent ERCP: only with cholangitis or persistent CBD obstruction
  • Antibiotics: only for infection (cholangitis, infected necrosis)
  • Mild biliary pancreatitis: cholecystectomy in the same admission
exam_pearl: Add fever plus jaundice (cholangitis) and the answer moves to antibiotics and ERCP.

stem: Child has severe pain in lower abdomen with guarding and the pain is in the groin area, what is the next appropriate step ?
highlight_terms_source: pain is in the groin area
why_right: In a child (implied boy) with severe lower abdominal pain radiating to the groin, testicular torsion must be excluded first, because it often presents as abdominal or groin pain and boys may not report scrotal pain. A genital (scrotal) examination is fast, bedside and can reveal a high-riding, tender testis with absent cremasteric reflex, or an incarcerated inguinal hernia. The time-critical lesion is found by examination, not by imaging.
why_wrong_block: B. CT: radiation in a child and a delay that can cost the testis; right only after examination for intra-abdominal causes when the diagnosis is still unclear. Doppler ultrasound, not CT, is the imaging for the scrotum.
key_concept:
Boy with lower abdominal or groin pain: examine the genitalia and groin every time.
  • Torsion: sudden severe pain, high-riding transverse testis, absent cremasteric reflex: urgent surgical exploration
  • Incarcerated inguinal hernia: tender irreducible groin lump
  • Equivocal torsion: Doppler ultrasound, without delaying surgery
  • Other alternatives a student may consider: abdominal exam for appendicitis, urinalysis
exam_pearl: Torsion in children often presents as abdominal pain; skipping the scrotal exam is the classic missed diagnosis.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Similar screenshot (male child with sudden lower abdominal and groin pain, which is most important to be examined: A-Abdominal exam, B-Groin exam, C-General exam) shows Answer: B. Alhomrani: if option C was 'GENITAL' then go for it (genital, not general).

stem: A 62-year-old man, DM and HTN, presents with 4-hour history of sudden left leg pain, history of claudication at 200 m, smoker for 40 years. Left: femoral present, absent popliteal and distal; right: intact femoral and popliteal but diminished distal pulses. ECG normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation?
highlight_terms_source: 4-hour history of sudden left leg pain
why_right: Sudden leg pain for 4 hours with absent popliteal and distal pulses on a background of claudication is acute (on chronic) limb ischemia. No sensory or motor loss is described, so the limb is not immediately threatened and there is time to image. The lead-in asks for the most appropriate investigation, i.e. the definitive anatomical test, which is CT angiography.
why_wrong_block:
B. Vascular ultrasound: a reasonable initial bedside screen, but it is not the definitive test that maps the occlusion and run-off for planning.
C. Conventional angiogram: invasive; now used mainly when an endovascular intervention is planned in the same sitting, not as the first diagnostic test.
D. MR angiogram: slower and less available in an acute setting; an alternative when CT contrast is contraindicated.
key_concept:
Acute limb ischemia ladder: heparin, then image (US first, CT angiography definitive), unless the limb is threatened.
  • 6Ps: pain, pallor, paresthesia, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paralysis
  • Sensory/motor deficit: skip imaging, go to revascularisation
  • AF / cardiac source: embolectomy
  • Atherosclerotic in situ thrombosis: catheter-directed thrombolysis
  • Irreversible ischemia: amputation
exam_pearl: "Initial" step = heparin; "most appropriate investigation" = CT angiography; altered motor exam = no imaging at all.

stem: A 40-year-old healthy woman with 4-hour history of sudden onset right lower limb pain. Intact femoral pulse but absent distal pulses, diminished sensory with altered motor exam. ECG: atrial fibrillation. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: Sudden limb pain with absent distal pulses in a healthy 40-year-old with atrial fibrillation is acute embolic limb ischemia, and the intact femoral pulse places the embolus at or just below the femoral bifurcation. Diminished sensation and altered motor exam mean a threatened limb that needs immediate revascularisation. Embolectomy is the treatment for an embolic occlusion.
why_wrong_block:
B. Above knee amputation: only for irreversible ischemia (fixed mottling, rigid paralysis) or a non-salvageable limb; at 4 hours this limb is still salvageable.
C. Catheter-directed thrombolysis: right for in situ thrombosis on atherosclerotic disease (acute on chronic ischemia) in a limb not yet severely threatened; it acts too slowly when motor function is already altered.
D. Heparinization and observation: heparin is the first step in all acute limb ischemia, but alone it does not restore flow to a threatened limb.
key_concept:
Acute limb ischemia treatment: decide embolus vs thrombosis.
  • Embolus (AF, healthy vessels, sudden onset): embolectomy
  • Thrombosis (claudication history, diabetes, smoker): catheter-directed thrombolysis
  • Motor or sensory deficit: no imaging, straight to revascularisation
  • Irreversible ischemia: amputation
  • Heparin first in every case
exam_pearl: AF plus a previously healthy patient = embolus = embolectomy; claudication history plus normal ECG = thrombosis = thrombolysis.

stem: A 40-year-old healthy woman with 4-hour history of sudden onset right lower limb pain. Intact femoral pulse but absent distal pulses, diminished sensory with altered motor exam. ECG: atrial fibrillation. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation?
why_right: This is acute embolic limb ischemia (AF, sudden onset, absent distal pulses) with diminished sensation and altered motor exam, i.e. a threatened limb. When motor function is affected, imaging is skipped because any delay risks limb loss; the source is clearly embolic, so the patient goes straight to embolectomy. That is why the best "investigation" answer here is no investigation.
why_wrong_block:
A. CT angiogram: the most appropriate investigation for acute limb ischemia when the limb is not threatened (no motor or sensory loss); here it would only delay revascularisation.
B. Vascular ultrasound: the initial imaging in a stable, viable limb; not when motor function is already altered.
C. Conventional angiogram: invasive and time-consuming; it may be done on the table during the procedure but must not delay surgery.
key_concept:
Acute limb ischemia: the motor exam decides whether to image.
  • Viable limb (no deficit): heparin, ultrasound, then CT angiography
  • Threatened limb (sensory or motor loss): no imaging, immediate revascularisation
  • Embolic (AF): embolectomy
  • Thrombotic (atherosclerosis): catheter-directed thrombolysis
exam_pearl: Same AF scenario without motor or sensory loss and the answer flips back to CT angiogram.

stem: A 62-year-old man, DM HTN, presents with 4-hour history of sudden left leg pain, history of claudication at 200 m, non-compliant, smoker 40 years. Left: femoral present, absent popliteal and distal; right: diminished distal pulses. Elevated BSL. ECG: Normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: A diabetic, hypertensive 40-year smoker with claudication at 200 m and bilateral pulse deficits now has sudden pain for 4 hours with absent popliteal and distal pulses: acute on chronic ischemia from in situ thrombosis on atherosclerotic disease. The normal ECG argues against a cardiac embolus. Thrombosis on diseased vessels is treated with catheter-directed thrombolysis, which also unmasks the underlying lesion for later angioplasty or bypass.
why_wrong_block:
B. Femoral thrombectomy: the operation for a cardiac embolus (e.g. AF) lodged in a healthy artery; with no embolic source and diffusely diseased vessels it is not first choice.
C. Above knee amputation: only for irreversible ischemia or a non-salvageable limb; nothing here suggests that.
D. Heparinization and observation: heparin is the first step but on its own does not reopen an acutely occluded artery.
key_concept:
Embolus vs thrombosis in acute limb ischemia.
  • Thrombosis: claudication history, risk factors, bilateral disease, normal ECG: catheter-directed thrombolysis
  • Embolus: AF or recent MI, sudden, healthy other limb: embolectomy
  • Heparin first in both
  • Irreversible ischemia: amputation
exam_pearl: Change the ECG to atrial fibrillation and the answer becomes embolectomy.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents with a 2-month history of right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Ultrasound shows a diffusely calcified gallbladder without stones. What is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: 2-month history of right upper quadrant abdominal pain
why_right: A diffusely calcified gallbladder on ultrasound is a porcelain gallbladder, which is associated with gallbladder carcinoma. This patient is also symptomatic (2 months of RUQ pain), so removal is indicated on both counts. The answer is cholecystectomy.
why_wrong_block:
B. Percutaneous biopsy: not used to work up a suspected gallbladder malignancy because it risks seeding the tract and a negative result does not exclude cancer; resection is diagnostic and therapeutic.
C. Cholecystostomy tube: a temporary drain for acute (often acalculous) cholecystitis in a patient too sick for surgery; it does not treat the cancer risk.
D. Observation: may be discussed only for an asymptomatic patient unfit for surgery; this patient has symptoms.
key_concept:
Gallbladder findings that call for cholecystectomy.
  • Porcelain (calcified) gallbladder: cholecystectomy
  • Symptomatic gallstones / biliary colic: elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy
  • Polyp 10 mm or more: cholecystectomy
  • Acalculous cholecystitis in the critically ill: cholecystostomy tube
exam_pearl: Calcified gallbladder wall = cancer risk = remove it; do not biopsy it.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's typed recall: 'Pts complaining of RUQ pain for 2 month, US showing diffuse calcified gall bladder without stones, next?' with A. cholecystectomy highlighted (options: cholecystectomy, percutaneous biopsy, cholecystectomy tube, observation). The 'Q:' restatement lists A-C only; Answer: A- Cholecystectomy.

stem: Female in her 30s underwent carpal tunnel syndrome surgery, when the surgeon applied lidocaine with adrenaline she started to have more pain and numbness, what is the most appropriate initial step? (I'm sure the stem like this)
OptC: Check signs of ischemia in her hand
why_right: Adrenaline in the local anaesthetic is a vasoconstrictor, so new or worsening pain after injection into the hand raises the fear of vasospasm and compromised perfusion. The lead-in is "most appropriate initial step": before any test, you examine the hand at the bedside (colour, temperature, capillary refill, radial/ulnar pulses, digit turgor). The clinical findings then decide whether anything further (reversal with an alpha blocker, imaging) is needed.
why_wrong_block:
A. BP and HR would matter if you suspected systemic adrenaline or anaesthetic toxicity (palpitations, tachycardia, agitation, perioral tingling); the complaint here is local pain and numbness in the operated hand.
B. Doppler US is a second step once examination shows signs of ischemia or is equivocal; imaging never comes before a bedside vascular exam.
key_concept:
Suspected limb or digit ischemia: clinical examination first, imaging second.
  • Check colour, temperature, capillary refill, pulses, pain on passive stretch
  • Local findings (pallor, cold, delayed refill) point to vasospasm or vascular compromise
  • Systemic symptoms (tachycardia, palpitations, CNS signs) point to systemic absorption: then check vitals
  • Examination findings guide whether Doppler or reversal is needed
exam_pearl: "Initial step" in a limb perfusion question = examine the limb, not order the Doppler.

stem: 48 years old male patient known with hyperlipidemia with recurrent history of acute pancreatitis for the last 10 years, presented with vomiting blood 1 day ago, all labs are normal, and on examination, the patient had splenomegaly; on radiological examination, esophageal varices are found. What is the diagnosis?
why_right: "Recurrent acute pancreatitis" for years, then hematemesis with varices and splenomegaly but "all labs normal" (no liver disease) is the classic picture of left-sided (sinistral) portal hypertension. The splenic vein runs along the back of the pancreas; inflammation thromboses it, splenic blood diverts through the short gastric veins and produces varices (classically gastric fundal) while the portal vein and liver are normal. Hyperlipidemia here is just the cause of the pancreatitis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Angiodysplasia causes painless GI bleeding, typically in the elderly (often with aortic stenosis or CKD), but it does not produce varices or splenomegaly.
B. An arteriovenous shunt into the portal system (e.g. after trauma or liver biopsy) raises pressure in the whole portal system; nothing in this history suggests it, and pancreatitis points to splenic vein thrombosis instead.
D. Splenic artery aneurysm can complicate pancreatitis and may rupture with sudden hemorrhage, but it is an arterial lesion and does not create varices.
key_concept:
Pancreatitis + varices + splenomegaly + normal liver = splenic vein thrombosis (sinistral portal hypertension).
  • Splenic vein lies on the posterior pancreas, so pancreatitis or pancreatic tumour can thrombose it
  • Collaterals via short gastric veins give isolated gastric (fundal) varices
  • Portal vein and liver function are normal
  • Definitive treatment: splenectomy (removes the inflow)
  • Portosystemic shunts are not indicated (portal pressure normal)
exam_pearl: Varices with NORMAL liver tests and a pancreatitis history: think splenic vein thrombosis, and the cure is splenectomy, not a shunt.

stem: A 30-year-old underwent a laparoscopic appendectomy 2 weeks ago (see report). Histology: carcinoid tumor at the tip of the appendix measuring 0.5 cm. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
OptD: CT scan of chest abdomen and pelvis
highlight_terms_source: carcinoid tumor at the tip of the appendix
why_right: An appendiceal carcinoid (neuroendocrine tumour) that is small ("0.5 cm", well under 2 cm) and at the "tip" of the appendix, with no mesoappendix or nodal involvement, is cured by the appendectomy already done. Its metastatic risk is negligible, so no further surgery, imaging or endoscopy is needed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Colonoscopy is for synchronous colonic pathology, e.g. after an appendiceal mass or abscess treated conservatively in an older patient; a small tip carcinoid does not require it.
C. Right hemicolectomy is reserved for carcinoid >2 cm, at the base of the appendix, or with mesoappendix or lymph node invasion (and for appendiceal adenocarcinoma).
D. Staging CT is used for larger or invasive tumours or adenocarcinoma; a 0.5 cm tip lesion does not need staging.
key_concept:
Appendiceal carcinoid: size, site and invasion decide.
  • <2 cm, at tip, no mesoappendix/node invasion: appendectomy alone, observe
  • >2 cm, OR at base, OR mesoappendix/node invasion: right hemicolectomy
  • Appendiceal adenocarcinoma: right hemicolectomy
exam_pearl: Same tumour at the BASE of the appendix (or >2 cm) flips the answer to right hemicolectomy.

stem: 33-year-old female patient presented with anal fistula; on examination: external opening at 7 o'clock; you are planning for fistulotomy. Where is the most likely site of internal opening?
why_right: By Goodsall's rule, draw a transverse line across the anus (3 to 9 o'clock). An external opening at "7 o'clock" lies posterior to that line, and posterior openings follow a curved tract to an internal opening in the posterior midline (6 o'clock). Knowing the internal opening is essential before fistulotomy so the whole tract is laid open.
why_wrong_block:
B. The anterior midline is not where this tract goes; anterior external openings (in front of the 3 to 9 line) track radially in a straight line to the nearest crypt, not to 12 o'clock specifically.
C. A lateral internal opening is not predicted by Goodsall's rule; anterior openings drain straight radially and posterior openings curve to the posterior midline.
D. A tract with no internal opening is a sinus, not a fistula; the stem states anal fistula, which by definition connects the anal canal to the skin.
key_concept:
Goodsall's rule (transverse line through 3 and 9 o'clock).
  • External opening POSTERIOR to the line: curved tract to posterior midline (6 o'clock)
  • External opening ANTERIOR to the line: straight radial tract to nearest crypt
  • Exception: anterior openings far from the anal verge (>3 cm) may still curve to the posterior midline
  • Low simple fistula: fistulotomy; high or complex: MRI then seton or sphincter-sparing surgery
exam_pearl: Any opening between 3 and 9 o'clock on the back half points to 6 o'clock midline, whatever its exact hour.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Highlight is on the 'Q:' restatement (A. Left lateral, B. Midline anterior, C. Midline posterior, D. Straight lateral) where C. Midline posterior is highlighted. 6 o'clock -> posterior; 12 o'clock -> anterior (Goodsall rule).

stem: A 34-year-old woman with progressive dysphagia diagnosed as a case of achalasia. She has no medical problem and not on any medications. She is clinically unremarkable (see lab results): RBC 4, Hb 10, platelets 455, WBC 9, urea 5, creatinine 98. Which of the following is the best treatment option?
why_right: This is a young ("34-year-old"), otherwise healthy woman with achalasia, so she should get definitive therapy. Heller myotomy is first line but is not offered; pneumatic dilatation is the other definitive, durable treatment and is the best listed choice. The mild labs (Hb 10, platelets 455) are distractors and do not contraindicate dilatation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fundoplication alone is an anti-reflux operation for GERD; in achalasia it is only added to a Heller myotomy, and on its own it would worsen the outflow obstruction.
C. Oral nitrates (isosorbide dinitrate) give weak, short-lived LES relaxation and are reserved for patients unfit for dilatation or surgery.
D. Botulinum toxin gives temporary relief and is reserved for elderly or high-risk patients unfit for definitive treatment, not a fit 34-year-old.
key_concept:
Achalasia treatment by fitness.
  • Fit patient: Heller myotomy (with partial fundoplication) first line
  • Pneumatic dilatation: other definitive option, chosen when myotomy is not offered
  • Unfit/elderly/high risk: botulinum toxin injection
  • Drugs (nitrates, calcium channel blockers): weakest, bridging or unfit patients
exam_pearl: Young and fit = definitive therapy (myotomy, or dilatation if myotomy is absent); Botox is the answer only when the patient is old or unfit.

stem: 70 years old male complain of severe chest pain and change in voice after 8 hours of pneumatic dilatation of esophageal stricture What is the cause ?
why_right: Severe chest pain hours after "pneumatic dilatation of esophageal stricture" is iatrogenic esophageal perforation until proven otherwise; endoscopic instrumentation is the commonest cause of esophageal perforation. The "change in voice" fits air tracking into the neck and mediastinum (subcutaneous/mediastinal emphysema). Work-up is neck and chest X-ray, then a water-soluble contrast study or CT with oral contrast, with NPO, IV antibiotics and resuscitation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Aspiration after endoscopy presents with cough, dyspnea, fever and hypoxia with lung infiltrates, not severe chest pain with voice change.
B. Bleeding after dilatation shows as hematemesis or melena and hemodynamic change, not severe retrosternal pain and voice change.
D. MI should be excluded with an ECG in a 70-year-old with chest pain, but the clear link to esophageal instrumentation plus voice change points to perforation.
key_concept:
Chest pain after esophageal instrumentation = perforation.
  • Clues: retrosternal pain, fever, tachycardia, subcutaneous emphysema/crepitus, Hamman crunch
  • Step 1: neck and chest X-ray (pneumomediastinum, effusion, surgical emphysema)
  • Confirm: water-soluble contrast esophagram, or CT with oral contrast if unstable
  • Initial care: ABC, NPO, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, IV PPI, analgesia
  • Large free leak: surgical repair; small contained, stable: nonoperative or endoscopic
exam_pearl: Post-dilatation or post-endoscopy chest pain is perforation, not cardiac, unless proven otherwise.

stem: Female PT with RLQ pain and no Fever, WBC within normal range, what to do?
OptB: discharge and tell them to return if the pain worsening
why_right: RLQ pain with "no fever" and a "normal WBC" is an equivocal picture: appendicitis is not excluded (early appendicitis can have normal labs), and in a woman ovarian and other pelvic causes remain possible. With only these two choices, the safe answer is active observation: admit, repeat clinical examination and labs (about 6 hours later) and image as needed. Note the recall says imaging and a pregnancy test were not among the options.
why_wrong_block: B. Discharge with return advice is suitable only once a serious cause has been reasonably excluded (low-risk score, reassuring exam and work-up); with unexplained RLQ pain and no imaging, sending her home risks missing appendicitis, ectopic pregnancy or torsion.
key_concept:
Equivocal RLQ pain: observe and reassess rather than discharge.
  • Normal WBC and no fever do not exclude early appendicitis
  • Woman of reproductive age: pregnancy test always (ectopic)
  • Imaging: CT best in non-pregnant adults, US in pregnancy and children
  • Pelvic differentials: ovarian torsion, ruptured cyst, PID, ectopic
  • Serial examination converts an equivocal case into a clear one
exam_pearl: When the picture is unclear, admitting for serial examination beats discharge; discharge only after the dangerous causes are excluded.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Note in recall: no US, no pregnancy test, no CT (among options).

stem: Female PT with RLQ pain and no Fever, primary investigation:
why_right: In a "female" with RLQ pain the first bedside investigations must cover the three big groups: CBC (inflammation, anemia from bleeding), pregnancy test (ectopic pregnancy, and it must be known before any CT radiation) and urinalysis (UTI, pyelonephritis, ureteric stone with hematuria). Only option C covers all three; imaging follows these results.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ultrasound is the usual next imaging (pelvic organs, appendix, especially if pregnant), but it comes after the basic labs, above all the pregnancy test, which changes what imaging and differential you pursue.
B. CBC alone misses the two key differentials in a woman with RLQ pain: pregnancy (ectopic) and urinary causes.
D. RFT and LFT are not targeted at RLQ pain causes and omit the pregnancy test and urinalysis.
key_concept:
Female with lower abdominal pain: CBC + pregnancy test + urinalysis first.
  • Pregnancy test: ectopic pregnancy and radiation safety before CT
  • Urinalysis: UTI, pyelonephritis, renal stone (hematuria)
  • CBC: leukocytosis, anemia
  • Then imaging: US in pregnancy or for pelvic causes; CT best for appendicitis in non-pregnant adults
exam_pearl: Any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain: pregnancy test before imaging.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Separate 'Q:' recall under 1581 with a different lead-in and options.

stem: A patient presents after trauma with: GCS = 14, Neurological weakness, CT scan shows intracranial hematoma. Blood pressure is low. What is the most appropriate initial management?
why_right: The decisive clue is "blood pressure is low" in a head-injured patient. Cerebral perfusion pressure = MAP minus ICP, so hypotension causes secondary brain injury and must be corrected first; ATLS order puts Circulation before Disability. With "GCS = 14" the airway is protected (no intubation needed), so the initial step is IV fluid resuscitation, followed by neurosurgery for the hematoma with weakness once the patient is resuscitated.
why_wrong_block:
A. Corticosteroids are not used in traumatic brain injury; they increased mortality in head injury trials. Steroids belong to vasogenic edema around tumours, not trauma.
C. Surgical evacuation is the definitive treatment for a hematoma with focal weakness, and would be the answer if the patient were normotensive; but hypotension must be corrected first.
D. Observation is for a small hematoma with no deficit in a stable patient; this patient has a focal deficit and shock.
key_concept:
Head injury + hypotension: fix C before D.
  • CPP = MAP minus ICP; hypotension worsens brain injury
  • GCS 8 or less: intubate first (airway)
  • Hypotensive: IV fluids, and search for another bleeding source
  • Stable with hematoma and focal deficit: urgent neurosurgical evacuation
  • Steroids: no role in TBI
exam_pearl: Same hematoma with normal BP flips the answer to neurosurgery; with GCS 8 or less it flips to intubation.
compiler_note: Compiler note: In patients with TBI, hypotension should be corrected immediately to maintain cerebral perfusion; fluid resuscitation is the first step. Comment (December File p1039): patient has weakness but is hypotensive, so fix ABC as initial; if GCS 8 or coma, intubation is initial; otherwise initial for weakness would still be surgery. Athar: Agree.

stem: Young male (around 20) Pt presented after he has a BLUNT abdominal trauma CT: there was Extravasation around the left kidney What are most appropriate step in management?
key_concept:
Blunt renal trauma: stability first, then CT findings.
  • Unstable despite resuscitation: surgery (exploration, nephrectomy if unreconstructable)
  • Stable, most grades: nonoperative, observe and repeat CT
  • Stable with active contrast extravasation, pseudoaneurysm or AV fistula: angioembolization
  • Urinary extravasation: observe, repeat CT; stent or nephrostomy if it persists
  • Renal pedicle avulsion: surgery
exam_pearl: "Extravasation" alone is not enough: contrast blush in a stable patient = angioembolization; urine leak = observe; unstable = theatre.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: No option marked on the numbered recall. Compiler: answer depends on URINARY vs CONTRAST/BLOOD extravasation; we also need to know option D. Blunt renal trauma: unstable -> surgery; stable -> by CT: grade 1-4 observe and repeat CT; grade 5 shattered kidney observe if stable; renal pedicle injury or grade 4-5 vascular -> surgery. Urinary extravasation -> observe and repeat CT (JJ stent or nephrostomy if persists); contrast extravasation -> observe +/- angio.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 40-something-year-old woman presents after blunt abdominal trauma. She is initially hypotensive despite resuscitation, but her blood pressure is now 100/80 mmHg. A CT scan shows contrast extravasation near the left kidney with a perirenal hematoma. What is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: contrast extravasation near the left kidney
why_right: She was hypotensive but has now responded to resuscitation ("BP is now 100/80"), so she is stable enough to stay out of theatre. CT shows active contrast extravasation with a perirenal hematoma, meaning an arterial bleed that will not reliably stop on its own. In a stable or responding patient with blunt renal injury and active extravasation, angioembolization stops the bleeding while preserving the kidney.
why_wrong_block:
A. Emergent nephrectomy is for the patient who stays unstable despite resuscitation (non responder) or has an expanding or pulsatile hematoma at laparotomy; she has responded, so a kidney sparing option comes first.
B. Repeat CT after 6 months ignores an active bleed now; delayed imaging is for follow up of a healed injury, not acute management.
D. Foley catheter and monitoring is conservative care for a stable, low grade renal injury with no active extravasation; contrast blush here means ongoing arterial bleeding.
key_concept:
Blunt renal trauma: decide by hemodynamics first, then by active bleeding on CT.
  • Stable, no extravasation: non operative (bed rest, monitoring, serial Hb).
  • Stable or transient responder with contrast extravasation: angioembolization.
  • Persistently unstable: operative exploration, nephrectomy if kidney not salvageable.
  • Unstable patients do not go to CT; they go to FAST then laparotomy.
exam_pearl: Contrast blush in a now stable patient = angioembolization; if the BP never recovers, the answer flips to surgery.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Unnumbered 'Q:' variant under 1589; options continue on p405 where C is highlighted. Compiler: contrast extravasation -> observe +/- angio; unstable -> surgery.

stem: Young male ( around 20) Pt presented after he has a BLUNT abdominal trauma CT : there was CONTRAST Extravasation around the left kidney I THINK Patient Was UNSTABLE What are most appropriate step in management ?
key_concept:
Blunt renal trauma: hemodynamics decide.
  • Stable, no blush: observe (fluids, bed rest, serial Hb).
  • Stable or responder with blush: angioembolization.
  • Persistently unstable: surgery (exploration, nephrectomy if not salvageable).
  • A truly unstable patient should not be in the CT scanner; instability is managed in theatre.
exam_pearl: The stem's word "UNSTABLE" pushes toward surgery; if the recall really meant a responder, angioembolization wins.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Unmarked. See approach under 1589: unstable blunt renal trauma -> surgery.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Patient KCO Rt inguinal hernia for 6 years (don't remember age) came complaining of irreducible swelling, pain in Rt inguinal region.
OptD: I don't remember 4th option maybe observe?
why_right: A long standing right inguinal hernia that has become irreducible and painful is an incarcerated hernia at risk of obstruction and strangulation, so it needs urgent operative exploration rather than further imaging or waiting. The recall keys this as exploratory laparotomy, and the other version of the question (obstruction with guarding and rigidity) points the same way: signs of compromised bowel mean surgery now.
why_wrong_block:
A. Diagnostic laparoscopy is for when the diagnosis is unclear (for example abdominal pain after surgery); here the diagnosis is clinically obvious and the hernia needs definitive repair.
C. Double contrast pelvic CT delays surgery in a clinically diagnosed painful irreducible hernia; imaging is for doubtful cases or an occult hernia.
D. Observation is never right for a painful irreducible hernia, because strangulated bowel can become gangrenous within hours.
key_concept:
Groin hernia states guide urgency.
  • Reducible: elective mesh repair.
  • Irreducible, painful: urgent surgery.
  • Obstructed (vomiting, distension): urgent surgery after resuscitation.
  • Strangulated (tense, very tender, red skin, systemic signs): emergency surgery, resect nonviable bowel.
exam_pearl: Painful irreducible hernia = operate now; scans and observation are the traps.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other version (Q:): intestinal obstruction, incarcerated hernia with guarding and rigidity, I think management is laparotomy? Options: A. Laparoscopy, B. Exploratory surgery for the hernia.

stem: 45 years old patient, came with history reducible hernia in inguinal area it pop out every two days with mild pain and he can manual reducible it by his finger, then he suddenly developed severe constant pain in early morning in that area and came to hospital, on examination of the inguinal area and scrotum examination and he is free from both them and pain is disappear, Now just have persistent nausea and vomiting, what is the next step ?
why_right: After "sudden severe constant pain" in a known hernia, the groin and scrotum are now empty and the pain has gone, yet he has persistent nausea and vomiting. This raises concern that a strangulated or obstructed segment was reduced into the abdomen (reduction en masse or reduced ischemic bowel), so the next step is CT abdomen and pelvis to look for obstruction or bowel ischemia before deciding on surgery.
why_wrong_block:
B. Hernia repair today after 2 hours treats the groin defect but does not address what is happening inside the abdomen; operative planning should follow imaging of the persistent vomiting.
C. Reassurance and discharge is unsafe because ongoing vomiting after an acute hernia episode can mean obstructed or ischemic bowel.
D. Hernia repair after 2 days fits an uncomplicated reducible hernia once symptoms settle; some recall versions mark this, but it ignores persistent vomiting that still needs explaining.
key_concept:
Hernia that went back in but symptoms persist: image the abdomen.
  • Empty groin + resolved pain + ongoing vomiting: suspect reduced ischemic bowel or reduction en masse.
  • CT abdomen and pelvis shows obstruction, ischemia or free fluid.
  • Positive CT or peritonitis: urgent laparotomy.
  • No symptoms after reduction: elective repair.
exam_pearl: Pain gone but vomiting persists after a hernia reduces = do not discharge; image for hidden obstruction.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Option D text in the recall ends with the word 'answer', while the compiler highlights A.
Other marked answers: Recall text: D. Hernia repair after 2 days

stem: Elderly male presents with massive LGIB (no PMHx). Most likely cause?
why_right: An "elderly male" with massive lower GI bleeding and no relevant history most likely has diverticulosis, the commonest cause of painless, large volume hematochezia in older adults. Diverticular bleeding is arterial, starts abruptly, and usually stops spontaneously.
why_wrong_block:
B. Colon cancer causes chronic, low volume blood loss with iron deficiency anemia, change in bowel habit or weight loss, not an acute massive bleed.
C. Angiodysplasia is the other main cause of painless bleeding in the elderly, typically recurrent and slower, and linked to aortic stenosis or CKD; when diverticulosis is also listed, diverticulosis is the more common cause of a massive bleed.
D. Ulcerative colitis gives bloody diarrhea with urgency and tenesmus in younger patients, not an isolated massive bleed in an elderly man.
key_concept:
Massive painless LGIB in the elderly: diverticulosis first.
  • Diverticulosis vs angiodysplasia: diverticulosis.
  • Diverticulitis vs angiodysplasia: angiodysplasia (diverticulitis does not bleed).
  • Chronic occult bleed with anemia or weight loss: colon cancer.
  • Bloody diarrhea with urgency: colitis.
exam_pearl: Diverticulosis bleeds, diverticulitis does not; the "osis" vs "itis" spelling flips the answer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Diverticulosis (not diverticulitis). Diverticulosis vs angiodysplasia -> diverticulosis; diverticulitis vs angiodysplasia -> angiodysplasia. Diverticulitis does NOT cause GI bleed.

stem: What signs indicate early decompensated shock?
key_concept:
Stages of shock.
  • Compensated: normal BP, tachycardia, tachypnea, cool peripheries, reduced urine output.
  • Decompensated: hypotension, worsening metabolic acidosis, renal failure (anuria).
  • Irreversible: multiorgan failure, poor response to inotropes.
  • Question asks "earliest sign of shock": tachycardia; asks "sign of decompensation": hypotension first.
exam_pearl: Tachycardia = earliest sign of shock; hypotension = first sign of decompensation.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Compiler wrote 'B/C??' (unsure). A screenshot variant (1638b) gives Athar: C = hypotension.
Other marked answers: Compiler: B/C??
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: The most initial sign of decompensated shocked:
why_right: In compensated shock, tachycardia and vasoconstriction hold the blood pressure normal; once these mechanisms fail, hypotension appears, and that is what defines decompensated shock. So the "most initial sign" of decompensation is a fall in blood pressure.
why_wrong_block:
A. Anuria follows the drop in BP as renal perfusion fails; choose it only if hypotension is not offered.
B. Decreased oxygen delivery to tissues is the underlying mechanism of all shock, present from the start, not a clinical sign of decompensation.
D. Cold and pale skin reflects compensatory vasoconstriction and is already present in compensated shock.
key_concept:
Compensated vs decompensated shock.
  • Compensated: normal BP, tachycardia, cool skin, reduced urine output.
  • Decompensated: hypotension, worsening acidosis, anuria.
  • Irreversible: multiorgan failure, refractory to inotropes.
exam_pearl: Earliest sign of shock is tachycardia; earliest sign of decompensation is hypotension.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot in the 1638 block. Athar: C. Hypotension, Then Anuria (If No Hypotension > Choose Anuria).

stem: female with upper and med pubic tubercle swelling irreducible , type of hernia
why_right: A swelling above and medial to the pubic tubercle is an inguinal hernia, whatever the patient's sex; that location alone excludes a femoral hernia. The swelling is "irreducible", and of the two options the key is obstructed inguinal hernia; strictly, the obstructed label requires bowel obstruction features such as vomiting and distension.
why_wrong_block: A. Strangulated femoral hernia: a femoral hernia lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, and strangulation needs a tense, very tender swelling with red skin and systemic signs; neither the site nor these features are described.
key_concept:
Groin hernia by relation to the pubic tubercle.
  • Above and medial: inguinal (direct or indirect).
  • Below and lateral: femoral (more common in women than men, especially elderly multiparous; highest strangulation risk). Inguinal is still the commonest groin hernia in women.
  • Irreducible: cannot be reduced, not tender, no obstruction.
  • Obstructed: irreducible with vomiting, distension, air fluid levels.
  • Strangulated: tense, very tender, discolored, systemic toxicity.
exam_pearl: Female sex tempts "femoral", but the site relative to the pubic tubercle decides.

stem: A patient presented with right iliac fossa pain, and description typical of appendicitis she did CT it shows Appendiceal mass with no collection WBC 15
key_concept:
Complicated appendicitis is managed by what CT shows.
  • Uncomplicated appendicitis: laparoscopic appendectomy
  • Mass/phlegmon, no collection: conservative (IV antibiotics)
  • Abscess (collection): percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics
  • Both mass and abscess routes end in interval appendectomy
  • Generalised peritonitis or deterioration: surgery
exam_pearl: The words "no collection" turn a drainage question into a conservative-management question.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A guy came from an RTA; did FAST and it shows fluid around the spleen and liver; blood pressure 96/80.
highlight_terms_source: fluid around the spleen and liver
why_right: After blunt trauma, the FAST pathway splits by haemodynamic status: positive FAST in a stable patient goes to CT to grade the solid organ injury, while positive FAST in an unstable patient goes to laparotomy. This recall treats "BP 96/80" (systolic above 90) as haemodynamically stable, so CT is the keyed next step.
why_wrong_block: B. Laparotomy: right for positive FAST in an UNSTABLE patient (persistent hypotension or non-responder to fluids), or for peritonitis or evisceration; this card frames the patient as stable.
key_concept:
Blunt abdominal trauma: FAST result + stability decides the next step.
  • Stable, FAST positive: CT abdomen
  • Stable, FAST negative: observe/re-examine
  • Unstable, FAST positive: laparotomy
  • Unstable, FAST negative: DPL / look for other bleeding source
  • Unstable stab wound: laparotomy without FAST
exam_pearl: If the stem says hypotensive or not responding to fluids, the same positive FAST flips the answer to laparotomy.

stem: 24-year-old woman with recurrent on-off PR bleeding after defecation. She has spontaneously reduced hemorrhoids. Hb was low. On examination: 3 hemorrhoids at 2, 7, 10 o'clock. How would you manage?
why_right: The keyed answer rests on the classic indications for haemorrhoidectomy: besides grade III to IV disease, bleeding severe enough to cause anaemia ("Hb was low") and failure of non-operative treatment ("recurrent on-off" bleeding) are surgical indications. She also has all three primary haemorrhoid columns involved ("2, 7, 10 o'clock"), favouring a definitive excisional operation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Observation: acceptable only for minor, asymptomatic haemorrhoids; recurrent bleeding with anaemia needs treatment.
B. Band ligation: right for grade I to III internal haemorrhoids bleeding without anaemia, as an outpatient first procedure; here the anaemic, recurrent bleeding is treated as an indication for surgery.
D. Conservative: fibre, stool softeners and sitz baths fit grade I to II haemorrhoids with mild symptoms; it will not reliably control bleeding that has already caused anaemia.
key_concept:
Haemorrhoid treatment ladder by grade and complications.
  • Grade I to II: conservative (fibre, softeners, sitz baths)
  • Grade III (manually reduced): band ligation / sclerotherapy
  • Grade IV or failed outpatient procedures: haemorrhoidectomy
  • Bleeding causing anaemia or mixed haemorrhoids: haemorrhoidectomy
  • Older patient or red flags (weight loss, change in bowel habit): colonoscopy first
exam_pearl: "Low Hb" from haemorrhoidal bleeding escalates even low-grade haemorrhoids to surgery in this exam's key.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Textbook excerpt: indications for haemorrhoidectomy include third- and fourth-degree haemorrhoids, second-degree not cured by non-operative treatment, mixed haemorrhoids with well-defined external component, and bleeding causing anaemia. A second version (next page): manual reduction (grade 3), 3 hemorrhoids at 2,7,10 o'clock, Hb and all labs normal, definitive treatment? 'Answer is Hemorrhoidectomy, Period'.

stem: Surgeon is performing a back lipoma excision under local anesthesia using lidocaine. He suspects an excessive dose of lidocaine may have been administered. What is the earliest sign of lidocaine toxicity?
why_right: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity follows a dose-related sequence: CNS excitation appears first, then seizures, then CNS and cardiovascular depression.
