⚠ Image audit: Page 418 highlights BOTH B and C in yellow with no Answer line or explanation to break the tie; card commits to B.
Compiler note: Both B and C are highlighted on the page; no further comment.
Other marked answers: Also highlighted: C. Viral exanthem unrelated to vaccine

stem: 3 Years Old Post TEF Repair, Present With Brassy Cough, 2 Days Earlier He Had Runny Nose, Normal Vitals, Good Air Entry Bilaterally With Expiratory Wheeze?
why_right: Tracheomalacia is the expected sequela of TEF repair: the trachea at the fistula site has weak cartilage and collapses on expiration, giving the classic brassy cough and expiratory wheeze. A simple viral cold ("runny nose 2 days earlier") makes it more noticeable, while the child stays well with normal vitals and good air entry.
why_wrong_block:
A. Asthma gives recurrent episodic wheeze with atopy and response to bronchodilators; it does not explain a brassy cough tied to a repaired TEF.
C. Croup gives a barking cough with inspiratory stridor, hoarseness and often fever and distress after a coryzal prodrome; here the noise is expiratory and the child is stable.
key_concept:
Post-TEF repair + brassy cough + expiratory wheeze = tracheomalacia.
  • Tracheomalacia: dynamic collapse of intrathoracic trachea, expiratory noise; diagnosis by bronchoscopy
  • Laryngomalacia: inspiratory stridor in early infancy, worse supine and with feeding; laryngoscopy
  • Croup: barky cough, inspiratory stridor, 6 months to 3 years
  • Other post-TEF problems: anastomotic stricture (dysphagia), recurrent fistula (cough with feeds), GERD
exam_pearl: Inspiratory stridor points above the thoracic inlet (larynx, croup); expiratory wheeze with brassy cough after TEF points to intrathoracic tracheomalacia.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's typed line: 'A CHILD AFTER TEF SURGERY DEVELOPED TRACHEAL STENOSIS?' followed by a screenshot (Q71) with handwritten pen answer B (a scribbled mark before it, apparently corrected to B).

stem: A child following up for being tall, has high arm span and long fingers, following up with ophthalmology for eye issues (written like this), no mental retardation. Most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: high arm span and long fingers
why_right: Tall stature, long arm span and long fingers (arachnodactyly) with eye problems needing ophthalmology follow up (myopia, ectopia lentis) and normal intelligence is Marfan syndrome. Normal cognition is what separates it from homocystinuria, which has a similar marfanoid body.
why_wrong_block:
B. Homocystinuria gives a marfanoid habitus with lens dislocation too, but adds intellectual disability and thrombosis; this child has no mental retardation.
C. Loeys-Dietz causes aortic aneurysms with hypertelorism, bifid uvula or cleft palate and arterial tortuosity; lens dislocation is not a feature, so the eye clue does not fit.
D. Ehlers-Danlos gives skin hyperextensibility, joint hypermobility and easy bruising; it is not defined by tall stature, long arm span or lens problems.
key_concept:
Marfanoid body: sort by eye and IQ.
  • Marfan: autosomal dominant, FBN1; upward lens dislocation, myopia, aortic root dilation, MVP, normal IQ
  • Homocystinuria: autosomal recessive; downward lens dislocation, intellectual disability, thrombosis
  • Loeys-Dietz: hypertelorism, bifid uvula, arterial tortuosity, aggressive aneurysms
  • Ehlers-Danlos: stretchy skin, hypermobile joints, poor wound healing
exam_pearl: Marfanoid child plus intellectual disability or thrombosis flips the answer to homocystinuria.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Tall stature + no eye symptoms = EDS; tall stature + eye symptoms = Marfan; tall stature + eye symptoms + retardation = Homocystinuria.

stem: 7-month-old pt. His mother noticed that he stopped smiling, low activity, fatigue. On examination he had multiple movements of neck flexion followed by extension of body & limbs lasting 1-2 seconds in a repetitive pattern. EEG showed slow wave & multifocal spikes (not sure, but it wasn't hypsarrhythmia or chaotic pattern). What's the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: multiple movements of neck flexion followed by extension of body & limbs lasting 1-2 seconds
why_right: A 7-month-old with developmental regression ("stopped smiling", low activity) and brief repetitive flexion then extension spasms of neck, trunk and limbs lasting 1 to 2 seconds in clusters is infantile spasms (West syndrome). The EEG described, slow waves with multifocal spikes, is in fact what hypsarrhythmia consists of, so even an imperfect recall fits the triad of spasms, regression and abnormal EEG.
why_wrong_block:
A. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy starts in adolescence with morning myoclonic jerks of the arms and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, normal development and generalized polyspike-wave EEG; it does not occur at 7 months.
C. Lennox-Gastaut presents later (usually 1 to 8 years) with multiple seizure types (tonic, atonic, atypical absence), intellectual disability and slow spike-wave EEG; West syndrome often evolves into it.
key_concept:
Infant + clustered flexor/extensor spasms + regression = West syndrome.
  • Age: peak 4 to 8 months
  • Triad: infantile spasms, developmental arrest/regression, hypsarrhythmia
  • Hypsarrhythmia: chaotic high-voltage slow waves with multifocal spikes
  • Look for tuberous sclerosis (ash leaf spots, Wood lamp)
  • Treatment: ACTH or high-dose steroids; vigabatrin first line in tuberous sclerosis
  • Lennox-Gastaut: childhood, multiple seizure types, slow spike-wave
exam_pearl: Same spasms in a teenager on waking are myoclonic jerks (JME); age is the first clue in childhood epilepsy syndromes.

stem: A mother brings her 6-month-old baby with pancytopenia and organomegaly. Labs show low hemoglobin. What is the most likely type of leukemia?
why_right: A child with pancytopenia, organomegaly and low hemoglobin has bone marrow replacement with extramedullary infiltration, typical of acute leukemia. ALL is the most common childhood leukemia (and the most common childhood cancer), so it is the most likely type.
why_wrong_block:
A. AML is the second most common childhood leukemia; favour it when the stem gives myeloid clues such as Auer rods, gum infiltration or DIC.
B. CML is rare in children and presents with marked leukocytosis and splenomegaly in the chronic phase, not pancytopenia.
D. Acute non-lymphoblastic leukemia is another name for AML, which is less common than ALL in children.
key_concept:
Child + pancytopenia + hepatosplenomegaly/lymphadenopathy = think acute leukemia; ALL is the most common.
  • ALL: most common childhood leukemia, peak in early childhood
  • AML (= acute non-lymphoblastic): second most common
  • CML: rare in children
exam_pearl: 'Acute non-lymphoblastic' is just AML in old wording; do not treat it as a separate answer.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1925).
Compiler note: Screenshot version: 'Which leukemia is the most common in pediatric age group?' with **C. Acute lymphoblastic marked.

stem: A 3-year-old child is seen in the clinic with fever and cough for 5 days following a flu-like prodrome. On examination, there is decreased air entry and crackles over the right lung middle zone. Chest X-ray is performed along with laboratory investigations. BP 90/64 mmHg, HR 110/min, RR 20/min, Temp 36.6 °C, SpO2 97%. Labs: Hb 12 g/dL, platelets 328 x10^9/L, WBC 22 x10^9/L, neutrophils 84%, lymphocytes 15%. What is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: crackles over the right lung middle zone
why_right: Fever and cough for 5 days with focal crackles and reduced air entry over the right middle zone, WBC 22 with 84% neutrophils, is bacterial community-acquired pneumonia, which needs antibiotics. The child is stable: SpO2 97%, normal RR and BP, no distress, so it is mild pneumonia managed at home with oral amoxicillin.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance fits a viral URTI; focal chest signs with neutrophilic leukocytosis mean bacterial pneumonia that needs antibiotics.
B. Bronchodilator and steroids treat asthma or wheeze; this child has focal crackles, not diffuse wheeze.
C. Admission for IV antibiotics is for severe pneumonia: SpO2 below 92%, respiratory distress, tachypnea, inability to take oral fluids, toxic look or complications such as empyema; none are present.
key_concept:
Pediatric CAP: severity decides where and how.
  • Mild (well, SpO2 ≥92%, feeding): oral amoxicillin at home
  • Severe: hypoxia, grunting, retractions, poor feeding, toxicity: admit, IV antibiotics, oxygen
  • First-line oral drug: amoxicillin (covers pneumococcus)
  • Stony dullness suggests parapneumonic effusion
exam_pearl: Hypoxia (SpO2 below 92%) is the single sign that flips management from oral home treatment to admission.

stem: 10 y.o child with high LDL cholesterol, low HDL, growing normally, no genetic diseases, no history of surgeries or medication, everything else is normal:
key_concept:
Child with high LDL: confirm, exclude secondary, then diet, then drugs.
  • Repeat fasting lipids and average two results
  • Secondary screen: TSH, renal (nephrotic), liver, glucose, medications
  • Family history and cascade screening for FH
  • Lifestyle diet trial first in most children
  • Statin considered from about 10 years if LDL stays ≥4.9 mmol/L (190 mg/dL), or lower with risk factors
  • A version of this recall that gives LDL 5 mmol/L is keyed to Further investigation.
exam_pearl: The deciding detail is the stage: a first unconfirmed profile (investigate), confirmed mild dyslipidemia without secondary cause (diet), or confirmed very high LDL or familial hypercholesterolemia (referral).
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 10 y.o child with LDL 5 mmol cholesterol, low HDL, growing normally, no genetic diseases, no history of surgeries or medication, everything else is normal:
why_right: An LDL of 5 mmol/L (about 193 mg/dL) in a 10-year-old who is otherwise healthy is markedly high and raises suspicion of familial hypercholesterolemia. The next step is further investigation: repeat fasting lipid profile, exclude secondary causes (hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestatic liver disease, diabetes) and take a family history, before committing to diet or specialist drug therapy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Teaching feeding habits is part of management for every child with dyslipidemia, but it comes after the result is confirmed and secondary causes are excluded, and diet alone is unlikely to correct LDL this high.
C. Referral to a cardiology or lipid prevention clinic is right once familial hypercholesterolemia is confirmed or LDL remains very high after diet, when a statin may be needed; it is premature on a single unconfirmed result.
key_concept:
Child with high LDL: confirm, exclude secondary, then diet, then drugs.
  • Repeat fasting lipids and average two results
  • Secondary screen: TSH, renal (nephrotic), liver, glucose, medications
  • Family history and cascade screening for FH
  • Lifestyle diet trial first in most children
  • Statin considered from about 10 years if LDL stays ≥4.9 mmol/L (190 mg/dL), or lower with risk factors
exam_pearl: Confirmed persistent LDL ≥4.9 mmol/L despite diet in a child aged 10 or older is when referral for statin therapy becomes the answer.

stem: Child presented with projectile vomiting, diagnosed with pyloric stenosis. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: Once pyloric stenosis is diagnosed, the condition is not a surgical emergency; the priority is to stop feeds (NPO) and correct dehydration and the hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis before pyloromyotomy. This recall's key is NPO because stopping oral intake is the first step of preoperative stabilization in a child who keeps vomiting every feed. The lead-in "next step" after diagnosis points to stabilization, not more imaging.
why_wrong_block:
A. An NGT can be used to decompress the stomach, but it is not routinely required and is not the defining first step; it is reserved for persistent vomiting or a distended stomach.
C. Bicarbonate would worsen the metabolic alkalosis that pyloric stenosis already causes; the correct fluid is 0.9% sodium chloride (with dextrose and potassium once urine output is confirmed).
D. Ultrasound is the first investigation to confirm pyloric stenosis, but the stem says the diagnosis is already made, so imaging is not the next step.
key_concept:
Pyloric stenosis: diagnose with US, stabilize first, operate later.
  • Age 2 to 8 weeks, projectile non-bilious vomiting, hungry vomiter, olive mass
  • Labs: hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis
  • Imaging: abdominal ultrasound first
  • Management: NPO + IV 0.9% saline resuscitation, correct K and Cl
  • Then pyloromyotomy once electrolytes are corrected
exam_pearl: Never take a pyloric stenosis infant to theatre with uncorrected alkalosis; and never give bicarbonate to an alkalotic child.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Second screenshot (another exam version): Pyloric stenosis initial management? A. NPO B. Nasogastric tube C. IV sodium chloride D. Surgery. Athar: IV Sodium Chloride; Alhomrani: NPO. Compiler: 'This is literally handicap question (unfortunately it's true). Anyhow, there is no way I give him saline while he is still drinking mother's milk!!!'
Other marked answers: Athar: IV sodium chloride

stem: 5-year-old child with high fever (I think 38) for 6 days, cracked red lips, rash, cervical lymphadenopathy, red eyes. What is the diagnosis?
why_right: Fever lasting 6 days plus cracked red lips, rash, cervical lymphadenopathy and red eyes (non-purulent conjunctivitis) gives fever ≥5 days with 4 principal features, which meets the criteria for Kawasaki disease. Diagnosis matters because untreated Kawasaki risks coronary artery aneurysms.
why_wrong_block:
A. Scarlet fever gives a sandpaper rash with strawberry tongue after streptococcal pharyngitis, but no conjunctivitis or cracked lips, and fever settles quickly with penicillin.
C. Rocky Mountain spotted fever follows a tick bite and gives headache with a petechial rash starting at wrists and ankles spreading centrally; it is not endemic here and lacks the lips plus conjunctiva plus node combination.
key_concept:
Kawasaki = fever ≥5 days + 4 of 5 (CRASH).
  • C: conjunctivitis, bilateral non-exudative
  • R: rash, polymorphous
  • A: adenopathy, cervical, usually unilateral
  • S: strawberry tongue, red cracked lips
  • H: hands and feet swelling, erythema, later peeling
  • Treat: IVIG + aspirin; echo for coronary aneurysm
exam_pearl: Persistent fever unresponsive to antipyretics with non-purulent conjunctivitis is Kawasaki until proven otherwise; purulent eyes point to an infection instead.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot version (next page): 2-year-old girl, relapsing fever 9 days, irritability, non-purulent conjunctivitis, red cracked lips, swollen erythematous hands and feet, maculopapular rash; Answer: B Kawasaki disease.

stem: Child presented with red urine and fever on examination there is abdominal discomfort. (It is a Long case) What is the diagnosis
key_concept:
Red urine in a child: look for infection signs vs nephritic signs.
  • Fever + abdominal/flank pain + pyuria: acute pyelonephritis
  • Dysuria, frequency, afebrile or low fever: cystitis (lower UTI)
  • Edema + HTN + RBC casts + recent strep or skin infection: PSGN
  • WBC casts: pyelonephritis; RBC casts: glomerulonephritis
exam_pearl: Fever with loin or abdominal pain and pyuria points to the upper tract; edema, hypertension and RBC casts point to the glomerulus.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 12-year-old patient presents to the clinic with diarrhoea, vomiting, miosis, bronchoconstriction, sweating, and excessive salivation. On examination, the breath has a garlic odour. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Diarrhoea, vomiting, miosis, bronchoconstriction, sweating and excessive salivation form the cholinergic toxidrome caused by acetylcholinesterase inhibition, which is organophosphate poisoning. The garlic odour on the breath is a classic supporting clue.
why_wrong_block:
B. DKA gives a fruity (acetone) breath, Kussmaul breathing, polyuria and polydipsia with hyperglycemia and ketosis; it does not cause miosis, salivation or bronchospasm.
C. Cyanide causes a bitter almond odour, sudden collapse, seizures and severe lactic acidosis with cherry red skin; there is no cholinergic picture.
D. Cocaine is sympathomimetic: mydriasis, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia and agitation; sweating occurs but pupils are dilated, not constricted.
key_concept:
Organophosphate = cholinergic excess (DUMBBELSS).
  • Diarrhea, Urination, Miosis, Bradycardia, Bronchospasm/bronchorrhea
  • Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation, Sweating
  • Nicotinic: fasciculations, weakness
  • Garlic breath odour
  • Treat: atropine + pralidoxime, decontamination
exam_pearl: Pinpoint pupils with wet secretions = cholinergic (organophosphate); pinpoint pupils with dry, quiet breathing = opioid.

stem: A 3-year-old asymptomatic child is examined prior to elective oral surgery. A grade 2/6 low-pitched continuous murmur is heard at the upper right sternal border when the child is sitting; the murmur disappears when the child is supine. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?
OptC: Antibiotic prophylaxis prior to oral surgery
OptD: Postpone oral surgery and re-evaluate the child
highlight_terms_source: murmur disappears when the child is supine
why_right: An asymptomatic child with a soft grade 2/6 continuous murmur at the upper right sternal border that is heard sitting and disappears supine has a venous hum, a classic innocent murmur. Positional change is the hallmark of innocence, so the child can be reassured and the surgery proceed.
why_wrong_block:
B. Cardiology referral is for pathological features: grade ≥3 or thrill, any diastolic component, abnormal S2, symptoms or a murmur that does not vary with position.
C. Endocarditis prophylaxis before dental procedures is only for high-risk cardiac lesions (prosthetic valve, previous endocarditis, certain cyanotic or repaired heart disease); an innocent murmur needs none.
D. Postponing would be right for a new pathological murmur or a murmur during acute febrile illness needing re-examination; a positional venous hum in a well child is no reason to delay.
key_concept:
Innocent murmur features (the S's).
  • Soft, Short, Systolic (venous hum is the continuous exception)
  • Normal heart Sounds, Symptomless
  • Special tests normal
  • Sitting/standing changes it
  • Venous hum: continuous, upper right sternal border or infraclavicular, louder sitting, gone supine or with neck compression
exam_pearl: A continuous murmur is usually pathological (PDA) unless it vanishes when supine: then it is a venous hum.

stem: Parents brought their child to the hospital for inability to move his arm Xray showed fracture at both distal ulna and radial bone. The child looks healthy and dressed well, and good hygiene they recall that 2 days ago the mom dropped a plate at the child arm and noticed he couldn't move his arm they didn't notice any bruising, so they thought it's just a strain. Which of the following is indicative of child abuse?
why_right: The parents noticed he couldn't move his arm after the injury but came only 2 days later. An unexplained delay in seeking care for an obvious injury is a recognized red flag for non-accidental injury, even when the family appears caring.
why_wrong_block:
A. A distal radius and ulna fracture is a common accidental injury in children; abuse-specific fractures are metaphyseal corner lesions, posterior rib fractures, multiple fractures of different ages or long bone fractures in non-mobile infants.
C. A consistent history argues against abuse; it is an inconsistent, changing or implausible history that raises concern.
D. A well-dressed, clean child argues against neglect but does not exclude physical abuse; appearance is not itself an indicator here.
key_concept:
Red flags for non-accidental injury.
  • Delay in seeking medical care
  • History inconsistent with injury or developmental stage, or changing story
  • Injuries of different ages, patterned bruises, burns
  • Metaphyseal corner fractures, posterior rib fractures
  • Fractures in non-ambulatory infants
  • Any concern: document and involve child protection
exam_pearl: Good hygiene and a caring look never rule out abuse; the timeline of presentation does the talking.

stem: 7 years female with eyelid erythema heliotrope rash and thickening of skin over metacarpophalangeal joints + proximal muscle weakness
highlight_terms_source: thickening of skin over metacarpophalangeal joints
why_right: Heliotrope rash of the eyelids plus thickened skin over the MCP joints (Gottron papules) plus proximal muscle weakness in a 7-year-old is the pathognomonic triad of juvenile dermatomyositis. The skin signs combined with myopathy separate it from other connective tissue diseases.
why_wrong_block:
A. Scleroderma causes skin tightening (sclerodactyly), Raynaud and morphea plaques; it does not give heliotrope rash or Gottron papules with proximal myopathy.
B. SLE gives a malar rash sparing nasolabial folds, oral ulcers, arthritis and cytopenias or nephritis; myositis can occur but heliotrope and Gottron papules point to dermatomyositis.
D. Rheumatic fever follows streptococcal pharyngitis with carditis, migratory arthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum and subcutaneous nodules; there is no myopathy or eyelid rash.
key_concept:
Juvenile dermatomyositis: rash + proximal weakness.
  • Heliotrope (violaceous) eyelid rash
  • Gottron papules over MCP and IP joints
  • Symmetric proximal weakness (Gowers sign)
  • Raised muscle enzymes (CK, aldolase), MRI or biopsy to confirm
  • Children: calcinosis is a typical complication
exam_pearl: Unlike adult dermatomyositis, the juvenile form is not linked to malignancy; its typical complications are calcinosis and vasculopathy.

stem: 4 years old came with URTI, high fever, drooling of saliva and multiple enlarged lymph node. He did not receive any vaccine. Which of following vaccine might prevent this condition?
why_right: This recall's key is the diphtheria vaccine: an unvaccinated child with a preceding URTI, drooling and multiple enlarged lymph nodes (bull neck) fits respiratory diphtheria, where the pharyngeal pseudomembrane causes dysphagia and airway obstruction. DTaP would have prevented it. The URTI prodrome and prominent lymphadenopathy are the clues used to argue against Hib epiglottitis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hib vaccine prevents epiglottitis: abrupt onset over hours, high fever, toxic child, drooling, tripod position and stridor, without a URTI prodrome or prominent lymphadenopathy.
B. No vaccine is used against group A streptococcus, and pneumococcal vaccine does not prevent this picture; streptococcal pharyngitis or lymphadenitis is not a vaccine-preventable answer here.
D. Polio presents with fever then asymmetric flaccid paralysis; it does not cause pharyngeal obstruction with drooling and lymphadenopathy.
key_concept:
Drooling + fever in an unvaccinated child: diphtheria vs Hib epiglottitis.
  • Diphtheria: gradual onset, low-grade fever, grey pseudomembrane that bleeds when removed, bull neck nodes
  • Epiglottitis (Hib): abrupt onset, high fever, toxic, drooling, tripod, stridor
  • Drooling occurs in both
  • Pseudomembrane or bull neck is the decider for diphtheria
  • Prevention: DTaP vs Hib conjugate vaccine
exam_pearl: A white membrane or bull neck = diphtheria; sudden toxic drooling child sitting forward = Hib.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Compiler: "I Always Wondered How This Recall Being Solved Hemophilus All The Time. Anyhow, My Answer Since July Is Diphtheria, Prior URTI Stands Against HIB (Assuming It Was Really URTI, Not Sore Throat). Don't rely on the recall because examinees write things from their understanding." Attached Telegram notes: one recall mentioned a white patch in oral cavity ("This Is For Sure Diphtheria"); Gradual onset (days) + low grade fever = Diphtheria; Abrupt onset (hours to 2 days) + high grade fever = Hemophilus; drooling occurs in both; pseudomembrane would differentiate.
Other marked answers: Common recall solution: A (Hemophilus)

stem: Child presented with bowed legs and Harrison sulcus suggestive of rickets. Most appropriate treatment/supplement?
why_right: Bowed legs and a Harrison sulcus are classic bony signs of rickets, which in a child is most often nutritional vitamin D deficiency. The lead-in asks for the treatment/supplement, so the answer is the vitamin D form used for treatment: daily vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol), with adequate calcium intake.
why_wrong_block: A. Vitamin A: deficiency causes night blindness, xerophthalmia and Bitot spots, not bone deformity. Right when the child has eye signs or measles needing supplementation, not bowing and a Harrison sulcus.
key_concept:
Rickets = defective mineralisation of growing bone; nutritional vitamin D deficiency is the commonest cause.
  • Signs: frontal bossing, craniotabes, widened wrists, rachitic rosary, Harrison sulcus, bowed legs
  • X-ray wrist: metaphyseal cupping and fraying
  • Nutritional rickets: treat with daily vitamin D3 plus calcium
  • Malabsorption (e.g. celiac) can also cause rickets: still vitamin D3, plus treat the cause
  • Hypophosphatemic rickets: phosphate low, calcium normal, does not respond to plain vitamin D
exam_pearl: If asked which type of vitamin D, the answer is D3 (cholecalciferol); if labs show low phosphate with normal calcium, think hypophosphatemic rickets instead.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's "Q:" restatement: A kid with rickets, what type of vitamin D do you give him? vitamin D1 / D2 / D3 / D4?. Answer: vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol).

stem: 10-year-old with polyuria/polydipsia, HbA1c 6.8%, C-peptide 0.09 (low). Most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A 10-year-old with polyuria/polydipsia and an HbA1c of 6.8% (diabetic range, ≥6.5%) has diabetes. The decisive clue is the low C-peptide: it means the beta cells are not making insulin, which is the hallmark of type 1 diabetes (autoimmune insulin deficiency), the commonest diabetes of childhood.
why_wrong_block:
B. Type 2 diabetes mellitus: insulin resistance with preserved or high C-peptide, usually in an obese adolescent with acanthosis nigricans. A low C-peptide argues against it.
C. MODY: autosomal dominant, with diabetes in several consecutive generations, mild hyperglycaemia and preserved C-peptide without autoantibodies. Right when there is a strong multigenerational family history and C-peptide is detectable.
D. Stress-induced hyperglycemia: transient high glucose during acute illness, with a normal HbA1c because it does not reflect 3 months of hyperglycaemia. Here the HbA1c is already raised and there are classic osmotic symptoms.
key_concept:
C-peptide separates insulin deficiency from insulin resistance.
  • Low C-peptide + child + osmotic symptoms = type 1 DM
  • Normal/high C-peptide + obesity + acanthosis = type 2 DM
  • Preserved C-peptide + dominant family history, antibody negative = MODY
  • HbA1c ≥6.5% is in the diabetic range; acute stress hyperglycaemia leaves HbA1c normal
  • Type 1 DM can present first as DKA
exam_pearl: High glucose with a normal HbA1c in an ill child is stress hyperglycaemia; a raised HbA1c with low C-peptide is type 1.

stem: A pediatric patient has been diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis. His brother and sister, who live in the same household, are asymptomatic. Which of the following regimens is appropriate for chemoprophylaxis in these close contacts?
why_right: Household contacts of meningococcal disease need chemoprophylaxis whether or not they have symptoms. Of the regimens listed, a single dose of ciprofloxacin is the only correct, standard regimen and it is the agent best suited to Neisseria meningitidis. The other options use the wrong drug or the wrong number of doses.
why_wrong_block:
A. Penicillin and rifampin for 1 week: penicillin does not clear nasopharyngeal carriage, and rifampicin prophylaxis is a short 2-day course, not a week. Right when only rifampicin for 2 days is offered for a child contact.
C. Penicillin for 1 week: penicillin treats invasive disease but does not eradicate carriage, so it is not used for prophylaxis. It is not right for any contact prophylaxis scenario.
D. IM ceftriaxone 4 doses: ceftriaxone is a valid prophylactic agent (preferred in pregnancy) but as a single IM dose; multiple doses is a treatment-type regimen, not prophylaxis.
key_concept:
Meningococcal contact prophylaxis: give to close/household contacts, symptomatic or not, as soon as possible.
  • Ciprofloxacin: single oral dose, best for N. meningitidis
  • Rifampicin: 2-day course; classic choice for children and for Hib contacts
  • Ceftriaxone: single IM dose; choice in pregnancy
  • Penicillin does not clear carriage, so it is never prophylaxis
  • Hajj pilgrims need meningococcal vaccination
exam_pearl: The count matters: ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone are single doses, rifampicin is 2 days; any option giving a week or multiple ceftriaxone doses is wrong.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1934).
Compiler note: Short recall version: 'Case about meningitis and family need Prophylaxis' with options A: ciprofloxacin single dose (highlighted), B: penicillin + rifampin, C: certificate.

stem: 4 y boy coming to clinic concerning about short stature has multiple dysmorphic features and Webbed neck and ejection murmurs at auscultation what is syndrome
why_right: The key words are a 4-year-old boy with short stature, webbed neck, dysmorphic features and an ejection murmur. Noonan syndrome is the Turner-like phenotype that occurs in boys (and girls) with a normal karyotype, and its typical heart lesion is pulmonary valve stenosis, which gives an ejection systolic murmur.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sotos: an overgrowth syndrome with tall stature, large head and advanced bone age. Right when the child is tall with macrocephaly, not short with a webbed neck.
B. Turner: 45,X affects girls only, with webbed neck, short stature, delayed puberty and coarctation or bicuspid aortic valve. It would be right if this were a girl; a boy rules it out.
C. Marfan: tall, thin, long limbs, arachnodactyly, lens dislocation and aortic root dilatation. Right with tall stature and lens subluxation, the opposite of this short child.
key_concept:
Webbed neck + short stature: sex decides between Turner and Noonan.
  • Girl, 45,X, coarctation or bicuspid aortic valve, ovarian failure = Turner
  • Boy (or girl with normal karyotype), pulmonary stenosis, cryptorchidism = Noonan (autosomal dominant)
  • Tall + arachnodactyly + lens dislocation = Marfan
  • Tall + macrocephaly + advanced bone age = Sotos
exam_pearl: A webbed neck in a boy is Noonan, never Turner; right-sided lesion (pulmonary stenosis) for Noonan, left-sided (coarctation) for Turner.

stem: Child with Multiple bruses and ptechia with echomosis after history of runny nose and flu symptoms and her brother has same symptoms Isolated thrombocytopenia in child Labs: Platelet 22 WBC 8 Hg 125 what is the most diagnostic test?
highlight_terms_source: after history of runny nose and flu symptoms
why_right: A child with bruises and petechiae after a viral (flu-like) illness and isolated thrombocytopenia (platelets 22 with normal WBC 8 and Hb 125) is the classic picture of immune thrombocytopenia. ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion, and the key test is the blood film: it confirms true thrombocytopenia (excludes clumping), shows large platelets, and excludes blasts, fragmented red cells (HUS/TTP) or abnormal platelet morphology that would point elsewhere.
why_wrong_block:
A. Coagulation profile: PT/aPTT are normal in ITP because the defect is platelet number, not clotting factors. Right when bleeding is into joints or muscles (haemophilia) or DIC is suspected in a sick child.
B. BM aspiration: not needed when only platelets are low and the film is typical. Right when there are other cytopenias, blasts, bone pain, organomegaly or a poor response to treatment (suspected leukaemia or aplasia).
D. Anti platelet antibody: neither sensitive nor specific, so it does not confirm or exclude ITP and is not part of routine work-up.
key_concept:
Childhood ITP: well child, petechiae/bruising 1 to 4 weeks after a viral illness, isolated low platelets.
  • Diagnose with CBC + blood film (exclusion diagnosis)
  • Bone marrow only if atypical: other cell lines abnormal, blasts, organomegaly, bone pain
  • Coagulation normal; antiplatelet antibodies not useful
  • Management in children is mostly supportive; steroids or IVIG for significant bleeding
  • A family history of low platelets raises inherited thrombocytopenia, also seen on the film (giant platelets)
exam_pearl: Isolated thrombocytopenia = blood film; add anaemia, high or low WBC or blasts = bone marrow aspiration.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1758).
