stem: Isolated jaundice in neonate 5 days old all other exam normal ( doctor notice yellow skin in pediatric clinic , parents came for postpartum checkup ) What is the diagnosis?
key_concept:
Neonatal jaundice by timing and examination.
  • First 24 hours = pathological (haemolysis) until proven otherwise
  • Days 2 to 3, well baby = physiological
  • First week with poor intake = breastfeeding jaundice
  • End of week 1 into weeks 2 to 3, thriving breastfed baby, normal exam = breast milk jaundice (observe, continue breastfeeding)
  • Beyond 2 weeks or conjugated bilirubin or pale stools = investigate (biliary atresia)
  • Neurological signs + very high bilirubin = kernicterus
exam_pearl: A normal neurological exam excludes kernicterus; jaundice only becomes kernicterus when the baby shows neuro signs.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: An 11-month-old boy is not moving his right hand and when he presented to the hospital it appeared that he had right ulnar and radial fracture presented after 2 days history of a fall on an outstretched hand when the doctor asked the parents why they didn't bring him earlier they said that they didn't see any bruises. child is dressed well, well-nourished and has had regular well baby visits.
OptA: Treat the child and inform the authorities
OptB: Believe the parents and treat the child
OptC: Treat the child and order head CT
why_right: An 11-month-old with a radius and ulna fracture, brought 2 days late, with an explanation that does not fully fit, must raise suspicion of non-accidental injury even if the child is well dressed, well nourished and attends well-baby visits. The doctor's duty is to treat the injury and report the concern to the child protection authorities, who investigate; the physician does not need proof, only reasonable suspicion.
why_wrong_block:
B. Believe the parents and treat the child: ignores the red flags (delayed presentation, long-bone fracture in an infant) and could send the child back to harm. Right only when the mechanism, age and timing fully match the injury.
C. Treat the child and order head CT: neuroimaging is for suspected abuse with neurological signs or in very young infants; this child has no head findings. The legal and ethical step being tested is reporting.
D. Call the police: the report goes through the hospital child protection team/social services, which involves the police if needed. Right if the child is in immediate danger from a violent adult at the scene.
key_concept:
Suspected child abuse: treat, protect, report.
  • Red flags: delay in seeking care, inconsistent or changing history, injury not matching developmental stage, fractures in non-ambulant infants
  • Good appearance and regular visits do not exclude abuse
  • Admit or keep the child safe if risk at home
  • Report to child protection on suspicion, no proof required
  • Work-up under 2 years: skeletal survey; neuroimaging if neuro signs or very young infant
exam_pearl: Suspicion is enough: report to child protection services, not straight to the police, and never just believe the parents.

stem: 5 years old with chronic productive cough , was admitted to hospital multiple times with wheezing and received antibiotics, neonatal admission for jaundice and treatment with phototherapy Brother has same condition What is the investigation:
why_right: A 5-year-old with chronic productive cough, repeated admissions with wheeze needing antibiotics, a sibling with the same condition (autosomal recessive) and a history of neonatal jaundice (prolonged neonatal jaundice is a recognised early CF feature) points to cystic fibrosis. The diagnostic investigation is the sweat chloride test.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cbc: may show infection but is non-specific and cannot diagnose the underlying cause of recurrent chest infections. Right when the question is about anaemia, infection markers or a haematological diagnosis.
B. Abg: assesses acute respiratory failure or acid-base status, not the cause of chronic suppurative lung disease. Right in an acutely hypoxic or exhausted child.
key_concept:
Chronic productive cough + recurrent chest infections + affected sibling = think cystic fibrosis.
  • Other clues: failure to thrive, steatorrhoea, rectal prolapse, meconium ileus, prolonged neonatal jaundice, nasal polyps
  • Diagnosis: sweat chloride test
  • Confirm/genetic: CFTR mutation analysis; also used to test asymptomatic siblings
  • Inheritance: autosomal recessive
exam_pearl: Recurrent wheeze is not always asthma: a productive cough with repeated antibiotic courses and a similar sibling means sweat test.

stem: Weight chart with plateauing after six month(after introduction of food) asking which food should be avoided:
key_concept:
Growth chart + timing of onset points to the cause.
  • Faltering after weaning onto cereals = celiac disease (avoid gluten: wheat, barley, rye)
  • Faltering from starting formula or dairy, with blood in stool or eczema = cow's milk protein allergy
  • Weight falls first, length preserved = nutritional/malabsorptive failure to thrive
  • Celiac serology must be done while still eating gluten
exam_pearl: Do not stop gluten before testing: serology and biopsy turn falsely negative on a gluten-free diet.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Newborn after CS has respiratory distress without desaturating. X ray shows: fluid in the lung fissure What is next step:
why_right: Newborn "after CS" with respiratory distress and "fluid in the lung fissure" on X-ray is transient tachypnea of the newborn (TTN), caused by delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid. TTN is self resolving, so management is supportive: low concentration supplemental oxygen (the recall's "30-40" oxygen) titrated to saturation, with monitoring, while the fluid clears over the first days.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV fluid does not treat retained lung fluid; IV fluids are used only if the baby is too tachypneic to feed safely, and fluid overload can worsen it.
C. The X-ray has already been done and shows the classic TTN finding; repeating it adds nothing unless the baby deteriorates or does not improve.
key_concept:
Term or near-term baby by C-section + tachypnea + fluid in fissures = TTN.
  • TTN: retained fetal lung fluid, CXR perihilar streaks / fluid in fissures, resolves within days
  • RDS: preterm, surfactant deficiency, diffuse ground glass (reticulogranular) CXR
  • TTN treatment: supportive, oxygen as needed, observe; no surfactant or antibiotics needed for TTN itself
  • Worsening or prolonged course: rethink (pneumonia, RDS, PPHN)
exam_pearl: Preterm with ground glass CXR is RDS (surfactant); term C-section with fluid in the fissure is TTN (supportive oxygen).

stem: Most diagnostic investigation for renal scarring
why_right: DMSA (technetium-99m dimercaptosuccinic acid) is a static cortical scan: the tracer binds to functioning proximal tubular cells, so scars appear as cortical defects. It is the most sensitive and diagnostic test for renal scarring (for example after pyelonephritis with vesicoureteral reflux), which is exactly what "most diagnostic ... renal scarring" asks.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ultrasound is the first, noninvasive screen (size, hydronephrosis, anatomy) but it misses many cortical scars; right as the initial imaging after a febrile UTI, not as the most diagnostic test for scarring.
B. MAG3 is a dynamic (renogram) scan for drainage, obstruction and split function, for example in suspected PUJ obstruction; it is not the test of choice for cortical scars.
key_concept:
Pediatric renal imaging by question:
  • Anatomy / first screen after UTI: ultrasound
  • Reflux (VUR): MCUG (VCUG)
  • Cortical scarring: DMSA (static scan)
  • Obstruction / drainage: MAG3 (dynamic renogram)
exam_pearl: Scar = DMSA (static); drainage or obstruction = MAG3 (dynamic); reflux = MCUG.

stem: A 10-year-old patient presents with a 3-day history of yellow discoloration of the sclera, anorexia and abdominal pain (see lab results).Test Result Normal Values Indirect bilirubin 140 <19 mol/L Total bilirubin 260 <20.5 mol/L Albumin 40 36-52 g/L Total Proteins 76 56-80 g/L Alanine aminotransferase 878 10-35 U/L Aspartate aminotransferase 1005 12-40 IU/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A 10-year-old with 3 days of scleral icterus, anorexia and abdominal pain, and transaminases near or above 1000 (ALT 878, AST 1005) has an acute hepatocellular injury, which in a child is most often acute viral (infective) hepatitis, classically hepatitis A. Bilirubin is raised with both conjugated and unconjugated parts, and albumin and total protein are normal, fitting an acute rather than chronic process.
why_wrong_block:
A. Gilbert syndrome gives a mild, isolated indirect hyperbilirubinemia with normal liver enzymes, often triggered by fasting or illness; enzymes in the 1000s exclude it.
C. Obstructive jaundice gives a predominantly direct bilirubin with high ALP and GGT and only modest transaminase rise, often with pale stools and dark urine; enzymes in the 1000s point to the hepatocyte instead.
D. Acute pancreatitis presents with epigastric pain radiating to the back and raised lipase or amylase; jaundice with transaminases near 1000 is not its picture.
key_concept:
Read the liver panel pattern:
  • Hepatocellular: ALT/AST very high (hundreds to thousands) = acute viral, toxic (paracetamol) or ischemic hepatitis
  • Cholestatic: ALP/GGT high, direct bilirubin predominant = obstruction
  • Isolated indirect bilirubin, normal enzymes = Gilbert or hemolysis
  • Low albumin suggests chronic disease or synthetic failure
exam_pearl: Transaminases near 1000 mean hepatitis, not obstruction or Gilbert, whatever the bilirubin split.

stem: Child w/ PMHx of Influenza vaccine flushing, SYNCOPE What to do in the future
OptA: don't give any vaccine in the future
OptC: give inactivated vaccine w/ antihistamine & steroid
OptD: Don't give influenza vaccine in the future
why_right: Flushing plus syncope after an influenza vaccine is read here as a serious (anaphylactic type) reaction to that vaccine. A serious allergic reaction to a previous dose of a vaccine is an absolute contraindication to further doses of that same vaccine, so the influenza vaccine should not be given again, while the rest of the schedule continues.
why_wrong_block:
A. Stopping all vaccines is wrong: a reaction to one vaccine contraindicates only that vaccine (or a shared component), not the whole immunization schedule.
B. The intranasal (live attenuated) vaccine is still an influenza vaccine with overlapping components, so a serious reaction to influenza vaccine contraindicates it as well.
C. Premedication with antihistamine and steroid does not make it safe to re-give a vaccine that caused a serious allergic reaction; mild local reactions or mild egg allergy need no premedication at all.
key_concept:
Vaccine contraindication ladder:
  • Absolute: anaphylaxis to a prior dose or to a vaccine component = do not give that vaccine
  • Precaution: moderate to severe acute illness; GBS within 6 weeks of a prior influenza vaccine
  • Not a contraindication: mild illness, local reaction, low to moderate fever after a dose, antibiotics, mild egg allergy for inactivated influenza vaccine
  • Live vaccines: avoid in immunodeficiency and pregnancy
exam_pearl: If the stem describes isolated fainting right after the injection (vasovagal), that is not a contraindication; flushing with collapse is treated as a serious reaction.

stem: Child w/ dilated CMP, CP, SOB, Fever, Tx ? There was associated CXR (i saw pulmonary edema (not sure)
why_right: A child with known dilated cardiomyopathy presenting with shortness of breath, chest pain and (per the recall) pulmonary edema on CXR is in acute decompensated heart failure with fluid overload, possibly triggered by the febrile illness. The first treatment for congestion is a loop diuretic, furosemide, together with oxygen, to offload the lungs and relieve dyspnea.
why_wrong_block:
A. Epinephrine is for anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest or refractory shock; it raises myocardial oxygen demand and is not the treatment of pulmonary edema in a perfused child.
B. Dobutamine is an inotrope for low cardiac output or cardiogenic shock (hypotension, poor perfusion); the stem describes congestion, not shock.
C. Milrinone (inodilator) is likewise reserved for low output states, usually in intensive care; it is not the first step for pulmonary edema with adequate perfusion.
key_concept:
Acute heart failure: decide wet vs dry and warm vs cold.
  • Warm and wet (congested, perfused): loop diuretic (furosemide) + oxygen; vasodilator if hypertensive
  • Cold and wet (low output, shock): add inotrope (dobutamine, milrinone)
  • Chronic DCM: ACE inhibitor, beta blocker, spironolactone
  • Fever + chest pain + new failure in a child: think myocarditis
exam_pearl: Inotropes only when the stem shows shock or poor perfusion; pulmonary edema alone gets furosemide.

stem: Ketone positive Characteristic odor Hypoglycemia Seizure Diagnosis?
why_right: "Marble urine syndrome" is the recall's spelling of maple syrup urine disease (MSUD), a branched chain amino acid (leucine, isoleucine, valine) metabolism defect. The clue combination is "ketone positive" + "characteristic odor" (sweet, maple syrup or burnt sugar smell of urine and sweat) + "hypoglycemia" + "seizure", typically in a neonate after starting feeds, with poor feeding, vomiting and encephalopathy.
why_wrong_block:
A. DKA also gives ketones and a fruity breath, but with hyperglycemia, polyuria, polydipsia and acidosis; hypoglycemia rules it out.
C. Galactosemia presents after milk feeds with jaundice, hepatomegaly, vomiting, cataracts and E. coli sepsis, with hypoglycemia and urinary reducing substances; there is no characteristic odor.
D. Hereditary fructose intolerance appears at weaning when fructose or sucrose (fruit, juice) is introduced, with vomiting, hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly; no typical odor and not in a milk-only neonate.
key_concept:
Metabolic odors and clues:
  • Maple syrup / burnt sugar urine + ketosis + encephalopathy: MSUD
  • Musty / mousy odor + fair skin + intellectual disability: phenylketonuria
  • Sweaty feet odor: isovaleric acidemia
  • Fruity breath + hyperglycemia: DKA
  • Milk then jaundice, cataract, E. coli sepsis: galactosemia
  • Fruit or sucrose at weaning then hypoglycemia: fructose intolerance
exam_pearl: Ketones with LOW glucose and a sweet urine odor is MSUD, not DKA.

stem: 4yo PRE SCHOOL the mother complains from nocturia
why_right: A "4yo" preschool child wetting at night (the recall's "nocturia" means bedwetting) is within the normal range: night dryness is the last continence skill, and bedwetting is not considered clinically significant enuresis before about 6 years. The right step is reassurance plus good toilet habits: regular daytime voiding, voiding before bed, limiting evening drinks and positive reinforcement without punishment.
why_wrong_block:
A. Postponing toilet training until 6 is wrong; the child should keep normal toileting routines, and age 6 is only the threshold for calling bedwetting enuresis, not for starting training.
C. Urology referral is for red flags: daytime wetting, secondary enuresis after a dry period, recurrent UTIs, poor stream or dribbling, polyuria or abnormal exam; none is described.
D. An enuresis alarm is a treatment for established nocturnal enuresis in an older, motivated school-age child (beyond the age 6 threshold), not for a normal 4-year-old.
key_concept:
Bedwetting by age:
  • Under about 6 years: normal; reassure, toilet habits, positive reinforcement
  • About 6 years and over: nocturnal enuresis; urinalysis, then alarm (first line) or desmopressin
  • Red flags (daytime symptoms, secondary, UTI, polyuria): investigate or refer
exam_pearl: The age decides: a 4-year-old gets reassurance and habits; a school-age child over 6 gets an alarm.

stem: A child brought by mother for development assessment. He can walk backwards, Follow simple commands. He started using a spoon and Pointing to things he is interested. What is the expected age for this child by months?
why_right: "Follows simple commands" and "pointing to things he is interested" are 15 month skills, and early independent walking with walking backwards and "started using a spoon" (just starting, not skilled) fit the same stage. No 18 month marker is given (running, pouring pellets, 6 to 10 words), so the expected age is 15 months.
why_wrong_block:
A. 18 months needs markers such as running, pouring pellets from a bottle or a vocabulary of about 6 to 10 words, none of which is given.
C. 24 months would show walking up stairs, kicking a ball and 2 word phrases; this child shows only early toddler skills.
D. 48 months is far beyond: a 4-year-old hops, tells stories and speaks in full sentences.
key_concept:
Toddler milestone anchors:
  • 12 months: walks alone, first words
  • 15 months: follows simple commands, points to show interest, tower of 3
  • 18 months: runs, pours pellets, about 6 to 10 words, tower of 4
  • 24 months: walks up stairs, 2 word phrases
  • Answer with the highest milestone the child has clearly achieved
exam_pearl: Add running or 6 to 10 words and the answer jumps to 18 months.

stem: A 10-days old boy presents in the ER after circumcision with 5-hours of bleeding from the operation site, what is the best step to do? Had high PTT
OptA: Applying pressure on the operation site
why_right: A 10-day-old with 5 hours of oozing after circumcision is actively bleeding, so the immediate best step is local hemostasis: firm direct pressure on the operation site. The "high PTT" points to an underlying coagulopathy (hemophilia, or vitamin K deficiency bleeding if vitamin K was missed), which is then worked up and corrected, but bleeding control with pressure comes first.
why_wrong_block:
B. Surgical exploration of the wound is for bleeding that persists despite pressure with a normal coagulation profile (a surgical vessel); with a prolonged PTT, operating before correcting the coagulopathy worsens bleeding.
C. The recall did not preserve this option's text; if it was factor replacement, vitamin K or FFP, that is the correction that follows once pressure is applied and the cause is identified.
D. Reassurance is unsafe: 5 hours of continuous bleeding in a neonate with a prolonged PTT is a true bleeding disorder until proven otherwise.
key_concept:
Post-circumcision bleeding in a neonate:
  • Step 1: direct pressure (local hemostasis)
  • Check PT, PTT, platelets; give vitamin K if not received
  • Isolated prolonged PTT in a boy: hemophilia A or B, give the specific factor
  • PT and PTT both prolonged: common pathway or vitamin K deficiency
  • Persistent bleeding with normal coagulation: surgical exploration
exam_pearl: Circumcision bleeding in a boy with high PTT is a classic first sign of hemophilia; pressure first, then factor.

stem: 4 years old boy, developed large neck swelling on the left side. On exam it is large 10cm in size, US FNA showed clear lymphatic fluid. What is the appropriate management?
why_right: A large lateral (left) neck swelling in a young child with "clear lymphatic fluid" on aspiration is a cystic hygroma (macrocystic lymphatic malformation). It is benign, so the aim is removal or ablation of the malformation; of the listed options only surgery treats it, and excision is the definitive option for a large 10 cm lesion.
why_wrong_block:
B. Observation is not appropriate for a large 10 cm lesion, which risks airway compression, infection and hemorrhage into the cyst; spontaneous regression is uncommon.
C. Chemotherapy is for malignancy (e.g. lymphoma, rhabdomyosarcoma); clear lymphatic fluid indicates a benign malformation.
D. Radiotherapy has no role in a benign lymphatic malformation in a child and carries growth and malignancy risks.
key_concept:
Pediatric neck masses:
  • Midline, moves with tongue protrusion: thyroglossal cyst, excision (Sistrunk)
  • Anterior border of sternocleidomastoid: branchial cyst, excision
  • Lateral / posterior triangle, soft, transilluminates, clear lymph fluid: cystic hygroma, sclerotherapy then surgery
  • Hard, fixed, systemic symptoms: think malignancy, biopsy
exam_pearl: Clear lymphatic fluid in a lateral neck mass = cystic hygroma; if sclerotherapy is offered, it is usually first for macrocystic lesions.

stem: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the Paediatric Outpatient Clinic because she is already showing breast development, appearance of pubic hair and acne. She is otherwise asymptomatic. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: breast development, appearance of pubic hair and acne
why_right: A 7 year old girl with breast development, then pubic hair and acne, who is "otherwise asymptomatic", is showing pubertal signs in their normal order. A normal sequence means the whole hypothalamic pituitary gonadal axis has switched on early, which is central (gonadotropin dependent) precocious puberty. In girls this is idiopathic in the large majority, so it is the most likely diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ovarian tumour: a peripheral (gonadotropin independent) source with suppressed LH and FSH and an out of order sequence; suspect it with rapid isolated estrogen effects, a pelvic mass or early vaginal bleeding.
C. Gonadotropin releasing tumour: rare and usually comes with other features; idiopathic central disease is far more likely in a well girl.
D. CNS lesion: an identifiable cause of central precocious puberty, but much more often found in boys or with neurological signs (headache, visual change); this girl is asymptomatic.
key_concept:
Normal sequence of pubertal signs = central; abnormal sequence = peripheral.
  • Central: pubertal LH/FSH, gonads make the steroids, always isosexual
  • Peripheral: prepubertal LH/FSH, source can be gonad, adrenal, ectopic or exogenous; iso or contrasexual
  • Girls: central is mostly idiopathic; boys: look harder for a CNS lesion
  • Workup: bone age, basal and GnRH stimulated LH, brain MRI
  • Treatment of central: GnRH agonist
exam_pearl: A boy with the same picture, or any girl with neurological signs, pushes you toward a CNS lesion.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer marked with ** in the screenshot.

stem: In which of the following conditions would you expect a bone age greater than the chronologic age?
why_right: The question asks where bone age exceeds chronological age. In congenital adrenal hyperplasia excess adrenal androgens accelerate epiphyseal maturation, so bone age runs ahead. These children are tall early but fuse early, ending with short adult height.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hypothyroidism: thyroid hormone is needed for skeletal maturation, so bone age is markedly delayed.
B. Chronic renal failure: chronic illness slows growth and delays bone age.
C. Familial short stature: bone age equals chronological age; the child is simply following short parents.
key_concept:
Sex steroid excess advances bone age; most growth failure delays it.
  • Advanced: CAH, precocious puberty, obesity, exogenous sex steroids
  • Delayed: hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, chronic illness (CKD, IBD), constitutional delay
  • Normal: familial short stature
  • CAH: commonest cause 21 hydroxylase deficiency; raised 17 hydroxyprogesterone
exam_pearl: Tall child now but short adult = advanced bone age from androgens or estrogens.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1999).
Compiler note: Answer marked with ** in the screenshot.

stem: A child with tall stature, long arms and fingers, following up with ophthalmology due to eye problems. On examination, he has mental retardation and skin bruising. What is his diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: tall stature, long arms and fingers
why_right: Tall stature with long arms and fingers plus an eye problem fits both Marfan syndrome and homocystinuria (marfanoid habitus with lens dislocation). The discriminating clue is mental retardation: intellectual disability is a feature of homocystinuria, while intelligence is normal in Marfan. Homocystinuria also carries a thrombotic tendency and osteoporosis, which Marfan does not.
why_wrong_block: A. Marfan: shares the tall habitus, arachnodactyly and ectopia lentis, but intelligence is normal; choose it when the picture adds aortic root dilation, mitral valve prolapse or pectus deformity with a normal intellect.
key_concept:
Marfan vs homocystinuria: same habitus, separated by intellect, lens direction and clotting.
  • Marfan: autosomal dominant, fibrillin 1; lens dislocates upward; aortic root dilation; normal IQ
  • Homocystinuria: autosomal recessive, cystathionine beta synthase deficiency; lens dislocates downward
  • Homocystinuria: intellectual disability, thromboembolism, osteoporosis
  • Other mimics: Ehlers Danlos (skin hyperelasticity, bruising), Klinefelter (tall, small testes)
exam_pearl: Marfanoid child plus intellectual disability or thrombosis = homocystinuria, not Marfan.

stem: A child came for a routine check up. He can walk steadily independently, and has an immature pincer grasp. Says 4-6 words, knows 2 body parts. What is the developmental age in months?
why_right: Place the child at the oldest milestone he has achieved. "Walks steadily independently" is past the 12 month stage of first steps, and the language clues are the decisive ones: about 4 to 6 words and knowing 2 body parts both belong to 15 months. The "immature pincer grasp" is a 9 month skill he has already passed, so it does not limit the age. He is not yet at the 18 month vocabulary of 6 to 10 words, so 15 months fits best.
why_wrong_block:
A. 24 months: expect 2 word phrases, about 50 words, climbing stairs and a 6 block tower; none are described.
B. 18 months: expect running and a vocabulary of 6 to 10 words; 4 to 6 words falls short.
D. 12 months: a child just starting to walk with only 1 to 3 words besides mama and dada; knowing body parts is later.
key_concept:
Developmental age = at or above the oldest achieved milestone, below the youngest missing one.
  • 12 m: walks alone, mature pincer, 1 to 3 words besides mama/dada, imitates
  • 15 m: walks well and backward, 3 to 6 words, points to body parts, uses spoon, 2 cube tower
  • 18 m: runs, 6 to 10 words, 4 cube tower, pours pellets from bottle
  • 24 m: 2 word phrases, about 50 words, stairs, 6 cube tower
exam_pearl: Word count is the tiebreaker: 4 to 6 words with body parts = 15 months; 6 to 10 words = 18 months.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Repeated below as 'Q:' version with Answer: C.

stem: Babay walking steady gate with wide steps and (rising both arms while walking) > i think the arm was like this im sure from the meaning
why_right: A wide based gait with both arms raised (the high guard posture) is the gait of a new independent walker, who keeps a broad base and lifts the arms for balance. Independent walking normally begins around 12 months and is established by about 15 months, so among these options 14 months is the age that fits a child who is walking alone but still with the immature high guard pattern.
why_wrong_block:
A. 8 m: at this age the child is sitting and starting to crawl; independent walking is not expected.
B. 9 m: pulls to stand and cruises at most; walking alone with any gait pattern is too early.
D. 15 m: by now walking is usually mature enough to walk backward, with arms lowered and a narrower base; the raised arm posture points slightly younger.
key_concept:
Early independent gait: wide base, arms high (high guard), short steps.
  • 9 m: pulls to stand, cruising
  • 12 m: first independent steps, wide base, arms raised
  • 15 m: walks well, walks backward, arms come down
  • 18 m: runs
exam_pearl: Arms up for balance = brand new walker (about 12 to 14 months); walking backward = 15 months.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Related variant recall under 1904.

stem: A baby is observed walking independently with a wide-based gait and arms raised for balance. At approximately what age is a child typically expected to walk independently with a wide-based gait and arms raised for balance?
highlight_terms_source: walking independently with a wide-based gait and arms raised for balance
why_right: The lead in asks when a child is typically expected to walk independently with a wide based gait and arms raised for balance. That high guard posture marks the onset of independent walking, which is a 12 month milestone. The broad base and raised arms are compensations for immature balance in the first weeks of walking.
why_wrong_block:
A. 9 months: the child pulls to stand and may cruise along furniture, but does not walk alone.
C. 15 months: walking is more mature by now (walks well, walks backward) and the arms are usually lowered.
key_concept:
Walking ladder:
  • 9 m: pulls to stand, cruises
  • 12 m: walks alone with wide base and arms raised
  • 15 m: walks well and backward
  • 18 m: runs
  • 24 m: up and down stairs
exam_pearl: Asked for the typical age, not a range: independent walking with high guard = 12 months.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Related variant recall under 1904.

stem: Child walking unsteady with raising hands when walking. How old is he in months:
why_right: "Walking unsteady with raising hands" describes the beginner walker: arms up in high guard to balance and an unstable, wide based gait. This is the picture of a child who has just started walking independently, the 12 month milestone.
why_wrong_block:
A. 15: walking is steadier by now, the child can walk backward and the arms have come down.
B. 18: the child runs and kicks a ball; an unsteady arms up gait would be immature for this age.
D. 24: the child climbs stairs and throws overhand; an unsteady beginner gait at 2 years would be delayed.
key_concept:
Gait matures fast after the first steps:
  • 12 m: unsteady, wide base, arms raised
  • 15 m: walks well, backward
  • 18 m: runs, kicks ball
  • 24 m: stairs, throws overhand
exam_pearl: Unsteady with hands up = 12 months; still like this at 18 months or later should prompt assessment.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Related variant recall under 1904.

stem: Baby with immature pincer grip, can say 5 to 6 words, and pointed 2 parts of his body, age in months
why_right: The decisive clues are language: 5 to 6 words and pointing to 2 body parts. Pointing to body parts is a 15 month skill and 3 to 6 words belongs to 15 months, while a vocabulary of 6 to 10 words is reached at 18 months. A child sitting at the top of the 15 month range but not yet at 18 months fits 17 months best among these options.
why_wrong_block:
A. 12: only 1 to 3 words besides mama and dada are expected and body part identification is not yet present.
C. 19: by now the child would be past the 18 month level with 6 to 10 words; 5 to 6 words is still below it.
D. 24: expect about 50 words and 2 word phrases; this child is well short of that.
key_concept:
Vocabulary ladder (single words):
  • 12 m: 1 to 3 words besides mama/dada
  • 15 m: 3 to 6 words, points to body parts
  • 18 m: 6 to 10 words
  • 24 m: about 50 words, 2 word phrases
  • 36 m: about 100 words, 3 word sentences
exam_pearl: Same options, different key: 5 to 6 words = 17 months (below 18); 6 to 10 words = 19 months (at or above 18).

stem: child can walk alone, steadily. Immature pincer grasp. Say 6-10 words and points to 2 body parts, how old is he by month?
why_right: The oldest milestone achieved is the vocabulary: 6 to 10 words is the 18 month level, so the child is at least 18 months. Steady independent walking and pointing to 2 body parts are earlier skills he has passed, and there are no 2 year skills such as 2 word phrases. The option at or just above 18 months and below 24 months is 19.
why_wrong_block:
A. 12: a child at 12 months is just starting to walk and has only 1 to 3 words besides mama and dada.
B. 17: fits 3 to 6 words with body parts; a full 6 to 10 word vocabulary means the 18 month level is reached.
D. 24: expect about 50 words and 2 word phrases, which are not described.
key_concept:
Age = at or above the oldest achieved milestone, below the youngest missing one.
  • 15 m: 3 to 6 words, points to body parts
  • 18 m: 6 to 10 words, runs
  • 24 m: about 50 words, 2 word phrases
exam_pearl: 6 to 10 words = 18 month level, so pick the option just above 18 (19), not the one below (17).

stem: Paedia walk back ward and use to eat spoon and from Age in month
why_right: The two clues are walking backward and using a spoon. Walking backward is a 15 month gross motor milestone, and starting to feed with a spoon (sloppily) is a 15 month self care skill. Both together place the child at 15 months.
why_wrong_block:
A. 12 month: the child has only just started walking forward and drinks from a cup; walking backward and spoon use come later.
C. 24 month: expect stairs, throwing overhand and 2 word phrases; a 2 year old would be described with those, not with first spoon use.
D. 9 month: pulls to stand and has an early pincer grasp; not walking at all.
key_concept:
15 month cluster:
  • Gross motor: walks well and backward
  • Fine motor: scribbles, 2 cube tower, inserts pellets into bottle
  • Self care: uses spoon (messily), helps in housework
  • Language: 3 to 6 words, follows commands, points to body parts
  • Uses spoon well, spilling little = 3 years
exam_pearl: Spoon used sloppily = 15 months; spoon used well = 3 years.

stem: A child brought by his mother to well baby clinic. On history and examination Language: say 2-3 words other than Mama & Dada Fine motor: walks backwards Cognitive: Stacks 2 blocks Social: follow one step command How old is the child?
highlight_terms_source: say 2-3 words other than Mama & Dada
why_right: Label each finding with its milestone age: walks backwards, stacks 2 blocks and follows a one step command are all 15 month skills. Saying 2 to 3 words besides mama and dada is a 12 month skill that is already achieved. The oldest milestones achieved sit at 15 months, so the child is 15 months.
why_wrong_block:
A. At 9 months the child only pulls to stand and says mama/dada nonspecifically; walking backwards and following commands are far beyond 9 months.
B. 12 months explains the extra words, but walking backwards, a 2 block tower and following one step commands are 15 month skills, so the child is older than 12 months.
D. A 24 month old walks up and down stairs, stacks about 6 blocks and puts 2 words together; this child shows none of these, so 24 months is too old.
key_concept:
Developmental age = the oldest milestone achieved, below the youngest one not achieved.
  • 12 months: walks, 2 to 3 words besides mama/dada, block in cup
  • 15 months: walks backward, tower of 2, 3 to 6 words, follows simple commands, uses spoon sloppily
  • 18 months: runs, tower of 4, 6 to 10 words
  • 24 months: stairs, tower of 6, 2 word phrases
exam_pearl: Walking backwards and a 2 block tower are the 15 month signature; do not stop at 12 months because of the word count.

stem: A child is assessed for developmental milestones. Findings include: Gross motor: walks backwards Fine motor: eats with spoon Language: speaks 5-6 words Social: plays with cubes What is the age in months?
why_right: Walks backwards is a 15 month gross motor skill, eats with a spoon (sloppily) appears at 15 months, and 5 to 6 words fits the 15 month range of 3 to 6 words. Playing with cubes is consistent with stacking 2 blocks at this age. All findings cluster at 15 months.
why_wrong_block:
A. A 6 month old sits alone, transfers objects and babbles; walking and real words are impossible at 6 months.
B. At 9 months the child pulls to stand and says mama/dada nonspecifically; walking backwards, spoon use and 5 to 6 words are well beyond 9 months.
D. At 24 months the child climbs stairs, uses about 50 words and joins 2 words into phrases; 5 to 6 single words is too few for 24 months.
key_concept:
Match each domain to its age, then pick the age where most findings converge.
  • 15 months: walks backward, uses spoon (sloppily), 3 to 6 words, tower of 2, follows simple commands
  • 18 months: runs, 6 to 10 words, tower of 4
  • 24 months: about 50 words, 2 word phrases, stairs
exam_pearl: Word count helps: 2 to 3 words at 12 months, up to 6 at 15 months, 6 to 10 at 18 months, about 50 at 24 months.

stem: Child came for routine check up. He can transfer objects hand-to-hand but hasn't developed pincer grasp. What is the developmental age in months?
key_concept:
Lower limit = oldest skill achieved; upper limit = youngest skill not achieved.
  • Transfer hand to hand, palmar grasp, sits alone: 6 months
  • Immature pincer grasp: 9 months
  • Mature pincer grasp: 12 months
  • Transfer present + no pincer = 6 to 8 months
exam_pearl: If the expected answer (about 7 months) is missing, the recall is probably garbled; learn the bracket, not the option.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: While at the clinic, an infant craw toward the doctor, rolls over, sits briefly, transfers objects from hand to hand and grasps objects using his radial palm. The infant is unable to use a pincer grasp. What is the approximate age in months?
highlight_terms_source: transfers objects from hand to hand
unable to use a pincer grasp
why_right: Transfers objects hand to hand and radial palmar grasp are 6 month skills, rolling over and sitting briefly fit 6 months, and crawling appears at 6 to 9 months. The infant is unable to use a pincer grasp, which appears at 9 months, so the age is above 6 but below 9 months: 7 months.
why_wrong_block:
A. At 3 months the infant only holds the head up and follows objects; crawling, sitting and transferring are not possible yet.
B. At 5 months the infant reaches and rolls front to back, but hand to hand transfer, sitting and crawling are 6 month or later skills.
D. At 9 months a pincer grasp is present; its absence here means the infant is younger than 9 months.
key_concept:
The skill the child cannot yet do sets the upper limit of the age.
  • 4 months: reaches, rolls prone to supine, no head lag
  • 6 months: sits, transfers, palmar grasp, rolls both ways
  • 6 to 9 months: crawls
  • 9 months: pincer grasp, pulls to stand
exam_pearl: Transfer present but no pincer grasp = between 6 and 9 months; pick the option inside that window.

stem: An infant lies with his head to one side and raises his head slightly, but the head lags when pulling up to a sitting position. The infant smiles when involved in social interactions and follows moving objects 180 degrees, but does not attempt to reach for them. What is the approximate developmental age in weeks?
why_right: Social smile and following objects 180 degrees are 2 month milestones. Head lag disappears and reaching begins at 4 months, so head lag on pull to sit and no attempt to reach place the infant below 4 months. 2 months in the unit asked is 8 weeks.
why_wrong_block:
A. At 4 weeks (1 month) social smiling and tracking through 180 degrees are not yet expected.
C. By 12 weeks (3 months) a prone infant lifts the head about 45 degrees with steadier control; here the head is raised only slightly, and every finding is already explained by the 8 week (2 month) milestones.
D. At 16 weeks (4 months) head lag has gone and the infant reaches for objects, both absent here.
key_concept:
Early infant milestones (convert to weeks when asked):
  • 2 months (8 weeks): social smile, coos, tracks past midline / 180 degrees
  • 4 months (16 weeks): no head lag, reaches, laughs, rolls front to back
exam_pearl: Read the unit: the question asks for weeks, so 2 months becomes 8 weeks.

stem: A newborn who is following objects 180 degrees, no head lag when pulled to sitting position, social smiling. Age by weeks?
why_right: Social smile and 180 degree tracking are 2 month skills, but the decisive clue is no head lag when pulled to sitting, which is achieved at 4 months. 4 months in weeks is 16 weeks, so the infant is at least 16 weeks developmentally (the word 'newborn' in the stem is loose wording).
why_wrong_block:
A. Read as 4 weeks (1 month), a social smile and 180 degree tracking are not yet expected, and head lag is still marked; 4 years is plainly far too old.
B. 8 weeks (2 months) fits the social smile and tracking, but head lag is still present at 2 months; here it has resolved.
C. At 12 weeks head control is improving, but full disappearance of head lag on pull to sit is the 4 month (16 week) marker.
key_concept:
Head lag is the switch between 8 and 16 weeks.
  • Smile + 180 degree tracking + head lag present = 8 weeks
  • Smile + tracking + no head lag (and reaching) = 16 weeks
exam_pearl: Same stem pattern as the 8 week card; the presence or absence of head lag flips the answer.

stem: Pediatric patient presented in ER with fever and barky cough a long senario but he was in distress Bp was 80/60, Oxygen was 80% What is the appropriate initial management?
OptC: Some type of intubation in the OR
key_concept:
Barky cough + distress: grade severity, then treat the airway.
  • Mild croup (no stridor at rest): single dose dexamethasone
  • Moderate/severe (stridor at rest, retractions): nebulized epinephrine + steroid + oxygen
  • Impending failure (hypoxia, fatigue, altered consciousness): secure airway
  • Toxic, high fever, drooling, tripod: epiglottitis, prepare for intubation + 3rd generation cephalosporin
  • Toxic with barky cough not responding to epinephrine: bacterial tracheitis
exam_pearl: SpO2 80% is never plain mild croup: oxygen and airway assessment come first, then look for severe croup versus a bacterial airway infection.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A mother brings her 6-month-old baby with complaints of pancytopenia and organomegaly. Labs has low Hemoglobin What is the most likely type of leukemia?
why_right: A child with pancytopenia, organomegaly and low hemoglobin has bone marrow replacement with extramedullary infiltration, typical of acute leukemia. ALL is the most common childhood leukemia (and the most common childhood cancer), so it is the most likely type.
why_wrong_block:
A. AML is the second most common childhood leukemia; favour it when the stem gives myeloid clues such as Auer rods, gum infiltration or DIC.
B. CML is rare in children and presents with marked leukocytosis and splenomegaly in the chronic phase, not pancytopenia.
D. Acute non-lymphoblastic leukemia is another name for AML, which is less common than ALL in children.
key_concept:
Child + pancytopenia + hepatosplenomegaly/lymphadenopathy = think acute leukemia; ALL is the most common.
  • ALL: most common childhood leukemia, peak in early childhood
  • AML (= acute non-lymphoblastic): second most common
  • CML: rare in children
exam_pearl: 'Acute non-lymphoblastic' is just AML in old wording; do not treat it as a separate answer.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1674).

stem: When do Screening for paedia for Irion defiency anemia?
why_right: Universal screening for anemia (hemoglobin/CBC) is done at 9 to 12 months, so 12 months is the screening age. Iron stores from birth are used up around 6 to 9 months while dietary iron is often low, which is why the screen is timed near the first birthday.
why_wrong_block:
A. 6 months is too early for routine screening in a healthy term infant; earlier testing is only for risk factors such as prematurity or low birth weight.
C. 15 to 18 months is the repeat screen for children with an underlying condition causing anemia, not the initial universal screen.
D. 24 months is too late for the initial screen; iron deficiency could already have affected development.
key_concept:
Well baby screening timing:
  • Anemia (CBC/Hb): all children at 9 to 12 months
  • Repeat at 15 to 18 months if an underlying anemia causing condition
  • Autism screening: around 2 years
exam_pearl: 18 months is the repeat (risk) screen, not the first one.

stem: Paedia with febrile convulsion her mother give paracetamol every 4h for 3days cae c/o jundice whate is case
key_concept:
Paracetamol toxicity stages:
  • Stage 1 (first 24 h): nausea, vomiting, malaise, normal labs
  • Stage 2 (days 2 to 3): RUQ pain, rising transaminases
  • Stage 3 (days 3 to 4): jaundice, encephalopathy, coagulopathy, liver failure
  • Repeated or unknown timing ingestion: no nomogram; send level + LFTs and start N-acetylcysteine
exam_pearl: Count the doses: every 4 hours around the clock is 6 doses a day, and jaundice from paracetamol liver injury typically appears around day 3.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Paedia ingestion of 20 tablets of iron how to do
why_right: The terse stem gives only "20 tablets of iron" in a child, which is a large, potentially toxic ingestion (the matching full question adds GI bleeding and tachycardia a few hours later). Symptomatic or severe iron poisoning is treated with chelation, and the specific antidote is parenteral (IV) deferoxamine, which binds free iron so it can be excreted in urine.
why_wrong_block:
A. Observation: acceptable only for a small, clearly non-toxic ingestion in a child who stays well with a normal serum iron; a large ingestion in a sick child needs active treatment, and the quiet latent phase can falsely reassure.
B. Gastric lavage: removes iron tablets poorly and does not treat the absorbed iron; it is not the definitive treatment once the child is symptomatic. Chelation is.
key_concept:
Iron overdose: symptomatic or high serum iron = IV deferoxamine.
  • Stage I (first hours): vomiting, abdominal pain, haematemesis, diarrhoea
  • Stage II: latent phase, falsely reassuring
  • Stage III: shock, metabolic acidosis, CNS depression
  • Stage IV: hepatotoxicity
  • Stage V: GI strictures/obstruction weeks later
  • Activated charcoal does NOT bind iron
exam_pearl: Antidote pairs: iron = deferoxamine; paracetamol = N-acetylcysteine. Do not be fooled by the latent phase.

stem: A 5-year-old child presents with drowsiness, abdominal pain, nausea and bloody diarrhea after ingesting an unknown number of iron tablets several hours before (see lab result). Test Result Normal Value: Iron 94 (9-21.5 umol/L). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
highlight_terms_source: ingesting an unknown number of iron tablets
why_right: The child is clearly poisoned: "drowsiness" (CNS depression) plus "bloody diarrhea" after iron tablets, and a serum iron of 94 umol/L, several times the upper normal limit of 21.5. Symptomatic iron toxicity with a markedly raised level is the indication for chelation with IV deferoxamine.
why_wrong_block:
A. Haemodialysis: does not effectively remove iron itself; it is used to clear the iron deferoxamine complex if renal failure develops.
B. Gastric lavage: poor at removing iron tablets and not useful several hours later in a symptomatic child; it does not treat absorbed iron.
C. Oral activated charcoal: does not bind iron (nor lithium, alcohols or other metals), so it is ineffective here. Right for many other recent toxic ingestions.
key_concept:
Iron poisoning: treat the sick child with chelation.
  • Indications for IV deferoxamine: GI bleeding, shock, metabolic acidosis, altered consciousness, or very high serum iron
  • Charcoal: does not bind iron
  • Dialysis: only for the chelate in renal failure
exam_pearl: Drowsiness plus bloody diarrhoea after iron tablets = severe toxicity; go straight to IV deferoxamine.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Question is a screenshot on the next page; option D marked with ** in the screenshot.

stem: 7-year-old child have neck stiffness and all meningitis symptoms. His CSF was obtained, and Gram stain showed Grampositive cocci Which chemoprophylaxis should be offered to his contacts?
key_concept:
Match the Gram stain to the bug, then the prophylaxis.
  • Gram-positive diplococci = pneumococcus: no contact prophylaxis
  • Gram-negative diplococci = meningococcus: rifampicin, ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone
  • Gram-negative coccobacilli = Hib: rifampicin
  • Child contact: rifampicin; pregnant contact: ceftriaxone
  • A version of this stem with Gram-negative coccobacilli (Hib) is answered with rifampicin
  • Patient himself: ceftriaxone + vancomycin (+ dexamethasone)
exam_pearl: Prophylaxis is about the organism, not the word "meningitis": pneumococcus spreads poorly and contacts need nothing.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A pediatric patient has been diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis. His brother and sister, who live in the same household, are asymptomatic. Which of the following regimens is appropriate for chemoprophylaxis in these close contacts?
why_right: Household contacts of meningococcal disease need chemoprophylaxis whether or not they have symptoms. Of the regimens listed, a single dose of ciprofloxacin is the only correct, standard regimen and it is the agent best suited to Neisseria meningitidis. The other options use the wrong drug or the wrong number of doses.
why_wrong_block:
A. Penicillin and rifampin for 1 week: penicillin does not clear nasopharyngeal carriage, and rifampicin prophylaxis is a short 2-day course, not a week. Right when only rifampicin for 2 days is offered for a child contact.
C. Penicillin for 1 week: penicillin treats invasive disease but does not eradicate carriage, so it is not used for prophylaxis. It is not right for any contact prophylaxis scenario.
D. IM ceftriaxone 4 doses: ceftriaxone is a valid prophylactic agent (preferred in pregnancy) but as a single IM dose; multiple doses is a treatment-type regimen, not prophylaxis.
key_concept:
Meningococcal contact prophylaxis: give to close/household contacts, symptomatic or not, as soon as possible.
  • Ciprofloxacin: single oral dose, best for N. meningitidis
  • Rifampicin: 2-day course; classic choice for children and for Hib contacts
  • Ceftriaxone: single IM dose; choice in pregnancy
  • Penicillin does not clear carriage, so it is never prophylaxis
  • Hajj pilgrims need meningococcal vaccination
exam_pearl: The count matters: ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone are single doses, rifampicin is 2 days; any option giving a week or multiple ceftriaxone doses is wrong.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1755).

stem: 2 year old pt want to go for hajj he didn't take any Prevention meningococcal vaccine what the best method of prophylaxis antibiotic
why_right: The question asks for antibiotic prophylaxis against meningococcus for a "2 year old" travelling to Hajj without the vaccine. In a young child the classic oral agent is rifampicin twice daily for 2 days; ciprofloxacin is given as a single dose, mainly to adults, and ceftriaxone as a single IM dose.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cefdinir 5 days BID: an oral cephalosporin for otitis, sinusitis or pharyngitis; it does not reliably eradicate nasopharyngeal meningococcal carriage and is not a prophylaxis regimen.
C. Ciprofloxacin 3 days BID: ciprofloxacin prophylaxis is a single oral dose, not a 3 day course, and exam keys favour rifampicin for a young child.
D. Ceftriaxone 5 days OD: ceftriaxone prophylaxis is a single IM dose (useful in pregnancy); a 5 day course is a treatment regimen, not prophylaxis.
key_concept:
Meningococcal chemoprophylaxis regimens.
  • Rifampicin: oral, twice daily for 2 days (children)
  • Hib contacts: rifampicin once daily for 4 days
  • Ciprofloxacin: single oral dose, adults
  • Ceftriaxone: single IM dose, pregnancy
  • Meningococcal ACYW135 vaccine is mandatory before Hajj
  • Pilgrims from the African meningitis belt: vaccine plus chemoprophylaxis on arrival
exam_pearl: Prophylaxis is short: rifampicin 2 days or a single dose of cipro/ceftriaxone; any 3 to 5 day course is a distractor.

stem: A newborn infant born from a mother with polyhydramnios presents with excessive salivation along with coughing and choking with the first oral feeding. An x-rav of the abdomen shows gas in stomach and a nasogastric tube coiled in the esophagus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: coughing and choking with the first oral feeding
nasogastric tube coiled in the esophagus
why_right: Maternal "polyhydramnios" (the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid), "excessive salivation", and "coughing and choking with the first oral feeding" mean the oesophagus ends blindly, confirmed by the "nasogastric tube coiled in the esophagus". The decisive clue is "gas in stomach": air can only reach the stomach through a distal fistula between trachea and lower oesophagus, so this is oesophageal atresia with distal TEF, the commonest type.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oesophageal atresia alone: would also coil the NG tube, but with no fistula the abdomen is gasless; gas in the stomach rules it out.
B. Tracheoesophageal fistula alone (H-type): the oesophagus is patent so the NG tube passes into the stomach; it presents later with recurrent chest infections and choking with feeds.
D. Omphalocele: a midline abdominal wall defect with bowel covered by a membrane at the umbilicus, visible at birth; it does not stop an NG tube.
E. Gastroschisis: uncovered bowel herniating to the right of the umbilicus; an abdominal wall defect, not an oesophageal one.
key_concept:
Coiled NG tube = oesophageal atresia; then look at the abdomen.
  • Gas in stomach = EA with distal TEF (commonest)
  • Gasless abdomen = isolated EA (or proximal fistula only)
  • NG passes, recurrent pneumonia = H-type TEF
  • Polyhydramnios + drooling + choking on first feed
  • Screen for VACTERL anomalies
exam_pearl: Gas in the stomach is the clue that upgrades "oesophageal atresia" to "atresia with TEF".

stem: Newborn has bubbling mucus and fluid from the nose after the first feed, xray revealed NGT coiled in esophageal pouch, which of the following is the diagnosis ?
highlight_terms_source: bubbling mucus and fluid from the nose after the first feed
why_right: "Bubbling mucus and fluid" after the "first feed" with an "NGT coiled in esophageal pouch" is the oesophageal atresia/tracheoesophageal fistula complex. Oesophageal atresia is not offered, and the commonest form of this anomaly is atresia with a distal fistula, so tracheoesophageal fistula is the keyed answer for this anomaly among the choices.
why_wrong_block:
B. Choanal atresia: causes cyanosis at rest that improves with crying and a catheter cannot pass through the nose; the oesophagus is normal, so an NG tube passed by mouth would not coil.
C. Tracheomalacia: a floppy trachea causes expiratory stridor and noisy breathing that worsens with crying or feeds; it does not block an NG tube.
key_concept:
Coiled NG tube = EA/TEF complex.
  • Most common type: proximal blind pouch + distal TEF (gas in stomach)
  • Clues: polyhydramnios, drooling, frothy secretions, choking on first feed
  • Choanal atresia: cyanosis relieved by crying
  • Tracheomalacia: stridor, tube passes
exam_pearl: If "oesophageal atresia" is missing from the options, pick TEF: they come together in most cases.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1938).
Compiler note: Shorter 'Q:' recall under 1936 with a different option set.

stem: A newborn presents with excessive drooling, bubbling from the mouth, and an inability to pass a nasogastric (NG) tube. Xray reveals the NG tube coiled in the upper esophageal pouch. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: inability to pass a nasogastric (NG) tube
NG tube coiled in the upper esophageal pouch
why_right: "Excessive drooling", "bubbling from the mouth" and an "inability to pass a nasogastric tube" that is seen "coiled in the upper esophageal pouch" are the defining picture of a blind-ending oesophagus, which is oesophageal atresia. The stem gives no abdominal gas finding, so the atresia itself is the diagnosis being asked.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hiatus hernia: stomach herniating through the diaphragm causes reflux and vomiting, but the NG tube still passes into the stomach.
C. Tracheoesophageal fistula: an isolated (H-type) fistula leaves the oesophagus patent so the tube passes; it presents with choking and recurrent chest infections. A fistula would be added only if gas is seen in the stomach.
D. Choanal atresia: blocked posterior nasal passages cause cyanosis that improves with crying and failure to pass a catheter through the nose into the pharynx, not a tube coiled in the oesophagus.
key_concept:
Coiled NG tube in an upper pouch = oesophageal atresia.
  • Clinical: drooling, frothy secretions, choking/cyanosis with feeds, maternal polyhydramnios
  • Gas in stomach: add distal TEF
  • Tube passes + recurrent pneumonia: H-type TEF
  • Cyanosis relieved by crying: choanal atresia
exam_pearl: The NG tube is the test: stuck in the chest = atresia; passes but chokes on feeds = H-type fistula.

stem: Newborn has bubbling mucus and fluid from the nose after the first feed, C-xray revealed NGT coiled in esophageal pouch, which of the following is the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: bubbling mucus and fluid from the nose after the first feed
why_right: "Bubbling mucus and fluid" after the "first feed" with an "NGT coiled in esophageal pouch" is the oesophageal atresia/tracheoesophageal fistula complex. Oesophageal atresia is not offered, and the commonest form of this anomaly is atresia with a distal fistula, so tracheoesophageal fistula is the keyed answer for this anomaly among the choices.
why_wrong_block:
B. Choanal atresia: causes cyanosis at rest that improves with crying and a catheter cannot pass through the nose; the oesophagus is normal, so an NG tube passed by mouth would not coil.
C. Tracheomalacia: a floppy trachea causes expiratory stridor and noisy breathing that worsens with crying or feeds; it does not block an NG tube.
key_concept:
Coiled NG tube = EA/TEF complex.
  • Most common type: proximal blind pouch + distal TEF (gas in stomach)
  • Clues: polyhydramnios, drooling, frothy secretions, choking on first feed
  • Choanal atresia: cyanosis relieved by crying
  • Tracheomalacia: stridor, tube passes
exam_pearl: If "oesophageal atresia" is missing from the options, pick TEF: they come together in most cases.

stem: Child Had URTI 2 Days Ago, Presented With Erythematous Rash That Covers The Jaw And Extends To The Shoulder And Back, WITHOUT Desquamation And Occipital, Posterior Cervical, Post Auricular Lymphadenopathy (Written In Case Like This):
highlight_terms_source: Occipital, Posterior Cervical, Post Auricular Lymphadenopathy
why_right: A mild prodrome ("URTI 2 days ago") followed by a pink-red rash that starts high on the face/jaw and spreads down to the "shoulder and back", plus "occipital, posterior cervical, post auricular lymphadenopathy", is classic rubella. Suboccipital and postauricular nodes are the hallmark that separates it from the other exanthems.
why_wrong_block:
B. Adenovirus: causes pharyngoconjunctival fever (fever, sore throat, conjunctivitis); a rash is non-specific and the occipital/postauricular node pattern is not typical.
C. Measles: high fever with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis and Koplik spots before a rash that starts behind the ears/hairline; it is a much sicker child and nodes are generalized rather than postauricular-predominant.
D. Erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19): "slapped cheek" facial redness then a lacy reticular rash on the limbs, with no prominent lymphadenopathy.
key_concept:
Viral exanthem forks.
  • Rubella: mild, low-grade fever, postauricular/suboccipital nodes, face-to-trunk pink rash, Forchheimer spots
  • Measles: high fever, 3Cs, Koplik spots
  • Parvovirus B19: slapped cheek, lacy limb rash
  • Roseola: high fever, rash appears as fever breaks
  • Scarlet fever: sandpaper rash then desquamation
exam_pearl: Postauricular plus suboccipital lymph nodes = rubella until proven otherwise.

stem: A 6-year-old unvaccinated girl is brought to the clinic by her mother with low-grade fever, rash, and swollen glands. Her mother reports The child was well until 2 days ago. Then developed mild fever, runny nose, and red eyes Yesterday, she developed a pink, non-itchy rash that started on the face and then spread to thetrunk and limbs What the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: pink, non-itchy rash that started on the face
why_right: An unvaccinated child with a "low-grade fever", mild coryza and red eyes, "swollen glands", and a "pink, non-itchy rash" that "started on the face" and spread to the trunk and limbs fits rubella. The mild course, low-grade fever and lymphadenopathy, with no Koplik spots, separate it from measles.
why_wrong_block:
A. Measles: shares the face-to-body spread and coryza/conjunctivitis, but presents with a HIGH fever, a sick child and Koplik spots before a darker, confluent rash; none of that is described here.
C. Epstein-Barr virus: infectious mononucleosis gives exudative pharyngitis, fatigue, generalized nodes and splenomegaly; a rash mainly appears after amoxicillin, not as a face-to-trunk pink exanthem.
key_concept:
Measles vs rubella hinges on severity.
  • Rubella: low-grade fever, mild, pink discrete rash, postauricular/suboccipital nodes
  • Measles: high fever, 3Cs, Koplik spots, ill child
  • EBV: sore throat, splenomegaly, rash after amoxicillin
exam_pearl: Same stem with HIGH fever and white oral spots flips the answer to measles.

stem: A 6-year-old child presents with a high-grade fever, malaise, conjunctivitis, coryza, and a cough. A rash of discrete pink macules recently began on the face and extends to the hands and feet. The child also had small, whitish spots inside the mouth before the rash appeared. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: small, whitish spots inside the mouth before the rash appeared
why_right: A "high-grade fever" with the 3Cs ("conjunctivitis, coryza, and a cough") and "small, whitish spots inside the mouth before the rash appeared" (Koplik spots, pathognomonic) followed by a rash starting on the face and spreading to the hands and feet is measles.
why_wrong_block:
A. Toxic shock syndrome: high fever with hypotension and a diffuse sunburn-like erythroderma that later desquamates, often linked to tampons or wounds; no Koplik spots or 3Cs.
B. Gonococcal bacteremia: a few acral pustules with arthritis/tenosynovitis in a sexually active patient, not a viral prodrome with a face-to-limb rash.
D. Rubella: similar face-to-body rash but with only low-grade fever, a mild illness, postauricular nodes and no Koplik spots.
key_concept:
Measles = high fever + 3Cs + Koplik spots, then rash.
  • Rash starts at hairline/face and spreads downward
  • Koplik spots: white spots on buccal mucosa opposite molars, before the rash
  • Rubella: low-grade fever, no Koplik
  • Complications: pneumonia, encephalitis, SSPE
exam_pearl: High vs low fever plus Koplik spots is the single switch between measles and rubella on this stem.

stem: A 5-year-old childis brought to the clinic with a febrile illness with a cough and separate irregularly shaped (blotchy) rashes. He has not had any routine vaccinations. On physical examination, there is enlarged tender cervical lymph nodes. There are also erythematous maculopapular rashes behind the ear, face and neck and to a lesser extent on the trunk. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: behind the ear, face and neck
why_right: An unvaccinated child with fever and cough and a blotchy, irregular erythematous maculopapular rash that begins behind the ears, face and neck and then spreads to the trunk to a lesser extent is the classic cephalocaudal measles exanthem. Measles rash tends to become confluent (blotchy), unlike the discrete pink macules of rubella, and the cough fits the measles prodrome (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis). Cervical lymphadenopathy is common in measles.
why_wrong_block:
A. Chickenpox gives itchy vesicles in crops at different stages (macule, papule, vesicle, crust), centred on the trunk; this rash is maculopapular and blotchy, not vesicular.
C. Mumps causes fever with parotid (or submandibular) gland swelling and no rash; think of it when the swelling is in front of the ear, not a rash behind it.
D. Rubella also spreads face to body, but it is a mild illness with low-grade fever, discrete pink macules that fade quickly and posterior auricular/suboccipital nodes; a prominent cough with a confluent blotchy rash points to measles.
key_concept:
Face-to-body maculopapular rash: decide measles vs rubella by severity, cough and rash texture.
  • Measles: high fever, 3 Cs (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis), Koplik spots, rash starts behind ears/hairline, becomes confluent/blotchy
  • Rubella: mild, low-grade fever, discrete pink macules, postauricular/suboccipital nodes
  • Varicella: vesicles in crops, trunk-centred
  • Mumps: parotitis, no rash
  • Unvaccinated status raises measles probability
exam_pearl: Rash starting behind the ears that turns blotchy and confluent in a coughing, unvaccinated child = measles; discrete pink macules in a well child = rubella.

stem: pediatric, rash in face or neck then go down, forgot it was desquamating or squamating not sure, no mention of murmur in qs , dx?
highlight_terms_source: rash in face or neck then go down
key_concept:
Face-down rash: measles vs rubella; desquamation shifts thinking toward Kawasaki (or scarlet fever).
  • Measles: 3 Cs + Koplik, confluent rash, fine branny peeling as it fades
  • Rubella: mild, discrete pink macules, posterior nodes
  • Kawasaki: fever ≥5 days + mucocutaneous signs, fingertip peeling later
  • Fifth disease: slapped cheek then lacy limb rash
exam_pearl: Peeling of the fingertips after prolonged fever is Kawasaki; fine branny peeling of a fading cephalocaudal rash after a cough/coryza prodrome is measles.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Screenshot recall under 1942; no answer marked.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A child is brought to Paediatric Clinic with cough, fever, rhinorrhoea, malaise, with conjunctival erythema. There are small, grayish, irregular lesions surrounded by an erythematous base, on the buccal mucus membrane near the second molar teeth. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: small, grayish, irregular lesions surrounded by an erythematous base, on the buccal mucus membrane near the second molar teeth
why_right: Small grayish lesions on an erythematous base on the buccal mucosa near the second molars are Koplik spots, which are pathognomonic for measles. Together with the prodrome of cough, rhinorrhoea (coryza) and conjunctival erythema (the 3 Cs) and fever, the diagnosis is measles, often before the rash appears.
why_wrong_block:
B. Rubella is a milder illness with discrete pink macules and posterior auricular/suboccipital nodes; it does not produce Koplik spots (any palatal petechiae are on the soft palate).
C. Parainfluenza causes croup: barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor; it has no buccal mucosal spots.
D. RSV causes bronchiolitis in infants: coryza followed by wheeze, crackles and respiratory distress; no Koplik spots or conjunctivitis-rash picture.
key_concept:
Koplik spots = measles until proven otherwise.
  • Prodrome: fever + cough, coryza, conjunctivitis
  • Koplik: grayish-white spots on red base, buccal mucosa opposite molars, appear before the rash
  • Rash: behind ears/face, spreads down, becomes confluent
  • Parainfluenza = croup; RSV = bronchiolitis
exam_pearl: Spots on the buccal mucosa opposite the molars = Koplik (measles); spots on the soft palate are not Koplik.

stem: A 2-year-old child weighing 12 kg is admitted to the pediatric ward for observation due to vomiting and poor oral intake. The medical team decides to initiate maintenance IV fluids. What is the appropriate daily fluid requirement for this child?
why_right: Maintenance fluid uses the Holliday-Segar rule: 100 mL/kg/day for the first 10 kg and 50 mL/kg/day for the next 10 kg. For a 12 kg child: 10 × 100 = 1000 mL plus 2 × 50 = 100 mL, giving 1100 mL/day. The child is only for observation with poor intake, so maintenance alone is asked, with no deficit added.
why_wrong_block:
A. 1200 mL comes from applying 100 mL/kg to all 12 kg; the kilograms above 10 kg are counted at only 50 mL/kg.
C. 1500 mL would be maintenance for a 20 kg child (1000 + 500); it overestimates for 12 kg and would only fit if a deficit were being added.
D. 1000 mL is the maintenance for exactly 10 kg; it ignores the extra 2 kg (another 100 mL).
key_concept:
Holliday-Segar daily maintenance:
  • First 10 kg: 100 mL/kg/day
  • Next 10 kg (11 to 20 kg): 50 mL/kg/day
  • Each kg above 20: 20 mL/kg/day
  • 12 kg: 1000 + 100 = 1100 mL/day
  • Hourly (4-2-1): 40 + 4 = 44 mL/h
exam_pearl: Do not multiply total weight by 100; only the first 10 kg get 100 mL/kg.

stem: A 14-month-old girt is brought to the clinic with vomi7ng and diarhoea. The mother reports her child is less ac7ve. On examina7on, she has mild dehydra7on with an es7mated fluid deficit of 5% (see lab results). Weigh 10 Kg Test Result Normal Values Sodium 128 134-146 mmol/L Potassium 3.3 3.5-5.1 mmol/L Chloride 94 97-108 mmol/L Bicarbonate 12 21-28 mmol/L How much intravenous fluid (mi/day) should be given?
why_right: Daily IV fluid = maintenance + deficit. Maintenance for 10 kg = 10 × 100 = 1000 mL. Deficit for 5% dehydration = 5% of 10 kg = 0.5 kg = 500 mL (weight × % × 10). Total = 1000 + 500 = 1500 mL/day. The low sodium, potassium and bicarbonate guide the fluid type and electrolyte replacement, not the volume.
why_wrong_block:
A. 1000 mL is maintenance only; it ignores the 5% deficit the stem tells you to replace.
B. 1250 mL adds only half the deficit (250 mL); the full 500 mL deficit belongs in the 24-hour total.
D. 1750 mL corresponds to a larger deficit (about 7.5%); the stem fixes the deficit at 5%.
key_concept:
Dehydration fluid volume = maintenance + deficit.
  • Maintenance: 100 mL/kg first 10 kg, 50 mL/kg next 10 kg, 20 mL/kg beyond
  • Deficit (mL) = weight (kg) × % dehydration × 10
  • 10 kg, 5%: 1000 + 500 = 1500 mL/day
  • Electrolytes (Na, K, HCO3) choose the fluid, not the volume
exam_pearl: When the stem gives a % deficit, add it to maintenance; answering maintenance alone (1000) is the trap.

stem: newborn with Maple Syrup ,What to give. A neonate presents with vomiting, lethargy, and signs of central nervous system depression. The baby has had episodes of seizures, and alternates between hypotonia and hypertonia. Diagnosed with maple syrup disease What's the treatment ?
OptC: Treat with high-dose sodium benzoate and sodium phenylacetate
OptD: Stop protein intake temporarily and start BCAA-free formula with IV glucose
why_right: Maple syrup urine disease is a defect in breaking down the branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine); leucine accumulation causes the neonatal encephalopathy described (vomiting, lethargy, seizures, alternating hypotonia/hypertonia). Acute management is to stop protein temporarily, give IV glucose (calories to stop catabolism) and then a BCAA-free formula; long term the diet restricts leucine, isoleucine and valine.
why_wrong_block:
A. This option is garbled in the recall and is not a recognized MSUD therapy; if it refers to nitisinone (NTBC), that drug is used for tyrosinemia type 1, not MSUD.
B. A phenylalanine-restricted diet treats phenylketonuria; MSUD needs restriction of the branched-chain amino acids, not phenylalanine.
C. Sodium benzoate and sodium phenylacetate are ammonia scavengers for hyperammonemia in urea cycle disorders, not the core treatment of MSUD.
key_concept:
Match the inborn error to its dietary fix:
  • MSUD: restrict leucine, isoleucine, valine (BCAA-free formula); acutely stop protein + IV glucose
  • PKU: restrict phenylalanine
  • Urea cycle disorders: sodium benzoate/phenylacetate, stop protein
  • Tyrosinemia type 1: nitisinone (NTBC)
exam_pearl: Sweet (maple syrup) smelling urine in an encephalopathic neonate = MSUD = branched-chain amino acids, not phenylalanine.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed recall 'newborn with Maple Syrup, What to give' plus screenshot with options (BCAA highlighted in red in option D). Q: Maple syrup urine disease: Restrict leucine, isoleucine and valine.

stem: Child was eating seeds and developed stridor, upon examination there was diminished air entry at right lung. (They gave a chext x-ray showing darker and hyperinflation of right lung)... it was obvious How to manage?
highlight_terms_source: diminished air entry at right lung
why_right: A child eating seeds who develops stridor with diminished air entry on the right and a CXR showing a hyperlucent, hyperinflated right lung (air trapping from a ball-valve obstruction) has an aspirated bronchial foreign body. When the diagnosis is this obvious, rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia is both diagnostic and therapeutic and is the management of choice for removal.
why_wrong_block:
A. A lateral neck X-ray helps for croup (steeple sign), epiglottitis (thumb sign) or a radiopaque upper airway object; the foreign body here is bronchial, already shown on CXR, and seeds are radiolucent anyway.
B. Laryngoscopy visualizes only the larynx (used for laryngomalacia or laryngeal foreign bodies); it cannot reach or remove an object in the right main bronchus.
D. A tracheal procedure (for example tracheostomy) is reserved for an airway that cannot be secured otherwise; a stable child with a bronchial foreign body needs removal by rigid bronchoscopy.
key_concept:
Suspected airway foreign body in a child: rigid bronchoscopy.
  • Clues: choking episode, nuts/seeds, sudden unilateral wheeze or reduced air entry
  • CXR: ipsilateral hyperinflation (air trapping), mediastinal shift away; expiratory/decubitus films help
  • Most organic objects are radiolucent; a normal CXR does not exclude
  • Rigid bronchoscopy = diagnostic and therapeutic
exam_pearl: Unilateral hyperinflation after eating nuts or seeds means a ball-valve bronchial foreign body; go straight to rigid bronchoscopy.

stem: A family brought their kid who has fever, cough, and runny nose. Symptoms started after hx of choking after he ingested of some seed. Chest exam: dec RT side breathing sound. X ray pictures was shown . What is the next thing to do?
OptC: Send home with antipyretic and nasal fluid
highlight_terms_source: choking after he ingested of some seed
why_right: Fever, cough and coryza that started after a choking episode on seeds, with decreased right-sided breath sounds, point to a retained bronchial foreign body (often right-sided because the right main bronchus is more vertical), possibly with distal infection. The next step is bronchoscopy (rigid) to confirm and remove the object; the history of choking must not be dismissed as a simple viral illness.
why_wrong_block:
A. Subcutaneous epinephrine treats anaphylaxis (urticaria, angioedema, wheeze, hypotension); there is no allergic picture here, and adrenaline does not remove an obstructing object.
C. Sending home with antipyretics fits a simple URTI; a choking history plus unilateral reduced air entry is a foreign body until proven otherwise, and missing it leads to recurrent pneumonia or bronchiectasis.
key_concept:
Choking history + unilateral chest signs = foreign body until bronchoscopy says otherwise.
  • Right main bronchus is the commonest site
  • Late presentation: fever, cough, persistent or recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe
  • Management: rigid bronchoscopy
exam_pearl: Fever and cough do not cancel a choking history; unilateral signs after a seed still mean bronchoscopy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: 'Q:' recall under 1974 with a different option set.

stem: 10 years old boy presented to the emergency department with fever, headache and sore throat for 2 days, in examination there were enlarged tonsils with exudate and pharyngeal petechiae. He had enlargement of anterior and posterior cervical lymph nodes. The rapid strep test was positive. BP: 100/65 T: 39 Others normal What's the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: Fever, tonsillar exudate, pharyngeal petechiae and tender cervical nodes in a 10-year-old fit group A streptococcal pharyngitis, and the rapid strep test is positive, which confirms it. A positive rapid antigen test is acted on directly: start antibiotics, with oral penicillin V (or amoxicillin) for 10 days to prevent rheumatic fever.
why_wrong_block:
B. Throat culture is the back-up test when the rapid strep test is negative in a child with a suggestive picture; after a positive rapid test it only delays treatment.
C. Reassurance fits viral pharyngitis (mild hyperemia, coryza, cough, negative rapid test); confirmed GAS needs antibiotics to prevent rheumatic fever and suppurative complications.
D. This option was not recalled, so it cannot be judged; with a confirmed positive rapid test, antibiotic treatment remains the next step.
key_concept:
Pediatric sore throat with GAS features: test, then treat by result.
  • Rapid antigen test positive: treat (penicillin V or amoxicillin, 10 days)
  • Rapid test negative in a child: confirm with throat culture
  • Penicillin allergy: macrolide or cephalosporin depending on reaction type
  • Treating prevents rheumatic fever
exam_pearl: Culture is for the negative rapid test in children; a positive rapid test goes straight to penicillin.
compiler_note: ⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-0131 → B. Throat culture. Confirm before the exam.

stem: down$ (didn't say down) depressed nasal bridge and Single Palmar Crease.
why_right: A depressed (flat) nasal bridge and single palmar crease are dysmorphic features of Down syndrome. The most common endocrine disorder in trisomy 21 is hypothyroidism (congenital or acquired, mostly autoimmune), which is why these children have repeated thyroid screening.
why_wrong_block:
B. Hypoparathyroidism with hypocalcaemia is the classic endocrine feature of DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion) syndrome, not Down syndrome.
C. Hypopituitarism is not a characteristic association of trisomy 21; it goes with midline defects such as septo-optic dysplasia.
D. Hyperthyroidism (Graves) is more frequent in Down syndrome than in the general population but far less common than hypothyroidism.
key_concept:
Down syndrome: recognize the face, then screen the associations.
  • Features: upslanting eyes, epicanthic folds, Brushfield spots, flat nasal bridge, protruding tongue, single palmar crease, hypotonia
  • Heart: endocardial cushion (AVSD) defect most typical
  • Endocrine: hypothyroidism most common
  • Also: duodenal atresia, Hirschsprung, leukaemia, atlantoaxial instability, early Alzheimer
exam_pearl: Hypoparathyroidism is the DiGeorge trap; Down syndrome = hypothyroid.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1627).
Compiler note: Recall is incomplete (stem missing the lead-in; recaller notes it did not say Down).

stem: A 4-month-old boy with down syndrome exhibits poor weight gain, tachypnea, a low-pitched grade 2 systolic murmur and a fixed splitting of S2. Chest X-ray reveals cardiomegaly and increased pulmonary vascularity. Electrocardiography documents biventricular hypertrophy and a superior frontal plane QRS axis. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: An infant with Down syndrome, failure to thrive, tachypnea, cardiomegaly and plethoric lungs has a large left to right shunt.
